skill.approach.obg.team_leader.title: Leading an obstetric emergency team
skill.approach.obg.team_leader.oneLine: Call for help first, give every task a name, and say the time
skill.approach.obg.team_leader.why: In a haemorrhage or an eclamptic fit the drugs are known. What goes wrong is that nobody calls for help, three people do the same task, and nobody watches the clock. Teamwork and personnel are what turn a protocol into treatment.

steps.text: Call for help at once: senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, blood bank, theatre, and a second pair of hands.
Give every task a name: airway and oxygen, IV access and bloods, drugs and fluids, someone to record times, someone to talk to the family. State the plan aloud.
Use closed-loop communication: say the order, hear it repeated, and hear that it has been done.
Note the time of the diagnosis and of each intervention. Reassess the patient at fixed intervals (vital signs and blood loss at least every 15 minutes in the PPH workflow).
Keep the woman informed, and explain to the family what is happening.

skill.approach.obg.team_leader.practice: Run a five-minute mock emergency where you are not allowed to touch the patient. If you cannot give every task to someone by name, you have not led.
pitfalls: Doing the procedure yourself and losing the overview.
Calling for help by shouting and not saying who is needed.
Not recording times, so the sequence cannot be reconstructed.
Forgetting the woman and her family.

probes.q: What is the first step in eclampsia and in postpartum haemorrhage?
probes.a: Call for help.

probes.q: How soon should the PPH treatment bundle be started after diagnosis?
probes.a: Ideally all bundle interventions are initiated within the first 15 minutes after a diagnosis of PPH.

probes.q: What does a team leader do that a team member does not?
probes.a: Keeps the overview, allocates and checks tasks, watches the time, and decides on escalation, rather than doing a single procedure.

rubric.text: Calls for help at once and says who is needed
Allocates named tasks: airway and oxygen, IV access and bloods, drugs and fluids, recording times
Uses closed-loop communication
Notes times of diagnosis and interventions and reassesses at fixed intervals
Keeps the woman informed and explains to the family

skill.tx.obg.pph_recognise.title: PPH (1): recognise it early
skill.tx.obg.pph_recognise.oneLine: Bleeding over 500 mL, or less with a racing pulse; shock index over 1 is a red flag
skill.tx.obg.pph_recognise.why: Women die of postpartum haemorrhage because it was recognised late, not because the drugs were unknown. Blood loss is usually underestimated, and a healthy young woman keeps her blood pressure until she is very short of blood. The pulse and the shock index warn before the pressure does.

steps.text: PPH is blood loss of more than 500 mL, or any bleeding that deranges the vital signs.

WHO (2025) advises acting on an objectively measured loss of 300 mL or more with any abnormal sign (pulse over 100, shock index over 1, systolic BP under 100 or diastolic BP under 60), or 500 mL or more, whichever comes first within 24 hours of birth, with particular vigilance in the first 2 hours. Measure loss with a calibrated drape where available.
Red flags in the Indian workflow: pulse over 120 per minute, systolic BP under 100 mmHg, SpO2 under 95%, shock index over 1 (pulse divided by systolic BP), or a deteriorating level of consciousness.
Assess uterine tone by palpating the abdomen in every woman.

Find the cause by what you feel: a flabby uterus (atony); a well-contracted uterus that is still bleeding (tears, retained tissue or rupture); a placenta that has not delivered; or bleeding with no apparent cause (coagulopathy).

skill.tx.obg.pph_recognise.practice: Given a pulse of 118 and a systolic pressure of 96, calculate the shock index aloud, name the red flags present, and say what the next 30 seconds are.
pitfalls: Estimating blood loss by eye and waiting for a fall in blood pressure.
Not checking the uterus, so atony is never named.
Treating all bleeding as atony when the uterus is well contracted.
skill.tx.obg.pph_recognise.dosingNote: CliniX does not prescribe. Doses here are quoted from the cited national or guideline document so a student can check them; the treating team's own protocol and the current formulary decide what is given.

probes.q: How is PPH defined in the ICMR workflow?
probes.a: Blood loss of more than 500 mL, or any amount of bleeding that causes derangement of vital signs.

probes.q: How is the shock index calculated, and what value is a red flag?
probes.a: Pulse rate divided by systolic blood pressure. A value over 1 is a red flag.

probes.q: Name the red flag signs of PPH in the Indian workflow.
probes.a: Pulse over 120 per minute, systolic BP under 100 mmHg, SpO2 under 95%, shock index over 1, and deterioration of sensorium.

probes.q: What is the WHO 2025 trigger for starting first-response treatment?
probes.a: Objectively measured blood loss of 300 mL or more with any abnormal haemodynamic sign, or 500 mL or more, whichever occurs first within 24 hours of birth.

probes.q: The uterus is well contracted but she is still bleeding. What are the causes?
probes.a: Genital tract trauma (cervical, vaginal or perineal tears), retained tissue, uterine rupture or scar dehiscence; and coagulopathy if there is no apparent cause.

rubric.text: States the definition: more than 500 mL, or any bleeding that deranges the vital signs
Measures blood loss objectively and knows the WHO trigger of 300 mL with an abnormal sign
Calculates the shock index (pulse divided by systolic BP) and knows that over 1 is a red flag
Checks the uterus: flabby (atony) or well contracted
Names the causes by what is found: atony, tears, retained placenta or tissue, rupture, coagulopathy

sources.source: ICMR and DHR, MoHFW: Standard Treatment Workflow, Postpartum haemorrhage (December 2025)
sources.locator: Definition; red flag signs; algorithm branches (placenta delivered or not, uterus contracted or flabby)

sources.source: WHO, Consolidated guidelines for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of postpartum haemorrhage (2025)
sources.locator: Recommendations 21 to 23 (objective measurement; diagnostic criteria 300 mL with abnormal signs or 500 mL; uterine tonus assessment)

skill.tx.obg.pph_first_response.title: PPH (2): the first-response bundle
skill.tx.obg.pph_first_response.oneLine: Help, two lines, fluids, oxygen, oxytocin, massage, tranexamic acid, all together
skill.tx.obg.pph_first_response.why: In PPH the first minutes are a set of things done together, not a list done in turn. The WHO bundle of uterine massage, an oxytocic, tranexamic acid, IV fluids, examination of the genital tract and escalation should ideally all be started within 15 minutes of the diagnosis.

steps.text: Call for help. Rapidly assess pulse, BP, respiratory rate and temperature, and check vitals and blood loss at least every 15 minutes.
Establish two IV lines with wide-bore (16 to 18 G) cannulas. Draw blood for grouping and cross-matching, and arrange blood and blood products at the earliest.
Start Ringer lactate or normal saline, 1 litre in 15 to 20 minutes. Initially replace each mL of blood lost with 3 mL of crystalloid, switching to blood as soon as it is available.
Give oxygen at 6 to 8 L per minute by mask. Insert an indwelling urinary catheter with a urobag and record input and output.

Give oxytocin 10 IU IM if it was not given after delivery, and start an oxytocin infusion of 20 IU in 500 mL Ringer lactate or saline at 40 to 60 drops per minute. Oxytocin is never given as an IV bolus.
Massage the uterus. Check whether the placenta has been delivered, and inspect it for completeness.

Give tranexamic acid 1 g by slow IV injection over 10 minutes for every PPH, whatever the cause, as early as possible and within 3 hours of birth. Repeat once after 30 minutes if bleeding continues. Carry on with all the other treatment meanwhile.

skill.tx.obg.pph_first_response.practice: Run the first five minutes of PPH in a mock scenario, naming who does each of the seven steps.
pitfalls: Giving oxytocin as an IV bolus, which can cause hypotension.
Doing the steps one after another instead of in parallel.
Delaying tranexamic acid past 3 hours, when it no longer helps.
Waiting for blood to arrive before starting crystalloid.
skill.tx.obg.pph_first_response.dosingNote: CliniX does not prescribe. Doses here are quoted from the cited national or guideline document so a student can check them; the treating team's own protocol and the current formulary decide what is given.

probes.q: What is the oxytocin regimen in the ICMR PPH workflow?
probes.a: 10 IU IM if not given after delivery, then an infusion of 20 IU in 500 mL Ringer lactate or saline at 40 to 60 drops per minute. Never an IV bolus.

probes.q: What is the tranexamic acid dose and time window?
probes.a: 1 g by slow IV over 10 minutes, as early as possible and within 3 hours of birth; it can be repeated once after 30 minutes if bleeding persists.

probes.q: How much crystalloid, and how fast, in the initial phase?
probes.a: 1 litre in 15 to 20 minutes, replacing each mL of blood lost with 3 mL of crystalloid at first, then switching to blood.

probes.q: Name the components of the WHO first-response treatment bundle.
probes.a: Uterine massage, an oxytocic, tranexamic acid, intravenous fluids, examination of the genital tract, and escalation of care.

rubric.text: Establishes two wide-bore IV lines (16 to 18 G), sends blood for grouping and cross-matching, and asks for blood products
Starts Ringer lactate or saline, 1 litre in 15 to 20 minutes
Gives oxygen 6 to 8 L per minute and inserts an indwelling catheter
Gives oxytocin 10 IU IM if not already given and starts 20 IU in 500 mL at 40 to 60 drops per minute, not as a bolus
Massages the uterus and checks whether the placenta has been delivered
Gives tranexamic acid 1 g slow IV over 10 minutes, within 3 hours of birth, whatever the cause
Checks vital signs and blood loss at least every 15 minutes

sources.locator: First-response box (call for help, two IV lines, fluids, oxygen, catheter, oxytocin IM and infusion, tranexamic acid)

sources.locator: Recommendations 24 to 29 (oxytocin, massage, tranexamic acid, isotonic crystalloids, first-response bundle within 15 minutes)

skill.tx.obg.pph_atony_escalate.title: PPH (3): atony, tears, tamponade, surgery and referral
skill.tx.obg.pph_atony_escalate.oneLine: Compress, add a drug that is safe for her, tamponade, then surgery, and never delay referral
skill.tx.obg.pph_atony_escalate.why: When the first response is not enough, what matters is doing the next step promptly and choosing a drug that will not harm her. Methylergometrine in a woman with pre-eclampsia, or carboprost in an asthmatic, turns a bleeding problem into a second emergency.

steps.text: Placenta not delivered: continue the oxytocin drip and, if the uterus is contracted, try controlled cord traction. If it still does not deliver, take her to theatre for manual removal.

Uterus well contracted and still bleeding: examine for cervical, vaginal and perineal tears and repair them. If bleeding persists after repair, suspect inadequate repair, rupture or scar dehiscence: examination under anaesthesia or laparotomy.

Flabby uterus: bimanual compression and drugs. Raise the oxytocin infusion to 10 to 20 units per hour. Add any of: methylergometrine 0.2 mg IM or slow IV, repeated after 15 minutes up to 5 doses (1 mg); carboprost 250 micrograms IM, repeated every 20 minutes up to 8 doses (2 mg); misoprostol 800 micrograms rectally or sublingually.
Check contraindications first: methylergometrine in hypertension (including pre-eclampsia and eclampsia), severe anaemia and heart disease; carboprost in asthma.

If bleeding continues, explore the uterus for retained bits, check coagulation and give blood and components, and use an intrauterine balloon (condom catheter tamponade). Aortic compression can reduce loss for a short time.

Surgery, in escalating order: uterine compression sutures; systematic devascularisation (uterine, then ovarian, then internal iliac artery ligation); hysterectomy. Uterine artery embolisation in selected women where it is available.

Refer early to a higher centre if blood, exploration or surgery are not available. Transport with the oxytocin infusion running, preferably with tamponade in place, in a non-pneumatic anti-shock garment if available, with an escort.

When bleeding is controlled: massage every 15 minutes for the first 2 hours, vital signs every 10 minutes for 30 minutes then every 15 minutes for 30 minutes then every 30 minutes for 3 to 6 hours, oxytocin 5 to 10 units per hour, and total oxytocin not over 100 IU in 24 hours.

skill.tx.obg.pph_atony_escalate.practice: Talk through what you would do for a woman with pre-eclampsia and a flabby uterus who is still bleeding after the first response, naming each drug you will not give and why.
pitfalls: Giving methylergometrine in pre-eclampsia or hypertension, or carboprost in asthma.
Continuing uterotonics for bleeding from a tear when the uterus is well contracted.
Referring without IV access, oxytocin running, tamponade or an escort.
Waiting for a falling haemoglobin or blood pressure before escalating.
skill.tx.obg.pph_atony_escalate.dosingNote: CliniX does not prescribe. Doses here are quoted from the cited national or guideline document so a student can check them; the treating team's own protocol and the current formulary decide what is given.

probes.q: Give the dose and a contraindication for methylergometrine in PPH.
probes.a: 0.2 mg IM or slow IV, repeated after 15 minutes up to 5 doses (1 mg). Contraindicated in hypertension including pre-eclampsia, severe anaemia and heart disease.

probes.q: Give the dose and a contraindication for carboprost.
probes.a: 250 micrograms IM, repeated every 20 minutes up to 8 doses (2 mg). Contraindicated in asthma.

probes.q: What is the misoprostol dose in PPH?
probes.a: 800 micrograms rectally or sublingually.

probes.q: Bleeding continues after all the drugs. What is the escalation order?
probes.a: Check for retained tissue and coagulopathy, intrauterine balloon tamponade, then uterine compression sutures, systematic devascularisation, and hysterectomy. Refer early if these are not available.

probes.q: What limits the total oxytocin in the first 24 hours?
probes.a: The total oxytocin must not exceed 100 IU in 24 hours.

rubric.text: Starts bimanual uterine compression for a flabby uterus and raises the oxytocin infusion to 10 to 20 units per hour
Chooses a second uterotonic and checks contraindications: no methylergometrine in hypertension or pre-eclampsia, severe anaemia or heart disease; no carboprost in asthma
Explores for retained tissue and, if the uterus is contracted, for tears, and repairs them
Uses intrauterine balloon tamponade if bleeding continues, then names the surgical steps in order
Checks for coagulopathy and gives blood and components
Refers early if transfusion or surgery is not available, with oxytocin running, tamponade in place and an escort
Plans monitoring once bleeding is controlled: massage every 15 minutes for 2 hours and regular vital signs

skill.tx.obg.eclampsia_abcd.title: Eclampsia (1): the first minutes
skill.tx.obg.eclampsia_abcd.oneLine: Call for help, turn her on her side, oxygen, a line, a catheter, then magnesium
skill.tx.obg.eclampsia_abcd.why: Eclampsia is a seizure in a woman with pre-eclampsia, and the seizure ends by itself. What kills is what happens around it: aspiration, hypoxia, injury, and a second and third fit that magnesium sulphate could have prevented. The first minutes are airway, breathing, circulation, and then the drug.

steps.text: Call for help. Follow the principles of ABCD critical management, with team work.
Airway: turn her to the lateral position, protect the mouth and airway and suction as needed (the FOGSI text lists a mouth gag and neck extension), and avoid injury.
Breathing: give oxygen by nasal prongs, use suction, and keep the oxygen saturation above 96%.
Circulation: secure IV access, send the hypertensive-disorder laboratory tests, give Ringer lactate or normal saline at 80 mL per hour, and insert a Foley catheter.
Control convulsions with magnesium sulphate (loading and maintenance), control blood pressure with antihypertensives, and give corticosteroids if under 34 weeks.
Delivery: deliver once the mother is stabilised. Neuroimaging is not recommended for every case of eclampsia.

skill.tx.obg.eclampsia_abcd.practice: Say the first ninety seconds of an eclamptic fit aloud in ABCD order, and then name the drug you give and the position she is in.
pitfalls: Trying to restrain her or put something between her teeth in a way that injures her.
Delaying magnesium to arrange investigations or imaging.
Giving large volumes of IV fluid.
Forgetting that eclampsia can occur after delivery.
skill.tx.obg.eclampsia_abcd.dosingNote: CliniX does not prescribe. Doses here are quoted from the cited national or guideline document so a student can check them; the treating team's own protocol and the current formulary decide what is given.

probes.q: What does ABCD stand for in the management of eclampsia?
probes.a: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Delivery (with the drug therapy for convulsions and blood pressure within circulation).

probes.q: At what rate is IV crystalloid given in eclampsia, and what oxygen saturation is the target?
probes.a: Ringer lactate or normal saline at 80 mL per hour, and an oxygen saturation above 96%.

probes.q: Is a brain scan needed in every case of eclampsia?
probes.a: No. Neuroimaging is not recommended universally; MRI may be needed for a diagnostic dilemma.

rubric.text: Turns her to the lateral position, protects the airway with suction and prevents injury
Gives oxygen and aims for a saturation above 96%
Secures IV access, sends blood tests, gives crystalloid at 80 mL per hour and inserts a Foley catheter
Names magnesium sulphate first and blood pressure control next
States that delivery follows once she is stabilised

sources.source: FOGSI, Gestosis (India) and ICOG: Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy, Good Clinical Practice Recommendations 2019
sources.locator: Management of eclampsia: principles (ABCD), airway, breathing, circulation, delivery; neuroimaging not universal

skill.tx.obg.mgso4.title: Eclampsia (2): magnesium sulphate, the Pritchard and Zuspan regimens
skill.tx.obg.mgso4.oneLine: Load at once, check three things before every maintenance dose, keep calcium gluconate at the bedside
skill.tx.obg.mgso4.why: Magnesium sulphate is the first-choice drug for eclampsia and to prevent it in severe pre-eclampsia. It works only if the loading dose is given at once, and it is safe only if the reflexes, the breathing and the urine are watched, because an overdose stops the breathing.

steps.text: Use 50% w/v ampoules if possible: each ampoule is 1 g, which makes the arithmetic easy.

Pritchard regimen (preferred). Loading, 14 g in all: 4 g IV slowly as 20 mL of a 20% solution (4 ampoules of 50% plus 12 mL distilled water in a 20 mL syringe) at 1 g per minute, and 5 g of 50% deep IM into each buttock (5 ampoules with 0.5 mL of 2% lignocaine, in a 10 mL syringe with a long 20 G needle).

Pritchard maintenance: 5 g deep IM in alternate buttocks every 4 hours, only if the respiratory rate is above 16 per minute, the patellar reflexes are present, and the urine output is more than 100 mL in the last 4 hours.
Zuspan (IV) regimen: 4 g IV loading as above, then 5 g (5 ampoules) in 500 mL Ringer lactate at 100 mL per hour, which is 1 g per hour, preferably by infusion pump.
Continue for 24 hours after delivery or after the last convulsion, whichever is later. Routine serum magnesium monitoring is not needed.
Overdose: stop further doses, give oxygen, intubate if required, and give 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate slowly IV over 10 minutes with ECG monitoring. Keep it at the bedside.

skill.tx.obg.mgso4.practice: Draw up the Pritchard loading dose on paper: how many ampoules, what diluent, how fast, and where each part goes. Then state the three checks before the first maintenance dose.
pitfalls: Giving a maintenance dose without checking reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output.
Delaying the loading dose while waiting for laboratory results.
Injecting the 50% solution IV undiluted.
Stopping at delivery when the drug should continue for 24 hours.
skill.tx.obg.mgso4.dosingNote: CliniX does not prescribe. Doses here are quoted from the cited national or guideline document so a student can check them; the treating team's own protocol and the current formulary decide what is given.

probes.q: What is the Pritchard loading dose of magnesium sulphate?
probes.a: 14 g in all: 4 g IV slowly (1 g per minute, as 20 mL of a 20% solution) plus 5 g of a 50% solution deep IM into each buttock.

probes.q: What three things must be present before each maintenance dose?
probes.a: Respiratory rate above 16 per minute, patellar reflexes present, and urine output over 100 mL in the last 4 hours.

probes.q: What is the Zuspan maintenance regimen?
probes.a: After a 4 g IV loading dose, 5 g in 500 mL Ringer lactate at 100 mL per hour, which is 1 g per hour, preferably by infusion pump.

probes.q: She becomes drowsy with no reflexes and slow breathing on magnesium. What do you do?
probes.a: Stop magnesium, give oxygen, intubate if needed, and give 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate slowly IV over 10 minutes with ECG monitoring.

probes.q: How long is magnesium continued, and is a serum level needed?
probes.a: For 24 hours after delivery or the last convulsion, whichever is later. Routine serum magnesium monitoring is not needed.

rubric.text: Gives the loading dose at once: Pritchard 4 g IV over about 4 minutes plus 5 g deep IM in each buttock, or the Zuspan 4 g IV load
Gives maintenance: 5 g deep IM 4-hourly (Pritchard) or 1 g per hour by infusion (Zuspan)
Checks respiratory rate, patellar reflexes and urine output before each maintenance dose
Keeps 10% calcium gluconate at the bedside and states the response to toxicity
Continues for 24 hours after delivery or the last convulsion, whichever is later

sources.source: FOGSI, Gestosis (India) and ICOG: Hypertensive Disorders in Pregnancy, Good Clinical Practice Recommendations 2019
sources.locator: Magnesium sulphate: Pritchard (intramuscular) and Zuspan (intravenous) regimens; management of magnesium over action

skill.tx.obg.eclampsia_bp_delivery.title: Eclampsia (3): blood pressure, steroids, delivery and transfer
skill.tx.obg.eclampsia_bp_delivery.oneLine: Treat 160/110 promptly but gently, steroids under 34 weeks, deliver when stable
skill.tx.obg.eclampsia_bp_delivery.why: Seizures are prevented by magnesium; strokes are prevented by treating severe hypertension. The blood pressure should come down promptly but slowly, because a woman who drops from 190/120 to 100/60 has a hypoperfused placenta and brain. Delivery follows stabilisation, and the plan must survive the transfer to another facility.

steps.text: Treat a systolic pressure of 140 or more and a diastolic of 90 or more, with a target below 140/90 and no hypotension. In severe hypertension lower the pressure promptly but gradually.

Nifedipine 10 to 30 mg orally, never sublingually. Repeat in 30 to 45 minutes if not controlled, to a maximum total of 120 mg, then move to a slow-release form. Contraindicated in heart failure and AV or SA nodal abnormalities.

Labetalol 10 to 20 mg slow IV, then 20 to 80 mg every 20 to 30 minutes to a maximum total of 300 mg, or an infusion of 1 to 2 mg per minute after the first dose; 200 mg orally in a conscious woman. Contraindicated in heart failure, diabetes (per FOGSI), asthma and bradycardia.

Delivery: eclampsia and HELLP are delivered once the mother is stabilised after magnesium sulphate. Non-severe pre-eclampsia is delivered at 37 completed weeks, and severe pre-eclampsia after 34 completed weeks. Induction is safe, and caesarean section is for obstetric indications.
Corticosteroids for delivery before 34 completed weeks: dexamethasone 6 mg IM 12-hourly for 4 doses, or betamethasone 12 mg IM 24-hourly for 2 doses.
After delivery monitor the blood pressure closely for the first 48 hours, avoid NSAIDs, treat a persistent pressure of 160 systolic or 110 diastolic within one hour and consider magnesium sulphate.

Before transfer: the Pritchard loading dose must have been given and the receiving centre told; give nifedipine 20 mg slow-release or labetalol 200 mg orally (never sublingual nifedipine); give a corticosteroid dose if indicated; send an escort with an eclampsia kit.

skill.tx.obg.eclampsia_bp_delivery.practice: For a woman at 32 weeks with a pressure of 180/115 after her fit, state which drug you give, its dose, the target, the checks, and what you decide about steroids and delivery.
pitfalls: Giving nifedipine sublingually.
Lowering the pressure too fast or below 140/90 into hypotension.
Using labetalol in a woman with asthma or bradycardia.
Sending her to another facility without a loading dose or a call ahead.
skill.tx.obg.eclampsia_bp_delivery.dosingNote: CliniX does not prescribe. Doses here are quoted from the cited national or guideline document so a student can check them; the treating team's own protocol and the current formulary decide what is given.

probes.q: By which route must nifedipine never be given in this setting?
probes.a: Sublingually.

probes.q: What is the blood pressure target in severe pre-eclampsia, and how fast should you get there?
probes.a: Below 140/90 without hypotension, lowering the pressure promptly but gradually.

probes.q: When is delivery advised in non-severe pre-eclampsia, in severe pre-eclampsia, and in eclampsia?
probes.a: 37 completed weeks for non-severe; after 34 completed weeks for severe; and in eclampsia once the mother is stabilised after magnesium.

probes.q: Give the IV labetalol regimen and its maximum.
probes.a: 10 to 20 mg slow IV, then 20 to 80 mg every 20 to 30 minutes, to a maximum total of 300 mg; or an infusion of 1 to 2 mg per minute after the first dose.

probes.q: Which antihypertensive would you avoid in a woman with asthma?
probes.a: Labetalol, which is contraindicated in asthma, heart failure and bradycardia.

probes.q: What must be done before transferring an eclamptic woman to another facility?
probes.a: Give the Pritchard loading dose and inform the receiving centre; give an oral antihypertensive (nifedipine 20 mg slow-release or labetalol 200 mg, no sublingual nifedipine); a steroid dose if indicated; and send an escort with an eclampsia kit.

rubric.text: Treats severe hypertension promptly: nifedipine 10 to 30 mg orally (never sublingual) or labetalol 10 to 20 mg slow IV, with a target below 140/90 and no hypotension
Checks contraindications: labetalol in asthma, heart failure and bradycardia; nifedipine in heart failure and nodal disease
States that delivery follows stabilisation after magnesium sulphate, with caesarean section for obstetric indications
Considers antenatal corticosteroids if the pregnancy is under 34 weeks
Plans postpartum monitoring of blood pressure for at least 48 hours and avoids NSAIDs
Before any transfer: loading dose given, an oral antihypertensive, steroids if indicated, an escort with an eclampsia kit, and the receiving centre informed

skill.exam.obg.pelvimetry.title: Clinical Pelvimetry and Bony Pelvis Assessment
skill.exam.obg.pelvimetry.oneLine: Systematic palpation of the sacral promontory, ischial spines, and subpubic arch
skill.exam.obg.pelvimetry.why: Recognising pelvic contraction before or during labour prevents obstructed labour, ruptured uterus, and hypoxic fetal injury. Failure to assess pelvic architecture risks embarking on an unsafe mid-cavity instrumental delivery or missing an inadequate mid-pelvis.

steps.text: Explain the examination, ensure the bladder is empty, and place the patient in dorsal lithotomy position with good lighting and privacy.
Don sterile gloves, lubricate the examining fingers with water-soluble antiseptic gel, and gently separate the labia with the non-dominant hand.
Introduce the gloved index and middle fingers into the vagina along the posterior vaginal wall toward the sacral hollow.
Palpate the sacral promontory: attempt to touch the promontory with the tip of the middle finger while raising the hand until the subpubic ligament touches the index finger base.
Mark the subpubic contact point with the other index finger, withdraw the hand, and measure the diagonal conjugate with a sterile ruler (normal 12 cm or greater).
Sweep the examining fingers down the sacrum to assess its curvature (smoothly concave versus straight or anteriorly inclined).
Palpate the ischial spines on each lateral pelvic wall: determine whether they are blunt, prominent, or encroaching, and estimate the interspinous diameter (normal 10 cm or greater).
Trace the sacrospinous ligament from the ischial spine to the sacrum, noting whether it admits two to three fingerbreadths.
Assess the pelvic outlet: place a clenched fist against the perineum between the ischial tuberosities to estimate the intertuberous diameter (normal 8.5 to 10 cm).
Palpate the subpubic arch: place the thumbs along the inferior pubic rami to determine whether the subpubic angle is rounded (normal 85 to 90 degrees) or narrow.

skill.exam.obg.pelvimetry.normal: Sacral promontory not reachable (diagonal conjugate 12 cm or greater), sacral hollow smoothly concave, ischial spines blunt and non-prominent (interspinous diameter 10 cm or greater), sacrospinous ligament admitting 3 fingerbreadths, subpubic angle rounded (85 to 90 degrees), and intertuberous diameter accommodating 4 knuckles (8.5 cm or greater).
skill.exam.obg.pelvimetry.abnormal: Easily reachable sacral promontory (diagonal conjugate under 11.5 cm), flat or jutting sacrum, prominent sharp ischial spines with narrowed mid-pelvis (under 10 cm), narrowed sacrospinous ligament (under 2 fingerbreadths), acute subpubic arch (under 85 degrees), or intertuberous diameter under 8 cm.
skill.exam.obg.pelvimetry.significance: Confirms contracted pelvis or mid-pelvic narrowing. Precludes mid-cavity instrumental delivery and warns of high risk of cephalopelvic disproportion, deep transverse arrest, and secondary arrest of labour requiring caesarean delivery.
skill.exam.obg.pelvimetry.practice: Rehearse digital estimation of the diagonal conjugate and palpation of the ischial spines on a pelvic mannequin, calibrating finger reach against a sterile ruler.
pitfalls: Mistaking a prominent sacral false promontory for the true promontory, miscalculating the inlet conjugate.
Performing clinical pelvimetry before 36 weeks or during active early labour without analgesia or consent.
Relying on clinical pelvimetry alone while ignoring dynamic assessment of fetal head descent and cranial moulding.

probes.q: What is the anatomical landmark for measuring the diagonal conjugate, and what is its normal clinical value?
probes.a: From the inferior border of the pubic symphysis to the sacral promontory; normal is 12 cm or greater.

probes.q: How is the obstetric conjugate estimated from the measured diagonal conjugate?
probes.a: By subtracting 1.5 cm from the diagonal conjugate, giving an obstetric conjugate of 10.5 cm or more in an adequate pelvis.

probes.q: Why is mid-pelvic contraction more dangerous during labour than inlet contraction?
probes.a: Inlet contraction prevents engagement entirely, allowing planned caesarean, whereas mid-pelvic contraction permits engagement followed by deep transverse arrest deep in the birth canal.

rubric.text: Explains procedure, ensures empty bladder, and positions patient in dorsal lithotomy
Palpates toward sacral promontory and measures diagonal conjugate accurately
Palpates ischial spines bilaterally and evaluates interspinous diameter
Assesses subpubic angle and intertuberous diameter at the pelvic outlet

teach.heading: Pelvic architecture and the four parent types
teach.body:
The female pelvis is classified by Caldwell and Moloy into four types: gynaecoid, android, anthropoid, and platypelloid.

The gynaecoid pelvis is the ideal female pelvis with a rounded inlet, blunt ischial spines, a wide sacral hollow, and an 85 to 90 degree subpubic arch.

The android pelvis has a heart-shaped inlet, prominent spines, and a narrow arch, which greatly predisposes to deep transverse arrest and obstructed labour.

teach.heading: The three obstetric planes and their critical diameters
Clinical pelvimetry: technique and safety boundaries
teach.body:
Clinical pelvimetry is performed at 36 to 37 weeks or in early labour when presentation is cephalic but engagement is delayed.

In an adequate gynaecoid pelvis, the sacral promontory cannot be reached with the examining fingers unless fingers exceed 12 cm in reach.

Prominent ischial spines with an interspinous diameter under 10 cm warn of mid-pelvic stenosis, making mid-cavity instrumental delivery dangerous.

skill.exam.obg.fetal_skull.title: Fetal Skull Anatomy: Sutures, Fontanelles and Moulding
skill.exam.obg.fetal_skull.oneLine: Identification of cranial bones, fibrous sutures, fontanelle geometry, and moulding grades
skill.exam.obg.fetal_skull.why: The sutures and fontanelles allow the fetal head to compress and change shape to navigate the maternal pelvis during labour. Palpating these landmarks on vaginal examination is the only reliable clinical method to identify fetal presentation, position, and degree of flexion.

steps.text: Inspect the cranial topography: identify the paired frontal bones anteriorly, paired parietal bones centrally, and the occipital bone posteriorly.
Palpate the frontal or metopic suture running in the midline between the two frontal bones from the glabella to the anterior fontanelle.
Trace the coronal sutures running laterally from the anterior fontanelle between the frontal and parietal bones on each side.
Follow the sagittal suture running along the midline between the two parietal bones, connecting the anterior and posterior fontanelles.
Locate the lambdoid sutures extending inferolaterally between the parietal bones and the occipital bone.
Examine the anterior fontanelle (bregma): verify its diamond shape, four radiating suture lines, and dimensions (approximately 2.5 to 3 cm by 2 to 3 cm).
Examine the posterior fontanelle (lambda): verify its triangular shape, three radiating suture lines, and smaller size (approximately 1.2 cm).
Assess cranial moulding: gently palpate whether parietal bones touch, overlap reversibly, or overlap permanently across the sagittal suture.
Differentiate caput succedaneum from cephalhaematoma by palpating whether the scalp swelling crosses cranial suture lines.
Correlate the position of the posterior fontanelle relative to the maternal pelvic quadrants to define the fetal occipital position.

skill.exam.obg.fetal_skull.normal: Soft, flat anterior fontanelle, triangular posterior fontanelle, patent sutures with minimal edge touching or grade 1 reducible moulding during active labour.
skill.exam.obg.fetal_skull.abnormal: Tense bulging fontanelle, widely separated sutures, grade 3 non-reducible overlapping of cranial bones, or severe caput obscuring all landmarks.
skill.exam.obg.fetal_skull.significance: Grade 3 non-reducible moulding in active labour indicates cephalopelvic disproportion and impending obstructed labour; fontanelle orientation determines fetal position.
skill.exam.obg.fetal_skull.practice: Practise identifying diamond and triangular fontanelles by touch alone inside an opaque pelvic simulator box.
pitfalls: Mistaking a large triangular anterior fontanelle for the posterior fontanelle due to failure to trace all radiating sutures.
Confusing caput succedaneum with cephalhaematoma, misjudging the true bony station of the fetal skull.
Ignoring grade 3 non-reducible moulding in the presence of strong contractions, missing obstructed labour.

probes.q: What shape is the anterior fontanelle and how many sutures meet at its margins?
probes.a: Diamond-shaped, formed by the junction of four sutures: frontal, sagittal, and two coronal sutures.

probes.q: How do you distinguish caput succedaneum from cephalhaematoma at the bedside?
probes.a: Caput succedaneum is serosanguinous subcutaneous edema that crosses suture lines, whereas cephalhaematoma is subperiosteal bleeding limited by suture lines.

probes.q: What are the three clinical grades of fetal skull moulding during labour?
probes.a: Grade 1: bones touch but do not overlap; Grade 2: bones overlap but are easily reducible; Grade 3: bones overlap and are non-reducible.

rubric.text: Traces sagittal suture and locates anterior and posterior fontanelles
Distinguishes diamond-shaped bregma from triangular lambda accurately
Evaluates and correctly grades cranial bone overlap and reversibility
Differentiates caput succedaneum from underlying bony cranial margins

teach.heading: Cranial topography and landmark fontanelles
teach.body:
The fetal skull consists of the vault, face, and base. The vault bones are compressible and held together by fibrous sutures.

Meeting points of sutures form membranous gaps called fontanelles.

The anterior fontanelle or bregma is diamond-shaped and closes by 18 months, whereas the posterior fontanelle or lambda is triangular and closes by 2 to 3 months of life.

teach.heading: Fontanelle comparison and clinical differentiation
Moulding classification and clinical significance
teach.body:
Moulding is the alteration of skull shape produced by compression of cranial bones under labour pressures.

Grade 1 moulding (touching suture edges) and grade 2 (reducible overlap) are physiological responses that reduce presenting diameters by 0.5 to 1 cm.

Grade 3 moulding (non-reducible overlap) warns of cephalopelvic disproportion and requires immediate delivery evaluation.

skill.exam.obg.fetal_diameters_station.title: Fetal Head Diameters, Engagement and Pelvic Station
skill.exam.obg.fetal_diameters_station.oneLine: Clinical correlation of fetal presenting diameters, abdominal fifths, and vaginal ischial station
skill.exam.obg.fetal_diameters_station.why: The outcome of labour depends on which diameter of the fetal skull engages in the maternal pelvis. Assessing station against the ischial spines and verifying engagement per abdomen prevents applying forceps or vacuum to an unengaged fetal head.

steps.text: Determine the presenting part and attitude of the fetal head by gentle abdominal palpation using Leopold manoeuvres.
Estimate engagement abdominally: determine how many fifths of the fetal head remain palpable above the upper border of the pubic symphysis.
Confirm engagement when two-fifths or less of the fetal head is palpable above the pelvic brim per abdomen.
Perform a gentle sterile vaginal examination to locate the bony landmarks of the maternal pelvis.
Palpate the ischial spines bilaterally along the lateral pelvic walls to define the zero station reference plane.
Locate the lowest bony point of the fetal skull (excluding caput succedaneum) relative to the ischial spines.
Designate station in centimetres: negative (-5 to -1) above the spines, zero (0) at the spines, and positive (+1 to +5) below the spines.
Identify the presenting diameter: in a fully flexed cephalic presentation, confirm the suboccipitobregmatic diameter (9.5 cm).
Detect deflexion attitudes: identify the occipitofrontal diameter (11.5 cm) in deflexed vertex, or the mentovertical diameter (13.5 to 14 cm) in brow presentation.
Correlate abdominal fifths with vaginal station to confirm true bony descent rather than progressive scalp edema.

skill.exam.obg.fetal_diameters_station.normal: Fully flexed vertex presentation presenting the suboccipitobregmatic diameter (9.5 cm), head engaged (2/5 or less palpable per abdomen, station 0 or lower).
skill.exam.obg.fetal_diameters_station.abnormal: Deflexed vertex, brow presentation (mentovertical 13.5 to 14 cm), unengaged head (3/5 or more palpable per abdomen, high negative station), or apparent low station caused entirely by caput succedaneum.
skill.exam.obg.fetal_diameters_station.significance: A deflexed head or brow presentation cannot deliver vaginally without flexion or caesarean delivery; high station with ruptured membranes warns of cephalopelvic disproportion or cord prolapse.
skill.exam.obg.fetal_diameters_station.practice: Practise assessing abdominal fifths and corresponding pelvic stations using simulated birth canal models.
pitfalls: Confusing a large caput succedaneum reaching station +1 with an engaged head when 3/5 of the skull remains above the brim abdominally.
Attempting vaginal delivery in a persistent brow presentation where the presenting diameter is 13.5 to 14 cm.
Documenting station without reference to the ischial spines.

probes.q: What is the presenting anteroposterior diameter in a well-flexed vertex presentation, and what is its normal measurement?
probes.a: The suboccipitobregmatic diameter, which measures 9.5 cm.

probes.q: What is station zero, and how is station defined above and below this point?
probes.a: Station zero is the level of the maternal ischial spines; station is measured in centimetres negative above the spines and positive below.

probes.q: What is the clinical definition of an engaged fetal head?
probes.a: The biparietal diameter has passed the pelvic inlet, corresponding to two-fifths or less palpable per abdomen and the leading bony skull at station zero.

rubric.text: Assesses abdominal descent in fifths above the pubic symphysis
Palpates ischial spines and records station in centimetres relative to zero
Identifies presenting cranial diameter and degree of flexion
Verifies bony landmark descent rather than superficial caput

teach.heading: Longitudinal presenting diameters and fetal attitude
Transverse cranial diameters and the engaging plane
teach.body:
The biparietal diameter (9.5 cm) is the greatest transverse diameter of the fetal skull.

When the biparietal diameter passes through the pelvic inlet, the head is engaged.

Other transverse diameters include the bitemporal (8.0 to 8.5 cm) and bimastoid (7.5 cm), which pass through the pelvis without difficulty in normal cephalic presentations.

teach.heading: The dual rule of engagement: abdominal fifths and station
teach.body:
Engagement is defined as the descent of the biparietal diameter through the pelvic brim.

Abdominally, engagement corresponds to 2/5 or less of the fetal head palpable above the pubic symphysis.

Vaginally, the leading bony point of the occiput reaches station zero (level of the ischial spines), provided extensive caput is not mistaken for skull.

skill.exam.obg.labour_abdomen.title: Abdominal Examination in Labour and Descent Assessment
skill.exam.obg.labour_abdomen.oneLine: Monitoring uterine contraction frequency, duration, resting tone, and descent of fetal head in fifths
skill.exam.obg.labour_abdomen.why: Abdominal examination provides non-invasive, objective evidence of labour progress and uterine dynamics. Measuring contractions and fetal head descent in fifths prevents unnecessary vaginal examinations and gives early warning of uterine hyperstimulation, tachysystole, or obstructed labour.

steps.text: Position the woman comfortably in semi-recumbent posture with a slight left lateral tilt to avoid supine hypotension.
Inspect the abdominal contour: observe for asymmetry, distended bladder, previous scars, or a pathological retraction ring (Bandl ring).
Place the warmed palm of the examining hand gently over the uterine fundus to monitor contractions continuously for at least 10 minutes.
Record the contraction frequency: count the number of contractions occurring within the 10-minute observation window.
Measure the duration of each contraction in seconds from initial palpable hardening to complete relaxation of the myometrium.
Evaluate contraction intensity: determine whether the fundus can be indented by the fingertips at the peak of the contraction (mild, moderate, or strong).
Verify uterine relaxation between contractions: confirm that the uterus becomes completely soft, excluding hypertonus or abruption.
Perform deep pelvic palpation using both hands to determine the number of fifths of the fetal head palpable above the pubic symphysis.

skill.exam.obg.labour_abdomen.normal: Active labour contractions 3 to 4 per 10 minutes, lasting 40 to 50 seconds, strong intensity, complete uterine relaxation between contractions, and progressive descent of the fetal head from 5/5 to 0/5.
skill.exam.obg.labour_abdomen.abnormal: Tachysystole (more than 5 contractions per 10 minutes), prolonged contractions (over 60 seconds), elevated resting tone, Bandl ring, or arrest of descent (head remains 4/5 or 3/5 despite strong contractions).
skill.exam.obg.labour_abdomen.significance: Tachysystole and hypertonus cause fetal hypoxaemia and uterine rupture; lack of descent in the presence of strong contractions signifies cephalopelvic disproportion or mechanical obstruction.
skill.exam.obg.labour_abdomen.practice: Practise palpatory timing of contractions and grading fifths of the head on an obstetric simulation mannequin.
pitfalls: Palpating contractions for only 2 or 3 minutes, which fails to capture true 10-minute frequency and variability.
Failing to palpate uterine relaxation between contractions, missing early concealed abruptio placentae or hyperstimulation.
Relying entirely on vaginal examination to determine fetal descent while ignoring abdominal fifths.

probes.q: What constitutes normal uterine contraction frequency and duration in the active first stage of labour?
probes.a: Three to four contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting 40 to 50 seconds, with complete relaxation in between.

probes.q: What is uterine tachysystole, and why is it dangerous for the fetus?
probes.a: More than five contractions in 10 minutes over a 30-minute window; it impedes intervillous blood flow and causes fetal hypoxia.

probes.q: How is descent of the fetal head graded in fifths by abdominal palpation?
probes.a: The width of five examining fingers above the symphysis: 5/5 is completely above brim, 2/5 indicates engagement, and 0/5 is completely in pelvis.

rubric.text: Positions mother with left lateral tilt to prevent supine vena caval compression
Palpates fundus for 10 minutes, recording contraction frequency, duration, and tone
Confirms complete uterine relaxation between contractions
Measures descent of fetal head in fifths above the pelvic brim

teach.heading: Palpatory assessment of uterine dynamics
teach.body:
Uterine contractions in active labour originate near the cornua and sweep downward across the myometrium.

Palpating the fundus for 10 minutes measures frequency, duration, and peak intensity.

A mild contraction indents easily under light finger pressure, a moderate contraction yields slightly, and a strong contraction feels rigid and cannot be indented at peak.

teach.heading: Grading descent in fifths above the brim
Warning signs on abdominal examination in labour
teach.body:
A visible transverse groove across the lower abdomen indicates Bandl's pathological retraction ring, marking extreme thinning of the lower segment in obstructed labour.

Tachysystole (more than 5 contractions per 10 minutes) or elevated basal tone reduces placental perfusion and requires immediate cessation of oxytocics.

skill.exam.obg.labour_pv.title: Intrapartum Vaginal Examination and Cervical Assessment
skill.exam.obg.labour_pv.oneLine: Aseptic digital assessment of cervical dilatation, effacement, membranes, liquor, station, and moulding
skill.exam.obg.labour_pv.why: Digital vaginal examination in labour tracks the objective milestones of active labour and confirms cephalic presentation. Performing it strictly every 4 hours or for clear indications reduces the risk of ascending chorioamnionitis and puerperal sepsis.

steps.text: Confirm the clinical indication, explain the procedure to the woman, ensure privacy, and obtain informed verbal consent.
Ensure the bladder is empty; wash hands thoroughly and don sterile gloves using strict aseptic technique.
Clean the vulva and perineal area with warm sterile water or normal saline using single downward strokes.
Gently separate the labia with the non-dominant hand and introduce the gloved index and middle fingers into the vagina.
Assess the cervix: determine consistency (firm, medium, soft), position (posterior, mid, anterior), and length or effacement percentage.
Measure cervical dilatation in centimetres by estimating the distance between the opposing internal cervical margins.
Check the fetal membranes: identify whether membranes are intact (smooth bulging fluid bag) or ruptured.
If membranes are ruptured, inspect the draining liquor for colour (clear, meconium-stained, blood-stained, or purulent) and odour.
Identify the presenting part, position, and station relative to the maternal ischial spines, noting caput and moulding.
Withdraw the fingers gently, clean the perineum, record findings immediately on the partograph, and explain findings to the woman.

skill.exam.obg.labour_pv.normal: Dilatation progressing at 1 cm per hour or more in active labour, full effacement, clear amniotic fluid, flexed vertex at station 0 or lower, absence of offensive odour.
skill.exam.obg.labour_pv.abnormal: Arrest of cervical dilatation, thick meconium-stained liquor, offensive liquor, cord presentation or prolapse, brow or face presentation, or high unengaged head.
skill.exam.obg.labour_pv.significance: Arrest of dilatation signifies labour dystocia; meconium-stained liquor indicates potential fetal compromise; foul liquor confirms intra-amniotic infection (chorioamnionitis).
skill.exam.obg.labour_pv.practice: Practise digital estimation of cervical dilatation (1 to 10 cm) on calibrated cervical simulation boards.
pitfalls: Performing vaginal examinations more frequently than every 4 hours without clinical indication, increasing sepsis risk.
Measuring dilatation at the external os rather than the internal os in an uneffaced cervix.
Failing to inspect liquor colour and odour immediately upon rupture of membranes.

probes.q: What is the standard recommended time interval for routine vaginal examination in uncomplicated active labour?
probes.a: Every four hours, unless there is a specific clinical indication to examine earlier.

probes.q: What is the difference between cervical effacement and cervical dilatation?
probes.a: Effacement is the progressive thinning and shortening of the cervix, whereas dilatation is the opening of the internal cervical os.

probes.q: What urgent action must be taken if a pulsating cord is felt on vaginal examination during membrane rupture?
probes.a: Elevate the presenting part digitally to relieve cord compression, place the mother in knee-chest position, and call an immediate emergency crash caesarean.

rubric.text: Ensures strict asepsis, sterile gloves, and perineal cleansing
Accurately measures cervical dilatation, effacement, and consistency
Identifies membrane state and inspects amniotic fluid colour and odour
Confirms presenting part, position, and station relative to ischial spines

teach.heading: Timing, indications and infection risks of vaginal examination
teach.body:
Vaginal examinations in labour should be limited to four-hourly intervals in uncomplicated active labour.

More frequent examinations increase the risk of ascending genital tract infection, chorioamnionitis, and neonatal sepsis.

Additional examinations are indicated only if contractions change, maternal urge to push develops, or fetal distress occurs.

teach.heading: Cervical effacement, dilatation and pelvic station
teach.body:
Effacement represents the incorporation of the cervical canal into the lower uterine segment, taken up from 2 to 3 cm length down to paper-thin thickness.

Dilatation is measured across the internal os from 0 to 10 cm.

Palpation of the presenting part identifies the anterior fontanelle, posterior fontanelle, and sagittal suture orientation relative to the maternal pelvic quadrants.

teach.heading: Membrane status, liquor colour and cord prolapse triage

skill.annex.obg.bishop_score.title: Bishop Pre-Induction Cervical Ripeness Score
skill.annex.obg.bishop_score.oneLine: Five pelvic parameters scoring cervical readiness for induction of labour
skill.annex.obg.bishop_score.why: Inducing labour with an unripe cervix leads to prolonged labour, failed induction, uterine exhaustion, and emergency caesarean delivery. Calculating the Bishop score identifies whether pre-induction cervical ripening with prostaglandins or mechanical methods is mandatory before oxytocin induction.
skill.annex.obg.bishop_score.practice: Calculate Bishop scores for three clinical scenarios and select the appropriate induction or ripening pathway.
pitfalls: Commencing oxytocin infusion when the Bishop score is 5 or less without prior cervical ripening.
Confusing effacement percentage with cervical length in centimetres.
Failing to re-evaluate the Bishop score 6 to 12 hours after placing a ripening agent before escalating to oxytocin.

probes.q: What five clinical parameters are assessed in the Bishop score?
probes.a: Cervical dilatation, effacement or length, station of fetal head, cervical consistency, and cervical position.

probes.q: What Bishop score defines an unfavourable cervix, and what intervention is indicated?
probes.a: A score of 5 or less indicates an unfavourable cervix requiring cervical ripening with prostaglandins or mechanical balloon before oxytocin.

probes.q: What Bishop score indicates a ripe cervix ready for amniotomy and oxytocin infusion?
probes.a: A score of 8 or more indicates a favourable cervix with high probability of successful induction.

rubric.text: Assesses all five Bishop parameters accurately on digital examination
Calculates the total Bishop score correctly out of 13
Selects ripening agent for score <=5 or direct induction for score >=8

teach.heading: The rationale for pre-induction cervical evaluation
teach.body:
The Bishop score is an objective numerical scoring system developed to predict the likelihood of successful vaginal delivery following induction of labour.

A closed, long, firm, posterior cervix offers high mechanical resistance to uterine contractions.

Assessing the score determines whether the patient requires pharmacological or mechanical cervical ripening before initiating oxytocin.

teach.heading: The modified Bishop scoring matrix
Score interpretation and clinical induction pathways
teach.body:
Total score ranges from 0 to 13 points.

A score of 5 or less indicates an unripe, unfavourable cervix: ripen with prostaglandin E2 gel, oral or vaginal misoprostol, or transcervical Foley catheter balloon.

A score of 8 or more indicates a ripe, favourable cervix: proceed directly with artificial rupture of membranes (amniotomy) and titrated intravenous oxytocin infusion.

skill.annex.obg.partograph.title: Modified WHO Partograph Plotting and Interpretation
skill.annex.obg.partograph.oneLine: Graphic recording of cervical dilatation, descent, contractions, and maternal-fetal vitals in active labour
skill.annex.obg.partograph.why: The partograph provides an early pictorial warning of prolonged or obstructed labour. Plotting dilatation and descent distinguishes normal active progress from protraction and arrest disorders, triggering timely transfer or intervention before maternal exhaustion, ketoacidosis, or fetal asphyxia supervenes.
skill.annex.obg.partograph.practice: Plot a sequential labour case on a blank partograph, identifying the exact hour the alert line is breached.
pitfalls: Starting to plot the partograph in the latent phase before active labour (dilatation under 4 cm) is established.
Failing to take decisive action when cervical dilatation reaches the action line 4 hours to the right of the alert line.
Recording only cervical dilatation while omitting moulding, liquor colour, maternal pulse, and urine output.

probes.q: At what cervical dilatation is plotting on the modified WHO partograph commenced?
probes.a: At 4 cm of cervical dilatation, representing the onset of the active first stage of labour.

probes.q: What is the clinical meaning of the alert line and action line on the partograph?
probes.a: The alert line represents a minimum dilation rate of 1 cm per hour; the action line is 4 hours to the right, signalling need for decisive intervention.

probes.q: What four signs on a partograph indicate cephalopelvic disproportion and obstructed labour?
probes.a: Dilation crossing action line, head arrested at high fifths, grade 3 moulding, and secondary arrest with maternal tachycardia.

rubric.text: Commences partograph plotting only when active phase (4 cm or more) is established
Plots cervical dilatation (X) and head descent (O) correctly on the time grid
Accurately records contraction frequency and duration using correct shading
Identifies breach of alert line and implements decisive action at the action line

teach.heading: The active phase and the geometry of the partograph
teach.body:
The modified WHO partograph is an intrapartum monitoring tool started when the cervix reaches 4 cm dilatation in the presence of regular rhythmic contractions.

The alert line extends from 4 cm to 10 cm at a slope of 1 cm per hour over 6 hours.

The action line runs parallel to the alert line, drawn exactly 4 hours to the right to provide a window for assessment before intervention.

teach.heading: Partograph parameter monitoring frequency
Reading deviation: alert line, action line and obstructed labour
teach.body:
Normal labour progress stays on or to the left of the alert line.

When dilatation crosses to the right of the alert line, it signals protraction: assess hydration, analgesia, and uterine contractions.

When dilatation reaches or crosses the action line (4-hour delay), it demands definitive management: amniotomy, oxytocin augmentation if contractions are weak, or caesarean delivery if obstruction is present.

skill.exam.obg.normal_delivery.title: Mechanism and Manual Conduct of Normal Vaginal Delivery
skill.exam.obg.normal_delivery.oneLine: Hands-on delivery of the fetal head, checking the cord, and safe delivery of the shoulders
skill.exam.obg.normal_delivery.why: Uncontrolled expulsion of the fetal head causes severe third-degree and fourth-degree perineal lacerations and sudden intracranial decompression. Gentle manual perineal support and controlled delivery of the shoulders prevent maternal obstetric anal sphincter injuries and neonatal brachial plexus trauma.

steps.text: Confirm full cervical dilatation, encourage rhythmic bearing-down efforts only during contractions, and support maternal positioning.
Don sterile gown and gloves, prepare delivery instruments, and ensure the neonatal resuscitation warmer is pre-heated.
Observe crowning: when 3 to 4 cm of fetal head remains visible at the introitus without receding between contractions.
Perform the modified Ritgen manoeuvre: place a sterile pad over the perineum, support the fetal chin through the perineum with one hand, and place the other hand on the occiput to maintain flexion.
Allow the vertex to deliver slowly by controlled extension between contractions, preventing explosive expulsion.
Wipe the infant face with a clean sterile gauze, then slip an index finger around the fetal neck to check for umbilical cord loops.
If a loose nuchal cord is felt, gently slip it over the fetal head; if tight, clamp twice with two artery forceps and divide between them.
Wait for spontaneous restitution and external rotation of the head, confirming that the shoulders have rotated into the anteroposterior diameter.
Place hands biparietally on the fetal head and apply gentle downward traction along the birth axis until the anterior shoulder delivers under the pubic arch.
Apply gentle upward and forward traction to deliver the posterior shoulder over the perineum, then support the emerging trunk and limbs.

skill.exam.obg.normal_delivery.normal: Slow controlled delivery of vertex by extension, intact perineum or minor controlled tear, spontaneous external rotation, smooth delivery of shoulders, and vigorous crying infant.
skill.exam.obg.normal_delivery.abnormal: Explosive delivery with third-degree or fourth-degree perineal tear, tight unyielding nuchal cord, or shoulder dystocia (turtle sign: fetal head retracts against perineum).
skill.exam.obg.normal_delivery.significance: Perineal trauma causes long-term anal incontinence; unrecognized shoulder dystocia results in permanent brachial plexus injury, fetal asphyxia, or death.
skill.exam.obg.normal_delivery.practice: Practise hands-on Ritgen manoeuvre and biparietal shoulder traction technique on an obstetric delivery model.
pitfalls: Applying excessive lateral or downward traction on the fetal head during shoulder delivery, stretching the brachial plexus.
Letting the fetal head deliver abruptly during the height of a contraction without maintaining flexion.
Clamping and cutting a loose nuchal cord that could easily have been slipped over the infant head.

probes.q: What is crowning of the fetal head?
probes.a: The largest diameter of the fetal head stretches the vulval introitus and does not recede between contractions.

probes.q: What is the purpose of the modified Ritgen manoeuvre during delivery of the head?
probes.a: To control the speed of delivery and maintain flexion, allowing the head to deliver slowly by extension without tearing the perineum.

probes.q: How should the fetal shoulders be delivered to prevent brachial plexus injury?
probes.a: Gently pull downwards along the pelvic axis until the anterior shoulder appears, then lift upwards to deliver the posterior shoulder.

rubric.text: Controls head delivery at crowning with modified Ritgen manoeuvre
Checks neck systematically for umbilical cord loops before delivering shoulders
Applies gentle axis traction to deliver anterior then posterior shoulder safely
Maintains manual perineal support throughout second stage delivery

teach.heading: The cardinal movements of normal labour
teach.body:
As the fetus navigates the pelvic canal, it undergoes sequential positional adaptations.

These cardinal movements are engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution, external rotation, and expulsion.

Flexion substitutes the smaller suboccipitobregmatic diameter (9.5 cm) for the larger occipitofrontal diameter (11.5 cm).

teach.heading: Manual perineal protection: the modified Ritgen technique
teach.body:
During crowning, the head must not deliver abruptly at the height of a contraction.

The modified Ritgen manoeuvre employs the operator fingers through the perineum to support the fetal chin while the other hand controls the occiput.

This slows the passage of the head and guides extension between contractions, protecting the anal sphincter from tears.

teach.heading: Shoulder delivery mechanics and avoidance of brachial traction
teach.body:
Following restitution, the shoulders rotate into the anteroposterior pelvic diameter.

The operator places hands over the parietal bones and exerts gentle downward traction along the pelvic curve until the anterior shoulder slips beneath the symphysis.

Jerking, twisting, or forceful lateral traction must never be used, as it directly strains the roots of the brachial plexus.

skill.approach.obg.amtsl.title: Active Management of the Third Stage of Labour (AMTSL)
skill.approach.obg.amtsl.oneLine: Uterotonic administration, delayed cord clamping, controlled cord traction, and uterine massage
skill.approach.obg.amtsl.why: Postpartum haemorrhage from uterine atony is the leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide. AMTSL reduces the incidence of postpartum haemorrhage by more than 60 percent, prevents severe maternal anaemia, and reduces the need for emergency blood transfusion.

steps.text: Palpate the maternal abdomen immediately after delivery of the infant to rule out the presence of an undiagnosed second twin.
Administer a prophylactic uterotonic drug (oxytocin 10 IU intramuscularly) within one minute of delivery of the baby.
Wait 1 to 3 minutes after birth before clamping the umbilical cord, supporting delayed cord clamping for neonatal blood volume and iron stores.
Apply two sterile clamps to the umbilical cord and divide the cord between the clamps using sterile blunt-ended scissors.
Watch for signs of placental separation: uterine fundus rises and becomes firm and globular, a sudden gush of blood occurs, and the cord lengthens.

Perform controlled cord traction (Brandt-Andrews manoeuvre): place one hand suprapubically pushing the uterus upward and backward (counter-traction) while the other hand applies gentle steady downward traction on the clamped cord during a contraction.
As the placenta emerges at the introitus, support it with both hands and rotate it gently in a continuous circular direction to twist the membranes into a rope so they peel off intact.
Perform immediate abdominal uterine massage to ensure the myometrium is firmly contracted, and thoroughly inspect the maternal cotyledons and fetal membranes for completeness.

skill.approach.obg.amtsl.practice: Practise performing controlled cord traction with suprapubic counter-traction on an obstetric simulator.
pitfalls: Applying cord traction without simultaneous suprapubic counter-traction, which can cause acute uterine inversion.
Pulling vigorously on the cord when the uterus is completely relaxed and uncontracted.
Administering oxytocin before ruling out an undiagnosed second twin in the uterus.
Failing to rotate the delivering placenta, tearing membranes and leaving retained fragments in utero.

probes.q: What are the three core components of the Active Management of the Third Stage of Labour?
probes.a: Prophylactic uterotonic within one minute, controlled cord traction with counter-traction, and uterine massage.

probes.q: Why must the uterine fundus be pushed upwards during controlled cord traction?
probes.a: Suprapubic counter-traction prevents uterine inversion while the placenta is being extracted by cord traction.

probes.q: What classic clinical signs indicate that the placenta has completely separated from the uterine wall?
probes.a: The uterus becomes globular, firm, and rises in the abdomen, the umbilical cord lengthens, and a sudden gush of blood appears.

rubric.text: Palpates abdomen to exclude an undiagnosed second twin before giving uterotonic
Administers prophylactic oxytocin within one minute of infant delivery
Executes controlled cord traction only with simultaneous suprapubic counter-traction
Inspects maternal cotyledons and fetal membranes for completeness and tears

teach.heading: The physiological third stage versus active management
teach.body:
The third stage begins after delivery of the fetus and ends with complete delivery of the placenta and fetal membranes.

In physiological management, separation relies entirely on endogenous oxytocin surges.

AMTSL speeds placental separation and shortens the third stage, reducing primary postpartum haemorrhage by two-thirds without increasing retained placenta rates.

teach.heading: The Brandt-Andrews manoeuvre: counter-traction mechanics
teach.body:
Controlled cord traction must never be exerted on a soft, flaccid uterus.

The operator waits for a strong uterine contraction following oxytocin administration.

One hand places the palm above the pubic symphysis, pressing the lower uterine segment upwards and backwards while the other hand exerts steady, non-jerky downward traction on the clamped cord.

teach.heading: Placental inspection: cotyledons, membranes and vascular anatomy

skill.exam.obg.episiotomy.title: Mediolateral Episiotomy: Indications, Timing and Incision
skill.exam.obg.episiotomy.oneLine: Surgical enlargement of the posterior vaginal introitus at 45 to 60 degrees during crowning
skill.exam.obg.episiotomy.why: Routine episiotomy causes unnecessary perineal trauma and pain, but selective episiotomy is life-saving in fetal distress or instrumental delivery. Infiltrating local anaesthetic adequately and angling the incision at 45 to 60 degrees from the fourchette protects the anal sphincter from catastrophic extension.

steps.text: Establish a clear clinical indication: instrumental delivery, shoulder dystocia, rigid perineum with impending ragged tear, or fetal distress requiring expedited birth.
Explain the procedure to the mother and obtain informed verbal consent between contractions.

Infiltrate 10 mL of 1% lignocaine into the perineum: insert needle at fourchette, aspirate to rule out intravascular puncture, and fan local anaesthetic subcutaneously and into the perineal body muscles.
Wait 1 to 2 minutes for adequate local anaesthesia; pinch the perineal skin gently with toothed forceps to test for sensory loss.
Time the incision: wait until the perineum is thinned and bulged by the fetal head and 3 to 4 cm of vertex is visible during a contraction (crowning).
Insert the index and middle fingers of the non-dominant hand between the fetal head and the posterior vaginal wall to protect the infant scalp.
Place the blunt blade of the episiotomy scissors inside the vagina and the sharp blade outside on the perineal skin.
Begin the incision at the posterior fourchette in the midline.
Cut downwards and outwards at an angle of 45 to 60 degrees towards the maternal ischial tuberosity for a length of 3 to 4 cm in a single decisive cut.
Control maternal bleeding with direct gauze pressure until delivery of the head and completion of the third stage.

skill.exam.obg.episiotomy.normal: Clean 3 to 4 cm mediolateral incision angled at 45 to 60 degrees, sparing the anal sphincter and rectum, with prompt delivery of the infant.
skill.exam.obg.episiotomy.abnormal: Extension of the incision into the external anal sphincter or rectum, severe arterial bleeding from severed perineal vessels, or median cut risking fourth-degree tear.
skill.exam.obg.episiotomy.significance: A midline incision or an incision angled at less than 45 degrees substantially increases the risk of third-degree and fourth-degree perineal tears.
skill.exam.obg.episiotomy.practice: Practise infiltration and scissor angulation (45 to 60 degrees) on perineal repair simulation blocks.
pitfalls: Cutting too early before the head crowns, which causes excessive blood loss from uncompressed perineal vessels.
Directing the cut at less than 45 degrees from the midline, allowing the incision to extend directly into the anal sphincter.
Failing to place two fingers inside the vagina to protect the fetal skull from the scissor blades.

probes.q: What is the recommended angle and starting point for a mediolateral episiotomy?
probes.a: Started at the posterior fourchette in the midline and directed laterally at 45 to 60 degrees toward the ischial tuberosity.

probes.q: Why is routine episiotomy not recommended in modern obstetric practice?
probes.a: Routine episiotomy increases severe perineal trauma, postpartum pain, blood loss, and dyspareunia compared to restrictive, selective use.

probes.q: What structures are divided during a standard mediolateral episiotomy?
probes.a: Vaginal mucosa, posterior fourchette, perineal skin, bulbospongiosus, superficial transverse perineal muscle, and perineal body fascia.

rubric.text: Aspirates before infiltrating 10 mL of 1% lignocaine into the perineal body
Times incision accurately at crowning when 3 to 4 cm of vertex is visible
Inserts two fingers inside vagina to protect fetal head during incision
Cuts mediolaterally at 45 to 60 degrees towards the ischial tuberosity

teach.heading: Indications and selective versus routine episiotomy policy
teach.body:
Modern obstetric evidence strongly refutes routine episiotomy for uncomplicated vaginal births.

Selective episiotomy is reserved for clear indications: operative vaginal delivery (forceps or ventouse), shoulder dystocia manoeuvres, rigid unyielding perineum, or urgent delivery for acute fetal distress.

Restrictive use halves the incidence of posterior perineal trauma without increasing anterior trauma.

teach.heading: Mediolateral versus midline episiotomy comparison
Surgical anatomy, nerve block and precision incision technique
teach.body:
The perineal body is innervated by the pudendal nerve.

Infiltration of 10 mL of 1% lignocaine into the perineal muscles provides effective anaesthesia within two minutes.

The incision begins in the midline fourchette and angles 45 to 60 degrees towards the ischial tuberosity, extending 3 to 4 cm.

This completely bypasses the external anal sphincter while creating adequate room.

skill.exam.obg.perineal_repair.title: Perineal Laceration Classification and Layered Surgical Repair
skill.exam.obg.perineal_repair.oneLine: Systematic classification of tears and anatomical restoration of rectum, sphincters, muscle, and mucosa
skill.exam.obg.perineal_repair.why: Obstetric anal sphincter injuries affect up to 5 percent of vaginal deliveries. Failure to diagnose a sphincter tear or inaccurate repair leads to faecal incontinence, flatus incontinence, chronic pain, and rectovaginal fistula formation.

steps.text: Inspect the perineum and birth canal under excellent lighting, ensure adequate analgesia (pudendal block or regional anaesthesia), and position the patient in lithotomy.
Perform a digital rectal examination to assess the integrity of the anal canal and external anal sphincter before starting repair.

Classify the injury: first-degree (skin/mucosa only), second-degree (perineal muscles), third-degree (sphincter complex: 3a <50% EAS, 3b >50% EAS, 3c IAS torn), or fourth-degree (rectal mucosa involved).
If rectal mucosa is torn (fourth degree): identify the apex and close rectal mucosa and submucosa with 3-0 polyglactin using interrupted sutures with knots in the submucosa.
Identify and repair the internal anal sphincter (IAS): approximate the pale glistening circular fibrous band with interrupted 2-0 or 3-0 polyglactin sutures.
Repair the external anal sphincter (EAS): approximate the red striated muscle ends using either end-to-end mattress sutures or overlap technique with 2-0 or 3-0 polyglactin.
Identify the apex of the vaginal tear: place an anchoring suture 1 cm above the apex into healthy vaginal tissue.
Close the vaginal mucosa down to the hymenal ring with a continuous 2-0 polyglactin suture, re-approximating the rectovaginal septum.
Approximate the perineal body muscles (bulbospongiosus and transverse perinei) with 2 or 3 interrupted 2-0 polyglactin sutures to restore the perineal body.
Close the perineal skin with a continuous subcuticular or interrupted absorbable suture, and perform a final digital rectal examination to verify sphincter reconstruction.

skill.exam.obg.perineal_repair.normal: Restored anatomical perineal body, intact functioning anal sphincter on rectal examination, smooth closed vaginal mucosa, and absence of sutures traversing the rectal mucosa.
skill.exam.obg.perineal_repair.abnormal: Unrecognized full-thickness anal sphincter defect, persistent rectal mucosal gap, palpable suture in the rectal lumen, or expanding perineal haematoma.
skill.exam.obg.perineal_repair.significance: Inadequate sphincter repair leads to permanent faecal incontinence and rectovaginal fistula; suture through rectal lumen creates a contaminated tract and fistula.
skill.exam.obg.perineal_repair.practice: Practise tiered identification of rectal mucosa, IAS, and EAS on three-dimensional layered perineal models.
pitfalls: Omitting the preliminary and concluding digital rectal examination, which leaves 30 percent of third-degree tears undetected.
Mistaking the internal anal sphincter for the external anal sphincter or vaginal fascia.
Leaving dead space in the perineal body, predisposing to large occult haematoma formation.

probes.q: How are third-degree perineal tears subclassified into 3a, 3b, and 3c?
probes.a: 3a is less than 50% of the external sphincter torn; 3b is more than 50% torn; 3c includes the internal anal sphincter.

probes.q: Why must a digital rectal examination always be performed after completing a perineal repair?
probes.a: To confirm sphincter tone, ensure symmetrical reconstruction, and verify that no suture has penetrated the rectal mucosa.

probes.q: What suture materials and techniques are recommended for repairing the external anal sphincter?
probes.a: A 2-0 or 3-0 polyglactin or PDS suture using either an end-to-end interrupted mattress technique or an overlap repair.

rubric.text: Performs digital rectal examination to diagnose tear depth before repair
Accurately categorises tear into first, second, 3a/3b/3c, or fourth degree
Approximates internal and external anal sphincters separately and securely
Performs concluding rectal examination to exclude intra-luminal suture and confirm tone

teach.heading: Classification of perineal tears: the OASIS grading system
Surgical repair sequence: from deep rectal mucosa to perineal skin
teach.body:
Repair of third-degree and fourth-degree tears requires an operating theatre, regional anaesthesia, and strict asepsis.

Surgical closure proceeds strictly from deep to superficial.

First, rectal mucosa is closed with 3-0 polyglactin, followed by the internal sphincter with interrupted sutures, the external sphincter with end-to-end or overlap technique, and finally the vaginal mucosa and perineal skin.

teach.heading: Postoperative care, laxatives, antibiotics and follow-up
teach.body:
Postoperative management following third-degree or fourth-degree repair includes broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics for five days to prevent wound infection.

Stool softeners (such as lactulose) are mandatory for 10 days to prevent hard stools straining the repair.

Bulking agents are contraindicated, and pelvic floor physiotherapy is scheduled at 6 to 12 weeks.
