skill.approach.obg.instrumental_precondi.title: Preconditions and Safety Checklist for Operative Vaginal Delivery
skill.approach.obg.instrumental_precondi.oneLine: Systematic maternal, fetal, operator, and facility safety verification before forceps or vacuum
skill.approach.obg.instrumental_precondi.why: Attempting instrumental delivery without verifying all safety preconditions leads to failed operative delivery, extensive maternal genital tract destruction, uterine rupture, and fatal neonatal intracranial or subgaleal haemorrhage. A strict checklist enforces safe decision-making.

steps.text: Verify cervical dilatation: confirm by careful digital examination that the cervix is 10 cm and fully dilated with no rim palpable.
Verify membrane status: confirm that membranes are completely ruptured; perform amniotomy if membranes remain intact.
Verify presentation and position: confirm cephalic presentation, identify the exact position (occiput anterior versus posterior/transverse) and attitude.

Verify engagement and station: ensure the head is engaged (less than 1/5th palpable abdominally, leading bony skull at station +2 or lower for low forceps, or at least station 0 for mid-cavity vacuum).
Assess pelvic adequacy: confirm no clinical evidence of cephalopelvic disproportion and that the mid-pelvis and outlet are clinically adequate.
Prepare maternal conditions: catheterise the bladder completely with a sterile catheter, verify adequate regional or pudendal analgesia, and obtain informed written consent.
Verify operator competence: ensure a skilled operator is present and experienced in operative vaginal delivery and emergency caesarean section.
Verify facility readiness: ensure the operating theatre is on standby for immediate crash caesarean, neonatal resuscitation team is present, and blood products are accessible.

skill.approach.obg.instrumental_precondi.practice: Run through the FORCEPS safety mnemonic aloud with a colleague prior to simulated instrumental extraction.
pitfalls: Applying forceps or vacuum through an incompletely dilated cervix (e.g. 8 or 9 cm), causing catastrophic cervical laceration.
Attempting operative vaginal delivery when the fetal head is unengaged (more than 2/5 palpable per abdomen).
Neglecting to empty the bladder, causing bladder trauma, urinary retention, and obstructing fetal descent.

probes.q: What are the essential cervical and membrane preconditions for instrumental delivery?
probes.a: The cervix must be completely dilated (10 cm) and the membranes must be fully ruptured.

probes.q: What abdominal and pelvic station findings are required to define low forceps delivery?
probes.a: The head must be less than 1/5th palpable per abdomen and the leading bony skull must be at station +2 or lower.

probes.q: What are three absolute contraindications to ventouse (vacuum) extraction?
probes.a: Gestation less than 34 weeks, face or brow presentation, and suspected fetal bleeding diathesis.

rubric.text: Confirms complete cervical dilatation (10 cm) and ruptured membranes
Verifies fetal head engagement and station <= 1/5th per abdomen
Catheterises bladder and ensures adequate maternal analgesia and consent
Ensures operating theatre and neonatal resuscitation team are immediately available

teach.heading: The safety philosophy of operative vaginal delivery
teach.body:
Instrumental delivery is a major surgical procedure performed to expedite birth for maternal exhaustion, medical co-morbidities, or fetal distress.

Every instrumental delivery must be conducted as a trial with willingness to abandon if progress does not occur.

Strict adherence to safety preconditions prevents severe birth trauma and medicolegal catastrophe.

teach.heading: The FORCEPS safety checklist
Classification: outlet, low, and mid-cavity operative delivery
teach.body:
Operative deliveries are classified by station and rotation under RCOG and ACOG criteria.

Outlet delivery occurs when scalp is visible without parting labia and rotation is 45 degrees or less.

Low delivery requires the leading bony skull at station +2 or lower.

Mid-cavity delivery involves the head engaged above station +2 but at station zero or below, requiring a consultant obstetrician in theatre.

sources.locator: operative_obstetrics_forceps_vacuum_caesarean: Prerequisites and safety checklist for operative vaginal delivery
Green-top Guideline No. 26: Operative Vaginal Delivery

skill.exam.obg.forceps_delivery.title: Obstetric Forceps Application and Axis Traction Technique
skill.exam.obg.forceps_delivery.oneLine: Left blade first, gentle articulated locking, check application, and traction along the pelvic curve
skill.exam.obg.forceps_delivery.why: Forceps provide direct mechanical traction and rotation to deliver a compromised or delayed fetus in the second stage. Correct cephalic application prevents facial nerve palsy, skull fractures, and maternal third-degree tears, while forceful traction causes catastrophic trauma.

steps.text: Assemble the forceps blades outside the patient: articulate the blades to confirm matching pair, verify cephalic and pelvic curves, and check the locking mechanism.
Hold the left blade in the left hand using a gentle pencil grip, holding the shank vertically near maternal right groin.
Insert two to four fingers of the right hand into the left side of the vagina to protect maternal tissues and guide the blade along the fetal parietal bone.
Gently glide the left blade along the maternal right hand into the left lateral pelvis, allowing the handle to sweep downwards into the horizontal plane without force.
Hand the left blade handle to an assistant to hold steadily without rotation.
Hold the right blade in the right hand using a pencil grip, and insert the fingers of the left hand into the right side of the vagina.
Glide the right blade gently into the right lateral pelvis until it lies opposite the left blade and the handle drops horizontally.
Articulate and lock the blades gently without applying force; if they do not lock easily, disengage, re-check fetal position, and re-apply.
Perform safety check: confirm sagittal suture runs midway between shanks, posterior fontanelle lies one fingerbreadth above shanks, and fenestrations are barely palpable.
Apply intermittent traction along the pelvic curve (Pajot manoeuvre: downwards, horizontally, then upwards as head crowns), disengaging blades as the head crowns.

skill.exam.obg.forceps_delivery.normal: Blades articulate easily without resistance, sagittal suture exactly bisects shanks, head descends smoothly with first and second traction efforts, and blades disengage easily.
skill.exam.obg.forceps_delivery.abnormal: Blades refuse to lock, asymmetry of application, excessive space between blade and fetal head, lack of descent with traction, or sudden maternal pain.
skill.exam.obg.forceps_delivery.significance: Difficulty in locking blades indicates improper application or incorrect diagnosis of position; lack of descent warns of unrecognized cephalopelvic disproportion.
skill.exam.obg.forceps_delivery.practice: Practise phantom blade introduction, articulation, and curve-of-Carus traction on an obstetric mannequin.
pitfalls: Forcing the blades to articulate when they do not lock naturally, compressing the fetal skull.
Applying traction in a straight horizontal line rather than following the downward-outward-upward curve of Carus.
Applying blades when the sagittal suture is oblique or rotated without specialised rotational forceps training.

probes.q: Which forceps blade is introduced first, and with which hand is it held?
probes.a: The left blade is introduced first, held in the left hand using a pencil grip into the left side of the maternal pelvis.

probes.q: What three clinical checks confirm correct cephalic application of obstetric forceps before traction?
probes.a: Sagittal suture midway between shanks, posterior fontanelle one fingerbreadth above shanks, and fenestrations barely palpable.

probes.q: What is the direction of traction during a low forceps delivery as the head emerges?
probes.a: Downwards and backwards initially, then horizontally, and finally upwards and forwards as the head crowns and extends.

rubric.text: Assembles blades outside the body to verify matching pair and locking
Introduces left blade first using pencil grip guided by contralateral fingers
Verifies correct cephalic application before applying any traction
Applies gentle, intermittent traction synchronous with contractions along pelvic curve

teach.heading: Forceps anatomy: curves, shanks, locks and fenestrations
teach.body:
Obstetric forceps possess two blades designed to grasp the fetal head symmetrically.

Each blade has a cephalic curve matching the fetal head and a pelvic curve matching the maternal birth canal.

The shanks connect the blades to the handles, terminating in an English lock, French screw, or German sliding lock.

Fenestrated blades allow maternal scalp to bulge through, improving grip without slippage.

teach.heading: Stepwise blade application and the non-forced locking rule
teach.body:
The left blade is always introduced first because its shank lies below the right blade in the standard English lock.

The operator guides the blade over the fetal parietal bone using the opposite hand inside the vagina.

The handles must drop together and lock without any resistance.

If resistance is met, force must never be applied; remove both blades and re-examine.

teach.heading: Checking application and traction along the curve of Carus

skill.exam.obg.vacuum_delivery.title: Vacuum Extraction (Ventouse): Flexion Point Cup Placement and Safety Limits
skill.exam.obg.vacuum_delivery.oneLine: Correct cup placement on the flexion point, 360-degree sweep, and traction rules
skill.exam.obg.vacuum_delivery.why: Vacuum extraction assists delivery by promoting fetal flexion and descent. Correct placement on the flexion point maintains optimal presenting diameters and prevents detachment, while paramedian or deflexing application causes fatal subgaleal haemorrhage, scalp avulsion, and failed delivery.

steps.text: Verify all instrumental delivery preconditions: full dilatation, ruptured membranes, engaged head, empty bladder, and known position.
Select the appropriate cup: rigid metal or plastic Bird cup, soft silastic cup, or handheld OmniCup device.
Lubricate the cup and introduce it into the vagina sideways by depressing the posterior perineum with the non-dominant hand.
Place the cup squarely over the flexion point on the fetal skull: on the sagittal suture, 3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle (and 6 cm posterior to the anterior fontanelle).
Perform a 360-degree finger sweep around the circumference of the cup to ensure no maternal vaginal or cervical tissue is trapped beneath the rim.
Secure the cup against the fetal head and generate an initial negative pressure of 0.2 kg/cm2 (150 mmHg) with the vacuum pump.
Re-check the rim for trapped maternal tissue, then increase negative pressure to the therapeutic level of 0.8 kg/cm2 (600 mmHg).
Apply traction only during uterine contractions, pulling perpendicularly to the base of the cup along the pelvic axis while the mother pushes.
Observe safety stop rules: verify descent with the first pull, achieve delivery within three pulls, limit cup pop-offs to maximum two, and never exceed 20 minutes total application.
As the head crowns, release the vacuum pressure completely, detach the cup gently, and support normal delivery of the face and shoulders.

skill.exam.obg.vacuum_delivery.normal: Cup placed symmetrically over flexion point, prompt descent with first traction effort, delivery achieved within 2 or 3 pulls, and small harmless chignon resolving in 24 hours.
skill.exam.obg.vacuum_delivery.abnormal: Cup applied over anterior fontanelle (deflexing), trapped maternal cervix under rim, failure of descent on first pull, repeated pop-offs, or expanding scalp haematoma.
skill.exam.obg.vacuum_delivery.significance: Paramedian placement increases traction force and detachment; subgaleal haematoma from excessive traction can hold the infant entire blood volume, causing hypovolaemic shock and death.
skill.exam.obg.vacuum_delivery.practice: Practise identifying the flexion point and performing the 360-degree safety sweep on an obstetric skull and pelvis model.
pitfalls: Placing the cup too far anteriorly over the anterior fontanelle, which deflexes the fetal head and increases the presenting diameter to 11.5 cm.
Applying traction between contractions without maternal expulsive effort, pulling the cup off the scalp.
Continuing traction after three pulls or two pop-offs, causing massive subgaleal haemorrhage.

probes.q: Where is the flexion point located on the fetal skull for correct vacuum cup placement?
probes.a: On the sagittal suture, 3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle and about 6 cm posterior to the anterior fontanelle.

probes.q: Why must a 360-degree finger sweep be performed around the cup rim before increasing vacuum pressure?
probes.a: To ensure no maternal vaginal wall or cervical tissue is trapped under the rim, preventing severe maternal lacerations.

probes.q: What are the four strict safety rules for abandoning a vacuum extraction attempt?
probes.a: No descent with the first pull, failure to deliver in three pulls, two cup detachments (pop-offs), or application exceeding 20 minutes.

rubric.text: Places cup precisely over flexion point on sagittal suture 3 cm anterior to lambda
Performs 360-degree digital sweep to exclude trapped maternal tissue before suction
Raises vacuum pressure incrementally to 0.8 kg/cm2 and applies perpendicular traction
Adheres strictly to abandonment rules: 3 pulls, 2 pop-offs, 20 minutes maximum

teach.heading: The physics of the flexion point and pelvic descent
teach.body:
The flexion point lies on the sagittal suture 3 cm anterior to the posterior fontanelle.

Applying traction at this pivot point promotes maximum flexion of the fetal head.

Flexion replaces larger cranial diameters with the minimal suboccipitobregmatic diameter (9.5 cm), allowing the head to descend smoothly through the maternal pelvic axis.

teach.heading: Stepwise pressure generation and the 360-degree safety check
teach.body:
After placing the cup on the flexion point, the operator must sweep a gloved index finger completely around the 360-degree rim.

Trapping cervical or vaginal mucosa under the cup causes catastrophic soft-tissue tears during traction.

Vacuum is raised initially to 0.2 kg/cm2 to check seal, and then to 0.8 kg/cm2 (600 mmHg) to create the artificial caput (chignon).

teach.heading: The four safety stop rules and vacuum-associated complications

skill.ix.obg.ctg_interpretation.title: Systematic Cardiotocography (CTG) Interpretation
skill.ix.obg.ctg_interpretation.oneLine: Dr C BRAVADO framework for evaluating contractions, baseline rate, variability, accelerations, and decelerations
skill.ix.obg.ctg_interpretation.why: Misinterpreting intrapartum CTG traces is the leading cause of preventable birth asphyxia and unnecessary emergency caesareans. Following a systematic structured reading framework prevents tunnel vision and ensures objective evaluation of fetal oxygenation.
skill.ix.obg.ctg_interpretation.practice: Analyse five intrapartum CTG strips systematically using the Dr C BRAVADO worksheet.
pitfalls: Evaluating decelerations without first establishing the baseline heart rate and baseline variability.
Mistaking an early deceleration for a late deceleration due to poorly synchronized tocodynamometer tracing.
Failing to recognize a sinusoidal fetal heart rate pattern, which signifies severe fetal anaemia or feto-maternal haemorrhage.

probes.q: What are the normal baseline fetal heart rate and normal baseline variability ranges?
probes.a: Normal baseline heart rate is 110 to 160 bpm; normal baseline variability is 5 to 25 bpm.

probes.q: How do early and late decelerations differ in their timing relative to uterine contractions?
probes.a: Early decelerations mirror contractions with nadir at peak, while late decelerations start after contraction onset with nadir after peak.

probes.q: What physiological mechanism causes variable decelerations, and what CTG feature distinguishes atypical variables?
probes.a: Umbilical cord compression causes variable decelerations; atypical features include loss of shoulders, prolonged secondary rise, and reduced variability.

rubric.text: Applies systematic Dr C BRAVADO framework to read the CTG strip
Correctly measures baseline fetal heart rate (110-160) and variability (5-25)
Differentiates early, late, variable, and prolonged decelerations accurately
Formulates accurate overall assessment of fetal oxygenation status

teach.heading: The Dr C BRAVADO systematic interpretation mnemonic

rows: Direct window to fetal brain oxygenation

teach.heading: Deceleration morphology: early, late and variable
teach.body:
Decelerations are transient episodes of fetal heart rate slowing by 15 bpm or more lasting 15 seconds or more.

Early decelerations mirror the contraction and are caused by benign fetal head compression.

Late decelerations have a delayed nadir after the peak of contraction, reflecting uteroplacental insufficiency.

Variable decelerations exhibit rapid drops and recovery, reflecting cord compression.

teach.heading: Variability abnormalities and the sinusoidal trace
teach.body:
Baseline variability is the single most reliable indicator of intact fetal central nervous system oxygenation.

Variability under 5 bpm lasting more than 30 to 50 minutes indicates hypoxia, deep fetal sleep, or maternal sedatives.

A sinusoidal pattern is a smooth, regular wave repeating at 3 to 5 cycles per minute with absent variability, pathognomonic for severe fetal anaemia or feto-maternal haemorrhage.

sources.locator: cardiotocography_and_intrapartum_fetal_monitoring: Systematic CTG interpretation and feature analysis
Intrapartum care for healthy women and babies: Electronic fetal monitoring

skill.ix.obg.ctg_classification.title: Intrapartum CTG Categorisation and Intrauterine Resuscitation
skill.ix.obg.ctg_classification.oneLine: FIGO/NICE classification into Normal, Suspicious, or Pathological and intrauterine resuscitation measures
skill.ix.obg.ctg_classification.why: Recognising a pathological CTG without knowing the immediate corrective measures wastes critical minutes. Systematic categorisation guides whether to continue routine care, initiate conservative intrauterine resuscitation, perform fetal scalp sampling, or expedite immediate delivery.
skill.ix.obg.ctg_classification.practice: Rehearse the intrauterine resuscitation response drill on a labour ward simulation mannequin.
pitfalls: Administering high-flow maternal oxygen routinely when maternal oxygen saturation is already normal (> 95%), which causes uteroplacental vasoconstriction.
Leaving an oxytocin infusion running while trying to correct late decelerations or tachysystole.
Delaying decision to deliver beyond 30 minutes in the presence of an unresolving pathological CTG or prolonged bradycardia.

probes.q: What four features define an abnormal or pathological CTG trace under FIGO/NICE guidelines?
probes.a: Baseline under 100 or over 180 bpm, variability under 5 bpm for over 30 minutes, persistent late decelerations, or acute prolonged bradycardia.

probes.q: What immediate conservative measures make up intrauterine fetal resuscitation?
probes.a: Turn mother to left lateral position, stop oxytocin, give IV fluid bolus, perform vaginal examination, and consider acute tocolysis.

probes.q: What is the recommended decision-to-delivery interval for a Category 1 crash caesarean section for acute fetal distress?
probes.a: Delivery should be achieved as rapidly as possible, ideally within 30 minutes of the decision.

rubric.text: Categorises trace accurately as Normal, Suspicious, or Pathological
Stops oxytocin infusion immediately in the presence of decelerations or tachysystole
Implements intrauterine resuscitation: left lateral position, IV bolus, vaginal exam
Escalates to senior review and expedites delivery when pathological trace persists

teach.heading: The three-tier CTG classification: Normal, Suspicious, Pathological
The intrauterine resuscitation bundle
teach.body:
Intrauterine resuscitation restores uteroplacental blood flow during acute fetal compromise.

First, reposition the mother into the left lateral position to relieve aortocaval compression by the gravid uterus.

Second, immediately stop any oxytocin infusion.

Third, infuse a 500 to 1000 mL intravenous crystalloid fluid bolus.

Fourth, give acute tocolysis (terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously) if hyperstimulation persists.

teach.heading: Fetal scalp blood sampling and decision-to-delivery intervals
teach.body:
When a CTG is pathological in the first stage of labour without acute collapse, fetal scalp blood sampling measures pH or lactate.

A scalp pH 7.25 or greater is reassuring; 7.21 to 7.24 warrants repeat sampling in 30 minutes; a pH 7.20 or less indicates severe acidosis requiring immediate delivery.

A Category 1 crash section mandates delivery within 30 minutes.

Intrapartum care for healthy women and babies: Intrauterine resuscitation and fetal monitoring

skill.approach.obg.newborn_immediate_car.title: Essential Immediate Newborn Care at Birth
skill.approach.obg.newborn_immediate_car.oneLine: Drying, thermal protection, delayed cord clamping, skin-to-skin contact, vitamin K, and breast crawl
skill.approach.obg.newborn_immediate_car.why: The first minutes of life determine neonatal survival and thermal stability. Routine suctioning of vigorous infants causes reflex bradycardia and mucosal trauma, while delayed cord clamping and immediate skin-to-skin contact prevent hypothermia, neonatal anaemia, and intraventricular haemorrhage.

steps.text: Note the exact time of birth; immediately receive the infant on a pre-warmed, dry sterile towel.
Thoroughly dry the infant body and head within the first 60 seconds to prevent evaporative heat loss, discarding the wet towel immediately.
Rapidly assess breathing, crying, and muscle tone; avoid routine oral or nasal suctioning if the baby is crying and breathing vigorously.
Place the naked infant prone directly onto the mother bare chest in uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact, covering both with a dry warm blanket and cap.
Wait 1 to 3 minutes after birth before clamping the umbilical cord, supporting delayed cord clamping in vigorous infants.
Clamp the cord with a sterile cord clamp 2 to 3 cm from the infant umbilical base, apply a second clamp distal to it, and cut with sterile scissors.
Support early initiation of breastfeeding (the breast crawl) within the first hour of birth.
Administer prophylactic vitamin K1 (1 mg intramuscularly for term infants, 0.5 mg for preterm <1000g) into the anterolateral thigh, apply prophylactic eye care, and place identification bands.

skill.approach.obg.newborn_immediate_car.practice: Practise immediate drying, skin-to-skin positioning, and cord clamping on a neonatal manikin within 60 seconds.
pitfalls: Performing routine, aggressive bulb suctioning of the oropharynx in a vigorously crying newborn, causing vagal bradycardia.
Clamping the umbilical cord immediately (< 30 seconds) in a vigorous infant, depriving the newborn of placental transfusion.
Leaving the wet delivery towel wrapped around the newborn, causing rapid hypothermia and metabolic acidosis.
Forgetting intramuscular vitamin K1 administration, leading to fatal late vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

probes.q: Why is immediate drying and removal of wet linen the top priority in newborn care?
probes.a: Newborns have a large surface-area-to-mass ratio; evaporative cooling rapidly causes hypothermia, hypoglycaemia, and acidosis.

probes.q: What is the recommended timing for clamping the umbilical cord in a healthy vigorous term infant, and why?
probes.a: Between 1 and 3 minutes after birth, to allow placental transfusion which improves neonatal iron stores and haemodynamics.

probes.q: What dose and route of vitamin K1 is recommended at birth, and what condition does it prevent?
probes.a: A single dose of 1 mg intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

rubric.text: Dries newborn immediately, discards wet linen, and maintains warmth with skin-to-skin
Avoids routine suctioning in a vigorous crying infant
Delays cord clamping for 1 to 3 minutes in vigorous infants
Administers vitamin K1 IM and promotes breastfeeding initiation within one hour

teach.heading: The golden minute: drying, thermal care and breathing assessment
teach.body:
The first 60 seconds after birth (the Golden Minute) determine extrauterine adaptation.

Immediate drying with a warm towel stimulates breathing and stops evaporative heat loss.

Vigorous infants who cry immediately require no suctioning, as catheter suction induces vagal bradycardia, laryngeal spasm, and mucosal tearing.

The infant must be placed directly onto the mother chest for thermal security.

teach.heading: Delayed cord clamping and skin-to-skin physiological benefits
teach.body:
Clamping the cord between 1 and 3 minutes allows placental transfusion of 80 to 100 mL of blood, increasing newborn red cell mass and iron reserves for 6 months.

In preterm infants, it reduces mortality and intraventricular haemorrhage.

Continuous skin-to-skin contact regulates neonatal heart rate, stabilizes blood glucose, colonises the infant with maternal flora, and facilitates the breast crawl.

teach.heading: Prophylaxis at birth: vitamin K, eye care and early breastfeeding

sources.locator: newborn_resuscitation_care_long_case: Essential newborn care at birth, warmth, cord care and vitamin K
Standards for maternal and neonatal care: immediate newborn care

skill.annex.obg.apgar_score.title: Apgar Score Assessment and Clinical Interpretation
skill.annex.obg.apgar_score.oneLine: Five objective signs scored at 1 and 5 minutes to document neonatal transition
skill.annex.obg.apgar_score.why: The Apgar score provides an established, standardised clinical shorthand to record the infant physiological transition after birth and evaluate response to resuscitation. Misunderstanding the score leads to delaying life-saving bag-mask ventilation while waiting to calculate the 1-minute score.
skill.annex.obg.apgar_score.practice: Score simulated newborn video vignettes at 1 and 5 minutes, documenting parameters accurately.
pitfalls: Waiting until 1 minute has elapsed to calculate the Apgar score before starting resuscitation in an apnoeic newborn.
Scoring peripheral cyanosis (acrocyanosis) as 0 instead of 1 in an infant with a pink trunk and blue hands.
Using the Apgar score alone to diagnose birth asphyxia without umbilical cord arterial blood gas analysis.

probes.q: What five physiological parameters are assessed in the Apgar score?
probes.a: Appearance (colour), Pulse (heart rate), Grimace (reflex response), Activity (muscle tone), and Respiration.

probes.q: How is an Apgar score interpreted at 1 minute and 5 minutes?
probes.a: 7 to 10 is normal transition, 4 to 6 indicates moderate depression needing resuscitation, and 0 to 3 is severe depression.

probes.q: Should neonatal resuscitation be delayed until the 1-minute Apgar score is calculated?
probes.a: Never. If the infant is apnoeic or heart rate is under 100, resuscitation begins immediately within the first 60 seconds.

rubric.text: Accurately scores all five Apgar components at 1 and 5 minutes
Stratifies score correctly into normal (7-10), moderate (4-6), or severe (0-3)
Initiates resuscitation immediately if apnoeic without waiting for 1-minute score

teach.heading: The Apgar scoring matrix: five physiological signs
Score interpretation and clinical resuscitation action
teach.body:
The score is recorded at 1 minute and 5 minutes, continuing every 5 minutes up to 20 minutes if the score remains under 7.

A score of 7 to 10 is normal.

A score of 4 to 6 indicates moderate depression requiring airway clearance and bag-mask positive pressure ventilation.

A score of 0 to 3 signifies severe depression requiring immediate advanced resuscitation including intubation and chest compressions.

teach.heading: Limitations of the Apgar score and medicolegal realities
teach.body:
The Apgar score was designed to evaluate clinical status, not to predict long-term neurological outcome or diagnose intrapartum asphyxia.

A low 1-minute score is common in healthy preterm infants due to physiological immaturity of tone and respiratory drive.

Diagnosing hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy requires umbilical cord arterial blood gas pH under 7.00, base deficit 12 mmol/L or worse, and multi-organ dysfunction.

skill.exam.obg.newborn_exam.title: Initial Newborn Physical Examination and Anomaly Screening
skill.exam.obg.newborn_exam.oneLine: Systematic head-to-toe clinical assessment within the first 24 hours of birth
skill.exam.obg.newborn_exam.why: A structured newborn examination detects congenital malformations, birth trauma, and signs of cardiorespiratory failure before discharge. Missing an imperforate anus, tracheo-oesophageal fistula, or congenital heart defect leads to rapid neonatal collapse.

steps.text: Examine under warm lighting in the presence of parents, checking general appearance, posture (flexed), and cry.
Measure vital signs: heart rate (120 to 160 bpm), respiratory rate (40 to 60 breaths/min), and axillary temperature (36.5 to 37.5 degrees C).
Inspect the head: palpate sutures and fontanelles, differentiating caput succedaneum from cephalhaematoma.
Inspect the face, eyes, and palate: inspect for facial symmetry, cleft lip, and palpate the hard and soft palate with a clean gloved finger for clefts.
Auscultate the chest: assess symmetry of air entry, absence of grunting or retractions, and check heart sounds and murmurs.
Palpate the abdomen: verify soft, non-distended contour, palpate liver edge, and inspect umbilical stump for two arteries and one vein.
Inspect genitalia: in males confirm bilateral descended testes in rugated scrotum and urethral meatus at tip; in females verify labia majora covering minora.
Check anal patency: inspect anus for normal anatomical position and confirm passage of meconium within 24 hours.
Examine the back and spine: run finger along vertebral column to exclude meningomyelocele, hairy tuft, or deep sacral pit.
Test musculoskeletal and neonatal reflexes: perform Barlow and Ortolani tests for hip instability, check digits for polydactyly, and elicit Moro, grasp, and suck reflexes.

skill.exam.obg.newborn_exam.normal: Active flexed posture, pink colour, heart rate 120-160, respiratory rate 40-60, soft fontanelles, intact palate, 3-vessel umbilical cord, patent anus, stable hips, and intact neonatal reflexes.
skill.exam.obg.newborn_exam.abnormal: Respiratory grunting, central cyanosis, cleft palate, single umbilical artery, imperforate anus, dislocatable hip clunk, spinal midline defect, or absent Moro reflex.
skill.exam.obg.newborn_exam.significance: Single umbilical artery prompts renal ultrasound screening; dislocatable hip requires prompt Pavlik harness splinting to prevent permanent hip dysplasia.
skill.exam.obg.newborn_exam.practice: Perform a systematic head-to-toe examination on a neonatal training simulator, vocalising all normal and abnormal findings.
pitfalls: Failing to visually inspect and palpate the roof of the mouth, missing an isolated cleft of the soft palate.
Assuming an anus is patent based on visual appearance without confirming the passage of meconium or gentle inspection.
Omission of hip screening with Barlow and Ortolani manoeuvres.

probes.q: What are the normal ranges for heart rate, respiratory rate, and temperature in a healthy term newborn?
probes.a: Heart rate 120 to 160 bpm, respiratory rate 40 to 60 breaths per minute, axillary temperature 36.5 to 37.5 degrees Celsius.

probes.q: How do you distinguish caput succedaneum from cephalhaematoma on palpation of the newborn skull?
probes.a: Caput succedaneum crosses suture lines and is present at birth, while cephalhaematoma is restricted by suture lines and appears hours later.

probes.q: What do the Barlow and Ortolani tests evaluate in the newborn?
probes.a: Developmental dysplasia of the hip: Barlow tests if a stable hip can be dislocated posteriorly, Ortolani tests if a dislocated hip can be reduced.

rubric.text: Measures newborn vitals accurately and assesses posture, colour, and cry
Palpates fontanelles, excludes skull birth trauma, and palpates palate
Verifies 3-vessel umbilical cord and checks anal patency and meconium
Screens hips with Barlow and Ortolani tests and inspects entire spine

teach.heading: Systematic head-to-toe examination sequence
teach.body:
The neonatal examination should be conducted within 24 hours of birth in a warm, draught-free room.

Begin with quiet observations (respiratory pattern, colour, posture) before disturbing the baby with auscultation and palpation.

Normal term posture is symmetrical flexion of all four limbs with spontaneous purposeful movements and a lusty cry.

teach.heading: Birth trauma identification: scalp, clavicle and nerves
Screening for critical anomalies: palate, hips, heart and anus
teach.body:
Always palpate the palate directly with a gloved little finger, as visual inspection misses submucous or posterior clefts.

Examine the umbilical cord cross-section to confirm two muscular arteries and one thin-walled vein.

Palpate femoral pulses to exclude aortic coarctation, and perform Barlow and Ortolani tests to detect developmental hip dysplasia early.

skill.exam.obg.puerperal_exam.title: Postnatal Physical Examination and Uterine Involution
skill.exam.obg.puerperal_exam.oneLine: BUBBLE-HE clinical bedside examination: breasts, fundus, bladder, lochia, perineum, and calf veins
skill.exam.obg.puerperal_exam.why: The puerperium is a high-risk period for fatal postpartum haemorrhage, puerperal sepsis, and pulmonary embolism. Daily systematic physical examination detects uterine subinvolution, infected lochia, and calf vein thrombosis before maternal septic shock or thromboembolic collapse develops.

steps.text: Greet the mother, ensure privacy, ask her to empty her bladder, and position her supine with head supported and legs extended.
Assess general appearance, maternal mood, and measure vital signs: temperature, blood pressure, pulse, and respiratory rate.
Examine the breasts: inspect for symmetrical enlargement, engorgement, nipple cracks or fissures, and palpate for localized tenderness or heat (mastitis).
Position examining hands on the abdomen and palpate the uterine fundus: locate the fundus relative to the umbilicus using fingerbreadths.
Measure fundal height: verify that the fundus descends approximately 1 cm (one fingerbreadth) per day, becoming non-palpable abdominally by day 10 to 14.
Assess uterine consistency and tenderness: confirm the uterus is firm and well-contracted; check for exquisite tenderness suggesting endometritis.
Assess bladder and bowel function: check for suprapubic fullness indicating urinary retention, and inquire about spontaneous voiding and flatus.
Inspect lochia on the perineal pad: evaluate volume, colour (rubra days 1 to 4, serosa days 5 to 9, alba days 10 to 15+), and smell (foul odour confirms sepsis).
Examine the perineum and episiotomy site: place woman in lateral position, inspect for REEDA criteria (Redness, Oedema, Ecchymosis, Discharge, Approximation), and check for haematoma.
Inspect the lower limbs: look for unilateral calf swelling, erythema, localized calf tenderness, or palpable cord-like veins suggesting deep vein thrombosis.

skill.exam.obg.puerperal_exam.normal: Afebrile, normal vitals, soft non-tender breasts, firm well-contracted uterus descending 1 fingerbreadth daily, non-offensive physiological lochia, healing perineum, and non-tender calf veins.
skill.exam.obg.puerperal_exam.abnormal: Fever >= 38 C, boggy tender subinvoluted uterus, foul-smelling or excessively heavy lochia, perineal wound breakdown or haematoma, and unilateral calf swelling or tenderness.
skill.exam.obg.puerperal_exam.significance: A tender, boggy uterus with foul lochia confirms puerperal endometritis requiring parenteral antibiotics; unilateral calf tenderness indicates deep vein thrombosis requiring therapeutic anticoagulation.
skill.exam.obg.puerperal_exam.practice: Practise measuring fundal involution against postpartum day milestones on simulation mannequins.
pitfalls: Palpating the uterine fundus with a full bladder, which displaces the uterus upwards and to the right, mimicking subinvolution.
Overlooking foul-smelling lochia because the pad was not directly inspected and smelled.
Performing vigorous dorsiflexion of the foot (Homan sign), which can dislodge a deep venous clot and cause fatal pulmonary embolism.

probes.q: What is the normal rate of uterine fundal involution in the puerperium, and when does it become non-palpable?
probes.a: The fundus descends about 1 cm or one fingerbreadth daily, becoming non-palpable abdominally by 10 to 14 days postpartum.

probes.q: Describe the normal progression of lochia in the postpartum period.
probes.a: Lochia rubra (red, days 1-4), lochia serosa (pinkish-brown, days 5-9), and lochia alba (yellowish-white, days 10-15 up to 3-4 weeks).

probes.q: What clinical triad strongly indicates puerperal endometritis on physical examination?
probes.a: Maternal fever, a tender and subinvoluted uterus, and offensive or foul-smelling lochia.

rubric.text: Checks vital signs and examines breasts for engorgement, nipple cracks, or mastitis
Accurately locates uterine fundus, assesses firm tone, and excludes tenderness
Directly inspects lochia colour and odour and evaluates perineal healing
Examines calves for unilateral swelling, warmth, and deep vein thrombosis signs

teach.heading: The physiology of myometrial involution and fundal landmarks
teach.body:
Involution is the physiological process whereby the postpartum uterus returns from approximately 1000 grams immediately post-delivery to its pre-pregnant weight of 60 grams by six weeks.

Immediately after delivery, the fundus is palpable midway between the umbilicus and symphysis pubis, rising to umbilicus level within 12 hours.

It descends by one fingerbreadth (1 cm) daily, sinking into the true pelvis by day 12.

teach.heading: Lochia characteristics across the puerperium
The BUBBLE-HE systematic postnatal examination framework
teach.body:
The BUBBLE-HE mnemonic provides a reliable bedside examination sequence.

Assess Breasts (soft, filling, engorged, nipple cracks), Uterus (firmness, fundal height, tenderness), Bladder (spontaneous voiding, retention), Bowel (flatus, distension), Lochia (colour, odour, clots), Episiotomy (REEDA score), Homan/Legs (unilateral calf pain, DVT signs), and Emotional status (maternal-infant bonding, blues).

skill.hx.obg.puerperal_complications.title: Postpartum Danger Signs and Puerperal Morbidity History
skill.hx.obg.puerperal_complications.oneLine: Screening for puerperal sepsis, secondary PPH, venous thromboembolism, and postpartum depression
skill.hx.obg.puerperal_complications.why: Most maternal deaths occur in the first six weeks following delivery. Structured history taking identifies early symptoms of life-threatening puerperal sepsis, secondary postpartum haemorrhage, deep vein thrombosis, and severe postnatal depression before irreversible morbidity occurs.

asks.text: Have you had any fever, shivering, or chills since giving birth? Ask specifically about temperature spikes occurring after the first 24 hours.
How is your vaginal bleeding? Ask if bleeding has suddenly increased in volume, turned bright red, contains large clots, or requires changing more than one soaked pad an hour.
Have you noticed any foul or bad smell from your vaginal discharge (lochia), or worsening pain in your lower tummy?
Do you have any pain, redness, or hard lumps in your breasts, or pain when feeding the baby? Ask whether nipples are cracked or bleeding.
Do you have any pain, swelling, or warmth in one of your calves or legs, or any sudden shortness of breath or chest pain?
How have you been feeling emotionally? Ask about crying spells, severe exhaustion, feeling unable to cope, lack of interest in the baby, or scary thoughts of harming herself or the baby.

skill.hx.obg.puerperal_complications.practice: Role-play taking a postnatal history from a mother on day 7 with fever and foul lochia, triaging for immediate hospital admission.
pitfalls: Dismissing persistent sadness and crying spells beyond day 10 as normal baby blues, missing major postpartum depression.
Failing to ask specifically about calf pain or unilateral leg swelling in a woman complaining of mild breathlessness.
Attributing sudden heavy bleeding on day 8 to a normal menstrual period rather than secondary postpartum haemorrhage.

probes.q: What defines puerperal pyrexia, and what is its leading cause?
probes.a: A temperature of 38.0 C or higher on any two of the first 10 days postpartum excluding the first 24 hours; leading cause is genital tract infection (endometritis).

probes.q: What is secondary postpartum haemorrhage, and what are its two most common causes?
probes.a: Excessive vaginal bleeding occurring between 24 hours and 6 to 12 weeks postpartum; commonest causes are retained placental fragments and endometritis.

probes.q: How do postpartum blues differ from postpartum depression in onset and duration?
probes.a: Blues peak around day 3 to 5 and resolve by day 10 without impairing maternal functioning; depression develops over weeks and causes persistent functional impairment.

rubric.text: Asks systematically about fever, chills, lower abdominal pain, and foul lochia
Quantifies bleeding volume, colour, and clots to screen for secondary PPH
Screens for unilateral calf pain, leg swelling, and sudden breathlessness
Screens for postpartum blues, depression, bonding difficulties, and red flags

teach.heading: The puerperal pyrexia diagnostic framework: the five Ws
teach.body:
Puerperal pyrexia is defined as a temperature of 38.0 degrees C or higher on any two of the first 10 days postpartum, excluding the initial 24 hours.

Investigate using the classic five Ws framework: Wind (atelectasis, pneumonia), Water (urinary tract infection), Womb (endometritis), Wound (episiotomy breakdown or caesarean surgical site infection), and Walking (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism).

teach.heading: Secondary postpartum haemorrhage and breast complications
teach.body:
Secondary PPH occurs between 24 hours and 6 to 12 weeks postpartum.

It is caused by retained placental cotyledons, subinvolution of the placental site, or endometritis.

Breast complications range from physiological engorgement (bilateral generalized tenderness resolving with feeding) to acute bacterial mastitis (unilateral wedge-shaped erythema with fever, usually Staphylococcus aureus) and fluctuant breast abscess.

teach.heading: Postnatal mental health triage: blues, depression and psychosis

skill.exam.obg.prolapse_popq.title: Pelvic organ prolapse staging and POP-Q examination
skill.exam.obg.prolapse_popq.oneLine: Systematic compartmental evaluation of vaginal descent at maximal Valsalva
skill.exam.obg.prolapse_popq.why: Pelvic organ prolapse causes urinary retention, recurrent infections, defecatory dysfunction, and severe quality of life impairment. Staging with the Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification system replaces subjective grades with reproducible centimetres relative to the hymen, directing whether conservative pessary care, anterior or posterior repair, apical suspension, or hysterectomy is indicated.

steps.text: Place the patient in dorsal lithotomy or left lateral position with an empty bladder and adequate illumination, explaining every step and ensuring a female chaperone is present.
Inspect the resting vulva and perineum for visible mucosal protrusion, ulceration, or excoriation before introducing any instrument.
Instruct the patient to perform a sustained, maximal Valsalva strain or vigorous cough to demonstrate the maximum extent of descent of all compartments.

Insert a single-blade Sims speculum against the posterior vaginal wall to retract it, exposing the anterior wall to evaluate point Aa (3 cm proximal to external urethral meatus) and point Ba (most dependent point of anterior wall).
Turn or re-insert the Sims speculum anteriorly to retract the anterior wall, measuring posterior points Ap (3 cm proximal to hymen) and Bp (most dependent point of posterior wall).
Identify apical descent at maximal strain by measuring point C (most distal edge of cervix or vaginal vault cuff) and point D (posterior fornix in women with a uterus).

Measure the three external distances in centimetres: genital hiatus (gh) from external urethral meatus to posterior hymen, perineal body (pb) from posterior hymen to mid-anal aperture, and total vaginal length (tvl) with prolapse manually reduced.

skill.exam.obg.prolapse_popq.normal: All six anatomical points (Aa, Ba, Ap, Bp) remain at -3 cm; points C and D remain high in the upper pelvis near -tvl; no protrusion beyond the hymenal ring on maximal Valsalva strain.
skill.exam.obg.prolapse_popq.abnormal: Descent of vaginal walls or cervix toward or beyond the hymen (points Aa, Ba, Ap, Bp, C, or D reaching between -1 cm and greater than +1 cm), widened genital hiatus (>4 cm), or deficient perineal body (<2 cm).
skill.exam.obg.prolapse_popq.significance: Defines prolapse compartment and stage: anterior wall descent (cystocele), apical descent (uterine prolapse or vault prolapse), and posterior wall descent (rectocele or enterocele), determining suitability for pelvic floor physiotherapy, pessaries, or surgical reconstruction.
skill.exam.obg.prolapse_popq.practice: Rehearse measuring all nine POP-Q parameters on a pelvic simulator and derive the stage from 0 to IV.
pitfalls: Examining only at rest without asking the patient to perform a sustained maximal Valsalva manoeuvre.
Failing to use a single-blade Sims speculum to isolate the anterior, apical, and posterior compartments sequentially.
Confusing point C (cervix or vaginal vault) with point D (posterior fornix in women with a uterus).

probes.q: What anatomical landmark serves as the zero reference plane in the POP-Q staging system?
probes.a: The hymenal ring or hymen serves as the fixed reference plane of zero.

probes.q: How is stage III pelvic organ prolapse distinguished from stage IV procidentia in POP-Q?
probes.a: In stage III the most distal part is more than 1 cm beyond the hymen but less than total vaginal length minus 2 cm; in stage IV complete eversion extends to at least total vaginal length minus 2 cm.

probes.q: Why is point D omitted in the POP-Q examination of a woman who has previously undergone total hysterectomy?
probes.a: Point D represents the posterior fornix and pouch of Douglas attachment to the cervix; after total hysterectomy there is no cervix or pouch of Douglas attachment.

rubric.text: Asks patient to perform maximal Valsalva or cough while inspecting introitus
Uses Sims speculum blade to isolate anterior, posterior, and apical compartments separately
Measures descent of landmarks in centimetres relative to the hymenal ring
Assigns POP-Q stage correctly based on the leading edge of prolapse

teach.heading: Principles of the Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification system
teach.body:
POP-Q is the international standardised system for quantifying pelvic organ prolapse. It measures six defined anatomical points and three landmark distances in centimetres relative to the hymen.

The hymen represents the reference plane of zero. Points proximal to the hymen inside the vagina receive negative numbers; points distal to the hymen outside the introitus receive positive numbers.

teach.heading: The six anatomical points and three landmarks

rows: Anterior wall, 3 cm proximal to urethral meatus
Most dependent leading edge of anterior wall
Most distal edge of cervix or vaginal cuff

teach.heading: POP-Q stages 0 to IV defined by the leading edge
teach.body:
Stage 0: no prolapse; points Aa, Ba, Ap, Bp are -3 cm; C and D are between -tvl and -(tvl - 2) cm.

Stage I: the most distal portion of prolapse is >1 cm above the hymen (<-1 cm).

Stage II: the leading edge is between 1 cm above and 1 cm below the hymen (-1 cm to +1 cm).

Stage III: leading edge is >1 cm beyond hymen but <(tvl - 2) cm.

Stage IV: complete eversion; leading edge extends to at least (tvl - 2) cm.

skill.annex.obg.popq_system.title: POP-Q Nine-Point Staging Grid and Stage Criteria
skill.annex.obg.popq_system.oneLine: The 3 by 3 measurement grid and stage definitions for pelvic organ prolapse
skill.annex.obg.popq_system.why: Descriptive terms such as mild or severe cystocele lack inter-observer reliability. The POP-Q 3x3 grid provides a precise anatomical record that allows clinicians to compare pre-operative and post-operative results and track prolapse progression objectively.
skill.annex.obg.popq_system.practice: Fill out the 3 by 3 POP-Q grid for a clinical vignette of third-degree uterine descent with cystocele.
pitfalls: Mixing positive and negative signs when recording distances relative to the hymen.
Measuring genital hiatus and perineal body while the patient is resting rather than at maximal straining.
Recording point D in a post-hysterectomy patient who has no cervix or pouch of Douglas attachment.

probes.q: What are the three columns and rows in the POP-Q 3x3 documentation grid?
probes.a: Top row has Aa, Ba, C; middle row has gh, pb, tvl; bottom row has Ap, Bp, D.

probes.q: What do the measurements gh and pb represent in the POP-Q grid?
probes.a: gh is genital hiatus from middle of external urethral meatus to posterior midline hymen; pb is perineal body from posterior hymen to mid-anal aperture.

probes.q: If a woman has total vaginal length of 8 cm and point C is at +7 cm, what POP-Q stage is present?
probes.a: Stage IV procidentia, because the leading edge exceeds total vaginal length minus 2 cm which is 6 cm.

rubric.text: Records all 9 grid parameters in centimetres accurately
Applies correct negative and positive signs relative to the hymen
Derives the correct stage 0 through IV from the leading edge coordinate

teach.heading: The 3 by 3 POP-Q documentation grid
Diagnostic criteria for POP-Q clinical stages
teach.body:
Stage 0: Aa, Ba, Ap, Bp all -3 cm, C or D <= -(tvl - 2) cm.

Stage I: Leading edge < -1 cm (more than 1 cm above hymen).

Stage II: Leading edge between -1 cm and +1 cm (within 1 cm of hymen).

Stage III: Leading edge > +1 cm but < +(tvl - 2) cm.

Stage IV: Complete eversion; leading edge >= +(tvl - 2) cm.

skill.exam.obg.gynae_abdominal.title: Gynaecological abdominal examination and pelvic mass evaluation
skill.exam.obg.gynae_abdominal.oneLine: Inspect, palpate lower abdomen, determine pelvic origin, and rule out ascites
skill.exam.obg.gynae_abdominal.why: Pelvic tumours such as large uterine fibroids, ovarian cysts, and pelvic inflammatory masses frequently present as abdominal swellings. Systematic abdominal examination determines whether a mass arises from the pelvis, differentiates uterine from ovarian origin, and identifies ascites or malignant metastasis.

steps.text: Ensure the patient has completely emptied her urinary bladder immediately before examination, positioning her comfortably supine with knees slightly bent and abdomen exposed from xiphisternum to pubic symphysis.
Inspect the abdominal contour for localized asymmetry, distension, striae, dilated abdominal veins, surgical scars, and movement of swellings with respiration.
Perform gentle superficial palpation over all nine abdominal regions, noting areas of muscular guarding, rigidity, or tenderness.
Palpate deeply from the epigastrium downwards into the hypogastrium to define the upper border, lateral margins, surface texture, consistency, and tenderness of any abdominal swelling.
Attempt to palpate the lower border of the mass just above the pubic symphysis: inability to get fingers below the lower border confirms the mass arises from the pelvic cavity.
Assess mobility of the mass in transverse and vertical planes, noting whether moving the mass elicits discomfort or transmits motion to the cervix.
Percuss systematically over the dome of the mass and in both flanks: central dullness with resonant flanks suggests an encapsulated mass or cyst; flank dullness with central tympany suggests ascites.
Perform tests for shifting dullness and fluid thrill if free abdominal fluid is suspected, and auscultate over the mass for bowel sounds or a vascular uterine souffle.

skill.exam.obg.gynae_abdominal.normal: Abdomen flat or soft, no palpable masses or organomegaly, resonant on percussion, normal bowel sounds, no tenderness, no shifting dullness.
skill.exam.obg.gynae_abdominal.abnormal: Palpable hypogastric or adnexal mass, inability to get fingers below the lower border, dullness over mass, shifting dullness in flanks, tenderness or rigidity.
skill.exam.obg.gynae_abdominal.significance: Differentiates uterine enlargement (central, firm, mobile with cervix, fingers cannot get below) from ovarian neoplasms (often cystic or firm, may be unilateral, mobile, distinct sulcus from uterus), full urinary bladder, or mesenteric cysts.
skill.exam.obg.gynae_abdominal.practice: Palpate lower abdomen on a torso model to demonstrate the inability to get below the lower border of a pelvic-abdominal mass.
pitfalls: Examining a patient with a full bladder, which can mimic a large cystic pelvic mass.
Failing to start palpation at the xiphisternum and moving downwards, missing the upper border of large pelvic masses.
Confusing the dullness of a giant ovarian cyst (central dullness, resonant flanks) with ascites (central tympany, dull flanks).

probes.q: What clinical sign confirms that an abdominal mass arises from the pelvic cavity?
probes.a: The examiner cannot get fingers below the lower border of the mass above the pubic symphysis.

probes.q: How does percussion differentiate a giant ovarian cyst from general peritoneal ascites?
probes.a: A giant ovarian cyst produces central dullness with resonant flanks; free ascites produces central periumbilical resonance with dull flanks and shifting dullness.

probes.q: What physical findings distinguish a large uterine fibroid from an ovarian mass on abdominal-pelvic examination?
probes.a: A fibroid is typically firm, central, moves with the cervix on bimanual palpation, and has no separating groove; an ovarian mass is often adnexal or cystic, moves independently of the cervix, and exhibits a palpable groove between mass and uterus.

rubric.text: Confirms bladder is emptied before palpating the lower abdomen
Attempts to palpate below the lower border to determine pelvic origin
Systematically assesses size, consistency, mobility, surface, and tenderness
Percusses across abdomen to distinguish central tumour dullness from flank ascites

teach.heading: Determining whether an abdominal mass arises from the pelvis
teach.body:
A mass arising from the pelvic cavity expands upwards into the abdomen as its volume increases.

The key diagnostic physical sign of pelvic origin is the inability to get fingers below the lower edge of the mass above the pubic symphysis.

Always ensure the urinary bladder is emptied completely before examination, as an overdistended bladder is the most frequent mimic of a cystic pelvic mass.

teach.heading: Differentiating a giant ovarian cyst from ascites
Differentiating uterine fibroid from ovarian neoplasm
teach.body:
Uterine leiomyomas are firm to hard, well-circumscribed, often nodular, situated centrally in the hypogastrium, and move synchronously with the cervix on bimanual examination.

Ovarian masses are commonly cystic or variable in consistency, lie lateral to or in the pouch of Douglas, can be moved independently of the cervix, and often feature a palpable notch or groove between the mass and the uterine fundus.

skill.exam.obg.breast_exam.title: Clinical breast examination in women
skill.exam.obg.breast_exam.oneLine: Inspect in multiple postures and systematically palpate all four quadrants, axilla, and supraclavicular fossae
skill.exam.obg.breast_exam.why: Breast lumps, nipple discharge, and skin changes are frequent presentations in gynaecological practice. Clinical breast examination detects palpable breast malignancies, differentiates benign fibroadenomas and cysts from invasive carcinomas, and forms the first pillar of the mandatory triple assessment.

steps.text: Explain the examination clearly, obtain informed verbal consent, provide a private environment, and ensure a female chaperone is present throughout.
Inspect both breasts with the patient sitting upright and arms relaxed at her sides, observing symmetry, contour, size, skin changes (erythema, edema, peau d orange), and nipple shape or inversion.
Ask her to raise both arms above her head, watching for subtle skin dimpling, tethering, or fixation of tissue that becomes apparent as the breasts lift.
Instruct her to press both hands firmly on her hips while leaning slightly forward, contracting the pectoralis major muscles to accentuate deep tethering.
Position her comfortably supine with the ipsilateral hand placed behind her head, flattening the breast tissue evenly against the thoracic cage.

Palpate systematically using the finger pads of the middle three fingers with light, medium, and deep pressure in a vertical strip or circular pattern covering all four quadrants and the axillary tail of Spence.
Palpate the nipple-areolar complex gently for subareolar thickening, and inspect for spontaneous or expressible nipple discharge without forceful squeezing.

Examine the axillary lymph nodes with the patient seated, supporting her relaxed forearm with one hand while systematically palpating the anterior, central, posterior, lateral, and apical groups, followed by the supraclavicular fossae.

skill.exam.obg.breast_exam.normal: Symmetrical breasts, smooth contour, no skin dimpling or tethering, nipples everted without discharge, supple breast tissue without dominant discrete lump, no axillary or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
skill.exam.obg.breast_exam.abnormal: Discrete hard irregular lump, skin dimpling, tethering to pectoral fascia, peau d orange, nipple retraction, spontaneous bloody or serous nipple discharge, fixed hard axillary lymph nodes.
skill.exam.obg.breast_exam.significance: Essential component of gynaecological well-woman examination and workup of palpable mass; positive findings mandate complete triple assessment (clinical exam, bilateral mammography or ultrasound, core needle biopsy).
skill.exam.obg.breast_exam.practice: Practise systematic vertical strip breast palpation on a breast model to detect simulated deep and superficial lumps.
pitfalls: Examining only in the seated position without palpating the flattened breast in the supine position.
Missing the axillary tail of Spence and the axillary lymph node groups.
Pinching breast tissue between the fingers rather than compressing it flat against the chest wall.

probes.q: Why is the patient asked to press her hands firmly against her hips during breast inspection?
probes.a: It contracts the pectoralis major muscle, accentuating skin tethering or dimpling caused by an underlying carcinoma.

probes.q: What three modalities comprise the triple assessment for any suspicious breast lesion?
probes.a: Clinical breast examination, imaging with mammography or ultrasound, and histopathology via core needle biopsy.

probes.q: What physical characteristics distinguish a benign fibroadenoma from an invasive breast carcinoma on palpation?
probes.a: A fibroadenoma is firm, smooth, well-defined, painless, and highly mobile like a breast mouse; a carcinoma is hard, irregular, poorly circumscribed, fixed to skin or pectoral fascia, and often associated with lymphadenopathy.

rubric.text: Inspects breasts in sitting position with arms raised and hands pressed on hips
Palpates systematically in supine position with ipsilateral hand behind head
Uses finger pads of three middle fingers compressing tissue against ribs
Palpates all axillary lymph node stations supporting the relaxed arm

teach.heading: The structural principles of clinical breast examination
teach.body:
Clinical breast examination evaluates the parenchyma, skin envelope, and regional lymphatic basins.

Palpation must cover the entire rectangular area from the clavicle superiorly to the inframammary fold inferiorly, and from the midsternal line medially to the midaxillary line laterally, including the axillary tail of Spence.

Tissue must be compressed gently against the thoracic cage using the finger pads, never pinched between fingers.

teach.heading: The triple assessment protocol for palpable breast lumps
Axillary lymph node examination technique
teach.body:
To examine the left axilla, support the patient's left forearm with your left hand to completely relax her shoulder girdle and pectoral muscles.

Use your right fingertips to explore the axillary apex, sweeping down along the chest wall (central group), behind the anterior pectoral fold (pectoral group), along the latissimus dorsi (subscapular group), and along the upper humerus (lateral group).

Repeat on the right side and finish by examining the supraclavicular fossae.

WHO position paper on mammography screening and clinical breast examination

skill.exam.obg.endometrial_sampling.title: Outpatient endometrial sampling using Pipelle suction curette
skill.exam.obg.endometrial_sampling.oneLine: Flexible manual suction curette sampling of endometrium without cervical dilatation
skill.exam.obg.endometrial_sampling.why: Abnormal uterine bleeding in perimenopausal women and any postmenopausal bleeding carries a significant risk of endometrial hyperplasia and adenocarcinoma. Outpatient Pipelle sampling provides tissue diagnosis with 99 percent sensitivity for endometrial carcinoma, avoiding general anaesthesia and hospitalisation.

steps.text: Confirm the patient is not pregnant, explain the procedure and temporary cramping sensation, and perform a bimanual pelvic examination to assess uterine size, version, and flexion.

Insert a Cusco bivalve speculum to expose the cervix, clean the ectocervix and external os with aqueous antiseptic solution, and apply a single-tooth tenaculum to the anterior lip if counter-traction is required.

Introduce the flexible polypropylene Pipelle gently through the external and internal cervical os until resistance is felt at the uterine fundus, noting the uterine cavity length against the outer sheath markings.
Stabilise the outer sheath at the external os and withdraw the internal plunger or piston smoothly and completely to create negative pressure suction within the lumen.
Rotate the Pipelle sheath 360 degrees continuously while gently moving it back and forth between the fundus and internal os three to four times, drawing tissue strips into the cannula.
Withdraw the Pipelle from the uterus, cut off the distal sampling tip or depress the plunger to express the tissue specimen into a container of 10 percent neutral buffered formalin.
Remove the tenaculum and speculum, inspect the cervix for haemostasis, and ensure the patient is comfortable before discharge.

skill.exam.obg.endometrial_sampling.normal: Smooth passage through internal os, thin uniform tissue strips, histopathology confirms proliferative or secretory endometrium or atrophic endometrium.
skill.exam.obg.endometrial_sampling.abnormal: Inability to negotiate stenotic internal os, copious friable necrotic tissue, histopathology demonstrates atypical hyperplasia or endometrial adenocarcinoma.
skill.exam.obg.endometrial_sampling.significance: First-line investigation for postmenopausal bleeding (endometrial thickness >4 mm on transvaginal ultrasound) and abnormal uterine bleeding in women aged >=40-45 years or with risk factors (PCOS, obesity, tamoxifen, Lynch syndrome).
skill.exam.obg.endometrial_sampling.practice: Practise Pipelle insertion, piston withdrawal to create vacuum, and 360-degree rotation on a uterine model.
pitfalls: Failing to withdraw the internal piston fully, resulting in inadequate vacuum and an insufficient tissue sample.
Moving the Pipelle only in one plane rather than rotating it 360 degrees to sample the entire cavity.
Attempting Pipelle sampling in a patient with acute pelvic infection or suspected pregnancy.

probes.q: What clinical threshold on transvaginal ultrasound in a postmenopausal woman mandates endometrial sampling?
probes.a: Endometrial thickness greater than 4 mm or heterogeneous irregular endometrium.

probes.q: How does the Pipelle curette generate the negative pressure required to draw endometrial tissue into its lumen?
probes.a: The inner plunger or piston is withdrawn completely while the device tip rests at the fundus, creating a vacuum.

probes.q: If a Pipelle biopsy yields insufficient tissue in a postmenopausal woman with recurrent bleeding and thickened endometrium, what is the next step?
probes.a: Hysteroscopy with directed biopsy or fractional curettage, because focal lesions such as polyps or focal carcinomas can be missed by blind aspiration.

rubric.text: Assesses uterine size and position before inserting Pipelle
Withdraws piston fully to generate reliable suction before curettage
Rotates curette 360 degrees while traversing cavity between fundus and os
Transfers tissue strip immediately into 10 percent neutral buffered formalin

teach.heading: Indications and patient selection for outpatient endometrial biopsy
teach.body:
Outpatient Pipelle sampling is the gold standard initial tissue test for abnormal uterine bleeding.

Indications include postmenopausal bleeding with endometrial thickness exceeding 4 mm, abnormal uterine bleeding in women aged 40 to 45 years or older, and younger women with persistent bleeding and risk factors such as obesity, chronic anovulation in polycystic ovary syndrome, or tamoxifen therapy.

teach.heading: Steps of Pipelle aspiration curettage
teach.body:
Visualise the cervix with a bivalve Cusco speculum under good illumination.

Gently introduce the flexible polypropylene Pipelle through the cervical canal until the fundus is contacted, noting the depth using centimetre markings on the sheath.

Withdraw the inner piston steadily and completely to create negative pressure. Rotate the sheath 360 degrees while moving it between the fundus and internal os to aspirate tissue from all walls.

teach.heading: Diagnostic accuracy and limitations of blind biopsy

rows: Small focal lesion may be missed
Atrophic rigid external or internal os

teach.heading: Managing the insufficient or failed outpatient biopsy
teach.body:
If the Pipelle cannot pass through the cervical canal due to cervical stenosis, misoprostol cervical priming or ultrasound guidance can assist entry.

When histopathology reports insufficient tissue in a woman with persistent bleeding and an endometrial stripe >4 mm, blind sampling cannot exclude malignancy. The patient must be scheduled for outpatient or operative hysteroscopy with targeted biopsy.

skill.exam.obg.pap_smear.title: Cervical cytology sampling using Ayre spatula and cytobrush
skill.exam.obg.pap_smear.oneLine: Sample squamocolumnar junction, smear or suspend in liquid medium, and fix immediately
skill.exam.obg.pap_smear.why: Cervical cancer is the second most common cancer in Indian women and is entirely preventable by detecting pre-invasive cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. Correct sampling of the transformation zone without air-drying artifacts ensures adequate diagnostic cytology under the Bethesda reporting system.

steps.text: Position the patient in dorsal lithotomy with good lighting, insert an unlubricated or warm water-moistened Cusco bivalve speculum, and visualise the entire ectocervix and external os.
Gently swab away excess mucus or inflammatory discharge with a dry cotton swab without vigorously scrubbing or traumatising the cervical epithelium.
Insert the longer tip of the Ayre wooden or plastic spatula into the external cervical os, resting the curved shoulder against the ectocervix.
Rotate the spatula a full 360 degrees while maintaining firm, continuous contact to harvest squamocolumnar junction cells.
Introduce the endocervical cytobrush gently into the canal until only the lowest bristles remain visible, and rotate 90 to 180 degrees only to avoid inducing bleeding.

Transfer cells immediately: for conventional smears, spread evenly across a pre-labelled glass slide and apply 95 percent ethyl alcohol fixative spray within 10 to 15 seconds; for liquid-based cytology, rinse the brush vigorously into the preservative vial.
Withdraw the speculum gently, ensure patient comfort, and complete the pathology request form with LMP, age, and clinical details.

skill.exam.obg.pap_smear.normal: Smooth pink squamous ectocervix, central circular or slit external os, transformation zone visible, cytology negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy (NILM).
skill.exam.obg.pap_smear.abnormal: Contact bleeding, acetowhite epithelium, friable erosion or ulcer; cytology shows ASC-US, LSIL, ASC-H, HSIL, AGC, or invasive squamous cell carcinoma.
skill.exam.obg.pap_smear.significance: Triage tool detecting cytological atypia; abnormal results direct patient to high-risk HPV testing, repeat cytology, colposcopy, or immediate excisional treatment.
skill.exam.obg.pap_smear.practice: Practise rotating the Ayre spatula 360 degrees and cytobrush 180 degrees on a cervical simulator and applying rapid fixative spray.
pitfalls: Applying lubricating jelly on the speculum before sampling, which coats cervical cells and causes severe cytological artifacts.
Delayed slide fixation beyond 10 to 15 seconds, resulting in air-drying artifacts that mimic dyskaryosis or render the smear unsatisfactory.
Over-rotating the endocervical brush multiple full turns, producing bleeding that obscures epithelial cells with red blood cells.

probes.q: Why must a conventional Pap smear be sprayed with fixative within 10 to 15 seconds of application to the slide?
probes.a: To prevent air-drying artifacts that distort cellular and nuclear morphology.

probes.q: What anatomical region must be sampled to ensure a cervical cytology specimen is adequate?
probes.a: The transformation zone, containing the squamocolumnar junction.

probes.q: What are the primary technical advantages of liquid-based cytology over conventional Pap smears?
probes.a: Liquid-based cytology reduces inadequate smears, removes obscuring blood and mucus, eliminates air-drying artifacts, and allows reflex HPV testing on the same sample.

rubric.text: Visualises cervix without contaminating lubricating jelly
Samples the squamocolumnar junction rotating spatula 360 degrees
Fixes conventional smear in 95 percent alcohol within 10 to 15 seconds or rinses in LBC vial
Labels container with patient identifiers and clinical details

teach.heading: The squamocolumnar junction and transformation zone
teach.body:
The transformation zone is the dynamic area of physiological metaplasia where columnar epithelium is replaced by stratified squamous epithelium.

Over 90 percent of cervical precancers and invasive squamous carcinomas arise within this transformation zone.

Sampling must harvest cells from both the ectocervix and the endocervical canal to confirm adequacy by the presence of endocervical or metaplastic cells.

teach.heading: Conventional Pap smear versus liquid-based cytology
The 2014 Bethesda reporting system categories
teach.body:
NILM: Negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy.

ASC-US: Atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance.

LSIL: Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (CIN 1 and transient HPV infection).

ASC-H: Atypical squamous cells, cannot exclude HSIL.

HSIL: High-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (CIN 2 and CIN 3, true cancer precursors requiring colposcopy).

skill.exam.obg.via_screening.title: Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) for cervical screening
skill.exam.obg.via_screening.oneLine: Direct inspection of the transformation zone 1 minute after 3 to 5 percent acetic acid application
skill.exam.obg.via_screening.why: In low-resource health settings lacking laboratory infrastructure, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) provides immediate, real-time cervical screening. It enables the single-visit screen-and-treat approach with thermal ablation or cryotherapy, preventing progression of pre-cancerous lesions without loss to follow-up.

steps.text: Prepare freshly diluted 3 to 5 percent acetic acid solution and position the woman in dorsal lithotomy with bright halogen or LED lighting.
Insert a Cusco speculum, adjust illumination, and inspect the cervix for pre-existing leukoplakia, discharge, polyps, or visible exophytic tumours.
Apply 3 to 5 percent acetic acid generously over the ectocervix and external os using a soaked cotton swab, making thorough contact with the transformation zone.
Wait exactly one full minute (60 seconds) by the clock to allow cellular dehydration and intracellular protein coagulation to occur.
Inspect the transformation zone systematically, noting whether the squamocolumnar junction is fully visible around its entire 360-degree circumference.
Evaluate any acetowhite lesions: assess opacity, sharp borders, location relative to the squamocolumnar junction, and entry into the endocervical canal.
Record the result as VIA negative, VIA positive, or suspicious for cancer, and assess eligibility for immediate outpatient thermal ablation or cryotherapy.

skill.exam.obg.via_screening.normal: Cervix remains pink, or exhibits faint, diffuse, translucent, ill-defined pale areas distant from the squamocolumnar junction; VIA negative.
skill.exam.obg.via_screening.abnormal: Sharp, well-defined, dense, opaque, dull acetowhite lesions touching the squamocolumnar junction or entering the external os; VIA positive.
skill.exam.obg.via_screening.significance: Enables immediate bedside decision-making under national screening guidelines (such as India s Operational Framework for Common Cancers); eligible VIA-positive women can undergo same-day thermal ablation or cryotherapy.
skill.exam.obg.via_screening.practice: Identify VIA-positive versus VIA-negative cervical photographs and delineate the margins of the transformation zone.
pitfalls: Interpreting the cervix before waiting one full minute, missing slow-developing acetowhitening in true dysplastic lesions.
Mistaking physiological immature squamous metaplasia or endocervical mucus for pathological acetowhite lesions.
Performing ablative treatment when the lesion extends into the endocervical canal or covers more than 75 percent of the ectocervix.

probes.q: What concentration of acetic acid is used for visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA)?
probes.a: Dilute 3 to 5 percent acetic acid.

probes.q: Why must the examiner wait exactly one minute after applying acetic acid before reading the cervix?
probes.a: To allow sufficient time for cellular dehydration and reversible protein coagulation in dysplastic epithelium with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio.

probes.q: What anatomical criteria make a VIA-positive lesion ineligible for outpatient ablative therapy like cryotherapy or thermal ablation?
probes.a: Lesion extends into the endocervical canal out of view, covers more than 75 percent of the cervix, extends to the vaginal wall, or has features of invasive carcinoma.

rubric.text: Applies freshly prepared 3 to 5 percent acetic acid generously over the cervix
Waits one full minute (60 seconds) before interpreting cervical whitening
Inspects whether acetowhite lesion touches the squamocolumnar junction
Assesses suitability for ablative therapy versus excisional biopsy

teach.heading: The biochemical mechanism of acetowhitening
teach.body:
Dilute 3 to 5 percent acetic acid acts as an osmotic dehydrating agent.

Normal mature squamous cells have small nuclei and abundant glycogen-rich cytoplasm; light penetrates and reflects the underlying vascular stroma as pink.

Pre-cancerous cervical intraepithelial neoplasia has a high nuclear density and increased cytokeratin content. Acetic acid coagulates nuclear proteins, preventing light transmission and creating an opaque white appearance (acetowhitening).

teach.heading: VIA interpretation categories and criteria

rows: Uniform pink or faint translucent pale lines
Dense, sharp, opaque white touching the SCJ

teach.heading: Criteria for the single-visit screen-and-treat approach
teach.body:
Eligibility for ablative therapy (thermal ablation or cryotherapy) requires three conditions:

The entire transformation zone and the complete upper border of the lesion must be visible on the ectocervix.

The lesion must not extend into the endocervical canal or involve more than 75 percent of the ectocervical surface.

There must be no clinical suspicion of microinvasive or invasive cervical carcinoma.
