skill.ix.obg.hpv_dna_screening.title: High-risk HPV DNA molecular testing and screening algorithm
skill.ix.obg.hpv_dna_screening.oneLine: High-sensitivity molecular assay for 14 oncogenic genotypes with triage of positive results
skill.ix.obg.hpv_dna_screening.why: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus (primarily types 16 and 18) is the necessary causal agent for over 99 percent of cervical carcinomas. Primary HPV DNA testing provides greater sensitivity (>95%) and longer negative predictive value than cytology, allowing safe 5- to 10-year screening intervals.
skill.ix.obg.hpv_dna_screening.normal: Negative for high-risk HPV DNA genotypes (16, 18, 31, 33, 35, 39, 45, 51, 52, 56, 58, 59, 66, 68).
skill.ix.obg.hpv_dna_screening.abnormal: Positive for high-risk HPV DNA (specifically HPV 16/18 or other 12 pooled high-risk genotypes).
skill.ix.obg.hpv_dna_screening.significance: Positive result indicates persistent infection and risk of high-grade CIN; mandates triage with partial genotyping, reflex cytology, or colposcopy.
skill.ix.obg.hpv_dna_screening.practice: Map the triage pathway for an HPV 16-positive woman versus an HPV non-16/18 positive woman.
pitfalls: Initiating high-risk HPV screening before age 25 to 30 years, detecting transient infections that resolve spontaneously.
Proceeding to invasive excisional therapy based solely on a positive HPV test without secondary triage.
Testing for low-risk HPV types (types 6 and 11), which cause genital warts but do not cause cervical cancer.

probes.q: Which two high-risk HPV genotypes are responsible for approximately 70 percent of all cervical cancers worldwide?
probes.a: HPV genotypes 16 and 18.

probes.q: Why does the WHO recommend primary HPV DNA screening starting at age 30 rather than earlier in women of average risk?
probes.a: Transient HPV infections are highly prevalent in women under 30 and clear spontaneously; testing younger women leads to unnecessary colposcopies and overtreatment.

probes.q: If a 35-year-old woman tests positive for high-risk HPV non-16/18 types, what is the recommended reflex triage step?
probes.a: Reflex cervical cytology or VIA; if cytology shows ASC-US or worse, proceed to colposcopy; if cytology is normal, repeat co-testing in 12 months.

rubric.text: Collects cervical specimen into transport media or verifies validated self-sampling kit
Distinguishes high-risk genotypes 16 and 18 from pooled other high-risk types
Applies reflex cytology or colposcopy triage rather than immediate blind excision
Recommends 5 to 10 year screening interval following a negative high-risk HPV test

teach.heading: The oncogenic role of high-risk human papillomavirus
teach.body:
Persistent infection with high-risk HPV genotypes is the prerequisite for cervical carcinogenesis.

Viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 drive malignant transformation: E6 binds and degrades p53 tumour suppressor protein, while E7 binds and inactivates retinoblastoma (pRb) protein, disabling cell cycle checkpoints.

Genotypes 16 and 18 account for 70 percent of cervical cancers; other high-risk types (31, 33, 45, 52, 58) account for an additional 20 percent.

teach.heading: WHO primary HPV screening recommendations
Triage algorithm for HPV-positive screening results
teach.body:
When primary HPV testing is positive, management depends on genotyping and triage.

HPV 16 or 18 positive: direct referral for immediate colposcopy or treatment, because 1 in 5 such women harbour CIN 3 or invasive cancer.

Other 12 high-risk types positive: reflex cervical cytology. If cytology shows ASC-US or higher, perform colposcopy; if cytology is negative (NILM), repeat HPV testing in 12 months.

skill.ix.obg.colposcopy_basics.title: Colposcopic assessment of the cervix and directed biopsy
skill.ix.obg.colposcopy_basics.oneLine: Binocular magnified inspection of the transformation zone under white, green, and iodine illumination
skill.ix.obg.colposcopy_basics.why: Colposcopy bridges abnormal screening (abnormal Pap, positive HPV, or positive VIA) and definitive tissue management. Magnified binocular visualisation identifies the transformation zone, delineates pre-cancerous lesions, and guides targeted punch biopsies of the most abnormal areas.
skill.ix.obg.colposcopy_basics.normal: Complete visualisation of the squamocolumnar junction (Type 1 or 2 transformation zone); smooth translucent pink squamous epithelium; fine uniform network of vessels; diffuse uniform dark brown-black staining with Lugol iodine (Schiller negative).
skill.ix.obg.colposcopy_basics.abnormal: Dense opaque acetowhitening, coarse punctation, coarse mosaicism, atypical hairpin or corkscrew vessels, non-staining mustard-yellow areas on Lugol iodine (Schiller positive); Type 3 transformation zone (squamocolumnar junction within endocervical canal).
skill.ix.obg.colposcopy_basics.significance: Scores lesion severity using validated systems (Swede score or Reid Colposcopic Index); guides directed punch biopsy or immediate excisional treatment (LLETZ or cone biopsy).
skill.ix.obg.colposcopy_basics.practice: Score a series of colposcopy images using the Swede score criteria to decide between biopsy and immediate excision.
pitfalls: Calling a colposcopic examination adequate when the squamocolumnar junction extends deeply into the endocervical canal out of view.
Taking a random non-directed biopsy rather than targeting the area of densest acetowhitening or coarsest mosaicism.
Failing to apply the green filter to evaluate abnormal vascular patterns (punctation, mosaicism, and atypical vessels).

probes.q: What vascular changes are visualised under the colposcope green filter in high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia?
probes.a: Coarse punctation and coarse mosaicism.

probes.q: What is the biological basis of the Lugol iodine (Schiller) test on the cervix?
probes.a: Normal mature squamous cells contain glycogen, which stains dark mahogany brown with iodine; dysplastic cells are glycogen-depleted and remain unstained, appearing mustard yellow.

probes.q: How does the International Federation of Cervical Pathology and Colposcopy (IFCPC) classify transformation zone types 1, 2, and 3?
probes.a: Type 1 is completely ectocervical and fully visible; Type 2 has an endocervical component but is completely visible; Type 3 extends into the endocervical canal and is not fully visible.

rubric.text: Assesses and documents transformation zone type 1, 2, or 3
Uses green/blue optical filter to evaluate punctation, mosaicism, and abnormal vessels
Applies 3 to 5 percent acetic acid followed by Lugol iodine solution systematically
Obtains punch biopsy from the area of highest colposcopic abnormality

teach.heading: The optical stages of colposcopic examination
teach.body:
Colposcopy uses a binocular stereoscopic microscope with 6x to 40x magnification.

Stage 1 (Saline): moisten with normal saline to evaluate native architecture and discharge.

Stage 2 (Green filter): green light is absorbed by red haemoglobin, rendering capillary vessels dark and distinct to detect punctation and mosaic patterns.

Stage 3 (Acetic acid): apply 3 to 5 percent acetic acid to evaluate acetowhitening.

Stage 4 (Lugol iodine): apply iodine to assess glycogen uptake.

teach.heading: Colposcopic markers of high-grade dysplasia (CIN 2/3)
The IFCPC transformation zone classification
teach.body:
Type 1: The entire transformation zone is located on the ectocervix and is 100 percent visible.

Type 2: The transformation zone has an endocervical component, but the entire upper limit of the squamocolumnar junction remains fully visible with or without an endocervical speculum.

Type 3: The squamocolumnar junction extends deeply into the endocervical canal and cannot be fully visualised, precluding ablative therapy and requiring diagnostic excisional conisation.

skill.exam.obg.iucd_insertion.title: Intrauterine contraceptive device insertion using the withdrawal technique
skill.exam.obg.iucd_insertion.oneLine: Sound cavity, set cervical stop, and deploy arms at fundus by withdrawing inserter sleeve
skill.exam.obg.iucd_insertion.why: Copper-bearing IUCDs (such as Copper T 380A) and levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine systems (LNG-IUS) are premier long-acting reversible contraceptives providing >99 percent efficacy for 5 to 10 years. Performing the correct no-touch withdrawal insertion prevents fundal perforation, device expulsion, and pelvic infection.

steps.text: Perform a bimanual pelvic examination to assess uterine size, version (anteverted or retroverted), flexion, and mobility, confirming no cervical motion tenderness or adnexal mass.

Insert a Cusco bivalve speculum to expose the cervix, clean the ectocervix and external os with water-based antiseptic solution, and apply a single-tooth tenaculum to the anterior lip (posterior lip if retroverted) with gentle traction to straighten the canal.
Gently pass a sterile uterine sound through the cervical os to the fundus, noting the resistance of the fundal wall to measure the exact uterocervical depth in centimetres.
Set the blue plastic flange on the inserter sleeve to the measured sound depth, maintaining strict asepsis within the sterile packaging.
Fold the horizontal arms of the Copper T into the insertion tube within the sterile packet immediately before insertion, keeping the white plunger rod inserted.
Advance the loaded inserter tube through the cervical canal until the blue flange touches the external cervical os, ensuring the arms lie in the transverse uterine plane.
Execute the withdrawal deployment: hold the white plunger rod stationary while pulling the outer inserter tube back towards your hand, releasing the T-arms gently at the fundus.

Advance the inserter tube upward slightly until resistance is felt to ensure high fundal positioning, withdraw the plunger rod, withdraw the sheath, and cut the threads 3 to 4 cm from the external os.

skill.exam.obg.iucd_insertion.normal: Sound depth 6 to 8 cm, smooth fundal deployment without severe resistance, strings visible exiting external os at 3 to 4 cm, minimal spotting.
skill.exam.obg.iucd_insertion.abnormal: Sound depth <6 cm or >9 cm, sudden loss of resistance indicating uterine perforation, severe pelvic pain or vasovagal syncope, visible expulsion.
skill.exam.obg.iucd_insertion.significance: First-line long-acting reversible contraception (LARC); immediate efficacy; Copper T 380A effective for 10 years, LNG-IUS (Mirena) for 5 to 8 years (also treats heavy menstrual bleeding).
skill.exam.obg.iucd_insertion.practice: Practise loading a Copper T 380A into its insertion sleeve within the sterile packet and executing the withdrawal deployment on a pelvic model.
pitfalls: Pushing the plunger forward to deploy the IUCD rather than holding it stationary and withdrawing the outer sheath, risking uterine perforation.
Failing to straighten the uterocervical angle with gentle tenaculum traction, leading to cervical laceration or false passage.
Folding the Copper-T arms into the inserter tube more than 5 minutes before insertion, causing loss of arm memory and incomplete opening.

probes.q: What is the primary mechanism of action of copper-bearing intrauterine contraceptive devices?
probes.a: Copper ions induce a sterile inflammatory reaction in the endometrium and are toxic to spermatozoa and ova, inhibiting fertilisation.

probes.q: Why is the withdrawal technique used to deploy the T-arms of an IUCD at the fundus?
probes.a: Holding the central rod stationary while pulling the outer tube back releases the arms at the fundus without pushing the device forward against the myometrium, preventing fundal perforation.

probes.q: How long can a Copper T 380A remain in situ for effective contraception, and what is its approved duration under national programmes?
probes.a: Up to 10 years of effective continuous contraception.

rubric.text: Performs bimanual exam and sounds uterine cavity before opening IUCD package
Sets the cervical stop flange on the inserter to the exact sounded depth
Deploys IUCD by holding plunger rod still and withdrawing outer sleeve
Trims strings 3 to 4 cm from the external os using sterile scissors

teach.heading: Technical stages of the withdrawal insertion method
teach.body:
The Copper T 380A and levonorgestrel-releasing systems are placed using a no-touch withdrawal technique.

After uterine sounding confirms cavity length and direction, the movable plastic flange on the inserter tube is set to the exact measured depth in centimetres.

The horizontal arms are loaded into the tube inside the sterile pack just prior to insertion to preserve memory.

The tube is introduced to the fundus until the flange touches the external os.

The plunger rod is held stationary while the outer tube is withdrawn, allowing the arms to open safely at the fundus.

teach.heading: Comparison of common intrauterine devices
Complications and emergency red flags
teach.body:
Uterine perforation occurs in approximately 1 to 2 per 1000 insertions, most commonly in lactating women or with an undiagnosed retroverted uterus.

Device expulsion occurs in 2 to 5 percent of users, predominantly during the first three cycles or menses.

Pelvic inflammatory disease risk is elevated only within the first 20 days after insertion and relates to pre-existing untreated cervical infection.

skill.exam.obg.iucd_removal.title: Intrauterine contraceptive device removal and management of missing threads
skill.exam.obg.iucd_removal.oneLine: Gentle traction on visible threads, with ultrasound and instrumentation if strings are retracted
skill.exam.obg.iucd_removal.why: IUCD removal is requested for desired pregnancy, reaching expiry date, or complications (pain, bleeding, PID). When strings are missing from the external os, systematic evaluation differentiates unrecognized expulsion from uterine perforation or intrauterine retraction, avoiding blind intrauterine trauma.

steps.text: Position the patient in dorsal lithotomy, explain the removal sensations, and insert a Cusco bivalve speculum under good illumination.
Locate the cervical threads protruding from the external cervical os, cleansing any excess discharge.
Grasp both threads firmly close to the external os using sterile sponge-holding forceps or curved artery forceps.
Apply gentle, steady, continuous traction downward in line with the longitudinal axis of the cervical canal, allowing the flexible T-arms to fold upwards as the device passes through the internal os.
Inspect the retrieved IUCD immediately to confirm that both horizontal arms, the vertical stem, and all copper bands or hormone sleeves are completely intact.
If threads are missing at the external os: gently explore the endocervical canal with a sterile cytobrush or thread retriever rotated 360 degrees to tease curled threads down.

If threads cannot be retrieved: perform transvaginal pelvic ultrasound to confirm the device is within the uterine cavity before attempting intrauterine extraction with an IUCD hook or narrow forceps.
If ultrasound demonstrates an empty uterine cavity, obtain a plain abdominal-pelvic X-ray to rule out extrauterine peritoneal migration from silent perforation.

skill.exam.obg.iucd_removal.normal: Strings visible at external os, smooth extraction with steady gentle traction, intact IUCD retrieved, patient experiences mild transient cramp.
skill.exam.obg.iucd_removal.abnormal: Missing strings; broken thread on traction; resistance to traction suggesting myometrial embedment; device absent on ultrasound and visible in peritoneal cavity on radiograph.
skill.exam.obg.iucd_removal.significance: Restores fertility immediately upon removal; missing strings workup prevents unintended pregnancy (if expelled) and severe intra-abdominal complications or visceral adhesions (if perforated).
skill.exam.obg.iucd_removal.practice: Demonstrate gentle straight-line thread traction on an intact model and describe the algorithm for lost threads.
pitfalls: Tugging sharply on strings, which can snap aged or brittle monofilament threads.
Blindly instrumenting the uterine cavity with forceps without prior ultrasound confirmation that the IUCD is inside the uterus.
Assuming a missing IUCD has been expelled without ordering an abdominal X-ray to rule out silent extrauterine perforation.

probes.q: What is the first-line imaging modality to evaluate an IUCD with missing cervical threads?
probes.a: Transvaginal pelvic ultrasound.

probes.q: If pelvic ultrasound demonstrates an empty uterine cavity and no adnexal mass in a woman with a missing IUCD, what test must be ordered next?
probes.a: Plain abdominal-pelvic X-ray, to detect or rule out intraperitoneal migration following uterine perforation.

probes.q: How should an IUCD that is embedded deep within the myometrium be removed?
probes.a: Hysteroscopic visualisation and grasping under direct vision or operative laparoscopy.

rubric.text: Applies gentle, steady straight-line traction to visible strings using forceps
Thoroughly inspects extracted device to verify all arms and stem are complete
Orders transvaginal ultrasound before attempting blind intrauterine extraction for missing strings
Requests plain abdominal radiograph when ultrasound shows an empty cavity

teach.heading: Standard removal technique for visible IUCD threads
teach.body:
Ensure the patient is in dorsal lithotomy position and visualise the cervix with a Cusco speculum.

Grasp both threads firmly close to the external os using a sterile sponge forceps or curved artery clamp.

Apply gentle, continuous traction in line with the cervical canal.

The flexible arms fold upwards as the device traverses the internal os.

Inspect the retrieved device to confirm that both arms, the stem, and the copper or hormone reservoir are fully intact.

teach.heading: Diagnostic workup for the missing IUCD thread
Managing the lost intrauterine device
teach.body:
If transvaginal ultrasound confirms the IUCD is in the uterine cavity but threads are not reachable at the external os, removal can be achieved using an IUCD hook, Novak curette, or narrow alligator forceps under local anaesthesia.

If the device is deeply embedded in the myometrium, blind manipulation risks perforation and fracture.

Operative hysteroscopy under direct vision provides safe, controlled dislodgement and extraction.

skill.approach.obg.injectable_contracept.title: Injectable contraception counselling, eligibility and administration
skill.approach.obg.injectable_contracept.oneLine: DMPA 150 mg every 12 weeks: counsel on amenorrhoea, bone mineral density, and delayed fertility
skill.approach.obg.injectable_contracept.why: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA, Antara scheme in India) and norethisterone enanthate (NET-EN) are highly effective progestin-only injectables (>99% efficacy) independent of coitus. Thorough pre-injection counselling regarding irregular spotting, eventual amenorrhoea, and 6 to 10 month delay in fertility return prevents high discontinuation rates.

steps.text: Confirm reasonably certain she is not pregnant, ideally initiating during days 1 to 5 of menses or 6 weeks postpartum if breastfeeding.
Screen medical eligibility using WHO MEC criteria: measure blood pressure, and verify absence of active breast cancer, ischemic heart disease, stroke, or active viral hepatitis.
Explain the contraceptive mechanism: profound suppression of the mid-cycle LH surge to inhibit ovulation, thickening of cervical mucus, and endometrial thinning.

Counsel extensively on predictable bleeding pattern changes: irregular spotting and prolonged light bleeding during the first 3 to 6 months, progressing to amenorrhoea in over 50 percent of users by 1 year.
Discuss bone mineral density and fertility return: explain small reversible decrease in bone density and reassure that a 7 to 10 month delay in conception is common and completely reversible.
Administer DMPA 150 mg deep intramuscularly into the deltoid or upper outer quadrant of the gluteus maximus, shaking the aqueous vial thoroughly.
Instruct the patient firmly not to rub, massage, or apply hot compresses to the injection site, as pressure accelerates absorption and reduces duration of efficacy.
Schedule the repeat injection for exactly 12 weeks (84 days) later, informing her of the 4-week late grace window.

skill.approach.obg.injectable_contracept.practice: Roleplay counselling a patient requesting DMPA who is anxious about stopping her periods.
pitfalls: Vigorously massaging the injection site after administering DMPA, which accelerates depot absorption and shortens contraceptive duration.
Failing to warn the woman about amenorrhoea, leading to panic and fear of pregnancy when periods stop.
Prescribing DMPA without advising about the potential 6 to 10 month delay in the return of fertility in women desiring near-future conception.

probes.q: What is the dose and injection schedule of depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) under India s Antara programme?
probes.a: 150 mg intramuscularly every 12 weeks or 3 months.

probes.q: Why must the injection site not be massaged following intramuscular DMPA administration?
probes.a: Massaging hastens drug absorption from the depot, potentially shortening the duration of contraceptive cover.

probes.q: What is the typical delay in the return of fertility following the discontinuation of DMPA?
probes.a: Median 7 to 10 months, occasionally up to 18 months, unrelated to the duration of use.

rubric.text: Screens for WHO MEC contraindications including current breast cancer and severe vascular disease
Counsels proactively on irregular spotting progressing to benign amenorrhoea
Administers deep IM and instructs patient not to rub or massage the injection site
Explains expected 7 to 10 month delay in return of fertility upon stopping

teach.heading: Pharmacology and administration schedules of progestin injectables
teach.body:
Injectable progestins provide highly effective, reversible contraception independent of coitus.

DMPA (Depo-Provera, Antara) contains 150 mg in 1 mL aqueous suspension, administered deep intramuscularly every 12 weeks (3 months).

NET-EN (Noristerat) contains 200 mg in an oily solution, given intramuscularly every 8 weeks (2 months).

Do not massage the injection site, as rubbing accelerates release from the muscle depot.

teach.heading: Comparison of DMPA and NET-EN
Key counselling domains: bleeding, bones, and fertility return
teach.body:
Bleeding changes: irregular spotting occurs in the initial months; after one year of use, approximately 50 to 60 percent of women develop amenorrhoea, which is harmless.

Bone mineral density: slight reversible decrease occurs, which recovers after stopping; encourage weight-bearing exercise and dietary calcium.

Fertility delay: return of ovulation takes an average of 7 to 10 months following the last injection; reassure that long-term fertility is unimpaired.

skill.approach.obg.emergency_contracepti.title: Emergency contraception counselling and regimen selection
skill.approach.obg.emergency_contracepti.oneLine: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg within 72h, ulipristal 30 mg within 120h, or copper IUCD within 120h
skill.approach.obg.emergency_contracepti.why: Unprotected intercourse, condom slippage, or sexual assault carries a substantial risk of unintended pregnancy. Timely emergency contraception provides an effective safety net, with the Copper IUCD being the most effective method (>99.8%) and oral regimens reducing risk significantly if taken promptly.

steps.text: Calculate the exact hours elapsed since unprotected sexual intercourse, establishing cycle day and probability of pregnancy.
Present the three primary methods without bias: the Copper IUCD (most effective), oral ulipristal acetate (effective up to 120 hours), and oral levonorgestrel (effective up to 72 hours).
Advise that the copper-bearing IUCD provides >99.8 percent protection if inserted within 120 hours (5 days) of intercourse and can remain as ongoing long-term contraception.
If oral contraception is selected: administer levonorgestrel 1.5 mg single dose within 72 hours (or ulipristal acetate 30 mg single dose within 120 hours).
Instruct the patient that if vomiting occurs within 2 hours of levonorgestrel (or 3 hours of ulipristal), she must take a repeat dose immediately.
Explain that emergency contraception will not protect against future unprotected coitus in the same cycle and counsel on barrier protection until next menses.
Advise that next menses should arrive within a week of the expected date; if delayed by more than 7 days, a pregnancy test is required.

skill.approach.obg.emergency_contracepti.practice: Counsel a simulated patient presenting 60 hours after condom breakage and explain the advantages of the copper IUCD versus oral pill.
pitfalls: Refusing emergency contraception because more than 72 hours have elapsed, forgetting that Ulipristal and the Copper IUCD are effective up to 120 hours.
Failing to repeat the oral dose when the patient vomits within 2 to 3 hours of ingestion.
Assuming oral emergency contraception protects against subsequent coitus within the same cycle.

probes.q: What is the single oral dose of levonorgestrel used for emergency contraception, and within what timeframe should it ideally be taken?
probes.a: 1.5 mg single oral dose, taken within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse.

probes.q: What is the most effective method of emergency contraception available, and within what timeframe can it be placed?
probes.a: The copper-bearing intrauterine device, effective within 120 hours or 5 days of intercourse, with failure rate <0.2%.

probes.q: If a woman vomits 45 minutes after taking a 1.5 mg levonorgestrel emergency contraceptive pill, what action must be taken?
probes.a: She must take a replacement 1.5 mg dose immediately, optionally accompanied by an antiemetic.

rubric.text: Accurately calculates hours elapsed since unprotected sexual contact
Offers copper IUCD as the most effective method alongside oral regimens
Instructs patient to repeat oral dose if vomiting occurs within 2 to 3 hours
Establishes a plan for ongoing reliable contraception and STI testing

teach.heading: Indications and timing of emergency contraception
teach.body:
Emergency contraception is indicated after unprotected sexual intercourse, condom breakage or slippage, missed oral contraceptive pills, or sexual assault.

Efficacy is highest when administered as soon as possible after intercourse.

Emergency contraception prevents ovulation or fertilisation; none of the available methods acts as an abortifacient or interrupts an established, implanted pregnancy.

teach.heading: Comparison of emergency contraceptive methods
Post-administration guidance and follow-up
teach.body:
Vomiting: If vomiting occurs within 2 hours of levonorgestrel or 3 hours of ulipristal, the full dose must be repeated immediately.

Menstrual timing: Next menses usually arrives within a week of the expected date; if menses is delayed by more than 7 days, perform a urine pregnancy test.

Ongoing cover: Barrier contraception must be used for the remainder of the cycle; oral pills can be initiated immediately after levonorgestrel or after 5 days with ulipristal.

skill.approach.obg.permanent_contracepti.title: Permanent female and male contraception counselling and surgical options
skill.approach.obg.permanent_contracepti.oneLine: Voluntary informed surgical sterilisation: minilap Pomeroy, laparoscopic Falope ring, and no-scalpel vasectomy
skill.approach.obg.permanent_contracepti.why: Permanent sterilisation is chosen by millions of couples worldwide who have completed their family. Because it is irreversible, rigorous pre-procedure counselling confirming voluntary choice without coercion, explanation of failure rates (1 in 200), and comparison with no-scalpel vasectomy (safer, simpler) are legal and ethical requirements.

steps.text: Confirm that the request is completely voluntary, confirming that both partners agree their family is complete, with no coercion during labour or financial stress.
Review age, marital status, and parity criteria in accordance with national guidelines, ensuring a minimum waiting reflection period.
Explain unequivocally that surgical sterilisation is intended to be permanent and irreversible, discussing the poor success rates and invasiveness of reversal surgery.
Present no-scalpel vasectomy (NSV) for the male partner as a simpler, safer alternative that avoids peritoneal cavity entry and general anaesthesia.
Detail female surgical options: postpartum minilaparotomy with Pomeroy tubal excision, or interval laparoscopic tubal occlusion using silastic Falope rings or spring clips.

Disclose surgical risks and failure rates: explain that tubal ligation carries approximately a 0.5 percent failure rate (1 in 200), and that any subsequent pregnancy carries a high risk of being ectopic.
Explain post-vasectomy care: male sterilisation is not immediately effective, requiring alternative barrier contraception for 12 weeks until semen analysis proves azoospermia.
Obtain signed, informed, voluntary consent from the client on standard national consent forms.

skill.approach.obg.permanent_contracepti.practice: Conduct a mock pre-sterilisation counselling session addressing a couple where the husband assumes female sterilisation is the only option.
pitfalls: Pressuring a woman to undergo sterilisation while she is in active labour or immediately following a traumatic delivery.
Failing to offer no-scalpel vasectomy (NSV) for the male partner as a safer, simpler alternative to female tubal surgery.
Failing to explain that vasectomy is not immediately effective, leading to pregnancy before 3-month semen clearance.

probes.q: What is the Pomeroy technique for tubal ligation during postpartum minilaparotomy?
probes.a: A loop of the mid-isthmic fallopian tube is elevated, ligated at its base with absorbable suture, and the knuckle of the loop is excised.

probes.q: How do silastic Falope rings achieve tubal occlusion during laparoscopic sterilisation?
probes.a: A 2 to 3 cm loop of the fallopian tube is drawn into a cone applicator and a stretched silastic band is released around the loop, causing ischaemic necrosis and fibrosis.

probes.q: Why must a couple use barrier contraception for 3 months following a no-scalpel vasectomy?
probes.a: Sperm stored in the distal vas deferens and ampulla can fertilise an ovum until cleared; azoospermia must be confirmed on semen analysis at 3 months.

rubric.text: Confirms voluntary informed consent free of coercion or financial duress
Emphasises that surgical sterilisation must be considered permanent and irreversible
Actively discusses no-scalpel vasectomy as a safer and simpler partner option
Explains surgical failure rates and the risk of ectopic pregnancy if failure occurs

teach.heading: Ethical and legal principles of voluntary sterilisation
teach.body:
Sterilisation is an irreversible surgical procedure.

Counselling must confirm that the decision is entirely voluntary, free from coercion, and arrived at when the couple has completed their desired family size.

Consent must never be obtained during acute stress, active labour, or immediately following an obstetric emergency.

Spousal consent is not legally mandated under Indian law, but couple counselling is strongly encouraged.

teach.heading: Surgical techniques for female tubal occlusion

rows: Loop ligated with plain gut, excised

teach.heading: No-scalpel vasectomy versus female sterilisation
teach.body:
No-scalpel vasectomy (NSV) is performed under local anaesthesia through a single puncture in the midline scrotal raphe.

Compared with female tubal ligation, NSV has shorter operative time, lower complication rates, zero risk of peritoneal entry, and faster recovery.

Crucially, vasectomy is not immediately effective: stored sperm take approximately 12 weeks or 20 ejaculations to clear, and semen analysis demonstrating azoospermia is required.

skill.approach.obg.hormonal_implants_rin.title: Subdermal contraceptive implants and vaginal contraceptive rings
skill.approach.obg.hormonal_implants_rin.oneLine: Etonogestrel single-rod implant for 3 years, and ethinylestradiol/etonogestrel monthly vaginal ring
skill.approach.obg.hormonal_implants_rin.why: Subdermal implants represent the most effective reversible contraceptive available (Pearl Index 0.05), providing continuous progestin cover for 3 to 5 years. Vaginal rings offer combined hormonal contraception with low systemic peaks and monthly self-administration. Clear counselling on insertion, side effects, and removal schedules ensures optimal compliance.

steps.text: Review medical eligibility using WHO MEC criteria, confirming the patient is not pregnant and discussing her lifestyle and preference for provider-dependent versus user-dependent methods.
Describe the single-rod subdermal implant (Nexplanon: 68 mg etonogestrel rod, 4 cm long, 2 mm diameter, effective for 3 years).
Explain implant insertion: performed under local anaesthesia in the inner non-dominant upper arm, 8 to 10 cm above the medial humeral epicondyle, avoiding the sulcus between biceps and triceps.
Verify implant placement: confirm that both the provider and the patient palpate the rod immediately after insertion, applying a pressure bandage for 24 hours.
Describe the combined contraceptive vaginal ring (NuvaRing: releasing 15 mcg ethinylestradiol and 120 mcg etonogestrel daily).

Teach ring insertion and cycle schedule: inserted into the upper vagina by the patient on days 1 to 5 of menses, left in place for 3 weeks (21 days), removed for 1 ring-free week, and replaced on the same weekday.

Provide anticipatory guidance: counsel that implants commonly cause irregular light bleeding or amenorrhoea, and explain that if a ring is expelled for >3 hours, backup barrier contraception is needed for 7 days.

skill.approach.obg.hormonal_implants_rin.practice: Demonstrate the 30-degree subdermal entry and horizontal advancement on an implant arm trainer model.
pitfalls: Inserting a subdermal implant too deeply into the subcutaneous fat or muscular fascia, leading to non-palpable rods and neurovascular injury.
Failing to ensure both clinician and patient palpate the implant immediately following insertion.
Leaving a vaginal ring out of the vagina for more than 3 hours without using backup barrier contraception.

probes.q: What is the active progestin and duration of efficacy of the Nexplanon single-rod contraceptive implant?
probes.a: 68 mg of etonogestrel, effective for 3 years.

probes.q: Where is the recommended anatomical site for subdermal insertion of a contraceptive implant?
probes.a: Subdermally in the inner aspect of the non-dominant upper arm, 8 to 10 cm above the medial humeral epicondyle.

probes.q: What should a woman do if her contraceptive vaginal ring falls out and remains out for more than 3 hours during the third week of use?
probes.a: Rinse with cool water, re-insert immediately, use barrier contraception for 7 days, and discard the ring at the end of the third week to start a new ring without a hormone-free break.

rubric.text: Identifies correct subdermal insertion site 8 to 10 cm above medial epicondyle
Verifies presence of implant by immediate dual palpation by provider and patient
Explains the 3-weeks-in, 1-week-out schedule for contraceptive vaginal rings
Counsels on irregular bleeding profiles associated with progestin-only implants

teach.heading: Characteristics and insertion of subdermal implants
teach.body:
Nexplanon is a single, flexible ethylene vinyl acetate rod measuring 4 cm by 2 mm, containing 68 mg of etonogestrel.

It is inserted subdermally in the inner non-dominant arm, 8 to 10 cm above the medial humeral epicondyle.

The preloaded applicator needle is inserted at 30 degrees until the dermis is punctured, then lowered to lie flat just beneath the skin before advancing.

Both the clinician and patient must immediately palpate the rod.

teach.heading: Vaginal contraceptive ring mechanism and schedule
teach.body:
The combined contraceptive vaginal ring (NuvaRing) is a flexible, transparent ring that slowly releases 15 mcg of ethinylestradiol and 120 mcg of etonogestrel daily.

It is compressed and placed into the upper vagina by the user, where exact placement is not critical for absorption.

It remains in place for 3 weeks (21 days) and is removed for 7 days, during which withdrawal bleeding occurs, before a new ring is inserted.

teach.heading: Troubleshooting: expulsion and non-palpable implants

rows: Rinse with cool water and re-insert
Review eligibility; trial NSAID or COCP

skill.approach.obg.mtp_counsel.title: Medical termination of pregnancy legal framework and counselling
skill.approach.obg.mtp_counsel.oneLine: MTP Act 2021 eligibility, statutory RMP opinions, confidentiality, and post-abortion contraception
skill.approach.obg.mtp_counsel.why: Unsafe abortion is a leading preventable cause of maternal mortality in India. The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act 2021 expanded access up to 24 weeks for vulnerable categories, recognised contraceptive failure for unmarried women, and codified absolute privacy. Comprehensive pre-abortion counselling ensures informed, confidential, and safe care.

steps.text: Confirm pregnancy, gestational age, and intrauterine location using clinical examination or ultrasound, ensuring privacy and non-judgmental communication.

Review eligibility under the amended MTP Act 2021: risk to the woman s life, grave injury to physical or mental health, pregnancy from rape, substantial fetal abnormalities, or failure of contraception in any woman or her partner.

Determine the required statutory opinions: one Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP) up to 20 weeks; two RMPs from 20 to 24 weeks for defined vulnerable categories; or State Medical Board approval beyond 24 weeks for substantial fetal abnormalities.
Obtain valid informed consent: the written consent of the woman herself is sufficient if she is 18 years or older; guardian consent is required only if she is under 18 years or mentally ill.
Explain that spousal or partner consent is not legally required under Indian law, and reassure her of strict statutory confidentiality regarding her identity.

Present the options: medical abortion (mifepristone and misoprostol up to 9 weeks) versus surgical abortion (manual vacuum aspiration up to 12 weeks), explaining the timings, sensations, and warning signs.
Counsel on post-abortion contraception and provide her chosen method (oral pills, injectables, or immediate post-procedure IUCD) before discharge.

skill.approach.obg.mtp_counsel.practice: Roleplay pre-abortion counselling for an unmarried 22-year-old student, explaining consent laws and confidentiality protections under the MTP Act.
pitfalls: Demanding spousal consent or presence of husband for an adult woman seeking MTP; legally, only her own consent is required.
Denying MTP for contraceptive failure to an unmarried woman, which was specifically corrected in the MTP Amendment Act 2021.
Breaching confidentiality by documenting patient identifying details in non-statutory records or revealing her identity to unauthorised third parties.

probes.q: Under the amended MTP Act 2021, how many Registered Medical Practitioners (RMPs) must certify an abortion up to 20 weeks of gestation?
probes.a: Opinion of one Registered Medical Practitioner.

probes.q: What gestational limit applies to MTP for vulnerable categories such as survivors of rape or minors, and how many RMP opinions are required?
probes.a: Up to 24 weeks, requiring the opinion of two Registered Medical Practitioners.

probes.q: Whose consent is legally required under the MTP Act for an adult woman aged 18 years or older?
probes.a: Only the consent of the woman herself; spousal or parental consent is not legally required.

rubric.text: Applies correct statutory RMP opinion rules based on gestational age
Obtains informed consent directly from the adult client without requiring spousal agreement
Guarantees statutory confidentiality of client identity under MTP Act rules
Integrates post-abortion contraceptive counselling and immediate method provision

teach.heading: Key provisions of the MTP (Amendment) Act 2021
teach.body:
Gestational limits: termination up to 20 weeks requires the opinion of one Registered Medical Practitioner; from 20 to 24 weeks requires two RMPs for defined vulnerable categories.

Contraceptive failure: applies to any woman or her partner, explicitly removing the marital requirement.

Fetal anomalies: beyond 24 weeks, termination is permitted without gestational ceiling for substantial fetal abnormalities diagnosed by a four-member State Medical Board.

teach.heading: Statutory categories eligible for MTP between 20 and 24 weeks

rows: Survivors of sexual violence or incest

teach.heading: Confidentiality and consent mandate
teach.body:
Consent: for any woman aged 18 years or older who is of sound mind, only her own written consent is legally valid.

Spousal, partner, or parental consent is never required, and denying MTP because a spouse is absent violates the Act.

Confidentiality: Section 5A mandates that no registered medical practitioner shall reveal the name or particulars of a woman terminating pregnancy except to an authority authorised by law; violation carries fine and imprisonment.

skill.approach.obg.mva_procedure.title: Manual vacuum aspiration and medical abortion regimens
skill.approach.obg.mva_procedure.oneLine: MVA handheld syringe up to 12 weeks, and mifepristone-misoprostol regimen up to 9 weeks
skill.approach.obg.mva_procedure.why: Manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) and combined medical abortion represent safe, non-traumatic alternatives to sharp curettage for first-trimester abortion and incomplete miscarriage. Both methods avoid general anaesthesia, have lower uterine perforation rates than metal curettage, and boast over 95 to 98 percent success.

steps.text: Confirm intrauterine pregnancy and determine precise gestational age using menstrual history and pelvic examination or ultrasound.

For medical abortion (gestations up to 9 weeks or 63 days): administer Mifepristone 200 mg single oral tablet on Day 1, followed 24 to 48 hours later by Misoprostol 800 mcg buccally, sublingually, or vaginally.
Counsel medical abortion patients on expected cramping, bleeding heavier than normal menses with clots, and prescribe oral ibuprofen for pain management.

For manual vacuum aspiration (MVA, gestations up to 12 weeks): position in lithotomy, administer paracervical block, insert Cusco speculum, and steady the cervix with sponge-holding forceps (avoiding tenaculum on pregnant cervix).
Charge the MVA double-valve syringe by locking the plunger clips backwards to establish a negative pressure of 60 mmHg.
Dilate the cervix if needed using gentle Hegar dilators corresponding to the selected Karman cannula diameter in millimetres.
Introduce the Karman cannula to the uterine fundus, attach the charged syringe, and release the valve buttons to apply suction.
Rotate the cannula 360 degrees while gently moving it back and forth between fundus and internal os, continuing until red/pink foam appears and a gritty uterine cry is felt.
Close valves, disconnect syringe, and express the aspirated tissue into a strainer floating in clean water to inspect for chorionic villi and gestational sac.

skill.approach.obg.mva_procedure.practice: Charge and discharge an MVA syringe, demonstrating the vacuum seal and practice float inspection of mock tissue in water.
pitfalls: Using sharp metal curettage routinely for first-trimester abortion instead of manual or electric vacuum aspiration.
Failing to inspect the aspirated tissue floating in water to identify branching chorionic villi and gestational sac.
Administering misoprostol simultaneously with mifepristone rather than waiting the requisite 24 to 48 hours.

probes.q: What negative pressure vacuum is generated by the double-valve manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) syringe?
probes.a: Approximately 60 mmHg or 26 inches of mercury.

probes.q: What is the standard combined medical abortion drug regimen and timing for pregnancies up to 9 weeks (63 days)?
probes.a: Mifepristone 200 mg single oral dose, followed 24 to 48 hours later by Misoprostol 800 mcg buccally, sublingually, or vaginally.

probes.q: How is completeness of evacuation confirmed immediately following manual vacuum aspiration?
probes.a: Inspecting the evacuated products floating in clean water or saline against a light to identify translucent gestational sac and white branching chorionic villi.

rubric.text: Charges MVA syringe by retracting and locking plunger to establish 60 mmHg vacuum
Rotates Karman cannula 360 degrees with gentle strokes until gritty uterine cry is felt
Floats tissue in clear water to verify presence of chorionic villi and gestational sac
Instructs 24 to 48 hour interval between mifepristone and misoprostol

teach.heading: The mechanics of manual vacuum aspiration
teach.body:
Manual vacuum aspiration uses a portable 60 mL syringe with single or double push-button valves and flexible Karman cannulae.

Retracting the plunger until the retaining clips snap outward establishes a vacuum of 60 mmHg (26 inches of mercury).

The cannula size in millimetres corresponds to gestational age in weeks (for example, an 8 mm cannula for 8 weeks gestation).

Evacuation is complete when red or pink foam appears, a gritty sensation (uterine cry) is felt, and the uterus contracts firmly around the cannula.

teach.heading: Medical abortion protocol up to 9 weeks (63 days)
Complications and emergency warning signs
teach.body:
Haemorrhage: soaking more than two large sanitary pads per hour for two consecutive hours requires immediate hospital assessment.

Incomplete abortion: persistent pain, heavy bleeding, or foul-smelling lochia warrants repeat misoprostol or MVA.

Uterine perforation: rare with flexible Karman cannulae (<1 per 1000); if cannula penetrates beyond expected depth or mesenteric fat is aspirated, stop suction immediately and laparoscopically evaluate.

skill.exam.obg.dilatation_curettage.title: Dilatation and fractional curettage procedure and complication prevention
skill.exam.obg.dilatation_curettage.oneLine: Fractional curettage of endocervix then endometrium, with gradual calibrated Hegar dilatation
skill.exam.obg.dilatation_curettage.why: Dilatation and fractional curettage remains a fundamental diagnostic procedure to sample tissue and rule out endometrial hyperplasia and malignancy in abnormal uterine bleeding. Careful technique prevents severe complications including uterine perforation, cervical laceration, and Asherman syndrome (intrauterine synechiae).

steps.text: Perform a thorough bimanual pelvic examination under anaesthesia to determine uterine position, version, flexion, mobility, and adnexal status.
Retract the posterior vaginal wall with a Sims speculum, clean the cervix, and grasp the anterior lip of the cervix with a single-tooth tenaculum or vulsellum.

Perform endocervical curettage first: introduce a small sharp curette into the cervical canal and scrape around 360 degrees without passing the internal os, placing curettings into a separate container labelled endocervix.
Gently pass a uterine sound through the cervical os to the fundus, recording the exact cavity depth and direction.
Dilate the cervix sequentially using graduated Hegar dilators held in a pencil grip between thumb and fingertips, advancing gently past the internal os without arm force.
Introduce the Sims uterine curette to the fundus, systematically curetting the anterior wall, posterior wall, lateral walls, and fundal corners down to the internal os.
Collect the endometrial tissue strips into a separate container labelled endometrium, confirm a firm gritty sensation (uterine cry), and inspect for haemostasis.

skill.exam.obg.dilatation_curettage.normal: Smooth calibrated dilatation up to 8 to 10 mm without false passages, cavity length 6 to 8 cm, moderate firm tissue retrieved from both fractions, myometrial contraction and gritty texture on curettage.
skill.exam.obg.dilatation_curettage.abnormal: Sudden loss of resistance with curette passing beyond sounded depth (uterine perforation), profuse bright red haemorrhage, necrotic friable exophytic tissue masses.
skill.exam.obg.dilatation_curettage.significance: Histological evaluation of endometrial causes of AUB (PALM-COEIN: polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy); fractional curettage determines whether endometrial carcinoma extends to involve the endocervix (affecting FIGO staging and surgical radicality).
skill.exam.obg.dilatation_curettage.practice: Practise fractional curettage steps on a phantom model, taking endocervical curettings before inserting the uterine sound.
pitfalls: Failing to take the endocervical sample before sounding the uterus, contaminating the endocervical specimen with endometrial tissue.
Holding Hegar dilators in the fist and using brute force, which easily perforates the lower uterine segment.
Vigorous, aggressive curettage of a postpartum or infected uterus, removing the basal endometrium and causing Asherman syndrome.

probes.q: Why must the endocervical curettage be performed before the uterine sound is inserted in fractional curettage?
probes.a: To prevent dislodging endometrial tissue into the endocervical canal, ensuring clean histological separation of the two fractions for cancer staging.

probes.q: How should a Hegar cervical dilator be held to minimize the risk of traumatic uterine perforation?
probes.a: Held between the thumb and fingers like a pen or pencil, using gentle wrist control rather than arm thrust.

probes.q: If a uterine sound or curette suddenly passes well beyond the previously established cavity length without resistance, what has occurred and what is the immediate action?
probes.a: Uterine perforation; stop the procedure immediately, withdraw instruments gently, monitor vitals, and assess for internal haemorrhage or bowel injury.

rubric.text: Performs endocervical curettage before sounding the uterine cavity
Holds Hegar dilators like a pencil, gently dilating without excessive force
Curettes fundus, anterior, posterior, and lateral uterine walls systematically
Sends endocervical and endometrial curettings in separately labelled formalin bottles

teach.heading: The rationale for fractional curettage in gynaecology
teach.body:
Fractional curettage samples the endocervix and endometrium as two separate histological fractions.

This distinction is vital when evaluating postmenopausal bleeding or suspected uterine malignancy.

Detecting cervical stromal involvement by an endometrial adenocarcinoma upgrades the disease to stage II under FIGO staging, altering the surgical approach from simple to radical hysterectomy.

teach.heading: Stepwise surgical sequence of fractional D and C
teach.body:
Step 1: Perform bimanual examination under anaesthesia to determine version and flexion.

Step 2: Clean and drape; retract posterior vaginal wall with Sims speculum and steady cervix with tenaculum.

Step 3: Curette the endocervical canal around 360 degrees without entering the internal os. Place in Container A.

Step 4: Sound the uterine cavity to verify depth and direction.

Step 5: Dilate the internal os with graduated Hegar dilators held in a pencil grip.

Step 6: Curette the endometrial cavity systematically. Place in Container B.

teach.heading: Intraoperative complications and their management

rows: Yellow fat or peristalsis at os

skill.exam.obg.cervical_biopsy_lletz.title: Cervical punch biopsy and large loop excision of the transformation zone
skill.exam.obg.cervical_biopsy_lletz.oneLine: Punch biopsy for focal lesions, and monopolar radiofrequency loop excision for CIN 2/3
skill.exam.obg.cervical_biopsy_lletz.why: Abnormal cervical screening requires tissue confirmation before or during definitive treatment. Directed punch biopsy provides diagnostic histopathology, while Large Loop Excision of the Transformation Zone (LLETZ/LEEP) provides single-session diagnosis and therapeutic excision of pre-cancerous cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN).

steps.text: Position the patient in dorsal lithotomy, insert an insulated non-conductive Cusco speculum with smoke evacuation tubing, and visualise the cervix under colposcopic guidance.
Apply 3 to 5 percent acetic acid followed by Lugol iodine to delineate the transformation zone and identify the most severe lesion areas.
For cervical punch biopsy: position Tischler or Kevorkian punch biopsy forceps perpendicular to the cervix, taking a 2 to 3 mm bite of epithelium and stroma at the abnormal border.
For LLETZ / LEEP: attach the patient return grounding pad, infiltrate the cervical stroma with 2 to 5 mL of 1 percent lignocaine with adrenaline 1:100,000 for anaesthesia and vasoconstriction.
Select an appropriately sized wire loop (typically 15 to 20 mm wide and 7 to 10 mm deep) based on the size of the transformation zone.
Activate the electrosurgical generator on blend cut-coagulation mode at 40 to 50 watts, advancing the loop smoothly across the transformation zone in a single continuous pass without stopping.
Retrieve the excised specimen intact, pin or ink the 12 o clock margin for pathology orientation, and place in 10 percent formalin.
Fulgurate the resection base and crater margins with a 3 to 5 mm ball electrode on coagulation mode or apply Monsel paste to ensure absolute haemostasis.

skill.exam.obg.cervical_biopsy_lletz.normal: Punch biopsy yields 2 to 3 mm stromal core; LLETZ yields single intact hemispherical tissue piece with clean endocervical and ectocervical margins; histopathology confirms CIN 1 or negative margins.
skill.exam.obg.cervical_biopsy_lletz.abnormal: Margins involved by high-grade CIN 3 or invasive squamous cell carcinoma; heavy arterial bleeding from cervical stroma during or after excision.
skill.exam.obg.cervical_biopsy_lletz.significance: Definitive diagnosis of cervical lesions; LLETZ cures >90 percent of high-grade CIN lesions while preserving fertility; avoiding excess excision (>10 mm depth) preserves cervical competence in future pregnancies.
skill.exam.obg.cervical_biopsy_lletz.practice: Practise sweeping a wire diathermy loop across a fruit model (such as a peach or foam cervix) at uniform speed without dragging or burning tissue.
pitfalls: Pausing or dragging the wire loop mid-excision during LLETZ, causing severe thermal artifact that destroys histological margins.
Excising more than 10 to 12 mm of cervical tissue depth in young nulliparous women, increasing the risk of cervical incompetence and preterm birth.
Failing to apply a non-conductive insulated speculum and smoke evacuator during electrosurgical loop excision.

probes.q: What is the primary clinical indication for Large Loop Excision of the Transformation Zone (LLETZ / LEEP)?
probes.a: Treatment and histological confirmation of high-grade cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, CIN 2 or CIN 3.

probes.q: Why should the depth of cervical tissue excised during LLETZ be restricted to less than 10 mm in reproductive-aged women?
probes.a: Excision depths exceeding 10 mm significantly increase the subsequent risk of mid-trimester miscarriage and preterm labour.

probes.q: What chemical haemostatic agent is commonly applied to the cervical crater following biopsy to stop capillary oozing?
probes.a: Monsel solution (ferric subsulphate paste) or silver nitrate.

rubric.text: Uses insulated speculum and active smoke evacuation system for LLETZ
Infiltrates cervical stroma with local anaesthetic containing adrenaline
Performs LLETZ excision in a smooth, single continuous pass without pausing
Orients and pins or labels tissue specimen for pathological margin evaluation

teach.heading: Principles of electrosurgical loop excision (LLETZ / LEEP)
teach.body:
LLETZ uses a fine tungsten or stainless steel wire loop energized by high-frequency radiofrequency current.

The alternating current produces rapid intracellular heating, vaporising cellular water and cutting tissue with minimal thermal artifact.

The goal is to remove the entire transformation zone and dysplastic lesion in a single contiguous specimen to allow accurate pathological margin assessment.

teach.heading: Instrument comparison: punch biopsy versus loop excision
Obstetric sequelae and depth regulation
teach.body:
Excision of cervical stroma weakens the mechanical integrity of the cervix.

Meta-analyses demonstrate that excisions deeper than 10 mm or exceeding 1 cm3 in volume double the baseline risk of preterm pre-labour rupture of membranes and preterm birth in future pregnancies.

In nulliparous women, depth must be carefully tailored to the transformation zone, avoiding excessive endocervical canal excision.

skill.exam.obg.bartholins_marsupialisati.title: Marsupialisation of Bartholin gland cyst and abscess
skill.exam.obg.bartholins_marsupialisati.oneLine: Incision at hymenal ring, evacuation of pus, and eversion of cyst wall with absorbable sutures
skill.exam.obg.bartholins_marsupialisati.why: Obstruction of the Bartholin gland duct leads to painful cysts or acute abscesses. Simple incision and drainage or needle aspiration results in recurrence rates exceeding 20 to 30 percent as the wound edges heal prematurely. Marsupialisation exteriorises the cyst lining to create a permanent epithelialised draining tract, preserving glandular function and preventing recurrence.

steps.text: Examine the vulva under good lighting to assess the fluctuant swelling in the posterior third of the labium majus and rule out surrounding cellulitis or necrotising fasciitis.
Administer local infiltration anaesthesia with 1 percent lignocaine or arrange conscious sedation.
Retract the labia majora to expose the introitus, identifying the mucosal surface of the labium minus overlying the medial bulge of the cyst just external to the hymenal ring.
Make a 1.5 to 2 cm vertical incision through the vaginal mucosa overlying the medial aspect of the cyst, deepening the incision until the fibrous cyst capsule is incised.
Allow pus or mucus to drain completely, collect a microbiological swab for Gram stain and culture (including gonococcus and chlamydia), and irrigate the cavity with saline.
Grasp the cyst wall margins with fine Allis forceps to mobilize the edges.
Evert the cyst wall and suture it with interrupted 3-0 polyglactin (Vicryl) sutures to the adjacent vaginal mucosa medially and introitus laterally, leaving a patent marsupial pouch.
In women aged 40 years or older, excise a small wedge of the cyst wall for histopathological examination to rule out underlying Bartholin gland carcinoma.

skill.exam.obg.bartholins_marsupialisati.normal: Wide patent pouch with neatly everted edges, free drainage of contents, complete relief of tension, healing with a functional permanent opening.
skill.exam.obg.bartholins_marsupialisati.abnormal: Excessive bleeding from vascular bed, failure to identify true cyst wall, closure of opening resulting in recurrence, extensive cellulitis requiring intravenous antibiotics.
skill.exam.obg.bartholins_marsupialisati.significance: Definitive surgical treatment of symptomatic Bartholin cyst and acute abscess; preserves lubrication function of the gland and prevents high recurrence rates of simple incision.
skill.exam.obg.bartholins_marsupialisati.practice: Practise suturing the everted edges of a simulated balloon cyst wall to the surrounding latex mucosal border.
pitfalls: Performing a simple incision and drainage without marsupialisation, which leads to rapid wound closure and cyst recurrence.
Placing the incision on the external skin of the labium majus rather than the medial mucosal surface at the hymenal ring, resulting in a visible, painful scar.
Failing to biopsy the cyst wall in a woman aged 40 years or older to exclude rare Bartholin gland adenocarcinoma.

probes.q: Why is marsupialisation preferred over simple incision and drainage for a Bartholin abscess?
probes.a: Simple incision and drainage closes prematurely with recurrence in up to 30 percent; marsupialisation creates a permanent fistulous tract that preserves drainage and glandular function.

probes.q: Where should the surgical incision for marsupialisation of a Bartholin cyst be placed?
probes.a: On the mucosal surface of the introitus just external to the hymenal ring, avoiding the external hairy skin of the labium majus.

probes.q: Why should a cyst wall biopsy be sent during marsupialisation in a woman older than 40 years?
probes.a: To rule out rare Bartholin gland carcinoma, which can present as a painless or indurated cyst in perimenopausal or postmenopausal women.

rubric.text: Places 1.5 to 2 cm incision on the medial mucosal surface near hymenal ring
Evacuates contents and takes microbiological swab for culture
Everts and sutures cyst wall edges to vaginal mucosa with interrupted absorbable sutures
Obtains cyst wall biopsy for histopathology in women aged 40 years or older

teach.heading: Anatomy of the Bartholin gland and pathogenesis of obstruction
teach.body:
The greater vestibular (Bartholin) glands are paired pea-sized mucus-secreting glands situated in the posterior third of the labia majora.

Their 2 cm ducts open into the vestibular groove between the hymen and the labium minus.

Obstruction of the duct orifice by trauma, inspissated mucus, or infection leads to cyst formation; secondary infection by polymicrobial flora or gonococcus produces an intensely painful, throbbing abscess.

teach.heading: Surgical steps of marsupialisation
teach.body:
Retract the labia and locate the fluctuant mass.

Incise the vaginal mucosa vertically for 1.5 to 2 cm at the junction with the hymen, then open the cyst wall and aspirate the purulent contents.

Grasp the cyst capsule with fine Allis forceps. Using 3-0 polyglactin or chromic catgut on a round-bodied needle, place interrupted sutures catching the edge of the cyst lining and the vaginal mucosa.

This exteriorises the mucosal cavity, creating an open pocket resembling a marsupial pouch.

teach.heading: Management options for Bartholin disease

rows: Everts cyst wall to skin edges
Inflatable balloon in cavity for 4 wks

skill.exam.obg.diagnostic_laparoscopy_gy.title: Diagnostic laparoscopy in gynaecology and pelvic inspection
skill.exam.obg.diagnostic_laparoscopy_gy.oneLine: Pneumoperitoneum creation, umbilical trocar insertion, and systematic pelvic survey
skill.exam.obg.diagnostic_laparoscopy_gy.why: Laparoscopy is the gold standard investigation for evaluating female infertility, chronic pelvic pain, endometriosis, and suspected ectopic pregnancy. Mastering safe entry techniques (Veress needle or open Hasson) and systematic pelvic inspection prevents devastating vascular or bowel trocar injuries.

steps.text: Ensure the patient is in modified lithotomy position under general endotracheal anaesthesia, with empty bladder (Foley catheter) and empty stomach (orogastric decompression).
Place an intrauterine cannula or uterine manipulator vaginally to permit full range of uterine mobility during laparoscopy.
Make a small vertical intraumbilical or curved infraumbilical skin incision, elevating the lower abdominal wall with the non-dominant hand.

Introduce the spring-loaded Veress needle directed toward the pelvic hollow at a 45-degree angle in normal-weight patients (90 degrees in obese patients), noting two distinct clicks as it crosses the rectus sheath and peritoneum.

Confirm peritoneal entry using safety tests: syringe aspiration (no blood, urine, or bowel content), followed by the saline drop test (saline drops in the hub are aspirated spontaneously into the cavity upon abdominal wall lift).
Connect carbon dioxide insufflation at low flow (1 L/min), verifying low initial pressure (<8 to 10 mmHg), and insufflate to a high-pressure entry plateau of 20 to 25 mmHg.

Introduce the primary 10 mm umbilical trocar, insert the 0 or 30 degree laparoscope, and immediately rotate the camera 360 degrees to verify that no bowel or retroperitoneal vessel trauma occurred at the entry site.

Reduce intra-abdominal working pressure to 12 to 15 mmHg, place the patient in steep Trendelenburg tilt, and insert secondary 5 mm working trocars under direct vision lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

Conduct a systematic survey of the pelvis: examine the anterior cul-de-sac, uterine fundus, both ovaries, fallopian tubes from isthmus to fimbriae, uterosacral ligaments, and pouch of Douglas, performing chromopertubation with dilute methylene blue to assess tubal patency.

skill.exam.obg.diagnostic_laparoscopy_gy.normal: Smooth peritoneal surfaces, pink mobile uterus, normal pearly white ovaries, patent fallopian tubes with free bilateral spill of methylene blue dye, clear pouch of Douglas without endometriotic powder burns or adhesions.
skill.exam.obg.diagnostic_laparoscopy_gy.abnormal: Powder-burn or red flame endometriotic implants, dense pelvic adhesions obliterating pouch of Douglas, swollen bluish ampulla with tubal haematoma (ectopic pregnancy), hydrosalpinx, tubal blockage (no dye spill).
skill.exam.obg.diagnostic_laparoscopy_gy.significance: Definitive diagnosis and staging of endometriosis (rASRM classification), tubal factor infertility, pelvic inflammatory disease, and ectopic pregnancy, enabling immediate operative intervention.
skill.exam.obg.diagnostic_laparoscopy_gy.practice: Practise Veress needle safety checks (quadruple click, syringe aspiration, and saline drop test) on a laparoscopic trainer box.
pitfalls: Failing to empty the urinary bladder and stomach before inserting trocars, risking catastrophic bladder or gastric perforation.
Inserting secondary lateral trocars blindly without transilluminating the anterior abdominal wall to avoid the inferior epigastric vessels.
Injecting carbon dioxide gas when high insufflation pressures (>8 to 10 mmHg) indicate the Veress needle is extraperitoneal in the preperitoneal space or omentum.

probes.q: What safety test confirms that a Veress needle tip is freely within the peritoneal cavity before starting gas insufflation?
probes.a: The saline drop test: a drop of saline placed in the open hub flows spontaneously into the abdomen under negative intra-abdominal pressure when the abdominal wall is lifted.

probes.q: What working intra-abdominal pressure of carbon dioxide is maintained during standard operative gynaecological laparoscopy?
probes.a: 12 to 15 mmHg.

probes.q: How are the inferior epigastric vessels identified and avoided when placing lateral secondary laparoscopic ports?
probes.a: By transilluminating the abdominal wall with the laparoscope and visualising the vascular pulsation on the peritoneal surface lateral to the obliterated umbilical artery.

rubric.text: Performs safety checks (saline drop and aspiration) before high-flow gas insufflation
Rotates laparoscope 360 degrees upon entry to exclude retroperitoneal or visceral trauma
Places secondary ports under direct visual guidance lateral to inferior epigastric vessels
Inspects uterus, adnexa, pouch of Douglas, and performs chromopertubation

teach.heading: Principles of peritoneal entry: closed Veress versus open Hasson
teach.body:
Closed entry uses a spring-loaded Veress needle inserted through the umbilicus, where the rectus sheath and peritoneum fuse.

Two distinct clicks correspond to the anterior rectus fascia and the peritoneum.

The open Hasson technique incises the fascia and peritoneum under direct vision, placing stay sutures to anchor a blunt cannula.

Hasson entry is preferred in patients with prior laparotomy scars to avoid adherent bowel.

teach.heading: Verification tests for peritoneal placement of Veress needle

rows: Drop of saline in needle hub
Drop sucked into cavity on lift

teach.heading: Systematic survey of the female pelvis and chromopertubation
teach.body:
Position the patient in steep Trendelenburg tilt once pneumoperitoneum is established, allowing gravity to displace bowel loops into the upper abdomen.

Manipulate the uterus anteriorly and systematically examine the anterior cul-de-sac, uterine fundus, both fallopian tubes from isthmus to fimbriae, ovaries, and the pouch of Douglas.

For chromopertubation, dilute methylene blue is injected through the uterine cannula, observing the fimbrial ends for blue dye spill.

skill.exam.obg.diagnostic_hysteroscopy.title: Diagnostic hysteroscopy and uterine cavity inspection
skill.exam.obg.diagnostic_hysteroscopy.oneLine: Transcervical endoscopy using rigid or flexible scope with fluid distension media
skill.exam.obg.diagnostic_hysteroscopy.why: Abnormal uterine bleeding, recurrent implantation failure, and missing intrauterine devices require direct visualization of the endometrial cavity. Diagnostic hysteroscopy allows immediate identification and directed biopsy of polyps, submucosal leiomyomas, and intrauterine adhesions, surpassing blind curettage.

steps.text: Position the patient in dorsal lithotomy, performing bimanual examination to verify uterine size, version, and flexion.
Assemble the hysteroscopy system: connect a 2.7 to 4 mm 30-degree rigid telescope to the light source, camera, and irrigation inflow tubing containing normal saline.
Flush the irrigation fluid through the sheath prior to entry to purge all air bubbles from the line, eliminating the risk of venous air embolism.
Introduce the scope into the external cervical os under direct camera visualization, utilizing continuous low-pressure saline distension to dilate the endocervical canal.
Negotiate the internal cervical os gently under visual guidance without blind cervical dilatation whenever feasible.
Perform a panoramic survey of the entire endometrial cavity: inspect the uterine fundus, right tubal ostium, left tubal ostium, anterior wall, posterior wall, and lateral walls.
Examine the endometrium for focal pathologies: polyps, submucosal fibroids, synechiae, or malignant vascular patterns, taking directed target biopsies as indicated.
Monitor fluid deficit (total irrigation volume infused minus collection canister output) continuously to ensure fluid absorption remains well below safety thresholds.

skill.exam.obg.diagnostic_hysteroscopy.normal: Smooth pinkish-orange endometrium, cavity fully distended, patent symmetrical bilateral tubal ostia, no focal intra-cavitary projections, smooth endocervical canal.
skill.exam.obg.diagnostic_hysteroscopy.abnormal: Pedunculated or sessile endometrial polyp, white firm submucosal leiomyoma (FIGO type 0, 1, or 2), dense fibrous synechiae (Asherman syndrome), friable atypical vascular endometrium (hyperplasia/carcinoma), missing IUCD embedded in wall.
skill.exam.obg.diagnostic_hysteroscopy.significance: Gold standard diagnostic modality for intra-cavitary uterine pathology; guides operative hysteroscopic resection (myomectomy, polypectomy, septoplasty, adhesiolysis).
skill.exam.obg.diagnostic_hysteroscopy.practice: Navigate a 30-degree hysteroscope inside a uterine trainer box, locating both tubal ostia and rotating the light post to scan lateral walls.
pitfalls: Failing to flush air bubbles from the irrigation tubing before entering the uterine cavity, risking fatal venous air embolism.
Failing to monitor irrigation fluid deficit (especially non-conductive distension media like glycine), leading to hyponatraemic encephalopathy or pulmonary edema.
Forcing the hysteroscope blindly through a tight internal os, creating a false passage into the myometrium or perforating into the peritoneal cavity.

probes.q: What physiological fluid distension medium is standard for diagnostic hysteroscopy and bipolar electrosurgery?
probes.a: Normal saline (0.9% sodium chloride).

probes.q: What is the fluid deficit threshold that mandates terminating an operative hysteroscopy when using non-conductive hypotonic media such as 1.5% glycine?
probes.a: 1000 mL in healthy women, or 750 mL in elderly patients with cardiovascular disease, to prevent hyponatraemia and brain edema.

probes.q: Why is a 30-degree angled telescope preferred over a 0-degree straight telescope in diagnostic hysteroscopy?
probes.a: Rotating the 30-degree scope around its longitudinal axis provides an expansive panoramic view of the tubal ostia, cornua, and lateral walls without tilting the instrument shaft.

rubric.text: Flushes irrigation tubing with saline to purge all air before entering the cervix
Navigates the endocervical canal and internal os under direct vision using fluid distension
Systematically visualises both tubal ostia, fundus, and all four uterine walls
Strictly monitors fluid input and output deficit to prevent fluid overload

teach.heading: Optics and distension media in hysteroscopy
teach.body:
Hysteroscopes utilize a 2.7 mm to 4 mm telescope housed within a protective sheath with fluid inflow and outflow channels.

A 30-degree angled lens allows inspection of the angled cornua and lateral walls by rotating the scope on its axis.

Isotonic normal saline (0.9% NaCl) is the preferred distension medium for diagnostic procedures and bipolar electrosurgery, minimizing electrolyte shifts.

teach.heading: Distension media comparison and safety thresholds
Technique of vaginoscopic no-touch entry (Bettocchi method)
teach.body:
Modern outpatient diagnostic hysteroscopy frequently avoids speculum and tenaculum instrumentation entirely.

The vaginoscopic technique introduces the miniaturized scope into the vaginal introitus.

Fluid distension distends the vaginal vault; the external os is visualised, and the scope gently traverses the canal under direct vision.

This dramatically reduces patient pain and vasovagal reactions, permitting office diagnosis without anaesthesia.
