skill.exam.obg.abdominal_hysterectomy_st.title: Total abdominal hysterectomy key surgical steps and ureteric safety
skill.exam.obg.abdominal_hysterectomy_st.oneLine: Orderly ligation of round, infundibulopelvic or ovarian, uterine, and cardinal ligaments with vault closure
skill.exam.obg.abdominal_hysterectomy_st.why: Total abdominal hysterectomy is among the commonest major gynaecological operations performed for uterine leiomyomas, adenomyosis, and pelvic malignancies. The ureter passes within 1.5 cm of the uterine artery and travels beneath it; meticulous anatomical dissection and staying close to the uterus prevents catastrophic ureteric transection or ligation.

steps.text: Catheterise the urinary bladder, enter the peritoneal cavity via a transverse suprapubic (Pfannenstiel) or midline vertical incision, and pack the intestines into the upper abdomen using moist laparotomy packs.
Apply straight Kocher or Heaney clamps across both uterine cornua to elevate and provide continuous traction on the uterus.
Clamp, divide, and ligate the round ligaments bilaterally with No. 1 absorbable suture, opening the anterior and posterior leaves of the broad ligament.
Incise the uterovesical peritoneal fold transversely and gently dissect the bladder base downwards off the lower uterine segment and upper cervix into the avascular vesicocervical space.

Manage adnexa: if removing ovaries (bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy), clamp, cut, and doubly ligate the infundibulopelvic ligaments taking care of the ureter at the pelvic brim; if preserving ovaries, clamp, cut, and ligate the utero-ovarian ligament and fallopian tube close to the cornu.

Skeletonize the uterine vessels: place a curved Heaney or Zeppelin clamp perpendicular to the uterine artery hugging the lateral border of the cervix at the internal os, divide, and transfix with No. 1 Vicryl.
Clamp, divide, and transfix the Mackenrodt (cardinal) and uterosacral ligaments bilaterally, releasing the cervix from its deep pelvic attachments.

Incise the anterior vaginal fornix, amputate the cervix circumferentially from the vaginal vault, and close the vaginal cuff with continuous or figure-of-eight absorbable sutures incorporating the lateral cardinal pedicles for vault suspension.

skill.exam.obg.abdominal_hysterectomy_st.normal: Specimen removed intact without visceral injury, haemostatic pedicles, clear bilateral ureteric peristalsis, intact closed vaginal vault, clear urine output in Foley catheter.
skill.exam.obg.abdominal_hysterectomy_st.abnormal: Uncontrolled arterial haemorrhage from slipped uterine or ovarian pedicle; thermal or sharp ureteric transection; accidental cystotomy of bladder base during flap dissection.
skill.exam.obg.abdominal_hysterectomy_st.significance: Primary operative procedure for benign and malignant pelvic disease; strict adherence to anatomical pedicle boundaries prevents life-threatening haemorrhage and ureteric injury.
skill.exam.obg.abdominal_hysterectomy_st.practice: Identify and trace the three classic anatomical hazard zones for ureteric injury during abdominal hysterectomy on an anatomical pelvic model.
pitfalls: Failing to dissect and reflect the urinary bladder adequately downwards off the cervix before clamping the uterine vessels, causing bladder laceration.
Clamping lateral to the uterine cervix rather than hugging the uterine stroma, which captures the ureter as it crosses beneath the uterine artery.
Attempting blind mass clamping during brisk haemorrhage from a retracted infundibulopelvic or uterine vessel, causing ureteric transection.

probes.q: What is the anatomical relationship between the uterine artery and the ureter near the level of the internal cervical os?
probes.a: The uterine artery crosses superior and anterior to the ureter: water under the bridge.

probes.q: What are the three classic anatomical danger zones where the ureter is most vulnerable to surgical injury during hysterectomy?
probes.a: At the pelvic brim beneath the infundibulopelvic ligament, at the level of the internal os where the uterine artery crosses over it, and at the lateral vaginal vault fornices during Mackenrodt clamp placement.

probes.q: How is the bladder safely separated from the anterior cervix and upper vagina during the development of the bladder flap?
probes.a: The uterovesical peritoneal fold is incised transversely and gentle blunt and sharp dissection is performed in the loose avascular vesicocervical fascial space, pushing the bladder base inferiorly.

rubric.text: Incises uterovesical fold and mobilises bladder base well below the cervicovaginal junction
Applies uterine artery clamps perpendicular and immediately adjacent to the cervical stroma
Incorporates lateral cardinal ligament pedicles into vault closure to prevent vault prolapse
Identifies course of the ureter and verifies bilateral peristalsis and clear urine output

teach.heading: The three surgical pedicles of abdominal hysterectomy
teach.body:
Abdominal hysterectomy proceeds through three distinct bilateral sets of clamps.

Pedicle 1: Round ligament and either the infundibulopelvic ligament (if removing adnexa) or the utero-ovarian ligament and tubal isthmus (if preserving adnexa).

Pedicle 2: Uterine vessels at the level of the internal os after reflecting the bladder.

Pedicle 3: Cardinal (Mackenrodt) and uterosacral ligaments anchoring the cervix to the vaginal vault.

teach.heading: Ureteric danger zones during pelvic surgery

rows: Ureter lies 1.5 cm lateral to cervix

teach.heading: Bladder reflection and vault closure
teach.body:
Developing an adequate bladder flap is the single most critical step protecting the urinary tract.

The loose avascular vesicocervical plane is entered after picking up the glistening uterovesical peritoneum.

The bladder must be rolled downwards until the anterior vaginal wall is palpated between the fingers.

The vaginal vault is closed with absorbable No. 1 polyglactin suture, anchoring the uterosacral ligaments to provide apical vault support.

Uterine Anatomy and Abdominal Hysterectomy

skill.exam.obg.vaginal_hysterectomy_step.title: Vaginal hysterectomy surgical steps and pelvic floor reconstruction
skill.exam.obg.vaginal_hysterectomy_step.oneLine: Circumferential cervical incision, pouch entry, retrograde clamp sequence, and vault suspension
skill.exam.obg.vaginal_hysterectomy_step.why: Vaginal hysterectomy is the least invasive, most cost-effective route for hysterectomy, associated with faster recovery, less pain, and no abdominal incisions. Because dissection proceeds from below upwards in reverse order to abdominal hysterectomy, systematic identification of tissue planes and careful bladder displacement are essential to prevent bladder and rectal injury.

steps.text: Place the patient in steep dorsal lithotomy with buttocks projecting over the table edge, catheterise the bladder, and insert a weighted Auvard speculum posteriorly.
Grasp the anterior and posterior cervical lips with vulsellum forceps, exerting firm downward traction to deliver the cervix toward the introitus.
Pass a female metal catheter into the bladder to identify the lower border of the bladder base, making a circular incision around the cervix 1 cm below this reflection.
Enter the pouch of Douglas sharply by picking up and incising the posterior peritoneum between the uterosacral ligaments, inserting a posterior retractor.
Dissect the bladder base upwards off the anterior cervix within the vesicocervical space and sharply incise the anterior uterovesical peritoneal fold under direct vision.

Execute the retrograde pedicle clamping sequence: Clamp 1: uterosacral and cardinal (Mackenrodt) ligaments, divided and transfixed with No. 1 Vicryl; Clamp 2: uterine artery and veins, clamped close to the cervix, divided and ligated.

Deliver the uterine fundus (Doderlein manoeuvre) anteriorly or posteriorly, and place Clamp 3 across the round ligament, fallopian tube, and utero-ovarian ligament bilaterally, freeing the uterus completely.
Perform McCall culdoplasty by placing non-absorbable or delayed-absorbable sutures through both uterosacral ligament stumps to elevate the vaginal cuff and close the cul-de-sac.
Perform anterior colporrhaphy and posterior colpoperineorrhaphy (Ward-Mayo repair) if cystocele or rectocele is present, close the vaginal epithelium, and insert a vaginal antiseptic pack.

skill.exam.obg.vaginal_hysterectomy_step.normal: Specimen removed intact with minimal blood loss, patent rectum and intact bladder confirmed, vaginal vault suspended high without descent, urine in catheter remains clear and blood-free.
skill.exam.obg.vaginal_hysterectomy_step.abnormal: Slipped uterine vessel pedicle retracting into retroperitoneal pelvis; accidental cystotomy into bladder base; entry into rectum during posterior pouch opening.
skill.exam.obg.vaginal_hysterectomy_step.significance: Primary approach for pelvic organ prolapse with uterine descent and benign mobile uteri <=12 weeks size; combining vault suspension (McCall culdoplasty) prevents post-hysterectomy vaginal vault prolapse.
skill.exam.obg.vaginal_hysterectomy_step.practice: Trace the retrograde clamp sequence of vaginal hysterectomy (uterosacral-cardinal, then uterine vessels, then cornual pedicle) on a surgical diagram.
pitfalls: Making the anterior mucosal incision too high without sounding the bladder limit, cutting directly into the bladder base.
Failing to enter the pouch of Douglas sharply, dissecting into the posterior uterine wall or stripping rectal serosa.
Failing to perform an apical vault suspension (such as McCall culdoplasty), leading to early postoperative vaginal vault prolapse.

probes.q: In what sequence are the vascular and ligamentous pedicles clamped during vaginal hysterectomy?
probes.a: From below upwards in retrograde order: first uterosacral and cardinal ligaments, second uterine vessels, third round and utero-ovarian ligaments.

probes.q: How is the lower limit of the urinary bladder confirmed before making the anterior cervicovaginal incision in vaginal hysterectomy?
probes.a: A female metal catheter or sound is passed into the bladder to identify the lowest point of the bladder base against the anterior cervix.

probes.q: What is the purpose of performing a McCall culdoplasty during the closure of a vaginal hysterectomy?
probes.a: To obliterate the pouch of Douglas and suspend the vaginal vault to the remnants of the uterosacral ligaments, preventing enterocele and vault prolapse.

rubric.text: Sounds bladder with metal catheter to identify vesicovaginal junction before incision
Successfully enters posterior (Douglas) and anterior (uterovesical) peritoneal spaces
Executes retrograde pedicle clamping: cardinal-uterosacral, uterine vessels, cornual pedicles
Performs McCall culdoplasty or uterosacral vault suspension to prevent vault prolapse

teach.heading: Anatomical principles of the vaginal approach
teach.body:
Vaginal hysterectomy works from the outside inward, reversing the sequence of abdominal hysterectomy.

Downwards traction on the cervix delivers the lower uterine segment toward the introitus.

Opening both the pouch of Douglas posteriorly and the uterovesical pouch anteriorly isolates the lateral ligamentous supports.

Pedicles are clamped, divided, and ligated from caudal to cranial, allowing progressive descent of the uterine body.

teach.heading: Vaginal versus abdominal hysterectomy pedicle sequence

rows: Round ligament, tube, and ovarian lig.

teach.heading: Reconstruction: the Ward-Mayo procedure and McCall culdoplasty
teach.body:
When vaginal hysterectomy is performed for uterovaginal prolapse, pelvic floor reconstruction must accompany uterine removal.

The classic Ward-Mayo operation combines vaginal hysterectomy with anterior colporrhaphy (plication of pubocervical fascia) and posterior colpoperineorrhaphy (plication of rectovaginal fascia and perineal body repair).

A McCall culdoplasty places non-absorbable or delayed-absorbable sutures across the bilateral uterosacral ligament stumps to elevate the vaginal cuff and close the cul-de-sac.

skill.exam.obg.instrument_gynae_specula.title: Gynaecological specula and vaginal retractors identification and use
skill.exam.obg.instrument_gynae_specula.oneLine: Identify Sims double-bladed speculum, Cusco self-retaining bivalve, and anterior wall retractor
skill.exam.obg.instrument_gynae_specula.why: Vaginal specula are the fundamental diagnostic instruments of outpatient and operative gynaecology. Differentiating the Cusco self-retaining bivalve speculum (which frees both hands for procedures) from the Sims double-bladed speculum (which visualises vaginal wall prolapse and requires an assistant) prevents examination errors and trauma.

steps.text: Inspect the instrument presented: check material (reusable stainless steel versus single-use disposable plastic), blade dimensions, hinge joints, and presence of locking thumb-screws.
Identify the Cusco self-retaining bivalve speculum: note two curved duckbill blades connected to a perpendicular handle with a ratcheted or threaded thumb-screw mechanism.

Demonstrate Cusco operation: insert with blades closed in the oblique or transverse vaginal diameter, rotate 90 degrees to horizontal, open blades gently in the upper vagina, and tighten the screw to keep the instrument self-retaining, freeing both hands for Pap smear, IUCD placement, or Pipelle biopsy.
Identify the Sims double-bladed speculum: note a central flat handle connecting two curved, trough-shaped blades of unequal width, each featuring a longitudinal drainage groove.
Explain Sims clinical use: patient in left lateral or semi-prone Sims position, assistant retracts posterior vaginal wall while examiner inspects anterior wall prolapse (cystocele) or apex.
Identify the Sims anterior vaginal wall retractor: note a long central metal shaft with two fenestrated curved loops set at 15 degrees, with serrations designed to fit into vaginal rugosities.
Explain the role of the anterior retractor: passed along the anterior wall to gently depress a lax, sagging anterior wall or cystocele that obscures the cervix during Sims speculum examination.

skill.exam.obg.instrument_gynae_specula.normal: Clean, smooth, non-pitted blades, functional locking screw, no sharp edges, sterilised by autoclaving.
skill.exam.obg.instrument_gynae_specula.abnormal: Stiff or cross-threaded locking screw, chipped or warped disposable plastic blades, bent retractor loop, bioburden or rust.
skill.exam.obg.instrument_gynae_specula.significance: Essential viva and OSCE practical station; matching the correct speculum to the clinical task ensures patient comfort, adequate cervical exposure, and accurate prolapse evaluation.
skill.exam.obg.instrument_gynae_specula.practice: Demonstrate insertion and locking of a Cusco bivalve speculum, and demonstrate retraction with a Sims speculum and anterior wall retractor on a pelvic trainer.
pitfalls: Attempting to evaluate anterior or posterior vaginal wall prolapse using a Cusco speculum, which splints and conceals both walls.
Opening the blades of a Cusco speculum before inserting it fully into the upper vagina, pinching sensitive introital tissue.
Using a metal speculum for electrosurgical loop excision (LLETZ) instead of an insulated non-conductive speculum.

probes.q: What is the primary operational advantage of a Cusco bivalve speculum over a Sims double-bladed speculum?
probes.a: The Cusco speculum is self-retaining with a screw lock, freeing both hands of the single clinician to perform procedures without requiring an assistant.

probes.q: Why is the Sims double-bladed speculum preferred over the Cusco speculum for evaluating pelvic organ prolapse?
probes.a: A single blade of the Sims speculum retracts one vaginal wall while leaving the opposite wall completely visible and mobile during straining, whereas a Cusco speculum holds both walls rigid.

probes.q: What is the clinical function of the fenestrations and serrations on the ends of a Sims anterior vaginal wall retractor?
probes.a: The serrations grip into the transverse vaginal rugosities, preventing slippage while retracting a lax, redundant anterior vaginal wall that would otherwise obscure the cervix.

rubric.text: Distinguishes Cusco self-retaining bivalve from Sims non-self-retaining double-bladed speculum
Inserts speculum with closed blades in oblique/transverse diameter before rotating
Selects Sims speculum for prolapse evaluation and Cusco for solitary procedures
Explains role of fenestrated anterior retractor in managing redundant cystocele

teach.heading: Design features of Sims versus Cusco specula
teach.body:
The Sims speculum is a non-self-retaining instrument featuring two curved trough-shaped blades of unequal dimensions connected by a handle.

The central groove collects cervical discharge or blood.

The Cusco speculum is a bivalve self-retaining instrument.

Its two hinged blades open via a lever and lock with a knurled thumb-screw, keeping both hands of the examiner free to perform Pap smears, IUCD placements, or biopsies.

teach.heading: Comparative features of gynaecological specula

rows: Vaginal hysterectomy, D and C in OT

teach.heading: Sims position and anterior wall retractor dynamics
teach.body:
The Sims speculum is ideally used in the Sims semi-prone position with buttocks brought to the table edge and the right thigh flexed towards the chest.

Retracting the perineum backwards allows atmospheric air to enter and balloon the vagina.

When a lax anterior wall bulges downward (cystocele), a Sims anterior wall retractor is passed along the anterior wall to gently elevate it, bringing the cervix into direct view.

skill.exam.obg.instrument_uterine_graspi.title: Uterine grasping forceps, tenacula and sounding instruments identification
skill.exam.obg.instrument_uterine_graspi.oneLine: Identify Vulsellum, Tenaculum, Green-Armytage, Sponge forceps, and Sims versus Bladder sound
skill.exam.obg.instrument_uterine_graspi.why: Stabilising the mobile uterus and measuring cavity dimensions are essential steps before any intrauterine instrumentation. Confusing a traumatic tenaculum or vulsellum on a soft pregnant cervix risks massive cervical tearing, while misidentifying an uncalibrated bladder sound for a uterine sound leads to undetected perforation.

steps.text: Inspect grasping forceps jaws and curvature: identify Teale vulsellum by its multiple fine sharp interlocking teeth (3 to 4 on each blade), gentle curve on the shaft, and ratcheted handle.
Identify the single-tooth tenaculum: note a single, sharp, inward-curving hook on each blade with a ratchet lock, used to steady the non-pregnant anterior cervical lip for IUCD insertion.
Identify Green-Armytage hemostatic forceps: note broad, triangular, flat jaws with deep transverse serrations and no sharp teeth, used to clamp bleeding myometrial edges during caesarean hysterotomy.
Identify sponge-holding forceps: note long straight shaft with oval fenestrated loop jaws, used for gentle, atraumatic grasping of the soft, hypervascular pregnant cervix during suction evacuation.

Identify Sims metallic uterine sound: note a 30 cm long stainless steel instrument with a 30-degree angulation approximately 5 cm from its rounded bulbous tip, with graduated calibration marks in centimetres or inches.
Demonstrate clinical use of the uterine sound: assess uterine cavity depth, confirm direction of flexion (anteverted or retroverted), and avoid sounding when pregnancy is suspected.

Compare with the female bladder sound: note a long chrome instrument with a continuous gentle curve, smooth round tip, and completely uncalibrated shaft, used to delineate the lower bladder margin before anterior colporrhaphy.

skill.exam.obg.instrument_uterine_graspi.normal: Sharp teeth aligned without crossing, functioning ratchet lock, clear graduated centimetre/inch markings on uterine sound, smooth unblemished shaft on bladder sound.
skill.exam.obg.instrument_uterine_graspi.abnormal: Sprung jaws, loose ratchet slipping under tension, blunted or broken teeth, bent shaft, missing calibration marks.
skill.exam.obg.instrument_uterine_graspi.significance: Primary surgical instrument station in viva and practical examinations; matching the correct grasping instrument to uterine status (non-pregnant vs pregnant cervix) prevents iatrogenic cervical laceration.
skill.exam.obg.instrument_uterine_graspi.practice: Distinguish between a Teale vulsellum, tenaculum, and Green-Armytage clamp, and explain why a tenaculum is avoided on a pregnant cervix.
pitfalls: Applying a sharp-toothed vulsellum or tenaculum to a soft, hypervascular pregnant cervix during suction evacuation, causing deep tearing.
Mistaking a bladder sound for a uterine sound, resulting in lack of depth calibration during sounding.
Using a uterine sound as a lever to force open a stenotic internal os, creating a false passage or myometrial perforation.

probes.q: How does a Teale vulsellum differ structurally from a single-tooth tenaculum?
probes.a: A vulsellum has multiple fine interlocking sharp teeth on each blade, whereas a tenaculum has a single sharp, inward-pointing hook on each blade.

probes.q: Why is a sponge-holding forceps used instead of a vulsellum or tenaculum to hold the cervix during suction evacuation in early pregnancy?
probes.a: The pregnant cervix is soft, vascular, and friable; toothed instruments like tenacula tear easily, whereas broad, fenestrated sponge forceps grasp gently without laceration.

probes.q: What physical characteristics distinguish a Sims metallic uterine sound from a female bladder sound?
probes.a: The Sims uterine sound has a 30-degree angulation near its blunt tip and is calibrated with graduated markings; a bladder sound has a gentle curve throughout and no calibration markings.

rubric.text: Differentiates multiple-toothed vulsellum, single-tooth tenaculum, and Green-Armytage clamp
Selects non-traumatic sponge-holding forceps over toothed instruments for pregnant cervix
Distinguishes angulated, calibrated uterine sound from curved, ungraduated bladder sound
Explains haemostatic role of Green-Armytage clamp during caesarean section

teach.heading: Structural features of uterine grasping instruments
teach.body:
Grasping forceps stabilize the cervix to allow intrauterine access.

The Teale vulsellum possesses 3 to 4 fine sharp teeth on each jaw that bite into the fibrous cervical stroma without crushing intervening tissue.

The single-tooth tenaculum provides intense focal traction but creates a deep puncture wound.

The Green-Armytage forceps has broad, heavy, serrated triangular blades designed to compress wide bleeding myometrial edges during caesarean hysterotomy.

teach.heading: Cervical grasping instruments comparison

rows: LSCS uterine cut edges for haemostasis

teach.heading: Uterine sound versus bladder sound
teach.body:
The Sims metal uterine sound is a 30 cm malleable chrome-plated instrument with a 30-degree bend located approximately 5 cm from its rounded bulbous tip.

The shaft is calibrated in inches or centimetres to measure uterocervical depth and determine flexion.

The female bladder sound has a continuous gentle curve, no sharp angles, and zero calibration markings, used to sound the bladder base and identify urethral diverticula or cystocele.

skill.exam.obg.instrument_dilators_curet.title: Cervical dilators, uterine curettes and evacuation instruments identification
skill.exam.obg.instrument_dilators_curet.oneLine: Identify Hegar dilators, Sims curette, Novak curette, Pipelle, Ovum forceps, and MVA syringe
skill.exam.obg.instrument_dilators_curet.why: Instrumental dilatation, curettage, and evacuation are central to gynaecological emergency and elective care. Differentiating double-ended Hegar dilators, sharp gynaecological versus blunt obstetric curettes, and vacuum aspiration cannulae prevents fatal myometrial perforation, cervical tearing, and missed incomplete abortion.

steps.text: Inspect Hegar cervical dilators: note double-ended solid stainless steel cylindrical rods with smooth, tapering, blunt ends and a gentle curve conforming to uterine flexion, with two diameter sizes stamped in millimetres on the central grip (e.g. 5/6, 7/8 mm).
Demonstrate pencil grip on Hegar dilator: hold between thumb and index finger, resting the hypothenar eminence on the patient s perineum to prevent sudden forceful thrusting through the internal os.

Inspect Sims double-ended uterine curette: identify the sharp oval loop at one end (used for non-pregnant diagnostic gynaecological scraping) and the blunt oval loop at the other end (used for gentle obstetric evacuation of retained products).
Inspect Novak biopsy curette: note a rigid metal cannula with a small side-cutting fenestration and serrated rim near its blunt tip, designed to connect to a syringe for endometrial sampling.

Inspect Pipelle endometrial suction curette: note a flexible 3.1 mm polypropylene tube with a distal side port and internal sliding piston that creates negative suction for painless outpatient biopsy.
Inspect ovum forceps: note long scissor-like instrument with spoon-shaped, fenestrated oval jaws without teeth, and specifically observe the complete absence of a ratchet lock on the handles.

Inspect manual vacuum aspiration (MVA) syringe: note 60 mL translucent syringe body, internal plunger with locking retaining clips, double push-button valves, and colour-coded semi-rigid Karman cannulae.

skill.exam.obg.instrument_dilators_curet.normal: Smooth dilator surfaces without burrs, undamaged sharp curette cutting loop, free movement of MVA plunger, airtight seal on MVA valve buttons.
skill.exam.obg.instrument_dilators_curet.abnormal: Chipped or notched dilator tip, bent curette stem, ovum forceps with missing pin or loose joint, cracked MVA plastic syringe barrel failing to hold vacuum.
skill.exam.obg.instrument_dilators_curet.significance: Viva spotter and practical OSCE station; correctly identifying instruments and their specific clinical safety rules ensures safe uterine evacuation and complication prevention.
skill.exam.obg.instrument_dilators_curet.practice: Select the appropriate Hegar dilator sequence for an 8-week gestation, assemble an MVA syringe, and differentiate sharp from blunt curettes.
pitfalls: Using a sharp uterine curette vigorously in a soft postpartum or post-miscarriage uterus, which easily shears off the basal endometrium or perforates.
Choosing an ovum forceps with a ratchet lock, which can crush and avulse the uterine wall if accidentally closed on myometrium.
Advancing Hegar dilators skipping multiple sizes (e.g. from 4 mm directly to 8 mm), causing cervical tears.

probes.q: Why does a standard ovum forceps lack a ratchet lock between its handles?
probes.a: To prevent accidental crushing, gripping, or avulsion of the uterine wall when grasping loose products of conception.

probes.q: What is the clinical distinction between the two ends of a double-ended Sims uterine curette?
probes.a: One end is sharp for gynaecological curettage of non-pregnant endometrium; the other end is blunt for obstetric evacuation of the soft pregnant uterus.

probes.q: How do the sizes on double-ended Hegar dilators correlate with clinical practice?
probes.a: The stamped numbers indicate the diameter in millimetres at each end, allowing gradual, sequential 1 mm dilatation of the internal os without tearing cervical tissue.

rubric.text: Identifies double-ended Hegar dilators and explains the pencil grip technique
Differentiates sharp gynaecological loop from blunt obstetric loop on Sims curette
Identifies ovum forceps and highlights the deliberate absence of a ratchet lock
Identifies MVA double-valve syringe and colour-coded flexible Karman cannulae

teach.heading: Design and safety features of Hegar dilators
teach.body:
Hegar dilators are solid double-ended metallic instruments with smooth, rounded, slightly curved tips.

Sizes range from 1/2 mm up to 19/20 mm, with each end increasing by 1 to 2 millimetres.

The slight curve conforms to the normal anteflexion or retroflexion of the uterine canal.

Dilators must be advanced in numerical order without skipping sizes, held lightly between the fingers like a pen to sense resistance at the internal os.

teach.heading: Comparison of uterine evacuation and sampling instruments
Novak curette versus Pipelle endometrial sampler
teach.body:
The Novak curette is a rigid metal cannula with a serrated lateral fenestration at its tip, connected to a 10 mL syringe for manual aspiration.

It has largely been replaced by the Pipelle endometrial suction curette.

The Pipelle is a 3.1 mm flexible polypropylene cannula with an internal piston that generates its own vacuum, allowing painless outpatient sampling without requiring local anaesthesia or cervical dilatation.

asks.text: Was your blood pressure raised before this pregnancy, or before 20 weeks this time? Chronic hypertension changes the diagnosis to superimposed disease.
Have you had raised blood pressure, fits, a very small baby, a stillbirth or an early delivery in a previous pregnancy? Ask what gestation each event happened at.
Do you have kidney disease, diabetes, lupus or antiphospholipid syndrome? Each of these raises the risk of pre-eclampsia.
Is this a twin or higher-order pregnancy? Multiple pregnancy stretches the placenta and raises the risk.
How old are you, and is this your first ongoing pregnancy? Age under 20 or over 35 and a first pregnancy both add risk.
Did your mother or sister have fits or very high blood pressure in pregnancy? A family history adds to the background risk.
Were you advised low-dose aspirin or calcium in this pregnancy, and did you take it regularly? This tells you both her risk category and her adherence.

skill.hx.preeclampsia.risk.oneLine: The background conditions that mark a woman as high risk
pitfalls: Stopping at this pregnancy and never asking about previous ones, when a prior hypertensive pregnancy is the strongest predictor.
Recording diabetes or kidney disease as incidental history without recognising them as pre-eclampsia risk factors.
Forgetting to ask about aspirin prophylaxis, which reveals whether someone already judged her high risk.
skill.hx.preeclampsia.risk.practice: Take the risk history from a booked antenatal mother: previous pregnancies with gestation and outcome, chronic hypertension, renal disease, diabetes, autoimmune disease, multiple pregnancy, and aspirin or calcium prophylaxis.

probes.a: Previous pre-eclampsia or eclampsia, chronic hypertension, kidney disease, diabetes, multiple pregnancy and antiphospholipid syndrome all raise the risk, and low-dose aspirin from early pregnancy lowers it in these women.
probes.q: Name three background conditions that raise the risk of pre-eclampsia.

probes.a: Because a previous hypertensive pregnancy is the strongest predictor of recurrence, and the gestation and severity of that episode guide how closely she is watched this time.
probes.q: Why does the previous obstetric history matter more than any other risk factor?

sources.locator: preeclampsia: clinicalPearls
Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

skill.hx.preeclampsia.risk.title: Risk factors for pre-eclampsia
skill.hx.preeclampsia.risk.why: Pre-eclampsia is not equally likely in every pregnancy. A small set of background conditions concentrates most of the risk, and finding them decides who gets aspirin prophylaxis, extra surveillance and a delivery plan made early rather than in a crisis.

asks.text: Headache: where is it, how severe, how long, and does it persist despite rest and paracetamol? A persistent severe headache is a warning symptom.
Vision: any flashing lights, blurring, blind spots or double vision? Visual disturbance reflects cerebral involvement.
Upper abdomen: any pain below the ribs on the right side or in the centre, or sudden nausea and vomiting? Right upper quadrant pain reflects liver involvement.
Swelling: sudden puffiness of the face or hands, rings or footwear suddenly tight, rapid weight gain? Distinguish this from gradual ankle swelling.
Urine: has the amount passed each day fallen noticeably? Oliguria signals renal involvement.
Fits: any episode of loss of consciousness with jerking of the limbs, tongue biting or incontinence, witnessed by family? Ask a relative directly.
Baby: are fetal movements normal in number, reduced, or absent? Reduced movements reflect uteroplacental compromise.
Blood pressure story: when was raised pressure first noticed, what were the readings, and was protein found in the urine at the same visit?

skill.hx.preeclampsia.symptoms.oneLine: The warning symptoms that herald fits and organ injury
pitfalls: Asking about headache without asking whether it persists despite rest and simple analgesia, which is what makes it a warning symptom.
Missing visual symptoms because the student never names flashing lights and blurring for the patient.
Forgetting to ask a relative about witnessed fits, which the woman herself cannot describe.
skill.hx.preeclampsia.symptoms.practice: Take the symptom history from a woman past 20 weeks with raised blood pressure: headache, visual symptoms, upper abdominal pain, sudden swelling, urine output, fits witnessed by family, and fetal movements, in that order.

probes.a: Persistent severe headache, visual disturbance such as flashing lights or blurring, right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, and sudden swelling of the face and hands are the warning symptoms that herald eclampsia.
probes.q: Name four warning symptoms of imminent eclampsia.

probes.a: Because the fit itself causes loss of consciousness with amnesia for the event, so only a witness can describe the jerking, tongue biting or incontinence that confirms it was a seizure.
probes.q: Why must you ask a relative about fits rather than the woman herself?

sources.locator: preeclampsia: clinicalPearls
Hypertension in pregnancy

skill.hx.preeclampsia.symptoms.title: Symptoms of pre-eclampsia and imminent eclampsia
skill.hx.preeclampsia.symptoms.why: Most women with pre-eclampsia feel well until late, and the symptoms that do appear are the direct voice of organ injury: brain, liver, kidney and placenta. Asking for them by name is what catches severe disease before the fit happens.

skill.presentation.preeclampsia.case.body: Present an obstetric case in a fixed order: mother and gestation first, then the story, the two-patient examination, the labs, the summary, and the delivery plan.
keyPoints: Open with particulars that carry obstetric meaning: age, parity, gestation, booking status and referral source. A 24-year-old unbooked primigravida at 34 weeks tells the listener the risk before the story starts.

Follow with the presenting complaints in the order that matters: pressure story, warning symptoms, urine output, fits, then fetal movements. End the history with antenatal care, previous pregnancies and medical background.

Report examination as mother then fetus: blood pressure with cuff and posture, oedema distribution, reflexes and clonus, abdominal findings with fundal height and lie, then fetal heart and liquor. State what was normal as well as what was not.

Read the laboratories as organs: platelets and haemolysis for blood, transaminases for liver, creatinine for kidney, then growth and Doppler for the fetus. Each value earns its place by changing the plan.

Close with the summary sentence and a concrete plan: stabilise, protect against fits, control pressure, steroids if preterm, and delivery by the route the mother and cervix allow, with postpartum surveillance stated, not assumed.
Keep a focused case to about two minutes. If it runs longer, the structure is wrong, not the content.
skill.presentation.preeclampsia.case.oneLine: Mother, gestation, two-patient findings, and a delivery plan
pitfalls: Presenting in the order the questions were asked rather than the fixed order the listener expects.
Reading every laboratory value without saying what each one means for delivery.
Ending at the diagnosis with no plan, when the plan is the whole point of an obstetric case.

probes.a: Particulars with parity and gestation, presenting complaints, antenatal and previous pregnancy history, maternal then fetal examination, laboratories read as organs, summary, and a delivery plan with postpartum surveillance.
probes.q: State the fixed order of an obstetric case presentation.

probes.a: Because the listener uses gestation to judge prematurity, severity to judge urgency, and fetal status to judge the route and timing, so without them the plan cannot be assessed.
probes.q: Why must gestation, severity and fetal status appear before the plan?

rubric.text: Presents in the fixed obstetric order
Reports maternal and fetal findings together
Ends with a delivery plan including postpartum surveillance

skill.presentation.preeclampsia.case.title: Presenting the pre-eclampsia case
skill.presentation.preeclampsia.case.why: An obstetric presentation is judged on whether the listener can make the delivery decision from it. Structure carries that decision: mother, gestation, both patients examined, and a plan that names delivery and the days after it.

asks.text: How old are you, have you had children, and is there anyone in the family with fibroids or an operation for them?
When did your periods start, and have you ever gone a long stretch without periods except in pregnancy?
Are you taking any hormones, have you used tamoxifen, and are you on any blood thinning medicine?
Tell me about each pregnancy: miscarriage, preterm birth, severe pain in mid pregnancy, heavy bleeding after delivery, or difficulty conceiving?
Have your periods stopped? If yes, when, and have you had any bleeding since they stopped?

skill.hx.fibroid.risk.oneLine: Age, parity, family, hormones and obstetric past that raise or lower the prior

probes.a: Reproductive age, nulliparity, obesity, early menarche and a family history of fibroids.
probes.q: Name three risk factors for fibroids.

probes.a: Anticoagulants and hormonal treatment worsen bleeding, and tamoxifen is associated with fibroid growth, so the drug history changes both the symptom burden and the options.
probes.q: Which drugs in her history change a fibroid presentation?

probes.a: Nulliparity raises the prior while higher parity lowers it, so a parous woman with the same lump and bleeding is slightly less likely to have fibroid than a nulliparous one, though the difference never rules anything out.
probes.q: How does parity shift your thinking before you examine her?

sources.locator: uterine_fibroid: clinicalPearls
Uterine leiomyoma (epidemiology and risk factors)

teach.heading: Who gets fibroids
points: Reproductive age is the dominant factor: lesions appear after menarche, grow through the thirties and forties, and regress after the menopause.
Nulliparity, obesity and early menarche raise the risk, while higher parity is protective.
A first degree relative with fibroids raises the risk substantially, so family history is never a formality here.
Black ethnicity carries higher prevalence and earlier onset, worth knowing when interpreting a young patient with severe disease.

teach.body:
Anticoagulants and hormonal medicines worsen the bleeding that brings her in, and tamoxifen is associated with fibroid growth, so list every drug before attributing the blood loss to the lesion alone.

A personal or family history of bleeding since menarche points to a coagulation disorder such as von Willebrand disease, which can coexist with fibroid and must be tested for rather than assumed absent.
teach.heading: Drugs and bleeding tendency that change the picture

teach.body:
Fibroids are linked with subfertility, miscarriage and preterm birth, and classically with acute red degeneration pain in mid pregnancy, so each pregnancy needs one line.

After the menopause the questions reverse: lesions should shrink, and any bleeding after the menopause needs exclusion of endometrial pathology rather than attribution to a known fibroid.
teach.heading: Obstetric and menopausal history

skill.hx.fibroid.risk.title: Risk factors and background that matter in fibroid
skill.hx.fibroid.risk.why: Age, parity, family history and drugs shift the pre-test probability before a hand is laid on her, and fertility wishes plus menopausal status decide which treatments are even on the table.

skill.presentation.fibroid.case.oneLine: Present a fibroid case the way a consultant expects to hear it

probes.a: Age, parity and fertility wishes, bleeding quantified in practical terms, uterine size in weeks with FIGO type, and the anaemia grade.
probes.q: What five facts must a fibroid presentation contain?

probes.a: Whether the uterus moves with the cervix, whether the fornices are free, and the size, consistency and mobility of the uterus.
probes.q: What bimanual findings does the consultant listen for?

rubric.text: Follows particulars, complaints, menstrual history, examination, investigations, diagnosis, plan
Quantifies bleeding, uterine size and haemoglobin rather than saying heavy, big or low
Justifies the plan from fertility wishes, FIGO type and anaemia

sources.locator: Presenting the case
uterine_fibroid: management

teach.body:
Open with age, parity and fertility wishes, then the chief complaints in her words with duration. Fertility wishes come first because they frame every option that follows.

Follow with the menstrual history in practical terms: pads per day, clots, flooding, night changes, days off work. Never present bleeding as heavy without these numbers behind it.
teach.heading: Opening and the menstrual history

teach.body:
Present the abdomen first: a firm midline mass of stated weeks size with an unreachable lower border. Then the speculum: healthy cervix with blood in the vault.

Then the bimanual: uterine size, firm nodular consistency, mobility with the cervix, and free fornices. Each negative, no cervical motion tenderness, no adnexal mass, is doing real work against PID and ovarian disease.
teach.heading: Examination findings in order

teach.body:
Close with investigations that matter: haemoglobin with iron studies, pregnancy test, ultrasound with FIGO type, and histology where taken. Then the diagnosis as one line.

Then the plan justified from three anchors: fertility wishes choose preservation or definitive care, FIGO type chooses the route, and anaemia decides the timing. End with what you will do about the anaemia before anything else.
teach.heading: Investigations, diagnosis and the justified plan

skill.presentation.fibroid.case.title: Presenting the fibroid case
skill.presentation.fibroid.case.why: A fibroid presentation is assessed on whether the listener can reconstruct the uterus and the plan from your words alone. Weeks size, FIGO type, anaemia grade and fertility wishes are the load bearing facts; without them the presentation is a story, not a case.

asks.text: Onset: when exactly did the bleeding start, and what were you doing at that moment? Was the start sudden, and did pain and bleeding begin together?
Amount: how much blood has come out? How many pads or cloths soaked, over how many hours, and did any clots pass? Ask what she uses and how often she changes it.
Colour and character: is the blood bright red or dark and stale looking? Dark blood that started with severe pain points towards a concealed separation rather than a fresh lower segment bleed.

Pain: describe the abdominal pain. Is it constant and severe with a hard tight feeling of the womb, or does it come and go like labour pains? Constant pain with a rigid womb is the voice of abruption.
Provocation: did anything precede it, a fall, a blow to the abdomen, a road accident, a sudden gush after the waters broke, or intercourse? Even a seemingly minor knock matters in late pregnancy.

Contractions and leak: is the womb tightening at intervals, and has watery fluid leaked per vaginam? Frequent tight contractions with little rest between them suggest hypertonus from a separating placenta.
Baby: when were fetal movements last felt normally, and are they reduced or absent now? Reduced or absent movements reflect that the separating placenta can no longer support gas exchange.

skill.hx.abruptio.bleed_pain.oneLine: Painful bleeding in late pregnancy: onset, amount, pain and provocation
pitfalls: Recording only the visible blood loss, which in concealed abruption badly underestimates the true haemorrhage.
Calling intermittent tightening labour without asking whether the womb ever fully relaxes between pains.
Skipping the trauma question because the fall seemed trivial, when minor abdominal trauma is a recognised trigger.
skill.hx.abruptio.bleed_pain.practice: Take the bleeding and pain history from a woman past 20 weeks with vaginal bleeding: suddenness, amount in pads, colour, constant versus intermittent pain, provocation or trauma, contractions, leak and fetal movements, in that order.

probes.a: Constant severe abdominal pain with a hard tender womb and dark bleeding, often with reduced fetal movements, points towards abruption, while painless bright red bleeding with a soft non tender womb points towards praevia.
probes.q: How does the bleeding and pain history separate abruptio placentae from placenta praevia?

probes.a: Because much of the blood can stay trapped behind the placenta as a concealed retroplacental clot, so the pads show only a fraction of what she has lost and the pulse, pressure and urine output tell the truer story.
probes.q: Why can a woman with only moderate visible bleeding already be in shock?

sources.locator: placental_abruption: clinicalPearls
Green-top Guideline 63: Antepartum haemorrhage

teach.body: Antepartum bleeding is any vaginal bleeding from viability onwards, and the very first fork in the history is pain. Painful bleeding with a tender tight womb is abruptio placentae until proven otherwise. Painless bleeding with a soft relaxed womb is placenta praevia until proven otherwise. That single distinction organises every question that follows.
teach.heading: Pain first, everything else after

points: Ask suddenness first: abruptio announces itself in minutes with pain, while praevia often starts unprovoked and without warning.
Ask amount in pads or cloths per hour, plus clots, because an estimate beats adjectives like spotting or heavy.
Ask colour: dark stale blood suggests blood trapped behind the placenta, bright red suggests a fresh lower segment source.
Ask whether the womb relaxes fully between tightenings; a womb that never softens is hypertonic from separation.
Ask about the baby every time: reduced or absent movements mean the placenta is failing at its main job.
teach.heading: Five questions that separate the two great causes

skill.hx.abruptio.bleed_pain.title: Bleeding and pain in suspected abruption
skill.hx.abruptio.bleed_pain.why: The amount of blood on the pads can lie, but the story rarely does. A history that pins down suddenness, pain, amount and provocation separates a concealed abruption from a praevia before a hand touches the abdomen, and it tells you how worried to be.

asks.text: Blood pressure: any raised pressure in this pregnancy or before it, swelling of face or hands, headache, visual flashing or fits? Hypertension and pre-eclampsia are the commonest predisposing conditions.

Previous pregnancies: any earlier abruption, stillbirth, preterm delivery, growth restricted baby or caesarean section? A prior abruption raises the recurrence risk, and a scarred uterus changes the differential towards rupture.
This pregnancy: twins or more, too much fluid around the baby, or waters breaking early with a sudden gush? Rapid decompression of an overdistended womb can shear the placenta off its bed.
Substances: tobacco in any form, beedi or cigarette smoking, chewing tobacco, alcohol, or cocaine? Smoking and cocaine injure the decidual vessels that later rupture.
Clotting and medical: any known clotting disorder, thrombophilia, diabetes, kidney disease or autoimmune illness? Ask what tablets she takes, especially aspirin or blood thinners.
Trauma and procedures: any fall, blow, accident, assault, external cephalic version or road travel on bad roads in recent days? Ask directly, because she may not connect a small knock to the bleed.

skill.hx.abruptio.risk.oneLine: The background that makes abruption more likely
pitfalls: Stopping at this pregnancy and never asking about a previous abruption or stillbirth, which is the strongest predictor of recurrence.
Asking about smoking but forgetting chewing tobacco, which is the commoner exposure in many Indian settings.
Missing chronic hypertension because all attention is on the bleeding, when it is part of the cause.
skill.hx.abruptio.risk.practice: Take the risk history from a woman with suspected abruption: pressure story, previous pregnancies and their outcomes, twins and fluid and early rupture, tobacco in every form, clotting and medical illness, and recent trauma, in that order.

probes.a: Hypertension and pre-eclampsia, a previous abruption, abdominal trauma, tobacco or cocaine use, twins or excess fluid with sudden decompression, early rupture of membranes, and clotting disorders.
probes.q: Name five risk factors for abruptio placentae.

probes.a: Because the decidual vessels were already fragile from high pressure or from smoking related injury, so a smaller trigger such as a minor fall or a sudden gush of fluid is enough to start the separation.
probes.q: Why does a hypertensive smoker abruption after seemingly minor trauma?

sources.locator: placental_abruption: clinicalPearls
Abruptio placentae

teach.body: Abruption begins when a maternal decidual vessel ruptures and blood splits the placenta from the womb. Anything that makes those vessels fragile or the placenta easier to shear raises the risk. Raised pressure injures the vessels, smoking injures them further, and a scarred or overdistended womb changes the mechanics of separation.
teach.heading: Fragile vessels plus shearing force

points: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, including pre-eclampsia, are the commonest background: control of pressure is prevention.
A previous abruption is the strongest single predictor, so every past pregnancy outcome must be recorded.
Twins, excess amniotic fluid and early rupture of membranes overdistend then suddenly decompress the womb.
Tobacco in any form and cocaine damage the decidual vessels directly.
Trauma, even a fall she calls minor, and clotting disorders complete the list to ask about.
teach.heading: Who to suspect before she bleeds

skill.hx.abruptio.risk.title: Risk factors for abruptio placentae
skill.hx.abruptio.risk.why: An abruption rarely comes from nowhere: the hypertensive mother, the previous stillbirth, the twin pregnancy or the recent fall were all visible beforehand. Knowing the risk list turns the history from a formality into a search, and it decides who is counselled and watched more closely.

asks.text: What do you eat on a normal day, do you eat meat or eggs, and do you drink tea with your meals? A vegetarian diet with tea at mealtimes sharply lowers iron absorption.

How many times have you been pregnant, how old were you at the first pregnancy, and how long after the last delivery did this pregnancy start? Teenage pregnancy, many births and a gap under two years all drain iron stores.
Is this a twin pregnancy? Two babies raise iron and folate demand well above a singleton pregnancy.
Were you told you had low blood in a previous pregnancy, did you bleed heavily after a delivery, and were your periods heavy before this pregnancy? Past loss predicts present anaemia.

Do you walk barefoot in the fields, were you given a deworming tablet after the first three months, and have you had fever with chills this pregnancy? Hookworm and malaria are treatable causes of anaemia here.
Do you have tuberculosis, kidney disease, thyroid disease or repeated infections? A long illness can keep anaemia from responding to iron alone.

Were you given iron and folic acid tablets at the health centre, how many do you take in a week, and what happens when you take them? Nausea and constipation are the common reasons tablets pile up untaken.

skill.hx.anaemia.risk.oneLine: The diet, pregnancies and parasites that concentrate the risk
pitfalls: Asking about diet as vegetarian or not and stopping there, without asking about tea with meals, which is the single most fixable eating habit.
Recording many previous pregnancies as background without recognising short gaps and teenage childbearing as the reason her stores never refilled.
Hearing that iron tablets were collected and assuming they were swallowed, when nausea is the usual reason they sit in a drawer.
skill.hx.anaemia.risk.practice: Take the background history from a booked antenatal mother with low haemoglobin: daily diet with tea habits, parity with gaps, twins, past anaemia and bleeding, barefoot work with deworming, chronic illness, and iron tablet adherence with reasons for missing.

probes.a: A vegetarian diet with tea at mealtimes, teenage pregnancy, many births with short gaps, twins, past anaemia or heavy bleeding, hookworm or malaria exposure, and chronic illness all raise the risk, and asking about iron tablet adherence shows whether prevention already failed.
probes.q: Name four background facts that raise the risk of anaemia in pregnancy.

probes.a: Because iron stores refill slowly over months, so a pregnancy that starts before the last one is repaid begins in deficit, and each further demand of twins or bleeding deepens it.
probes.q: Why does a short gap after the last delivery matter more than the number of children?

sources.locator: iron_deficiency_anemia: pathophysiology
Anaemia in pregnancy

skill.hx.anaemia.risk.title: Risk factors and background that matter in anaemia
skill.hx.anaemia.risk.why: Anaemia is not spread evenly across pregnancies. A small set of background facts, what she eats, how close her pregnancies are, whether she carries worms, and whether iron tablets are actually swallowed, concentrates most of the risk, and finding them decides whether she needs iron alone or iron plus deworming, diet change or a workup for chronic disease.

asks.text: Do you feel tired through the day, and has your capacity for housework or field work fallen? Fatigue that limits daily work is the commonest symptom of anaemia.
Do you get breathless climbing stairs or walking uphill, and does your heart pound after small effort? New breathlessness on effort with palpitations points to anaemia rather than normal pregnancy.
Do you feel giddy on standing, have you ever fainted, and do you get headaches? Postural giddiness with pallor suggests the haemoglobin has fallen substantially.
Do you crave clay, chalk, raw rice or ice? This craving, called pica, is a classic clue to iron deficiency even before the blood counts fall.

Do your legs feel restless or creeping at night, and do your nails break easily with cracks at the corners of the mouth or a sore tongue? Restless legs, brittle nails and a sore mouth all cluster with iron deficiency.
Have you bled from anywhere, piles, gums, nose, or spotting from below? Ongoing loss explains anaemia that diet alone cannot explain.
Have you had fever with shivering, burning while passing urine, or a cough? Fever and infection point away from simple iron deficiency and toward malaria or chronic disease.
Is the baby moving as before, and have you had any chest pain, fainting or swelling of the face? Falling movements, chest pain and fainting are red flags that need same-day assessment.

skill.hx.anaemia.symptoms.oneLine: Tired blood, its warning symptoms, and the red flags
pitfalls: Calling every tiredness of pregnancy normal and never asking about work capacity, which is the question that separates physiology from anaemia.
Missing pica because the mother is embarrassed to mention eating clay, so the most specific symptom is never volunteered.
Taking a symptom history without asking about the baby movements, forgetting this history has two patients.
skill.hx.anaemia.symptoms.practice: Take the symptom history from a pregnant woman with pallor: fatigue with work capacity, breathlessness with palpitations, giddiness, pica, restless legs with nail and mouth changes, bleeding, fever, and fetal movements with chest pain and fainting as red flags.

probes.a: Falling capacity for daily work, new breathlessness on effort with palpitations, giddiness on standing, pica for clay or ice, restless legs, and brittle nails with a sore tongue together build the symptom picture of iron deficiency.
probes.q: Name four symptoms that build the picture of anaemia in pregnancy.

probes.a: Chest pain, fainting, any vaginal bleeding, fever with shivering, and reduced fetal movements all need same-day assessment because they signal severe anaemia, an active cause, or a fetus already compromised.
probes.q: Which answers in this history are red flags, and what do they demand?

sources.locator: iron_deficiency_anemia: clinicalPearls
Anaemia in pregnancy

skill.hx.anaemia.symptoms.title: Symptoms of anaemia and red flags in pregnancy
skill.hx.anaemia.symptoms.why: Most anaemia in pregnancy announces itself through tiredness long before any crisis, but tiredness alone is also normal in pregnancy. A structured symptom history separates the two by asking about work capacity, effort tolerance and the small specific clues like pica, and it catches the red flags that move a mother from routine tablets to same-day care.

skill.present.anaemia.case.body: Present an obstetric anaemia case in a fixed order: mother and gestation first, then the story with cause, the two-patient examination, the blood results read as iron status, the severity grade, and the plan for mother and delivery.
keyPoints: Open with particulars that carry obstetric meaning: age, parity with gaps, gestation, booking status and diet. A 26-year-old unbooked G3P2 at 32 weeks with a 16-month gap tells the listener the cause before the story starts.

Follow with the presenting complaints in the order that matters: fatigue with work capacity, breathlessness with palpitations, pica, then bleeding and fever. End the history with tablets taken, deworming, previous pregnancies and medical background.

Report examination as mother then fetus: pallor grade with nail and mouth changes, pulse and pressure, oedema with chest signs, abdominal findings with fundal height and liquor, then fetal heart and movements. State what was normal as well as what was not.

Read the blood results as iron status: haemoglobin with grade, red cell size with ferritin, smear picture, then B12 with folate and stool with malaria. Each value earns its place by changing the plan.

Close with the summary sentence and a concrete plan: iron by the route her severity allows, deworming with diet counsel, transfusion only if she earns it, delivery where blood is available, and a follow-up haemoglobin date stated, not assumed.
Keep a focused case to about two minutes. If it runs longer, the structure is wrong, not the content.
skill.present.anaemia.case.oneLine: Mother, gestation, iron status, grade, and a plan
pitfalls: Presenting in the order the questions were asked rather than the fixed order the listener expects.
Reading every blood value without saying what each one means for iron replacement.
Ending at the diagnosis with no delivery plan, when blood availability at delivery is the whole point of grading her.

probes.a: Particulars with parity and gestation, presenting complaints with cause history, maternal then fetal examination, blood results read as iron status, severity grade, and a plan covering iron, deworming, transfusion threshold and delivery with a follow-up date.
probes.q: State the fixed order of an obstetric anaemia case presentation.

probes.a: Because the listener uses gestation to judge how little time iron has left to work, severity to judge the route of replacement, and fetal growth to judge whether the anaemia has already cost the baby, so without them the plan cannot be assessed.
probes.q: Why must gestation, severity and fetal growth appear before the plan?

rubric.text: Presents in the fixed obstetric order
Reports maternal and fetal findings together
Ends with an iron, transfusion and delivery plan with follow-up

sources.locator: iron_deficiency_anemia: management
Anaemia in pregnancy

skill.present.anaemia.case.title: Presenting the anaemia case
skill.present.anaemia.case.why: An obstetric anaemia presentation is judged on whether the listener can decide the route of iron and the place of delivery from it. Structure carries that decision: mother, gestation, both patients examined, iron status with grade, and a plan that names replacement, transfusion threshold and follow-up.

skill.hx.antenatal.symptoms.title: Symptoms of the current pregnancy
skill.hx.antenatal.symptoms.oneLine: Ordinary early symptoms first, then the danger symptoms, asked separately
skill.hx.antenatal.symptoms.why: Most early pregnancy symptoms are physiological and need only explanation, but a small set of symptoms marks a pregnancy that needs action that day. Asking the two groups separately stops a normal complaint hiding a dangerous one, and stops a dangerous one being dismissed as ordinary.

asks.text: Ask about the ordinary symptoms of early pregnancy one by one: nausea and vomiting and what time of day they come, heartburn, constipation, frequency of passing urine, tiredness, breast heaviness or tenderness, and any pica or unusual food craving.

Ask when she first felt the baby move, and whether movements have stayed regular since. First movements are usually felt around the middle of the pregnancy, earlier in a woman who has been pregnant before.

Ask the danger symptoms as a separate set, each with its own question: vaginal bleeding, leaking of fluid, persistent vomiting with inability to keep fluids down, fever, burning or pain while passing urine, reduced or absent fetal movements, severe headache with blurring of vision, sudden swelling of the face or hands, fits, and pain in the abdomen.

For every positive symptom, fix the onset, the course since it began, and what she has done about it: how many weeks pregnant she was when it started, whether it is getting better or worse, and whether she has sought care or taken any medicine for it.

skill.hx.antenatal.symptoms.practice: Take the symptom history from a partner playing a woman at twelve weeks with nausea and one danger symptom, and show that you asked the two groups separately.
pitfalls: Lumping ordinary and danger symptoms into one hurried question, so a red flag is never named.
Forgetting to ask about fetal movements once they should have begun.
Accepting persistent vomiting as ordinary morning sickness without asking about fluids, weight and urine output.

probes.q: Name four danger symptoms you must ask about separately at every antenatal visit.
probes.a: Vaginal bleeding, leaking of fluid, reduced or absent fetal movements, and severe headache with blurring of vision, together with fever, persistent vomiting, burning urination and sudden facial swelling.

probes.q: A woman at ten weeks reports vomiting several times a day but keeps fluids down and passes urine normally. What separates this from vomiting that needs urgent care?
probes.a: The ability to keep fluids down, normal urine output, no weight loss and no dehydration signs keep it in the ordinary range; inability to retain fluids, reduced urine, weight loss or a fast pulse move it to urgent care.

probes.q: She felt first movements two weeks ago and now reports they have stopped for a day. How do you respond?
probes.a: Treat absent movements after quickening as a danger symptom needing same-day assessment with fetal heart check and further testing, not reassurance alone.

sources.locator: diagnosis_pregnancy_antenatal_care_schedule: Signs symptoms hormones
Prenatal care: maternal symptoms and danger signs

skill.hx.antenatal.risk.title: Risk markers that change antenatal care
skill.hx.antenatal.risk.oneLine: Age, parity, previous outcomes and medical disease that move her to specialist care
skill.hx.antenatal.risk.why: Most pregnancies stay low risk and can be followed at a primary centre, but a short list of background markers predicts most serious complications. Finding them at the booking visit decides where she delivers, how often she is seen, and which extra tests she is offered, so missing them wastes the whole purpose of booking early.

asks.text: Ask her age and her obstetric score in full: number of pregnancies including this one, number of living children, and the outcome of each previous pregnancy with the gestation and birth weight where she remembers them.

Ask about previous pregnancy complications one by one: stillbirth or newborn death, preterm birth, a baby that grew poorly, high blood pressure or fits in pregnancy, heavy bleeding before or after birth, caesarean section or instrumental delivery, and diabetes detected in pregnancy.

Ask about medical disease before this pregnancy: high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid disease, heart disease, kidney disease, asthma or tuberculosis, epilepsy, sickle cell disease or thalassaemia, and any blood transfusion she has needed.

Ask about the present background: tobacco or alcohol use, consanguinity, age above 35 or below 18, a long gap or a very short gap since the last birth, twin pregnancy in the family or treatment taken to conceive, and whether she booked late with no care so far.

skill.hx.antenatal.risk.practice: Take the risk history from a partner playing a 32-year-old woman with one previous stillbirth and thyroid disease, and state whether she stays low risk and where she should deliver.
pitfalls: Recording parity as a number without the outcome of each previous pregnancy.
Asking about medical disease as one vague question instead of naming the diseases that change care.
Missing a previous stillbirth or preterm birth because the woman was not asked directly.

probes.q: Name four background markers that move a pregnancy out of the low risk group.
probes.a: Previous stillbirth, previous preterm birth, previous caesarean section, and medical disease such as hypertension, diabetes or thyroid disease, with age extremes and multiple pregnancy alongside them.

probes.q: Why do you ask the outcome of each previous pregnancy rather than just the number of children?
probes.a: Because a previous stillbirth, preterm birth, growth restricted baby or bleed predicts recurrence and changes surveillance, timing and place of delivery, while a bare count hides all of it.

probes.q: A healthy 24-year-old in her second pregnancy had a previous term vaginal birth with no complications. Where can she be followed?
probes.a: She stays low risk and can be followed at a primary centre with routine visits, provided each visit continues to find nothing new.

sources.locator: diagnosis_pregnancy_antenatal_care_schedule: High risk referral
Prenatal care: risk assessment

skill.presentation.antenatal.case.title: Presenting the antenatal booking case
skill.presentation.antenatal.case.oneLine: Mother, dates, risk, two-patient findings, and the plan to delivery
skill.presentation.antenatal.case.why: An antenatal case is presented to hand over two patients at once and the plan that keeps both safe. A fixed order lets the listener judge the dates, the risk group and the plan in under two minutes, and a story told in the order questions were asked hides exactly those three things.
skill.presentation.antenatal.case.body: Present an antenatal booking case in a fixed order: mother and dates first, then the story, the two-patient examination, the tests, the summary, and the plan to delivery.
keyPoints: Open with particulars that carry obstetric meaning: age, parity, gestation with how the dates were fixed, booking status and referral source. A 26-year-old booked primigravida at 12 weeks by certain dates tells the listener the risk before the story starts.

Follow with the presenting story in the order that matters: reason for this visit, ordinary symptoms, danger symptoms each answered, then antenatal care so far, previous pregnancies and medical background.

Report examination as mother then fetus: weight and blood pressure with cuff and posture, pallor and oedema, then abdominal findings with fundal height against gestation, lie and presentation where relevant, liquor, and fetal heart and movements. State what was normal as well as what was not.

Read the tests as answers: pregnancy test and dating scan for the dates, haemoglobin and blood group, urine protein and sugar, infection screening, thyroid and sugar testing where offered, and what each result changed.
Close with the summary sentence and a concrete plan: risk group, visit schedule, supplements and immunisation, counselling given, birth preparedness, and referral where the risk group demands it.
Keep a booking presentation to about two minutes. If it runs longer, the structure is wrong, not the content.
pitfalls: Presenting in the order the questions were asked rather than the fixed order the listener expects.
Stating a gestation without saying how the dates were fixed.
Ending at the diagnosis with no plan, when the plan to delivery is the whole point of a booking case.

probes.q: What is the fixed order of an antenatal case presentation?
probes.a: Mother with parity and gestation, presenting story, antenatal and previous pregnancy history, maternal then fetal examination, tests read as answers, summary, and the plan to delivery.

probes.q: Why must the presentation state how the dates were fixed?
probes.a: Because every later judgement about growth, preterm labour and post-term management rests on the dates, and dates from memory alone carry a different weight from dates confirmed by an early scan.

sources.locator: diagnosis_pregnancy_antenatal_care_schedule: Dating scan and EDD
Prenatal care: clinical examination

skill.hx.endometriosi.risk.title: Risk factors and background that matter in endometriosis
skill.hx.endometriosi.risk.oneLine: Family, menstrual pattern, parity, hormones and the surgical past
skill.hx.endometriosi.risk.why: Endometriosis clusters with a family history, early menarche with short cycles, and delayed childbearing, while higher parity and combined pill use lower the prior. Capturing that background before examining sets the prior that the fingers then test.

asks.text: How old were you at your first period, how many days apart do your periods come, and for how many days do you bleed?
Have you had children, at what age did you first give birth, and are you trying to conceive now? For how long?
Does your mother or sister have painful periods, difficulty conceiving, or an operation for chocolate cyst or fibroids?
Have you used birth control pills, injections or a hormonal coil, and did the pain ease while you used them?
Have you had any operation on the abdomen or pelvis, treatment for tuberculosis or pelvic infection, or a caesarean section?

teach.heading: Who carries the higher prior
points: A first degree relative with endometriosis raises the risk substantially, so family history is never a formality here.
Early menarche with short cycles means more lifetime retrograde flow, which the implantation theory links to deposits.
Nulliparity and delayed first birth raise the prior, while higher parity lowers it; the same pain in a parous woman weighs slightly less.
Prolonged combined pill use is protective, which is also why a pill trial that eased pain is retrospective evidence.

teach.heading: Drugs and the surgical past
teach.body:
Hormonal medicines mask the very symptoms you are chasing, so list every pill, injection and coil with dates before calling the pain absent. Prior GnRH analogue or danazol courses, and their side effects, shape what she will accept next.

A caesarean scar or laparoscopy scar that swells and pains with each period marks scar endometriosis. Prior surgery for chocolate cyst, pelvic infection or tuberculosis rewrites both the adhesions you will feel and the tubes you are trying to save.

probes.q: Name three risk factors for endometriosis.
probes.a: A first degree relative, early menarche with short cycles, and nulliparity with delayed childbearing.

probes.q: Why does the pill history matter in both directions?
probes.a: Pill use lowers the prior and masks symptoms, while pain that eased on pills proves hormone responsiveness.

probes.q: What in the surgical past changes your examination and plan?
probes.a: Prior cyst surgery, pelvic infection or caesarean section predict adhesions, tubal damage and scar deposits.

sources.locator: endometriosis_adenomyosis_chocolate_die: clinicalPearls
Endometriosis (epidemiology and risk factors)

skill.present.endometriosi.case.title: Presenting the endometriosis case
skill.present.endometriosi.case.oneLine: Present an endometriosis case the way a consultant expects to hear it
skill.present.endometriosi.case.why: An endometriosis presentation is assessed on whether the listener can grade the pain, picture the pelvis and choose the arm of treatment from your words alone. Quantified pain, fertility timeline, mobility with nodularity, and scan anchors are the load bearing facts.

teach.heading: Opening with pain and fertility
teach.body:
Open with age, parity, duration of trying and the pain story in her words with duration. Fertility wishes come first because they frame every option that follows.

Follow with the menstrual history in practical terms: pads per day, clots, days off work, analgesics per day. Never present pain as severe without these numbers behind it, and state plainly whether intercourse pains her.

teach.heading: Examination findings in order
teach.body:
Present the abdomen first: usually soft with only iliac fossa tenderness, stating that no mass reaches above the pubis. Then the speculum: healthy cervix with no discharge.

Then the bimanual: uterine version, mobility, tenderness, nodularity of the uterosacrals, and each fornix with the size and mobility of any mass. Each negative, no cervical motion tenderness, no discharge, is doing real work against PID.

teach.heading: Investigations, diagnosis and the justified plan
teach.body:
Close with investigations that matter: pregnancy test, ultrasound with ground glass size and junctional zone, CA-125 with AMH, and haemoglobin. Then the diagnosis as one line carrying both labels where both are met.

Then the plan justified from three anchors: today's priority of pain or conception chooses medical or fertility care, AMH and cyst size choose cystectomy or ablation, and anaemia decides the timing. End with what you will do about the anaemia before anything else.

probes.q: What five facts must an endometriosis presentation contain?
probes.a: Quantified pain, duration of trying, uterine mobility with nodularity, scan anchors and the anaemia grade.

probes.q: How does the presentation justify cystectomy over ablation?
probes.a: By anchoring AMH, cyst size and recurrence against the fertility priority already stated.

rubric.text: Follows particulars, pain quantified, fertility timeline, examination, investigations, diagnosis, plan
Quantifies pain, pads, analgesics, cyst size and haemoglobin rather than saying severe, big or low
Justifies the plan from pain versus conception priority, AMH with cyst size, and anaemia

asks.text: How many times have you given birth, and were any deliveries at home, prolonged, or assisted with instruments?
Have your periods stopped, and if so, at what age did they stop?
Do you have a long standing cough, constipation that needs daily straining, or work that needs lifting heavy loads?
Has your weight risen over the years, and does anyone in the family have a similar bulge or a hernia?
Have you had any operation on the uterus or vagina, and have you used hormones since the menopause?
Do you still wish to have children, and what contraception do you use at present?

skill.hx.genital.risk.oneLine: Parity, menopause, pressure factors and fertility wishes that set the prior

probes.a: Vaginal childbirth, ageing and the menopause, obesity, chronic cough, constipation with straining, and heavy lifting.
probes.q: Name four risk factors for genital prolapse.

probes.a: Because raised abdominal pressure drives descent, and treating cough and constipation with lighter work protects both pessary care and surgical repair.
probes.q: Why do you ask about cough, constipation and occupation in a woman with a bulge?

probes.a: The younger woman is counselled toward uterus sparing repair with fertility preserved, while the older unfit woman is managed with pessary and physiotherapy.
probes.q: Two women have the same stage III prolapse, one aged 32 wanting children and one aged 62 with heart disease. How does the history change the plan?

teach.heading: Parity and menopause carry the prior
points: Vaginal birth is the strongest risk factor: stretching and denervation of the levator muscles and endopelvic fascia during delivery weakens the supports for decades after.
Home deliveries, prolonged labour and instrumental delivery add trauma, so ask where and how each birth happened, not just how many.
Risk rises with age and after the menopause, as oestrogen loss thins the vaginal tissues and weakens connective tissue.
Higher parity raises the prior while nulliparity lowers it, though neither rules prolapse in or out on its own.

teach.body:
Chronically raised abdominal pressure drives descent: persistent cough, constipation with daily straining, heavy lifting at work, and obesity all add load to already weak supports.

Each of these can be treated or lightened, which is why they belong in the history and in the plan: weight, cough and constipation decide whether conservative care can hold and whether surgery will last.
teach.heading: Pressure, weight and bowels are the modifiable half

teach.body:
A younger woman who wants fertility preserved is a candidate for uterus sparing repair, while completed family opens vaginal hysterectomy with floor repair.

Fitness matters as much: heart disease, anaemia and poor mobility push toward pessary and physiotherapy, so ask about medical illness and drugs that raise surgical risk.
teach.heading: Fertility wishes and fitness frame the options

skill.hx.genital.risk.title: Risk factors and background that matter in genital prolapse
skill.hx.genital.risk.why: Parity, menopause and chronic pressure set the prior before examination, while fertility wishes and fitness decide which treatments are even available. A prolapse history that skips these ends with a stage but no plan.

skill.present.genital.case.oneLine: Present a prolapse case the way a consultant expects to hear it

probes.a: Age, parity, menopausal status and fertility wishes, the bulge with duration and diurnal pattern, the POP-Q points with the stage, and bladder, bowel and conjugal symptoms.
probes.q: What facts must a prolapse presentation contain?

probes.a: Which walls descend on straining, the state of the cervix and vault, any ulcer on the exposed part, uterine mobility with the cervix, and the POP-Q points with the stage.
probes.q: What examination findings does the consultant listen for?
