teach.body:
Open with age, parity, menopausal status and fertility wishes, then the bulge in her words with duration and what makes it worse through the day. Fertility wishes come early because they frame preservation against removal.

Follow with bladder, bowel and conjugal symptoms in that order, since each maps to a compartment and to an operation: leak on cough, incomplete emptying, and the need to press the bulge back.
teach.heading: Opening and the bulge history

teach.body:
Present the vulva first: lax perineum with the bulge seen on bearing down. Then the speculum: which walls descend, the state of the cervix and vault, and any ulcer or discharge on the exposed part.

Then the bimanual: uterine size, mobility with the cervix, and free fornices. Close the examination with the POP-Q points and the stage, since the stage is the number the plan hangs on.
teach.heading: Examination findings in order

teach.body:
Close with the investigations that matter: urine test, post-void residual, ultrasound with renal tract views where the prolapse is advanced, and cervical screening before surgery. Then the diagnosis as one line with compartment and stage.

Then the plan justified from three anchors: fertility wishes choose preservation or removal, fitness chooses pessary against surgery, and incontinence testing decides whether a continence procedure joins the repair.
teach.heading: Investigations, diagnosis and the justified plan

skill.present.genital.case.title: Presenting the genital prolapse case
skill.present.genital.case.why: A prolapse presentation is judged on whether the listener can picture the descent and the plan from your words alone. Compartment, stage, incontinence and fertility wishes are the load bearing facts; without them the presentation is a story, not a case.

skill.hx.infertility.trying.title: The trying history: duration, frequency and timing
skill.hx.infertility.trying.oneLine: How long they have tried, how often they meet, and whether a pregnancy ever began
skill.hx.infertility.trying.why: Infertility is defined by duration of regular unprotected intercourse, not by anxiety about conceiving. Pinning down months of trying, coital frequency, and any past conception separates a couple who need evaluation now from one who needs reassurance and timing advice.

asks.text: How long have you been having regular intercourse without any contraception, and have you ever conceived together, even if the pregnancy did not continue?
How often do you have intercourse, and do you time it to the fertile days in the middle of the cycle?
Have either of you used any contraception in the past, and when was it stopped?
Has the husband fathered a pregnancy with any partner before, and has the wife conceived before, whatever the outcome?
Is intercourse itself difficult: pain, vaginismus, erectile difficulty, or long separation for work?

teach.heading: Duration is the diagnosis
teach.body:
Infertility means no conception after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse. About 85 percent of couples conceive within 12 months and 95 percent within 24 months, so duration alone tells you whether this couple sits inside or outside the expected range.

Shorten the wait with age: start evaluation after 6 months of trying when she is over 35, and at once when she is over 40. Ask duration before anything else, since it frames every later question.

teach.heading: Frequency and the fertile window
teach.body:
The fertile window runs about 5 to 6 days before ovulation, and intercourse every 1 to 2 days through it gives the best chance. Many couples trying for a baby meet less often than they think, or only after the window has closed.

A basal temperature rise only confirms ovulation after it has happened, so it cannot be used to time intercourse. Ask what they actually do, not what they know.

teach.heading: Primary or secondary
points: Primary infertility means no conception ever; secondary means at least one prior pregnancy, whatever its outcome.
A past conception, even one ending in miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy, proves ovulation, sperm transport and fertilisation once worked.
Past contraception matters mainly for when it stopped; prolonged delay after stopping deserves the same workup, not reassurance.
Painful intercourse, vaginismus, erectile difficulty or work separation can explain everything and are volunteered only when asked directly.

probes.q: How is infertility defined, and what share of couples conceive within a year?
probes.a: No conception after 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse; about 85 percent conceive within 12 months and 95 percent within 24 months.

probes.q: When do you start evaluation earlier than 12 months?
probes.a: After 6 months of trying when she is over 35, and immediately when she is over 40.

probes.q: A couple times intercourse by the basal temperature rise and still fail. What is wrong with their method?
probes.a: The temperature rise only confirms ovulation after it has happened, so it cannot prospectively time intercourse; advise intercourse every 1 to 2 days through the fertile window instead.

skill.hx.infertility.risk.title: Risk factors and background that matter in infertility
skill.hx.infertility.risk.oneLine: Age of both partners, ovulation clues, tubal risks, weight, habits and drugs
skill.hx.infertility.risk.why: Most infertility is explained by a small set of background facts: her age, whether she ovulates, whether her tubes are scarred, his sperm production, and the habits and drugs acting on both. Asking these systematically is what stops the workup chasing one partner while the answer sits with the other.

asks.text: How old are both of you, and has there been rapid weight gain or loss, or heavy exercise and dieting?
Are her periods regular and monthly, is there milk leaking from the breasts, excess hair, acne, or thyroid swelling or tablets?
Has she had pelvic infection with discharge and lower abdominal pain, tuberculosis treatment, abdominal or pelvic surgery, or a ruptured appendix?
Do either of you smoke or chew tobacco, drink alcohol, use cannabis or opioids, and is he on testosterone supplements or medicines for fits, pressure or sugar?
Has he had mumps with testicular swelling, undescended testes, hernia or hydrocele surgery, or injury and heat exposure to the testes?
Is there diabetes, thyroid disease, early menopause or consanguinity in the family, and what work do both of you do?

teach.heading: Age first, of both
teach.body:
Her age dominates prognosis: fecundability falls about 14 percent by 34 to 35, about half by 40 to 41, and further after 42, mostly from chromosomal errors in ageing oocytes. No comparable fall occurs in men under 50.

Record his age too, since paternal age over 40 is linked with poorer outcomes, but never let a young husband reassure you about a 39 year old wife.

teach.heading: Ovulation and tubal clues
points: Regular monthly periods with premenstrual symptoms usually mean ovulation; long irregular gaps point to anovulation, most often polycystic ovary syndrome.
Galactorrhoea, hirsutism, acne and thyroid signs each name an endocrine cause: prolactin, androgens and thyroid hormone respectively.
Pelvic inflammatory disease, treated tuberculosis, pelvic surgery and ruptured appendix all scar tubes; endometriosis with painful periods scars and distorts as well.
Low weight with heavy exercise shuts ovulation down from the hypothalamus, while obesity blunts it from the ovary; both are reversible causes.

teach.heading: His history and shared habits
teach.body:
Male factors contribute to about half of couples, alone or combined, so his history is never optional: mumps orchitis, undescended testes, hernia surgery, heat and toxin exposure, and drugs that suppress sperm production, including exogenous testosterone.

Smoking, excess alcohol, cannabis and severe obesity impair fertility in both partners and are modifiable before any test is ordered. List every drug either partner takes before attributing the failure to disease.

probes.q: Name three background facts that raise the prior for infertility before any test.
probes.a: Her age over 35, irregular anovulatory cycles, and a past pelvic infection or pelvic surgery scarring the tubes.

probes.q: Which drugs and habits in his history can suppress sperm production?
probes.a: Exogenous testosterone, some antihypertensives and anticonvulsants, smoking, heavy alcohol, cannabis and severe obesity.

probes.q: She is 29 with regular cycles and he is 45 with normal semen. Who carries the higher age risk, and why?
probes.a: She does not: fecundability falls steeply with her age from the mid thirties through oocyte chromosomal errors, with no comparable fall in men under 50, though paternal age over 40 still worsens outcomes.

skill.present.infertility.case.title: Presenting the infertile couple
skill.present.infertility.case.oneLine: Present both partners, duration and frequency, examination, workup and plan
skill.present.infertility.case.why: An infertility presentation fails when it reports only the wife: the consultant cannot judge the couple from half the data. Duration of trying, coital frequency, both examinations and both halves of the workup are the load bearing facts; without them the presentation is a story, not a case.

teach.heading: Opening with both partners
teach.body:
Open with both ages, occupation and separation history, then duration of regular unprotected intercourse with coital frequency through the fertile window. State primary or secondary infertility and any past conception with its outcome.

Follow with her menstrual pattern in exact terms and his relevant past: mumps orchitis, undescended testes, hernia surgery, heat exposure and every drug either partner takes.

teach.heading: Examination of both
teach.body:
Present her general examination first: weight and body mass index, hirsutism and acne, galactorrhoea, thyroid signs and pelvic findings. Then his: build, secondary sexual characters and testicular examination.

Each negative is doing real work: regular cycles argue for ovulation, a normal semen analysis removes half the differential, and free fornices with a mobile uterus argue against tubal and endometriotic disease.

teach.heading: Workup, diagnosis and the justified plan
teach.body:
Close with the three workup limbs and what each showed: semen analysis, proof of ovulation with ovarian reserve, and tubal with uterine assessment. Then the diagnosis as one line naming the factor and the side.

Then the plan justified from anchors: modifiable habits first, ovulation induction for anovulation, surgery for tubal or cavity disease, assisted techniques where simpler measures fail, with referral thresholds stated.

rubric.text: Reports both partners with ages, duration of trying and coital frequency
States her ovulatory and pelvic findings and his genital examination
Justifies the plan from the identified factor, her age and what simpler measures have done

probes.q: What facts must an infertility presentation contain that most gynaecology presentations do not?
probes.a: Both partners with ages, duration of regular unprotected intercourse, coital frequency, his genital examination and his semen analysis.

probes.q: What examination negatives does the consultant listen for, and what does each exclude?
probes.a: Regular cycles with no galactorrhoea or hirsutism argue for ovulation without endocrine disease; normal testicular examination with normal semen removes male factor; free fornices argue against tubal and endometriotic disease.

asks.text: How old were you when your periods started, and have your cycles ever stayed regular for a full year at a stretch?
Tell me about your weight since your teenage years: slow steady gain, sudden gain, and everything you have tried in order to lose it.
Among your mother, sisters and aunts, is there anyone with irregular periods, excess facial hair, difficulty conceiving, or diabetes?
List every medicine you take, including hormonal pills, thyroid tablets, fits medicines, mind medicines, steroids and skin creams.
Has any hair growth, acne, hair thinning or voice change arrived suddenly or worsened very fast over the last few months?

skill.hx.pcos.risk.oneLine: Family, weight trajectory, drugs and tempo that raise or lower the prior

probes.a: A first degree relative with irregular periods, hirsutism or subfertility, and a family background of type 2 diabetes or obesity.
probes.q: What family history raises the prior for PCOS?

probes.a: Valproate, antipsychotics and steroids can disturb cycles and weight, while combined hormonal contraception masks the natural cycle and hides the oligomenorrhoea you are trying to assess.
probes.q: Which drugs in her history change a PCOS presentation?

probes.a: Gradual onset around menarche with years of slowly worsening oligomenorrhoea fits PCOS, while sudden or rapidly progressive virilisation points away from PCOS toward an androgen secreting tumour and needs urgent endocrine review.
probes.q: How does tempo shift your thinking before you examine her?

sources.locator: polycystic_ovary_syndrome: clinicalPearls
Polycystic ovary syndrome (risk factors and aetiology)

teach.body:
PCOS often declares itself around menarche with cycles that never settle into a regular pattern, then years of slowly lengthening gaps. That gradual tempo is itself informative, and it is the opposite of the sudden virilisation that should alarm you.

A first degree relative with irregular periods, excess hair or difficulty conceiving raises the prior substantially, and so does a family background of type 2 diabetes and obesity, since insulin resistance runs in the same households.
teach.heading: Whose prior is raised

teach.body:
Valproate, many antipsychotics and systemic steroids can all disturb cycles, weight and hair growth, so list every drug before attributing the picture to PCOS alone. Hormonal contraception needs special care: it imposes a regular withdrawal bleed that hides the natural oligomenorrhoea you are trying to assess.

Ask directly about sudden change. Hair growth, acne, scalp thinning or voice deepening that arrives over weeks to months, with clitoral enlargement or breast shrinkage, points away from PCOS toward an androgen secreting tumour and needs urgent endocrine review rather than routine reassurance.
teach.heading: Drugs and tempo that change the meaning
What else to ask before you examine
points: Fertility wishes and timeline, since they choose between cycle control now and ovulation induction later.
Usual diet, sugary drinks, daily activity and screen time, because lifestyle is the first line treatment and the history is where it starts.
Snoring, daytime sleepiness and low mood or anxiety, which are common fellow travellers and shape the plan as much as the periods do.
Smoking and alcohol, which add cardiovascular risk to a syndrome that already carries it.

skill.hx.pcos.risk.title: Risk factors and background that matter in PCOS
skill.hx.pcos.risk.why: Family history, weight trajectory, drugs and tempo shift the pre-test probability before a hand is laid on her, and fertility wishes plus metabolic risk decide which treatments are even on the table.

skill.present.pcos.case.oneLine: Present a PCOS case the way a consultant expects to hear it

probes.a: Age and fertility wishes, cycle pattern quantified in weeks and gaps, the two or three Rotterdam features with what excludes the mimics, and the metabolic screen.
probes.q: What five facts must a PCOS presentation contain?

probes.a: Whether the Rotterdam features are clinical or biochemical, which mimics were excluded and how, and what the plan is for cycles, hair, fertility and long term risk.
probes.q: What does the consultant listen for after the examination findings?

States which two Rotterdam features are present and names the exclusions that were checked
Justifies the plan from fertility wishes, endometrial protection and metabolic risk

teach.body:
Open with age, marital and fertility context, and body weight category, since all three shape the plan. Then quantify the cycles in practical terms: interval range, longest gap, number of bleeds a year, and any prolonged amenorrhoea with later heavy bleeding.

Name the hyperandrogenic features next with their course: where the hair grows and how it is managed, acne and scalp thinning, and the weight story since adolescence. Tempo matters here: gradual since menarche fits PCOS, sudden virilisation does not.
teach.heading: History in Rotterdam order

teach.body:
Give the examination as positives and relevant negatives: weight category, blood pressure, acne and hair pattern, acanthosis, and a normal pelvic examination with no virilisation and no palpable mass. State plainly that the ovaries are usually not reliably felt, so a normal bimanual examination neither confirms nor excludes PCOS.

Close with investigations grouped by job: exclusions checked, androgens found, morphology seen, metabolic screen done. Then the Rotterdam statement itself, the phenotype in plain words, and a plan split four ways: cycles and endometrial protection, hair and skin, fertility, and long term metabolic follow up.
teach.heading: Examination, investigations and the close

skill.present.pcos.case.title: Presenting the PCOS case
skill.present.pcos.case.why: A PCOS presentation that does not name which Rotterdam features are present, which mimics were excluded, and what the fertility wishes are leaves the consultant unable to judge the diagnosis or the plan, so this order exists to make all three explicit.

asks.text: When did the bleeding start, and how many weeks pregnant are you now? A first bleed in the second half of pregnancy frames everything that follows.

Did the bleeding come with any pain in the abdomen or back, any tightening of the uterus, or was it completely painless? Painless bleeding points toward praevia while pain with a tense uterus points toward abruption.
What did the blood look like: bright red or dark, with clots or without? Bright red fresh blood fits a low placental edge; dark blood suggests older or concealed bleeding.
How much was lost: how many pads or cloths were soaked, were clothes or bedding stained, and did you feel faint, dizzy or breathless? Amount and symptoms grade the emergency.
Is this the first bleed or has it happened before, and is each episode heavier than the last? Praevia typically bleeds repeatedly, often more heavily each time.
What were you doing when it started: resting, after intercourse, after straining or a fall, and what did you do next? Note anything that provoked it and whether rest slowed it.
Has there been any watery leaking, unusual discharge, fever, or injury? Leaking suggests ruptured membranes, discharge points to a local cause, and trauma changes the differential.
How are the baby movements since the bleeding began: normal, reduced or absent? Fetal wellbeing is half the assessment in any antepartum bleed.

skill.hx.placenta.bleeding.oneLine: Painless bright red bleeding: when it started, how much, how often, and what came with it
pitfalls: Recording the bleed without asking about pain, when painless versus painful is the single fastest separator of praevia from abruption.
Accepting heavy or light as an answer instead of counting soaked pads and asking about faintness, so the severity is never graded.
Forgetting to ask about fetal movements after the bleed, leaving the second patient unassessed.
skill.hx.placenta.bleeding.practice: Take the bleeding story from a woman past the middle of pregnancy with vaginal bleeding: onset and gestation, pain, colour and clots, amount with symptoms, recurrence, provocation, leaking or discharge, and fetal movements since, in that order.

probes.a: Onset with gestation, painless or painful character, bright red colour with or without clots, amount counted in soaked pads with faintness, recurrence with worsening episodes, provocation, leaking or discharge, and fetal movements since the bleed.
probes.q: List what the bleeding story must capture in suspected placenta praevia.

probes.a: Because a painless bleed from a low placenta leaves the uterus soft and relaxed, while abrupt separation makes it tense and tender with pain, so the pain question separates the two commonest causes at the bedside.
probes.q: Why is the pain question the most discriminating one in antepartum bleeding?

Placenta previa

skill.hx.placenta.bleeding.title: The bleeding story in suspected placenta praevia
skill.hx.placenta.bleeding.why: In antepartum bleeding the story examines the patient before your hands do: painless or painful, fresh or dark, first or repeated. Asking it in a fixed order is what separates praevia from abruption before a single examination step.

asks.text: Have you had a caesarean section or any other operation on the uterus, such as removal of a fibroid or repair after a rupture? Scarred muscle is where abnormal implantation takes hold.
Have you had bleeding from a low placenta in a previous pregnancy, or a previous pregnancy with a placenta that needed active management? Praevia recurs.
How many pregnancies and births have you had, and how old are you? Higher parity and older maternal age both raise the background risk.
Is this a twin or higher order pregnancy, and did it follow fertility treatment? Multiple gestation and assisted conception both predispose to low implantation.
Do you smoke tobacco or use it in any form, and did you smoke in earlier pregnancies? Smoking is a modifiable risk factor for praevia.
Have you had an early scan in this pregnancy that mentioned a low placenta, and were you asked to return for a repeat scan? A mid trimester low placenta often resolves and must be rechecked.
What is your blood group, and have you ever received anti-D immunoglobulin after a bleed, a procedure or a delivery? Rhesus status decides prophylaxis after every bleed.

skill.hx.placenta.risk.oneLine: The scarred uterus and the background that favour low implantation
pitfalls: Taking the surgical history as caesarean yes or no, without asking how many sections and whether the placenta lies over the scar this time, which is the accreta question.
Recording parity as a number without recognising multiparity itself as a risk factor for praevia.
Never asking the blood group, so anti-D prophylaxis after the bleed is missed in a rhesus negative woman.
skill.hx.placenta.risk.practice: Take the risk history from a woman with antepartum bleeding: uterine surgery with number of sections, previous praevia, parity and age, twins and fertility treatment, tobacco use, early scan findings with repeat imaging, and blood group with anti-D history.

probes.a: Previous caesarean section or other uterine surgery, previous praevia, multiparity, advanced maternal age, multiple pregnancy, assisted reproduction, and smoking.
probes.q: Name four risk factors for placenta praevia.

probes.a: Because implantation over scarred muscle can invade through deficient decidua into the myometrium, turning a praevia into an accreta spectrum with torrential bleeding at delivery.
probes.q: Why does a previous caesarean change a praevia from routine to high risk?

sources.locator: placenta_praevia: clinicalPearls
Placenta praevia and placenta accreta

skill.hx.placenta.risk.title: Risk factors for placenta praevia
skill.hx.placenta.risk.why: Praevia is a disease of where the placenta implants, and implantation follows scarring, parity and age. A risk history that names the scar count and the blood group is what triggers accreta surveillance and anti-D before the next bleed.

keyPoints: Open with particulars that carry obstetric meaning: age, parity with scar count, gestation, booking status and referral source. A 27 year old G3 with one previous section at 32 weeks tells the listener the risk before the story starts.

Follow with the bleeding story in the order that matters: onset and gestation, painless character, colour and amount, recurrence, provocation, and fetal movements since. End the history with antenatal scans, previous pregnancies and the risk background.

Report examination as mother then fetus, and state plainly that no vaginal examination was done: pallor and vitals with stability, soft non tender uterus, fundal height against dates, lie and presentation with engagement, then fetal heart and liquor. State what was normal as well as what was not.

Read the scan and laboratories as answers: placental edge distance from the internal os on transvaginal scan, anterior or posterior with relation to any scar, haemoglobin with group and crossmatch readiness, coagulation where bleeding was heavy, and the fetal trace.

Close with the summary sentence and a concrete plan: pelvic rest, steroids if preterm, anti-D if rhesus negative, inpatient observation or referral to a unit with blood and newborn care, and planned caesarean with accreta preparation where indicated.
Keep a focused case to about two minutes. If it runs longer, the structure is wrong, not the content.
skill.present.placenta.case.oneLine: Mother, gestation, bleeding story, two-patient findings, and a delivery plan
pitfalls: Presenting in the order the questions were asked rather than the fixed order the listener expects.
Omitting to say that vaginal examination was avoided, when that avoidance is a key safety decision the examiner marks.
Ending at the diagnosis with no plan, when the plan is the whole point of an antepartum bleeding case.

probes.a: Particulars with parity, scar count and gestation, the bleeding story, antenatal and risk history, maternal then fetal examination with no vaginal examination stated, scan and laboratories read as answers, summary, and a delivery plan with referral and postpartum vigilance.
probes.q: State the fixed order of a placenta praevia case presentation.

probes.a: Because gestation decides steroids and timing, stability decides resuscitation and referral, and fetal status with placental position decides the route, so without them the plan cannot be assessed.
probes.q: Why must gestation, stability and fetal status appear before the plan?

rubric.text: Presents in the fixed obstetric order
States that vaginal examination was avoided and why
Ends with a delivery plan including referral and blood readiness

skill.present.placenta.case.title: Presenting the placenta praevia case
skill.present.placenta.case.why: An antepartum bleeding presentation is judged on whether the listener can make the delivery decision from it. Structure carries that decision: mother, gestation, the bleed, both patients examined without a vaginal examination, and a plan that names blood, referral and delivery.

asks.text: How old are you, and have your periods stopped? If they have stopped, when was the last one, and has there been any bleeding since?
When did your periods begin, and have you ever gone months without bleeding except in pregnancy? Have you noticed weight gain, new facial hair, or acne?
Do you bruise easily, bleed for a long time after cuts or tooth removal, or suffer frequent nosebleeds? Did you bleed heavily after any delivery?
Are you taking any blood thinning medicine, hormonal tablets or injections, or thyroid medicine? Do you use a copper intrauterine device?
Tell me about each pregnancy: miscarriage, difficulty conceiving, heavy bleeding after delivery, or preterm birth?
Is there anyone in the family with heavy periods, a known bleeding disorder, fibroids, or cancer of the uterus or bowel at a young age?

skill.hx.abnormal.risk.oneLine: Age, cycle pattern, bleeding tendency, drugs and family that set the prior

probes.a: Adolescence with anovulation or a bleeding disorder, reproductive years with structural lesions, and perimenopause with anovulation and hyperplasia risk.
probes.q: How does age change the likely cause of abnormal bleeding?

probes.a: Anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs, hormonal medicines, tamoxifen, and the copper intrauterine device, which increases menstrual loss while the levonorgestrel system reduces it.
probes.q: Which drugs and devices in her history can cause or worsen the bleeding?

probes.a: Easy bruising, prolonged bleeding after cuts or dental work, frequent nosebleeds and heavy bleeding after delivery point toward a coagulopathy such as von Willebrand disease.
probes.q: What history suggests a bleeding disorder rather than a uterine cause?

sources.locator: abnormal_uterine_bleeding_and_palm_coein_classification: clinicalPearls
Abnormal uterine bleeding (risk factors and history)

teach.body:
In adolescence, most abnormal bleeding comes from anovulation in the first years after menarche, but a bleeding disorder is the important alternative: heavy bleeding from the very first period should always raise that question.

In the reproductive years, structural lesions dominate the prior: polyps, adenomyosis and fibroids. In perimenopause, cycles shorten and anovulation returns, and unopposed oestrogen over years raises the risk of hyperplasia. After the menopause, any bleeding is abnormal until proven otherwise, and cancer must be excluded first.
teach.heading: Age sets the prior

teach.body:
Anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs worsen any menstrual loss, so list every blood thinner before attributing the bleeding to the uterus.

Hormonal medicines, missed pills, injectables and implants commonly cause irregular spotting, especially in the first months. The copper device increases menstrual volume and cramping, while the levonorgestrel system usually lightens periods. Tamoxifen stimulates the endometrium and needs a bleeding history of its own.
teach.heading: Drugs and devices that bleed
The coagulopathy screen
points: Ask about easy bruising, bleeding gums, and nosebleeds that are frequent or hard to stop.
Ask how long cuts bleed, and about prolonged bleeding after tooth removal, surgery or childbirth.
Ask whether heavy periods have occurred since menarche, which favours an inherited disorder over an acquired one.
Ask about thyroid symptoms, weight change, galactorrhoea and features of polycystic ovary syndrome, which point to ovulatory causes.

skill.hx.abnormal.risk.title: Risk factors and background in abnormal uterine bleeding
skill.hx.abnormal.risk.why: Abnormal bleeding has nine FIGO categories, and the history is what narrows them before a finger is laid on the patient. Age, drugs and a structured bleeding screen together decide whether the next step is a scan, a biopsy, or a clotting test.

skill.present.abnormal.case.oneLine: Present an abnormal bleeding case the way a consultant expects to hear it

probes.a: Age and menopausal status, bleeding quantified in FIGO terms of frequency, regularity, duration and volume, uterine findings, and the anaemia grade.
probes.q: What six facts must an abnormal bleeding presentation contain?

probes.a: The PALM-COEIN category assigned with its evidence, the endometrial assessment, and the plan justified from fertility wishes, lesion site and anaemia.
probes.q: What does the consultant listen for after the examination findings?

rubric.text: Follows particulars, complaints, menstrual history in FIGO terms, examination, investigations, diagnosis, plan
Quantifies bleeding by frequency, regularity, duration and volume, uterine size in weeks, and haemoglobin
Assigns a PALM-COEIN category with evidence and justifies the plan from fertility wishes and anaemia

sources.locator: Presenting the case
abnormal_uterine_bleeding_and_palm_coein_classification: clinicalPearls

teach.body:
Open with age, parity, menopausal status and fertility wishes, then the chief complaints in her words with duration. Fertility wishes come early because they frame every option that follows.

Follow with the menstrual history in FIGO terms: how often periods come, how regular they are, how many days they last, how heavy they are in practical terms of pads, clots, flooding and nights disturbed, and any bleeding between periods or after intercourse.
teach.heading: Opening and the menstrual history

teach.body:
Present the general examination first: pallor and the anaemia grade, vitals with any postural change, weight and thyroid signs.

Then the abdomen: any palpable uterus with its weeks size. Then the speculum: whether blood or a polyp is seen and whether the cervix looks healthy. Then the bimanual: uterine size, shape, mobility with the cervix, tenderness, and whether the fornices are free. Each negative is doing real work against pregnancy, infection and ovarian disease.
teach.heading: Examination findings in order

teach.body:
Close with the investigations that matter: haemoglobin with iron studies, pregnancy test, thyroid function, ultrasound with what it showed, cavity assessment where done, and histology with what it excluded.

Then the diagnosis as one line with its PALM-COEIN category and the evidence for it. Then the plan justified from three anchors: fertility wishes choose preservation or definitive care, the category chooses the medical or surgical route, and anaemia decides the timing. End with what you will do about the anaemia before anything else.
teach.heading: Investigations, diagnosis and the justified plan

skill.present.abnormal.case.title: Presenting the abnormal bleeding case
skill.present.abnormal.case.why: An abnormal bleeding presentation is assessed on whether the listener can reconstruct the bleeding pattern, the uterus and the plan from it. FIGO terms for the history and a PALM-COEIN category for the diagnosis are what make that reconstruction possible.

skill.hx.breech.risk.title: Background that keeps a baby breech
skill.hx.breech.risk.oneLine: The previous pregnancies and uterine factors that explain why this baby did not turn
skill.hx.breech.risk.why: A breech at term is rarely random: a previous breech, more than one fetus, extra liquor, a low placenta, or a crowded uterus each raise the chance, and each changes what you offer next. Asking the background first is what stops an ECV being attempted where it should never have been tried.

asks.text: Have you had a baby that lay bottom-down before, or a previous premature birth? A past breech and past prematurity both recur, and the gestation of each earlier birth decides how this pregnancy is timed.
Is this a twin pregnancy, or have you been told there is extra water around the baby? More than one fetus and extra liquor both keep the presenting part high and mobile.
Have you had any bleeding in this pregnancy, and has anyone said the placenta lies low? A low placenta occupies the lower segment where the head should settle.

Do you have fibroids, or have you had any operation on the uterus such as a caesarean section or a surgery for a fibroid? A scarred or crowded uterus both limits turning and affects the delivery decision.
Did your waters leak early at any point, or did liquor drain suddenly in a gush? Sudden decompression with a high presenting part is the setting in which the cord slips down.
Was any anomaly seen in this baby or in a previous baby? Some fetal conditions present with persistent breech, so this question is asked routinely, not as an accusation.
Were you given anything to turn the baby, or advised any procedure for the breech before today? This tells you what has already been tried and what she understood of it.

skill.hx.breech.risk.practice: Take the risk background from a mother at 37 weeks with a breech: previous breech or preterm births with gestations, twins, bleeding with placental site, fibroids or uterine surgery, liquor history, and anything already tried for the breech.
pitfalls: Asking only about this pregnancy and never about previous breeches or preterm births, when recurrence is the strongest background clue.
Recording a fibroid or a previous caesarean as incidental history without recognising each as a reason ECV or vaginal birth may be unsuitable.
Forgetting to ask about bleeding and placental site, which is how an ECV gets attempted over a low placenta.

probes.q: Name four background factors that keep a baby breech.
probes.a: Prematurity, more than one fetus, extra liquor, a low placenta, and a crowded or unusually shaped uterus such as with fibroids all keep the baby breech.

probes.q: Why must you ask about bleeding and placental site before offering ECV?
probes.a: Because a low placenta occupies the lower segment, pressing on the uterus there risks bleeding, so ECV should not be attempted until the site is known to be clear.

Breech presentation

skill.present.breech.case.title: Presenting the breech case
skill.present.breech.case.oneLine: Mother, gestation, type of breech, ECV plan and delivery plan
skill.present.breech.case.why: A breech case is heard as a delivery decision, not as a story: the listener needs the type of breech, the gestation, the ECV offer and the fetal status before any plan can be judged. Presenting in that fixed order is what lets the consultant spot the one missing fact that changes the route of delivery.
skill.present.breech.case.body: Present a breech case in a fixed order: mother and gestation first, then the type of breech with how it was confirmed, then ECV suitability, then mother and fetus findings, then the summary and the delivery plan.
keyPoints: Open with particulars that carry obstetric meaning: age, parity, gestation, booking status and referral source. A 26-year-old booked second gravida at 37 weeks referred for breech tells the listener the options before the story starts.

State the type of breech and how it was confirmed: frank, complete or footling on abdominal examination with Leopold manoeuvres, confirmed on ultrasound with liquor, placental site and estimated weight.
Report ECV suitability explicitly: offered at 36 to 37 weeks when no contraindication exists, with consent, blood group and anti-D cover for an Rh-negative mother, and monitoring before and after.

Report examination as mother then fetus: general condition and vitals, abdominal findings with fundal height and the poles of the fetus, then fetal heart and liquor. State what was normal as well as what was not.

Close with the summary sentence and a concrete plan: ECV attempt or reason for skipping it, planned route of delivery with the conditions for a vaginal breech birth stated, and the referral destination where theatre, blood and newborn care are ready.
Keep a focused case to about two minutes. If it runs longer, the structure is wrong, not the content.
pitfalls: Presenting in the order the questions were asked rather than the fixed order the listener expects.
Naming breech without stating the type, leaving the listener unable to judge cord risk or ECV suitability.
Ending at the diagnosis with no delivery plan, when the plan is the whole point of a breech case.

probes.q: State the fixed order of a breech case presentation.
probes.a: Particulars with parity and gestation, type of breech with confirmation, ECV suitability, maternal then fetal examination, summary, and a delivery plan with the referral destination.

probes.q: Why must the type of breech appear before the plan?
probes.a: Because the type sets the cord risk and the ECV offer: a footling breech carries the highest prolapse risk and is not managed like a frank breech, so without the type the route of delivery cannot be assessed.

rubric.text: Presents in the fixed breech order
States the type of breech with confirmation
Closes with an ECV and delivery plan

skill.hx.carcinoma.risk.title: Risk factors and background that matter in carcinoma cervix
skill.hx.carcinoma.risk.oneLine: HPV exposure, parity, tobacco, immunity and screening past that set the prior
skill.hx.carcinoma.risk.why: Exposure, parity, tobacco, immunity and screening past set the pre-test probability before a speculum is passed, and fertility wishes plus screening access frame every option that follows.

asks.text: At what age did you marry or first have intercourse, and have you had more than one sexual partner in your life?
How many times have you been pregnant and given birth, and how old were you at your first delivery?
Do you smoke bidis or cigarettes, or chew tobacco, and for how many years?
Have you ever been told you have HIV or low immunity, or taken medicines that suppress immunity?
Have you ever had a Pap smear, a vinegar test of the cervix or an HPV test, and were you ever told the result was abnormal?

teach.heading: Why the sexual history matters here
points: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus causes almost every cervical cancer, and it passes through intimate contact, so exposure questions are clinical, not moral.
Most infections clear on their own; it is persistence over years, through preinvasive stages, that ends in invasion, which is why early first intercourse and more than one partner raise the risk.
Ask one explaining sentence first, then the questions, and offer to skip: a woman who understands why you ask answers more truthfully.

teach.heading: Parity, tobacco and immunity
teach.body:
High parity raises the risk, and tobacco, smoked or chewed, adds to it, so count both pregnancies and pack years in every case.

Low immunity impairs clearance of the virus, so HIV status, transplant medicines and long steroid courses belong in the same history.

teach.heading: Screening and vaccine history in one minute
teach.body:
Most cancers in India still present in women who were never screened, so one question, have you ever had a cervical test, carries more weight than a list of minor symptoms.

A past abnormal smear, a treated preinvasive lesion, or missed follow up after one, raises the urgency further, as does never having received HPV vaccine, which is offered from 9 years of age.

probes.q: Name four risk factors for carcinoma of the cervix.
probes.a: Early first intercourse, more than one sexual partner, high parity, smoking or tobacco chewing, immunosuppression, and never having been screened.

probes.q: Why does the screening history change your prior more than any single symptom?
probes.a: Most cancers arise in women who were never screened or were lost after an abnormal result, so a never-screened woman with bleeding carries a higher prior than a regularly screened one.

probes.q: How do you ask about sexual partners without shaming her?
probes.a: Explain that persistent viral infection of the cervix causes almost every case, that the questions are routine for every woman with bleeding, and that she may decline any question.

Cervical cancer: epidemiology and risk factors

skill.present.carcinoma.case.title: Presenting the carcinoma cervix case
skill.present.carcinoma.case.oneLine: Present a carcinoma cervix case the way a consultant expects to hear it
skill.present.carcinoma.case.why: A cervix cancer presentation is judged on whether the listener can stage the disease and plan treatment from your words alone. Parametrial status on each side, stage, anaemia and renal function are the load bearing facts; without them it is a story, not a case.

teach.heading: Opening and the bleeding story
teach.body:
Open with age and parity, then the bleeding in her words with duration: postcoital bleeding for stated months, intermenstrual spotting, discharge. Contact history comes first because it is the most specific symptom.

Follow with menstrual and obstetric background in one line each, plus screening past: never screened, or last test with result. A never-screened multiparous woman is the classic Indian presentation.

teach.heading: Examination: the cervix, the parametrium, the sidewall
teach.body:
Present the speculum first: a growth on the cervix of stated size, friable and bleeding on touch, or an ulcer replacing the cervix. Then the bimanual: uterine size and mobility, each parametrium free or involved and how far toward the sidewall, vaginal extent, fornices.

Each negative does work: free parametria keep her operable, a blocked ureter or sidewall fixation moves her to chemoradiation. State rectal findings where examined.

teach.heading: Proof, stage and the justified plan
teach.body:
Close with what proves it: biopsy histology with subtype, MRI extent, nodal imaging, haemoglobin and creatinine. Then the diagnosis as one line: squamous carcinoma of the cervix, FIGO stage stated, with anaemia and renal status.

Then the plan justified from three anchors: stage chooses surgery or chemoradiation, anaemia and renal function decide fitness and timing, and referral to a gynae oncology unit follows in every case. End with counselling points: what you told her and what she agreed to.

probes.q: What six facts must a carcinoma cervix presentation contain?
probes.a: Age and parity, bleeding quantified with contact history, the growth as seen on speculum, parametrial status on bimanual examination, and stage with fitness for treatment.

probes.q: What pelvic findings does the consultant listen for?
probes.a: Whether the growth bleeds on touch, whether each parametrium is free or involved and how far toward the sidewall, whether the fornices are free, and the rectal findings where examined.

rubric.text: Follows particulars, bleeding story, examination, biopsy and imaging, stage, plan
States parametrial status on each side and the resulting stage, not just that a growth exists
Justifies referral and treatment choice from anaemia, renal function and stage

asks.text: Age and parity: how old is she, and is this a first or a later pregnancy? Risk climbs steadily with maternal age.
Weight before pregnancy: what did she weigh before conceiving, and has weight risen steeply since? Excess weight is the strongest modifiable risk.
Earlier pregnancies: diabetes in any previous pregnancy, a previous unusually large baby, a difficult shoulder delivery, an unexplained stillbirth, or repeated early losses?
Family history: diabetes in parents or siblings, and at what age it appeared? Early onset in the family carries extra weight.
Polycystic ovary features: irregular cycles, unwanted hair growth, or difficulty conceiving before this pregnancy?
Other background: chronic hypertension, kidney disease, or prolonged use of drugs that raise glucose, such as steroids?
Birth weights of earlier children: how much did each baby weigh, and how was each delivered? A previous large baby predicts recurrence.
Population risk: South Asian women develop glucose intolerance at comparatively lower weight, so suspicion sits lower here than in European guidance.

skill.hx.gestational.risk.oneLine: The background that decides when she is tested and how closely she is watched
pitfalls: Recording risk as present or absent without letting it change the testing plan.
Forgetting to ask the birth weights of earlier children, the cheapest predictor available.
Treating one normal early test as a final answer in a high-risk woman.
skill.hx.gestational.risk.practice: Take the risk history from a newly booked pregnancy: age, weight, previous pregnancies with birth weights, family history, polycystic ovary features and background, then state when you would test her.

probes.a: Excess pre-pregnancy weight, higher maternal age, diabetes in a previous pregnancy or a previous unusually large baby, a family history of diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome, and South Asian background.
probes.q: Name four risk factors for gestational diabetes.

probes.a: No. Testing is repeated around 24 to 28 weeks, when placental resistance to insulin peaks, because risk persists after one normal early result.
probes.q: A high-risk woman tests normal at booking. Is testing finished?

probes.a: A previous unusually large baby is one of the strongest predictors of gestational diabetes in the current pregnancy, and it also warns of a repeat difficult delivery.
probes.q: Why do the birth weights of earlier children matter?

sources.locator: gestational_diabetes_mellitus: clinicalPearls
Diabetes mellitus in pregnancy

teach.body: A woman with strong risk factors is tested at booking, and tested again if that first test is normal, because waiting until mid pregnancy leaves overt diabetes untreated while the fetal organs are forming. A woman without risk factors follows routine screening around 24 to 28 weeks, when placental resistance peaks. The history therefore sets the calendar for testing, not just the level of suspicion.
teach.heading: Risk sets the timing of testing
The risk factors worth naming
points: Excess weight before pregnancy, and rapid gain in early pregnancy.
Maternal age above the mid twenties, with risk rising steadily after that.
Diabetes in a previous pregnancy, or a previous unusually large baby.
A parent or sibling with diabetes, especially with onset at a young age.
Polycystic ovary syndrome and chronic hypertension as accompanying risks.
South Asian background, which raises risk at comparatively lower weight.

teach.body: Two omissions recur on ward rounds. The first is never asking the birth weights of earlier children, although it costs nothing and predicts better than most tests. The second is treating a normal early test in a high-risk woman as a final answer. Risk persists after one normal result, so testing is repeated when placental resistance peaks.
teach.heading: What students miss

skill.hx.gestational.risk.title: Risk factors for gestational diabetes
skill.hx.gestational.risk.why: Testing every woman at the same visit misses the women whose diabetes started before conception. A careful risk history separates three groups: overt diabetes that needs finding in early pregnancy, high risk that needs early testing, and standard risk that follows routine screening. Without it, the whole screening plan is guesswork.

asks.text: Thirst: unusual thirst, a dry mouth, or drinking far more water than before this pregnancy?
Urine: passing urine unusually often, or waking repeatedly at night to pass urine?
Infection: itching or curdy discharge per vaginam, burning on passing urine, or repeated boils? High glucose feeds both thrush and bacterial infection.
Energy: unusual tiredness or exhaustion out of proportion to the stage of pregnancy?
Abdominal growth: has the abdomen enlarged unusually fast in recent weeks, or is she breathless lying flat? Rapid growth suggests extra liquor.
Fetal movements: are movements normal in number, reduced, or absent? Reduced movements reflect placental compromise and need same-day review.
Leaking: any watery leaking per vaginam, or a sudden gush? Rupture of membranes changes the plan whatever the glucose shows.
Overlap warnings: headache, flashing lights or blurring of vision, sudden swelling of face or hands, or pain below the ribs? Hypertension travels with diabetes and must be caught.

skill.hx.gestational.symptoms.oneLine: Usually silent, so screening finds it; symptoms point to poor control or a second problem
pitfalls: Waiting for symptoms before testing, when most affected women feel entirely well.
Missing thrush and urinary infection as the presenting clue to high glucose.
Asking about fetal movements without arranging same-day review when they are reduced.
skill.hx.gestational.symptoms.practice: Take the symptom history from a woman at 30 weeks with newly found high glucose: thirst, urine, infection, energy, abdominal growth, fetal movements, leaking and overlap warnings, in that order.

probes.a: Most women with gestational diabetes feel entirely well, so screening rather than symptoms makes the diagnosis. Symptoms suggest glucose has been high for some time, or point to a second problem.
probes.q: A woman asks why she needs a glucose test when she feels perfectly well. What do you tell her?

probes.a: Unusual thirst, frequent passing of urine, repeated thrush or boils, urinary burning, and unusual tiredness suggest glucose has been running high.
probes.q: Name four symptoms that suggest poorly controlled glucose in pregnancy.

probes.a: Rapid abdominal enlargement with breathlessness on lying flat suggests extra liquor, reduced fetal movements suggest placental compromise, and headache with visual change and sudden swelling suggest coexisting hypertension. Each changes urgency on the spot.
probes.q: Which warnings in a diabetic pregnancy change urgency on the spot, and what does each suggest?

sources.locator: gestational_diabetes_mellitus: redFlags
Diabetes in pregnancy
sources.source: NICE guideline on diabetes in pregnancy

teach.body: Most women with gestational diabetes feel entirely well, which is why screening rather than symptoms makes the diagnosis. A student who waits for the classic thirst and frequent urine of diabetes outside pregnancy will miss nearly every case. The test is offered because she is pregnant and the gestation is right, not because she complains.
teach.heading: Silence is the rule
Symptoms that suggest high glucose
points: Unusual thirst with a dry mouth, and drinking far more than before.
Passing urine unusually often, including repeated waking at night.
Itching or curdy discharge per vaginam, burning on urination, or repeated boils.
Tiredness out of proportion to the stage of pregnancy.
Any of these persisting for weeks suggests glucose has been high for some time.

teach.body: Three warnings change the visit whatever the glucose shows. Rapid abdominal enlargement with new breathlessness on lying flat suggests extra liquor around the baby. Reduced or absent fetal movements suggest the placenta is failing and need same-day review. Headache with visual change, sudden swelling, or pain below the ribs suggest hypertension travelling with the diabetes. Ask all three every time.
teach.heading: Warnings that change the visit

skill.hx.gestational.symptoms.title: Symptoms in gestational diabetes, and the warnings that overlap it
skill.hx.gestational.symptoms.why: Most women with gestational diabetes feel entirely well, which is why screening rather than symptoms makes the diagnosis. When symptoms do appear, thirst, frequent urine, repeated thrush or boils, and unusual tiredness suggest glucose has been high for some time. A separate set of warnings, rapid abdominal enlargement, reduced fetal movements, leaking fluid, and headache with swelling, changes urgency on the spot.

skill.present.gestational.case.body: Present in a fixed order and keep it to about two minutes. The listener should be able to reach your diagnosis before you say it, and should hear the delivery plan before you stop.
keyPoints: Open with age, parity, gestation and how the high glucose was found: routine screening, early testing for risk, or symptoms.
Give the risk background next: weight, previous pregnancies with birth weights, family history, and polycystic ovary features.
Give the current pregnancy: growth, liquor, blood pressure, urine protein, and fetal movements, positives then negatives.
State the examination in the same order every time: general, vitals with blood pressure, abdomen with fundal height and liquor assessment, fetal heart.
State the diagnosis with its basis: which test was above threshold and at what gestation, plus whether overt diabetes is excluded.
Name the two complications you are watching for: a large baby with extra liquor, and coexisting hypertension.
Close with the plan: glucose control, fetal surveillance, timing and mode of delivery, neonatal watch, and postpartum retesting.
skill.present.gestational.case.oneLine: Two minutes, in a fixed order, ending with the delivery plan
pitfalls: Presenting in the order the history was taken rather than in order of relevance.
Omitting birth weights of earlier children, which the listener needs for the delivery plan.
Ending on the diagnosis without stating timing and mode of delivery.
Quoting a glucose value without saying which test and at what gestation produced it.

probes.a: Age, parity, gestation and how the high glucose was found, then risk background, current pregnancy course, examination findings, diagnosis with its basis, watched complications, and the plan for control, surveillance, delivery and postpartum retesting.
probes.q: In what order should the gestational diabetes case be presented?

probes.a: The summary names the woman with her risk factors, the gestation and how glucose intolerance was found, the fetal size and liquor state, blood pressure, and control so far. A complete example is a 29 year old second pregnancy at 30 weeks with glucose intolerance on routine screening, a previous large baby, fundal height above dates with extra liquor, normal pressure, and fasting glucose above target despite diet.
probes.q: What belongs in the one-paragraph summary of this case?

rubric.text: Follows the fixed order: finding, risk, course, examination, diagnosis, plan
States timing and mode of delivery with reasons
Every glucose value is tied to its test and gestation
