teach.heading: The fixed order

rows: Age, parity, gestation, how high glucose was found
Weight, previous birth weights, family history
Vitals, fundal height, liquor, fetal heart
Grounds the plan in bedside facts
Which test, what gestation, overt excluded
Is what the listener will judge

teach.body: The delivery plan is the point of the whole presentation, so it comes last and complete: timing, mode, and the reason for each. A large baby with extra liquor points one way, a well grown baby with good control points another. Never end on the diagnosis and sit down; the listener is waiting to hear when and how this baby will be born.
teach.heading: End with the delivery plan

skill.present.gestational.case.title: Presenting the gestational diabetes case
skill.present.gestational.case.why: A case presentation is assessed on structure as much as content, and this case has a trap: students present the glucose values at length and run out of time before the delivery plan. The fixed order forces risk, fetal size, liquor and pressure before the numbers, so the listener can already see the delivery decision coming.

asks.text: How old are you, and is there anyone in the family who had an early menopause or weak bones with fractures?
Have your periods stopped? If yes, at what age, and did you have your uterus or ovaries removed by surgery?
Do you smoke or chew tobacco, and how much alcohol do you take in a week?
Have you had breast cancer, a clot in the leg or lungs, a stroke or heart attack, liver disease, or migraine with visual changes?
Are you taking any hormones, thyroid tablets, blood thinners, or medicines for fits or tuberculosis?

skill.hx.menopause.risk.oneLine: Age, family, clot and cancer background that set HRT safety

probes.a: Age at menopause and whether it was natural or surgical, smoking, and a family history of early menopause, breast cancer, clots or osteoporotic fractures.
probes.q: What background facts set the risk before you discuss HRT?

probes.a: Breast or endometrial cancer, a past clot or thrombophilia, stroke or heart disease, active liver disease and undiagnosed vaginal bleeding forbid systemic HRT.
probes.q: Which past illnesses forbid systemic HRT?

probes.a: Enzyme inducing drugs such as rifampicin and some anti epileptic medicines lower systemic oestrogen levels, so the drug list decides whether oral HRT will even work.
probes.q: A woman on tuberculosis treatment asks for HRT tablets. What do you check first?

sources.locator: menopause_and_postmenopausal_hormone_thera: management
Contraindications to hormone therapy

teach.heading: What raises the stakes
points: Age at stopping decides the label: under 40 is premature ovarian insufficiency, 40 to 45 is early menopause, and the average age of natural menopause is about 51.
Smoking brings the transition forward by roughly 2 years, so tobacco history is never a formality here.
Surgical menopause after removal of both ovaries starts abruptly and often severely, unlike the gradual natural transition.
A family history of early menopause, breast cancer, clots or hip fractures raises the prior for the same problem in her.

teach.body:
Ask directly about breast cancer, clots in the leg or lungs, stroke, heart disease, active liver disease and any bleeding after the periods stopped. Each of these changes whether systemic hormones can be offered at all.

Undiagnosed vaginal bleeding is never attributed to the transition until endometrial disease is excluded, so it is asked about in every first visit.
teach.heading: Illnesses that close the HRT door

teach.body:
List every medicine, including thyroid tablets, blood thinners, anti epileptic drugs and tuberculosis treatment. Enzyme inducers lower hormone levels and anticoagulants change the bleeding story.

Note calcium, vitamin D and osteoporosis treatment already taken, since they show what bone protection is in place before you add anything.
teach.heading: Drugs that change the plan

skill.hx.menopause.risk.title: Risk factors and background that matter in menopause
skill.hx.menopause.risk.why: HRT is offered only after weighing clot, cancer and liver risk against symptom burden, and that weighing is impossible without the background. Age, surgical history, tobacco, family and drugs each move the decision, so they are asked before symptoms are graded.

asks.text: When did your periods last come, and how has the pattern changed over the last few years?
Do you get sudden waves of heat with sweating in the day or night? How often, and do they wake you or stop your work?
Has sleep, mood, memory or interest in relations with your husband changed since the periods became irregular?
Do you have dryness or burning in the private parts, pain during relations, or burning while passing urine? Any urine leak on coughing or urgency?
Have you had any bleeding after the periods had stopped for a year, even spotting?
Do your joints ache, have you lost height, or broken a bone with a small fall?

skill.hx.menopause.symptoms.oneLine: Flushes, sleep, mood, dryness, leaks and aches asked in her words

probes.a: Cycle change with hot flushes and night sweats, sleep disturbance, vaginal dryness with dyspareunia, urinary urgency with recurrent infection, and joint aches.
probes.q: Name five symptom groups you must ask about in the menopause history.

probes.a: Flushes are strongly attributable to the transition while low mood, poor memory, incontinence and low desire are not clearly caused by ovarian ageing alone, so they need their own causes sought.
probes.q: She blames her low mood and forgetfulness on menopause. How do you respond?

probes.a: Any bleeding after 12 months without periods is never called a late period and always needs endometrial assessment, whatever else she reports.
probes.q: She mentions spotting a year after her periods stopped. What is your response?

sources.locator: menopause_and_postmenopausal_hormone_thera: clinicalPearls
Menopause transition: clinical manifestations

teach.body:
Start from the cycle: when the last period came and how the pattern changed over recent years. A persistent difference of 7 days or more between consecutive cycles marks the early transition, and 60 days or more without bleeding marks the late transition.

Then ask about heat waves with sweating by day and night: how often they come, whether they wake her, and whether they interrupt work or prayer. Frequency and night waking grade the burden better than any score.
teach.heading: Cycles first, then the heat

teach.body:
Ask about vaginal dryness, burning, itching and pain during relations, and about burning on passing urine, urgency, leaks on coughing and repeated urinary infections. These genital and urinary symptoms often outlast the flushes and are the ones women hesitate to volunteer.

Ask about sleep, mood, memory and interest in intimacy, but keep them separate from the flushes in your mind. Broken sleep from night sweats is expected; low mood, poor memory, leakage and low desire are not clearly caused by ovarian ageing and each needs its own enquiry.
teach.heading: Private symptoms and what they do not prove

teach.body:
Ask explicitly about any bleeding after a year without periods, even a single spot. Postmenopausal bleeding is never assumed to be hormonal and always needs the womb lining assessed.

Ask about joint aches, loss of height and fractures from small falls. Bone loss is silent until a fracture, so the history must go looking for it.
teach.heading: Bleeding and bones must be asked, not waited for

skill.hx.menopause.symptoms.title: Symptoms of the menopause transition
skill.hx.menopause.symptoms.why: Flushes are volunteered but dryness, leaks and low mood are not, so a fixed symptom list prevents the consultation from ending at the first complaint. Knowing which complaints the transition truly explains stops mood, memory and bladder symptoms being wrongly filed under menopause.

skill.present.menopause.case.oneLine: Present a menopause case the way a consultant expects to hear it

probes.a: Age with months since the last period, the flush burden with night waking, genital and urinary symptoms, and any postmenopausal bleeding stated as present or absent.
probes.q: What five facts must a menopause presentation contain?

probes.a: Blood pressure with BMI, breast findings, vulval and speculum findings with cervical health, bimanual uterine size with free fornices, and the baseline tests with dates.
probes.q: What examination and baseline facts does the consultant listen for?

rubric.text: Follows particulars, cycle story, symptoms by group, risk background, examination, baseline tests, diagnosis, plan
States months since last period, flush frequency, BP, BMI and endometrial thickness rather than saying long, frequent or normal
Justifies HRT choice from uterus status and risk, with review date and red flags explained

sources.locator: Presenting the case
menopause_and_postmenopausal_hormone_thera: management

teach.body:
Open with age, occupation and months since the last period, then the cycle story in her words with duration. Months without bleeding come first because the whole diagnosis hangs on that count.

Follow with symptoms by group: flushes with frequency and night waking, sleep and mood, genital dryness with pain during relations, urinary urgency with leaks and infections, and joint aches. State postmenopausal bleeding as present or absent in every presentation.
teach.heading: Opening and the symptom groups

teach.body:
Present blood pressure with BMI, then the breast examination, then the pelvis in order: vulval atrophy, speculum view of the vagina and cervix with any discharge or bleeding, and bimanual uterine size with fornix findings.

Then the baseline tests with dates: pregnancy test where relevant, thyroid, sugars, lipids, cervical screening, mammography, ultrasound with endometrial thickness, and bone density where done.
teach.heading: Examination and baseline tests in order

teach.body:
Close with the diagnosis as one line: menopause with troublesome vasomotor symptoms, or the relevant alternative where the picture did not fit.

Then the plan justified from three anchors: uterus present or absent chooses combined or single hormone treatment, clot and cancer risk chooses the route, and the review date with red flags closes the presentation. End with what she was told to return for.
teach.heading: Diagnosis and the justified plan

skill.present.menopause.case.title: Presenting the menopause case
skill.present.menopause.case.why: A menopause presentation is assessed on whether the listener can stage the transition and justify hormones from your words alone. Months since the last period, flush burden, bleeding status and risk background are the load bearing facts; without them the presentation is a story, not a case.

asks.text: How old are you, and have your periods stopped? If yes, at what age, and have you had any bleeding since?
How many children do you have, did you breastfeed, and have you ever used contraceptive pills or hormone treatment after the menopause?
Has anyone in your family had cancer of the ovary, breast, uterus or bowel, and has anyone been tested for BRCA or Lynch syndrome?
When did your periods start, do you have painful periods or known endometriosis, and have you ever been treated for pelvic infection or infertility?
Have you ever had surgery on the ovary or uterus, and have you noticed this kind of bloating or lump before?

skill.hx.ovarian.risk.oneLine: Age, menopause, parity, family cancers and hormones that raise or lower the prior

probes.a: Older age and postmenopausal status, nulliparity, a family history of ovarian or breast cancer, and inherited BRCA1, BRCA2 or Lynch syndrome mutations.
probes.q: Name four risk factors for ovarian malignancy.

probes.a: Combined oral contraceptives lower the risk substantially with longer use, while menopausal hormone treatment and prolonged ovulatory years raise it, so the full hormone history changes the prior.
probes.q: How does her hormone history change the risk?

probes.a: Endometriosis raises the risk of clear cell and endometrioid subtypes, and a past pelvic infection or infertility points toward tubal and inflammatory causes of an adnexal mass rather than a primary ovarian tumour.
probes.q: Why ask about endometriosis, pelvic infection and infertility in an adnexal mass?

sources.locator: ovarian_cancer: clinicalPearls
Ovarian cancer (epidemiology and risk factors)

teach.heading: Who carries the risk
points: Risk rises with age, and most malignant tumours present after the menopause, so a pelvic mass in a postmenopausal woman carries a far higher prior than the same mass at 25.
Nulliparity and prolonged ovulatory years without a break raise the risk, while pregnancy, breastfeeding and combined oral contraceptive use lower it.
A family history of ovarian, breast, uterine or bowel cancer raises concern, and known BRCA1, BRCA2 or Lynch syndrome mutations raise it markedly and should prompt genetic assessment.
Endometriosis is linked with clear cell and endometrioid subtypes, so a history of severe dysmenorrhoea or a known chocolate cyst belongs in the risk history.

teach.body:
Combined oral contraceptives protect against ovarian cancer, with the protection growing with longer use, so ask about them even when she stopped years ago.

Menopausal hormone treatment moves the risk the other way, and fertility drugs that repeatedly stimulate the ovary deserve one direct question, since repeated ovulation without a break is the proposed mechanism behind the parity effect.
teach.heading: Hormones that protect and hormones that add risk

teach.body:
Past pelvic infection, tuberculosis exposure and infertility point toward tubo ovarian inflammation and ectopic pregnancy as mimics of an ovarian mass.

Previous ovarian surgery matters twice: a cystectomy scar raises the chance of adhesions that fix a new mass, and any prior spill or rupture changes how you counsel about the next operation.
teach.heading: Pelvic past that points to mimics

skill.hx.ovarian.risk.title: Risk factors and background that matter in an ovarian tumour
skill.hx.ovarian.risk.why: An adnexal mass at 25 and at 60 carries a different prior before a single question is asked, and hormones, family cancers and pelvic infection each point to a different cause. The risk history is what sets that prior, so the examination is read against the right baseline.

skill.present.ovarian.case.oneLine: Present an ovarian tumour case the way a consultant expects to hear it

probes.a: Age with menopausal status, the bloating triad with tempo, whether the mass moves separately from the uterus, ascites and fixity, and the CA-125 with the RMI band.
probes.q: What six facts must an ovarian tumour presentation contain?

probes.a: Whether the uterus moves independently of the mass, whether a groove is felt between them, whether the mass is cystic or solid, fixed or mobile, and whether the pouch of Douglas is nodular.
probes.q: What bimanual findings does the consultant listen for?

rubric.text: Follows particulars, complaints with tempo, menopausal status, examination, CA-125 with RMI, diagnosis, referral plan
States uterus versus ovary separation, fixity, ascites and nodularity rather than just a lump
Justifies urgent gynaecological oncology referral from RMI band and red flags, not from worry alone

sources.locator: Presenting the case
ovarian_cancer: clinicalPearls

teach.body:
Open with age and menopausal status, then the chief complaints in her words with duration: months of bloating, early satiety and urinary urgency carry the weight here, not days of pain.

Follow with weight change, appetite, bowel habit and any bleeding after the menopause. Each of these is a staging clue, so present them before the examination, not after.
teach.heading: Opening, tempo and the systemic clues

teach.body:
Present the abdomen first: distension, shifting dullness for ascites, and a palpable mass with its size, surface and mobility. Then the speculum: a healthy or suspicious cervix and any bleeding.

Then the bimanual, which is the core of this presentation: uterine size and mobility, whether the mass moves separately from the uterus with a groove between, whether it is cystic or solid and fixed or mobile, and whether the fornices and pouch of Douglas are free or nodular.
teach.heading: Examination findings in order

teach.body:
Close with the investigations that triage her: CA-125 with menopausal status and the resulting RMI band, ultrasound features, and CT extent where done. Then the diagnosis as one line with the FIGO impression.

Then the plan justified from three anchors: the RMI band chooses routine versus urgent referral, red flags such as ascites with breathlessness or bowel change force immediate escalation, and completed staging leads to the gynaecological oncology team rather than a local operation.
teach.heading: Investigations, diagnosis and the justified plan

skill.present.ovarian.case.title: Presenting the ovarian tumour case
skill.present.ovarian.case.why: An ovarian tumour presentation is assessed on whether the listener can separate uterus from ovary and benign from malignant from your words alone. Menopausal status, independent mobility, fixity, ascites and the RMI band are the load bearing facts; without them the presentation is a story, not a case.

skill.hx.pelvic.risk_factors.title: Risk factors and background that matter in discharge and pelvic infection
skill.hx.pelvic.risk_factors.oneLine: Sexual history, contraception, instrumentation and past infection that set the prior
skill.hx.pelvic.risk_factors.why: Pelvic infection is a disease of exposure and opportunity: new or multiple partners, an unprotected interval, a recent procedure or a past episode each raise the prior before a single examination finding. Asked sensitively and without judgement, this background also decides partner treatment and prevention.

asks.text: Are you sexually active at present, and have you had a new partner or more than one partner in the last few months?
Do you or your partner use condoms regularly, and what contraception are you using now, including any intrauterine device and when it was fitted?
Have you had any vaginal discharge, pelvic infection or sexually transmitted infection before, and were your partners treated at the time?
Have you had any recent procedure through the cervix, such as termination of pregnancy, delivery, miscarriage, endometrial sampling or hysteroscopy, and have you used any vaginal douches or inserts?
When was your last menstrual period, could you be pregnant now, and when did you last have cervical screening?

teach.heading: Why the sexual history comes first
teach.body:
Infection reaches the upper tract by ascending from the cervix, so the organisms involved are most often sexually transmitted ones with vaginal flora alongside. A new partner, more than one recent partner, and inconsistent condom use each raise the likelihood substantially.

Ask with neutral language, explain why the questions matter, and see the partner alone for part of the history where local custom allows. A judgemental tone shuts down the exact answers the diagnosis depends on.

teach.heading: Contraception, procedures and past infection
points: An intrauterine device raises the risk mainly around insertion and with later bacterial vaginosis, and current pelvic infection is a reason not to fit one.
Any recent instrumentation of the uterus, including termination, delivery, miscarriage care, sampling or hysteroscopy, can carry organisms upward.
Vaginal douching disturbs the protective lactobacillus flora and favours overgrowth, so ask about it directly.

A past episode of pelvic infection or discharge matters twice: it raises the risk of tubal damage already present, and each repeat episode raises the chance of infertility and ectopic pregnancy further.

teach.heading: The two background facts that change management today
teach.body:
Always establish whether she could be pregnant, because pregnancy changes antibiotics, admission and the need to exclude ectopic gestation urgently.

Always ask about previous treatment and whether partners were treated, because an untreated partner guarantees reinfection and makes counselling, not just tablets, the intervention that breaks the cycle.

probes.q: Name three risk factors for pelvic inflammatory disease.
probes.a: A new or multiple sexual partners, inconsistent condom use, and a recent uterine procedure such as termination, delivery or sampling.

probes.q: Why does a past episode of pelvic infection matter in a woman presenting with discharge today?
probes.a: It raises the chance that tubal damage is already present, and each repeat episode further raises the risk of tubal infertility and ectopic pregnancy.

probes.q: A woman with discharge has an intrauterine device in place. How does that change your history and thinking?
probes.a: Ask when it was fitted and about recent bleeding or pain since, recognise the raised risk around insertion, and know that current pelvic infection is a reason not to fit a device while treatment of the present episode takes priority.

sources.locator: pelvic_inflammatory_disease: clinicalPearls
Pelvic inflammatory disease (risk factors)

skill.present.pelvic.case.title: Presenting the discharge and pelvic pain case
skill.present.pelvic.case.oneLine: Present a PID case the way a consultant expects to hear it
skill.present.pelvic.case.why: A pelvic infection presentation is judged on whether the listener can grade severity and name the next step from your words alone. Timing, tenderness mapped to structures, the pregnancy test, and the partner plan are the load bearing facts; without them the presentation is a story, not a case.

teach.heading: Opening and the history in one arc
teach.body:
Open with age, marital and pregnancy context, then the chief complaints with duration: lower abdominal pain, discharge described by colour, odour and amount, fever, deep pain during intercourse, and bleeding between periods.

Follow with the risk background in one line: partners, contraception including any intrauterine device, past infection and whether partners were treated. Never present discharge without describing it, and never present pelvic pain without the pregnancy possibility.

teach.heading: Examination findings in order
teach.body:
Present the abdomen first: temperature and pulse, then suprapubic tenderness with or without guarding, and any right upper quadrant tenderness that would raise perihepatitis. Then the speculum: discharge seen coming from the cervical os, with friability or bleeding on touch where present.

Then the bimanual: cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, adnexal tenderness and any mass, each stated with laterality. Each negative, no motion tenderness, no mass, is doing real work against tubo-ovarian abscess and ectopic gestation.

teach.heading: Investigations, diagnosis and the justified plan
teach.body:
Close with the tests that matter: urine pregnancy test first, microscopy and culture or nucleic acid testing where available, inflammatory markers, and ultrasound where a mass or abscess is suspected. Then the diagnosis as one line with severity.

Then the plan justified from four anchors: empirical antibiotics with the threshold stated, admission or outpatient care with the reason, partner notification and treatment with abstinence advice, and counselling on tubal risks with follow-up. End with what you will do about the partner before anything else is closed.

probes.q: What five facts must a pelvic infection presentation contain?
probes.a: The pregnancy possibility with the test result, tenderness mapped to cervix, uterus and adnexa, the discharge as seen at the os, severity with any abscess or sepsis features, and the partner plan.

probes.q: What bimanual findings does the consultant listen for, and what does each exclude?
probes.a: Cervical motion tenderness with uterine and adnexal tenderness mapping the infection to the upper tract, and the absence of a mass arguing against a tubo-ovarian abscess while a lateralised tender mass with fever argues for one.

rubric.text: Follows particulars, complaints with discharge described, risk background, examination, investigations, diagnosis, plan
States the pregnancy test, maps tenderness to structures, and grades severity with abscess or sepsis features
Justifies antibiotics, admission or outpatient care, partner treatment with abstinence, and counselling on tubal risks

sources.locator: Presenting the case
pelvic_inflammatory_disease: clinicalPearls

asks.text: When did the bleeding start in relation to the birth of the baby and the placenta? Bleeding before the placenta is out points to a different cause from bleeding after it.
How much has she bled, in her own words and in pads or cloths? Ask how many pads soaked through, how often she changes them, and whether blood flows continuously or in gushes.
Did she pass clots or pieces of tissue? Ask about the size of the clots and whether anything fleshy came away.
Was the placenta delivered whole? Ask whether the attendant checked both its maternal and fetal surfaces and whether all the membranes came out.
What did the attendant do after delivery? Ask about massage of the womb, any injection given, and whether the womb was felt to be hard or soft.
Is she dizzy, breathless, or faint, and has she passed urine since delivery? These answers grade the shock while the bleeding continues.

probes.a: The timing of bleeding against delivery of baby and placenta, an honest estimate of amount in pads or cloths with clots or tissue, whether the placenta came whole, what the attendant did including massage and injections, and shock symptoms with urine output.
probes.q: What must the bleeding story after delivery always establish?

probes.a: Because bleeding before the placenta separates suggests a different mechanism from bleeding after a complete placenta, when atony is commonest, and an incomplete placenta means retained tissue is keeping the womb from contracting.
probes.q: Why do you fix the bleeding against the moment the placenta came out?

sources.locator: postpartum_haemorrhage: clinicalPearls
Postpartum haemorrhage

teach.body: Primary bleeding starts within the first day after birth, and most of it starts within the first hour, while the womb should be clamping down. Secondary bleeding starts after the first day and can return as late as about three months, often with fever or foul discharge pointing to infection or leftover tissue.
teach.heading: Timing: primary bleeding and secondary bleeding

teach.body: Ask for amount in concrete terms: pads or cloths soaked per hour, clots the size of a lemon or larger, blood pooling under her, and whether it flows steadily or in gushes when the fundus is pressed. Then ask how she feels: dizziness on sitting, breathlessness, palpitation, and whether she has passed urine. The symptoms measure the loss the eyes underestimate.
teach.heading: Amount: pads, clots and how she feels

teach.body: A placenta that came whole with all membranes still leaves atony and tears on the table, but a placenta with a missing cotyledon or torn membranes means retained tissue until proven otherwise. Ask who checked it and what they saw, because this single answer decides whether the next step is massage and drugs or a manual exploration.
teach.heading: The placenta: whole or suspect

skill.hx.pph.bleed_story.title: The bleeding story after delivery
skill.hx.pph.bleed_story.why: The pads always understate the loss and the clock always matters more than it seems. A bleeding story fixed to the delivery of the placenta, counted in pads and clots, and graded by how she feels turns a frightened description into a measured emergency with a cause already half found.

asks.text: How many pregnancies and deliveries has she had, and were any labours very long, very fast, or delivered by forceps, vacuum or caesarean? Grand multiparity, prolonged or augmented labour, and operative delivery all tire the womb.
Was this pregnancy complicated by too much liquor, twins, a very big baby, or a low lying placenta? Each of these overstretches the womb or disturbs separation.

Did she have raised pressure, fits, severe anaemia, fever in labour, or bleeding before delivery? Pre-eclampsia, anaemia, chorioamnionitis and antepartum bleeding each raise the risk of bleeding after.
Has she bled heavily after a previous delivery, or needed blood, balloon treatment or surgery for it? A previous postpartum haemorrhage is the strongest warning of another.
Does she bleed easily elsewhere, take blood thinners or aspirin, or have a known clotting disorder? Ask about nose and gum bleeds, heavy periods, and any family history of bleeding.
Was this labour induced or speeded up with a drip, and was the third stage managed actively with an injection? Prolonged oxytocin tires the muscle it is meant to contract.

probes.a: Grand multiparity, overdistension from twins excess liquor or a big baby, prolonged or augmented labour, operative delivery, previous postpartum haemorrhage, pre-eclampsia, severe anaemia, infection in labour, fibroids or a scarred womb, and clotting disorders or blood thinners.
probes.q: Name the background risks you must ask about before the bleeding starts.

probes.a: Because a womb that has been overstretched or worked too long contracts poorly after the placenta separates, so the sinuses at the placental bed stay open and bleed. The risk history predicts the atony before it happens.
probes.q: Why do overdistension and prolonged labour predict atonic bleeding?

sources.locator: postpartum_haemorrhage: pathophysiology
Postpartum haemorrhage (risk factors)

teach.body: The womb that bleeds after delivery is usually the womb that was already tired or overstretched. Ask about grand multiparity, a labour that went on for many hours or was speeded with a drip, and delivery by forceps, vacuum or caesarean. Each of these leaves muscle that cannot clamp the placental bed shut.
teach.heading: The tired womb: parity, long labour and operative delivery

teach.body: Ask about twins, excess liquor, and a very big baby, because all three overstretch the fibres. Ask about fibroids, a previous caesarean scar, and a low lying placenta, because all three disturb how the placenta separates and how the womb contracts around it.
teach.heading: The overstretched womb: twins, liquor, big baby and fibroids

teach.body: Ask about raised pressure and fits, severe anaemia, fever in labour, and bleeding before delivery. Then ask the single most predictive question: did she bleed heavily after a previous birth. A previous postpartum haemorrhage outweighs every other risk factor, and a bleeding tendency or blood thinner completes the clotting side.
teach.heading: The rest of the risk: pressure, anaemia, infection and previous bleeding

skill.hx.pph.risk.title: Risk factors for postpartum haemorrhage
skill.hx.pph.risk.why: Most postpartum bleeding is predictable from the history taken before the birth, not from the bleeding itself. Finding the tired, overstretched or clotting-impaired womb in advance is what puts the uterotonic drawn up, the blood grouped, and the senior help nearby before the emergency starts.

probes.a: Parity and delivery details with time since birth, the quantified bleeding with the state of the placenta, uterine tone and fundal findings, maternal pulse pressure urine and clotting status, then severity and the resuscitation and cause-directed plan.
probes.q: What must a postpartum haemorrhage presentation contain, in order?

probes.a: Because a firm contracting uterus with continued brisk bleeding means the blood is coming from a tear or clotting failure rather than atony, so the plan changes from uterotonics to examination under good light, repair, and clotting correction.
probes.q: Why must the presentation state the uterine tone before the plan?

rubric.text: Follows the fixed order: parity and birth, quantified bleed, tone, maternal status, severity, plan
States uterine tone and fundal findings as the cause pointer
Grades severity from vitals and quantified loss, not from the pads alone

sources.locator: postpartum_haemorrhage: clinicalPearls
Postpartum haemorrhage

teach.body: Open with who she is and how she delivered: age, parity, gestation, mode of delivery, time since birth, birth weight and where she delivered. Then state the bleeding as primary or secondary with a quantified loss, the state of the placenta, and whether the third stage was managed actively. The listener should suspect the cause before you name it.
teach.heading: Open: parity, birth and quantified bleeding

teach.body: Give the uterine findings next: fundal height, whether the uterus is boggy or firm, and what happens to the bleeding when the fundus is massaged. A boggy uterus that firms with massage is atony. A firm uterus with continued bleeding is trauma or clotting failure until proven otherwise.
teach.heading: The middle: uterine tone as the cause pointer

teach.body: Give maternal status as its own sentence: pulse, pressure, breathing rate, pallor, urine output and clotting signs, stated plainly as stable or shocked. Close with severity, what has been given so far, and the plan: resuscitation, uterotonics, tranexamic acid, the cause-directed step, blood readiness, and referral if the setting cannot escalate.
teach.heading: Close: maternal status, severity and plan

skill.present.pph.case.title: Presenting the postpartum haemorrhage case
skill.present.pph.case.why: An obstetric presentation is judged on whether the listener can act from it. Bleeding cases are presented as tone first and plan second, because the state of the uterus decides the next pair of hands: drugs for atony, repair for tears, exploration for tissue, blood products for clotting failure.

skill.hx.preterm.symptoms.title: Pains, leaking, bleeding and discharge before term
skill.hx.preterm.symptoms.oneLine: Four separate stories that together stage threatened or established labour
skill.hx.preterm.symptoms.why: Early labour is diagnosed from the story plus the cervix, and the story also carries the two findings that forbid buying time: infected membranes and a separating placenta. A history that records only pain misses leaking, misses fever and sends the wrong patient for tocolysis.

asks.text: When did the pains start. Ask how often they come, how long each lasts and whether the gaps are regular. Ask if they ease with rest and fluids or keep mounting. Pains of hours with tightening every few minutes, each lasting most of a minute, favour true labour.

Has there been a gush or a steady leak of fluid down below. Ask when it started, how much there was, whether pads are soaked, the colour and the smell, and whether more escapes on coughing or on moving. Ask even when she complains only of pain.

Has there been vaginal bleeding. Ask the amount in pads, any clots, whether the pain is constant rather than coming and going, and whether the baby still moves. Constant pain with a uterus that never softens points away from labour.

Ask about discharge, itching and odour, and about burning or frequency on passing urine, loin pain and fever with shivering. Infection of the urine or genital tract can start contractions and forbids delaying treatment.
Ask about the baby: movements as usual, reduced or absent, and any recent fall, knock or intercourse. Then ask what she has already tried: rest, fluids, and any drug taken for the pains.

Close the story with the dates check: the last period, any early scan, and whether this pregnancy is single or twins. The week decides steroids, transfer and delivery, so it belongs in every history of pains before term.

skill.hx.preterm.symptoms.practice: Take this history from a partner playing a woman at 31 weeks with pains and leaking, and end with one sentence that stages threatened or established labour with membrane status.
pitfalls: Timing pains loosely as all day instead of counting gaps and duration, which cannot separate labour from Braxton Hicks tightening.
Taking only the pain story and never asking about leaking, so ruptured membranes are found late on the speculum.
Calling every leak urine without asking about gush, pads, coughing and smell, which misses the rupture that changes the examination.
Forgetting fever, burning urine and discharge, so the infection that forbids tocolysis stays hidden.

probes.q: What four stories must you take separately in suspected early labour.
probes.a: Pains with timing and regularity, leaking of fluid with colour and smell, vaginal bleeding with amount and pain, and discharge with burning or fever, plus fetal movements.

probes.q: How does the history separate true labour from Braxton Hicks tightening.
probes.a: True labour pains are regular and painful, come every few minutes and last most of a minute, and mount rather than ease with rest, while Braxton Hicks tightening is irregular and painless and settles with rest and fluids.

probes.q: What in the leaking story points to ruptured membranes rather than urine.
probes.a: A sudden gush followed by steady leaking that soaks pads, more fluid escaping on coughing, and pale watery fluid without the smell of urine, with continued leaking despite an empty bladder.

rubric.text: Counts contraction gaps and duration and judges regularity
Asks about gush, pads, colour, smell and escape on coughing
Asks about amount, clots and constant pain with bleeding
Screens for discharge, burning urine, loin pain and fever

teach.heading: Time the pains, do not summarise them
teach.body: True labour announces itself in numbers: pains of hours, coming every few minutes, each lasting most of a minute, regular and mounting. Braxton Hicks tightening is irregular and painless and settles with rest and fluids. Insist on gaps and duration before you accept the word pain, because the cervix is examined on the strength of these numbers.

teach.heading: Every leak gets the same five questions
teach.body: When it started, how much there was, the colour, the smell and what brings more: coughing or moving. A sudden gush that soaks pads, with pale watery fluid and continued leaking after passing urine, favours membranes over bladder. Never accept the label urine until these five answers are in, because a missed rupture invites a digital examination that seeds infection.

teach.heading: Fever changes the road
teach.body: Temperature with shivering, uterine tenderness, fast pulse of mother or fetus and foul fluid together mean infected membranes. That combination forbids tocolysis and means delivery with antibiotics, not delay. Ask about burning urine, discharge and recent fever in every case of pains before term, because infection is the one driver that history alone can expose.

sources.locator: preterm_labour: redFlags
Preterm labour

skill.hx.preterm.risk.title: The risk road to early labour
skill.hx.preterm.risk.oneLine: Previous early births, the cervix, this pregnancy and the habits that raise risk
skill.hx.preterm.risk.why: The strongest predictors of early birth are already written in her past: a previous spontaneous early birth and a short cervix. Finding them before the pains start is what allows progesterone, a stitch and planned transfer; finding them during pains still changes steroids, tocolysis and the newborn plan.

asks.text: Go through every previous pregnancy in order: the outcome, the week it ended, whether labour started on its own, the birth weight and whether the baby survived. Give most weight to a spontaneous birth before term and to any loss in the second trimester.

Take the cervical story by name: a stitch placed in an earlier pregnancy, a cervix measured short on scan, and any treatment that removed cervical tissue such as cone or loop removal. A cervix under 25 mm in the mid trimester marks high risk.

Ask what makes this pregnancy stretch or bleed: twins or more, excess fluid, bleeding in this pregnancy, and any hard tender episode that never relaxed. Each points to a different road: stretch, bleeding behind the membranes, or abruption.

Ask about infection past and present: urine infection treated or ignored, discharge with odour, fever in this pregnancy, and group B streptococcus carriage if it is known. Untreated infection of urine or genital tract can trigger contractions.

Ask about age, tobacco chewed and smoked, alcohol, heavy physical work and who supports her at home. Ask where she is booked and whether progesterone or a stitch was ever offered, because prevention offered and refused still counts as risk.

skill.hx.preterm.risk.practice: Take the risk history from a partner with a prior birth at 32 weeks and a cervical stitch, and close with the two factors that predict this event most strongly.
pitfalls: Recording the number of children without the week of each birth, which discards the single strongest predictor.
Skipping second trimester losses because attention stops at live births, hiding cervical weakness.
Never asking about cone or loop treatment and short cervix on scan, so a preventable cause goes unnamed.
Asking if anything was wrong instead of naming stitch, twins, bleeding and infection, and accepting a polite no.

probes.q: Name the two strongest predictors of spontaneous early birth.
probes.a: A previous spontaneous early birth and a short cervix seen on transvaginal scan.

probes.q: Which cervical history raises the risk of early labour.
probes.a: A stitch placed for weakness in an earlier pregnancy, removal of cervical tissue beyond a small depth, and a cervix measured under 25 mm in the mid trimester.

probes.q: Which features of the current pregnancy predispose to early labour.
probes.a: Twins or a larger multiple pregnancy, excess fluid overstretching the uterus, bleeding behind the membranes, and untreated infection of the urine or genital tract.

rubric.text: Records every pregnancy with its week, onset and outcome
Asks about stitch, short cervix and tissue removal procedures
Asks about twins, excess fluid, bleeding and infection in this pregnancy
Asks about tobacco, alcohol, booking and prevention offered

teach.heading: The past predicts more than the pains
teach.body: A previous spontaneous early birth raises the risk of another far more than any symptom of today, and a second trimester loss or a stitch points to the cervix rather than contractions as the driver. Record week, onset and outcome for every pregnancy, because risk without a week cannot set a plan.

teach.heading: Name the cervix, measure the cervix
teach.body: A cervix under 25 mm in the mid trimester marks high risk, and removal of cervical tissue beyond a small depth adds risk of its own. Ask about stitch, short cervix on scan and cone or loop treatment by name, and arrange measurement where the service exists rather than waiting for pains.

teach.heading: Stretch, bleed and infect: the three roads
teach.body: Twins and excess fluid overstretch the uterus, bleeding behind the membranes inflames them, and infection of urine or genital tract provokes contractions through inflammatory signals. Each road is found by asking, and each changes prevention: progesterone or stitch for the cervix, rest and review for stretch, treatment for infection.

skill.present.preterm.case.title: Presenting the early labour case
skill.present.preterm.case.oneLine: Mother, week, stage, membranes, infection, fetus and the clock
skill.present.preterm.case.why: A consultant judges the plan from the presentation alone, and in early labour the plan is entirely about time: has the steroid clock started, is transfer arranged, is delivery indicated. A presentation that omits the week or the infection screen cannot be acted on.
skill.present.preterm.case.body: Present this mother in a fixed order: mother and gestation first, then the stage with membranes, the infection screen, the two patient examination, the key results, and a time bound plan.
keyPoints: Open with particulars that carry obstetric meaning: age, parity with weeks of previous births, gestation with dating method, booking status and referral source.
Stage labour in one breath: threatened or established, contraction pattern, cervical dilatation and effacement, membranes intact or ruptured with colour and smell of fluid.
Report infection and bleeding before the fetus: temperature, pulse, tenderness, fluid odour, urine and swabs, then amount and pain of any bleeding.
Report the fetus as the second patient: lie, presentation, size against dates, liquor and heart pattern with the response to contractions.

Close with the clock and keep it short: steroids given or due, tocolysis to gain time for steroids and transfer, magnesium where the week demands it, transfer state, delivery route and the newborn team. About two minutes, ending with a plan.

steps.text: Open with mother and dates: age, gravidity and parity with the weeks of previous births, exact gestation with how it was dated, and booking and referral status.
Stage the labour: threatened or established, contraction gaps and duration, cervical dilatation and effacement, and membranes intact or ruptured with fluid colour and smell.
Report the infection screen and bleeding: temperature and pulse, uterine tenderness, fluid odour, urine and swab status, and any bleeding with its amount.
Report the fetus as the second patient: lie and presentation, size against dates, liquor volume, and heart pattern during and after contractions.
Close with the clock: steroids given or due, tocolysis purpose, magnesium protection, transfer arranged or awaited, delivery route if indicated, and the newborn team warned.
Keep the focused case to about two minutes, in this fixed order, ending with a plan rather than a diagnosis.

skill.present.preterm.case.practice: Present the 31 week case with ruptured membranes and no infection in two minutes, and let the listener state the plan before you reveal yours.
pitfalls: Presenting in the order the questions were asked rather than the fixed order the listener expects.
Omitting the week or the dating method, leaving the listener unable to judge any threshold.
Reporting the mother fully and the fetus barely, or the fetus fully with no infection screen, in the one case with two patients and a clock.
Ending at the diagnosis with no steroids, transfer or delivery times, when the plan is the whole point.

probes.q: State the fixed order of the early labour presentation.
probes.a: Mother with parity and gestation, labour stage with membranes, infection screen, fetal findings, then summary with steroids and transfer plan.

probes.q: Why must the week open the presentation.
probes.a: Because survival improves with each extra week inside, and steroids, magnesium protection, transfer and delivery thresholds all turn on gestation.

probes.q: What clock driven treatments must the closing plan time, and what does each buy.
probes.a: Steroids to mature the lungs, tocolysis to delay birth while steroids act and transfer happens, and magnesium to protect the brain, with antibiotics when infection or group B streptococcus carriage demands it.

rubric.text: Presents in the fixed order from mother and week to plan
Stages labour with cervix, membranes, fluid colour and smell
Reports infection screen with maternal and fetal findings together
Ends with steroids, tocolysis purpose, transfer and delivery route

teach.heading: The week opens every sentence that matters
teach.body: At 31 weeks the plan is steroids and transfer, near term it is delivery, and a wrong date picks the wrong plan. State gestation with its dating method before any finding, because every threshold in this disease turns on the week.

teach.heading: Membranes and infection travel together
teach.body: Pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix with escape on coughing confirms rupture, while fever with tenderness and foul fluid confirms infection that forbids tocolysis. Report colour and smell with the same care as dilatation, and state why no digital examination was done.

teach.heading: Close with a clock, not a label
teach.body: Steroids need a first dose now to help the lungs, tocolysis buys the hours for steroids to act and transfer to happen, and magnesium protects the brain at early weeks. A closing sentence that names dose state, transfer state and delivery route lets the consultant correct the plan instead of reconstructing it.

skill.hx.miscarriag.symptoms.title: Bleeding, pain and symptoms of early pregnancy loss
skill.hx.miscarriag.symptoms.oneLine: Characterising vaginal bleeding, tissue passage, and pelvic pain in early pregnancy
skill.hx.miscarriag.symptoms.why: Vaginal bleeding occurs in up to a quarter of first trimester pregnancies, but the clinical course ranges from benign spotting to life-threatening haemorrhage or ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Eliciting the precise onset, volume, colour, tissue passage, and pain pattern tells threatened miscarriage apart from inevitable or incomplete loss, and directs immediate resuscitation before examination.
skill.hx.miscarriag.symptoms.body: Ask systematically about vaginal bleeding, passage of clots or fleshy tissue, suprapubic cramping pain, shoulder tip pain or faintness, and any loss of subjective pregnancy symptoms.

asks.text: Bleeding onset and amount: when did the bleeding begin, how many sanitary pads have been soaked, is it fresh bright red blood or brownish spotting, and has it been getting heavier or lighter over the hours?
Tissue passage: have you noticed any solid pieces, fleshy fragments, or greyish tissue passed down below, or has the discharge contained only liquid blood and dark clots?
Pain character: where is the pain located, does it feel like period cramps coming in waves across the lower abdomen, or is it a sharp constant pain on one side?
Systemic symptoms: have you felt dizzy, light-headed on standing, faint, or experienced pain at the tip of the shoulder, which points towards intraperitoneal bleeding?
Pregnancy symptoms: have earlier early-pregnancy symptoms like nausea, morning sickness, and breast tenderness suddenly diminished or stopped over the preceding days?
Fever and discharge: have you had any chills, fever, shivering, or unpleasant smelling vaginal discharge that suggests infected products of conception?

keyPoints: Light bleeding with minimal or no pain points toward threatened miscarriage, where the pregnancy may yet continue safely.
Heavy fresh bleeding with rhythmical suprapubic cramps and passage of fleshy fragments suggests inevitable or incomplete miscarriage with cervical dilatation.
Sudden sharp unilateral pelvic pain with faintness or shoulder tip pain suggests ruptured ectopic pregnancy rather than miscarriage, demanding emergency ultrasound.
Resolution of earlier pregnancy nausea and breast fullness often precedes the onset of bleeding in a missed miscarriage or embryonic demise.
pitfalls: Failing to ask specifically whether fleshy tissue or only blood clots were passed, which is the key historical distinction between threatened and incomplete miscarriage.
Dismissing unilateral pain as simple uterine cramping without considering an ectopic pregnancy.
Neglecting to enquire about postural dizziness or syncope, which indicates significant occult blood loss.

teach.heading: Bleeding volume and tissue passage
teach.body:
First trimester vaginal bleeding must be quantified by pad count and colour. Brown spotting represents old altered blood and carries a lower risk of imminent loss, whereas bright red bleeding soaking more than one sanitary pad per hour signals active haemorrhage.

Ask whether the patient has passed recognisable tissue. Patients often mistake dark jelly-like blood clots for the conceptus; true products of conception appear firm, fleshy, grey-white or pinkish.

teach.heading: Pain characteristics and danger signs
teach.body:
Uterine cramping in miscarriage is typically midline, suprapubic, rhythmical, and accompanied by bleeding as the cervix softens and dilates to expel tissue.

Sharp, constant, or strictly unilateral iliac fossa pain should immediately raise suspicion of ectopic pregnancy. Shoulder tip pain reflects diaphragmatic irritation from haemoperitoneum and demands urgent surgical escalation.

probes.q: How does the pain of miscarriage differ characteristically from the pain of an ectopic pregnancy?
probes.a: Miscarriage pain is usually midline, suprapubic, rhythmical, and cramping like labour, whereas ectopic pain is often sharp, constant, and strictly unilateral in the iliac fossa.

probes.q: What is the clinical significance of passing fleshy greyish tissue compared to dark red blood clots?
probes.a: Passing fleshy greyish tissue indicates expulsion of products of conception such as gestational sac or decidua, confirming an incomplete or complete miscarriage rather than a threatened loss with simple clots.

skill.hx.miscarriag.risk.title: Risk factors and background in early pregnancy loss
skill.hx.miscarriag.risk.oneLine: Identifying maternal, genetic, endocrine, and anatomical factors predisposing to miscarriage
skill.hx.miscarriag.risk.why: While sporadic first trimester loss is most commonly caused by embryonic chromosomal aneuploidy, identifying maternal background factors is vital to prevent recurrence and uncover treatable systemic diseases such as antiphospholipid syndrome, thyroid disorders, or uncontrolled diabetes mellitus.
skill.hx.miscarriag.risk.body: Take a targeted background history covering maternal age, past pregnancy outcomes, medical comorbidities, endocrine disorders, prior uterine surgery or instrumentation, and medication exposures.

asks.text: Maternal age: what is your age, as chromosomal aneuploidy rises steeply in mothers over 35 years?
Obstetric history: have you had previous miscarriages, terminations, ectopic pregnancies, or premature deliveries, and at what gestations did they occur?
Medical disorders: do you have a history of thyroid disease, diabetes mellitus, systemic lupus erythematosus, or known blood clotting problems like thrombophilia?
Uterine conditions: have you been told of any fibroids, uterine anomalies such as a septate uterus, or had previous cervical procedures or curettage?
Medications and substances: are you taking any prescribed or over-the-counter medicines, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, or tobacco products?

keyPoints: Advanced maternal age is the strongest independent demographic predictor of spontaneous miscarriage due to rising rates of embryonic aneuploidy.
A history of two or more consecutive miscarriages meets the clinical definition of recurrent pregnancy loss and warrants systematic investigation.
Antiphospholipid syndrome is the primary treatable autoimmune cause of recurrent miscarriage and requires targeted anticoagulant prophylaxis in future pregnancies.
Uncontrolled maternal endocrine disorders, particularly overt hypothyroidism and poor glycaemic control in diabetes, substantially elevate early loss risk.
pitfalls: Attributing recurrent early losses to stress or physical exertion without investigating for parental translocations, antiphospholipid syndrome, or uterine anomalies.
Failing to review medication history for teratogens or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs taken in early pregnancy.
Overlooking previous surgical curettage or cervical trauma that could predispose to intrauterine adhesions or cervical weakness.

teach.heading: Genetic and maternal age contributions
teach.body:
Chromosomal aneuploidy accounts for approximately fifty percent of sporadic first trimester spontaneous miscarriages. Trisomies, monosomy X, and polyploidies are the predominant genetic defects.

The risk of embryonic aneuploidy climbs progressively with maternal age, rising from about ten percent in women under thirty years to over fifty percent in women aged over forty years.

teach.heading: Systemic and anatomical predisposing conditions
teach.body:
Acquired autoimmune thrombophilias, specifically antiphospholipid syndrome with lupus anticoagulant or anticardiolipin antibodies, produce microvascular placental thrombosis and early failure.

Structural uterine anomalies, including congenital uterine septa, submucosal fibroids, and intrauterine adhesions, impede adequate decidualisation and blastocyst implantation.

probes.q: What is the single most common cause of sporadic first trimester spontaneous miscarriage?
probes.a: Embryonic chromosomal aneuploidy, which accounts for around fifty percent of all early spontaneous miscarriages.

probes.q: Which treatable autoimmune condition should be actively investigated in recurrent pregnancy loss?
probes.a: Antiphospholipid syndrome, identified by lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin antibodies, or anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I antibodies, which responds to low-dose aspirin and heparin.

skill.present.miscarriag.case.title: Presenting the early pregnancy bleeding and miscarriage case
skill.present.miscarriag.case.oneLine: Two-minute structured case presentation synthesising history, examination, stage, and plan
skill.present.miscarriag.case.why: Presenting a patient with early pregnancy loss requires concise, compassionate clarity that immediately communicates haemodynamic stability, gestational age, clinical stage, sonographic findings, and a definitive management plan with emotional support.
skill.present.miscarriag.case.body: Deliver a concise two-minute case presentation structured into problem representation, clinical examination findings, ultrasound and laboratory results, definitive stage diagnosis, and therapeutic plan.
keyPoints: Open with a precise problem representation stating maternal age, gravidity, parity, exact gestational age, and chief complaint of bleeding and pain.
State haemodynamic stability immediately, including pulse, blood pressure, and estimated blood loss.
Report cervical os state from speculum examination and uterine size relative to dates from bimanual examination.
Synthesise transvaginal ultrasound findings regarding intrauterine sac, embryonic pole, and cardiac activity.
Conclude with a clear management choice (expectant, medical, or surgical), anti-D administration status, and bereavement counselling.
pitfalls: Failing to state whether the internal cervical os was open or closed on examination, which is the physical hallmark of stage classification.
Omitting the maternal Rhesus blood group and requirement for anti-D immunoglobulin.
Focusing entirely on evacuation procedures while forgetting psychological support and grief counselling.

teach.heading: Structuring the opening statement
teach.body:
Begin with a crisp summary: Mrs Sunita is a twenty-four year old primigravida at nine weeks gestation presenting with six hours of vaginal bleeding and lower abdominal cramping.

Immediately declare maternal stability: She is haemodynamically stable with normal blood pressure and pulse, and has had no syncopal episodes or signs of acute peritonism.

teach.heading: Synthesising physical and sonographic findings
teach.body:
Present pelvic findings clearly: Speculum examination reveals active dark red bleeding with the internal os admitting one fingertip and tissue in the canal. Bimanual examination shows an eight-week sized uterus with no adnexal mass.

Integrate imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrates retained irregular echoes in the endometrial cavity without a viable fetal pole, confirming an incomplete miscarriage.

probes.q: What essential pieces of information must be stated in the opening thirty seconds of a miscarriage case presentation?
probes.a: Maternal age, parity, verified gestational age, duration and severity of bleeding and pain, and maternal haemodynamic stability.

probes.q: Why must the Rhesus status always be mentioned when concluding the case presentation?
probes.a: Because non-sensitised Rhesus-negative women require anti-D immunoglobulin within seventy-two hours of early pregnancy bleeding or evacuation to prevent isoimmunisation.

skill.hx.ectopic.risk.title: Risk factors for ectopic pregnancy
skill.hx.ectopic.risk.oneLine: Identifying previous ectopic, tubal surgery, PID, endometriosis, and IUCD conception
skill.hx.ectopic.risk.why: Recognising predisposing tubal factors alerts the clinician early, although one-third of women with ectopic pregnancy have no identifiable risk factors.
skill.hx.ectopic.risk.body: Ask systematically about past ectopic gestations, pelvic infections, pelvic surgery, assisted reproduction, and contraception at the time of conception.

asks.text: Past ectopic pregnancy: Have you ever had an ectopic pregnancy before? A previous ectopic is the strongest single risk factor, carrying a ten-fold increase in recurrence.

Tubal and pelvic surgery: Have you had surgery on your fallopian tubes, sterilisation, or surgery for appendicitis or pelvic adhesions? Prior tubal surgery alters ciliary motility and lumen architecture.

Pelvic infections and PID: Have you been treated for pelvic inflammatory disease, sexually transmitted infections like chlamydia or gonorrhoea, or chronic pelvic pain? Salpingitis produces endosalpingeal damage and intraluminal synechiae.

Contraceptive history: Were you using an intrauterine device or progestogen-only contraception when you conceived? While IUCDs reduce the overall rate of pregnancy, if pregnancy occurs with an IUCD in situ, up to fifty percent are ectopic.
Fertility treatments: Did this pregnancy occur following in vitro fertilisation or ovulation induction? Assisted conception increases the risk of both tubal and heterotopic gestations.
Endometriosis and smoking: Do you have a diagnosis of endometriosis, or do you smoke cigarettes? Endometriosis causes peritubal distortion, while cigarette smoking impairs tubal ciliary motility.

keyPoints: A history of a previous ectopic pregnancy carries a ten-fold increased risk of recurrence, reaching ten to fifteen percent after one ectopic and over twenty-five percent after two.
Approximately one-third of women presenting with ectopic pregnancy have no identifiable risk factors, so the absence of risk factors must never be used to rule out the diagnosis.
If a woman conceives with an intrauterine contraceptive device in situ, the likelihood of that pregnancy being extrauterine is substantially heightened.
Assisted reproduction carries a risk of heterotopic pregnancy where an intrauterine and extrauterine gestation coexist simultaneously.
skill.hx.ectopic.risk.practice: Take a focused risk-factor history in two minutes from a simulated patient presenting with positive pregnancy test and pelvic pain, covering previous ectopic, pelvic surgery, PID, and IUCD use.
pitfalls: Assuming absence of documented risk factors excludes the possibility of an ectopic gestation.
Failing to ask about contraception at the time of conception, especially an intrauterine contraceptive device.
Neglecting the possibility of heterotopic pregnancy in women who have undergone assisted reproductive technologies.

probes.q: What is the single strongest clinical risk factor for an ectopic pregnancy?
probes.a: A previous ectopic pregnancy is the strongest clinical risk factor, increasing recurrence risk to about ten to fifteen percent.

probes.q: Why does a history of pelvic inflammatory disease increase the risk of tubal implantation?
probes.a: Pelvic inflammatory disease causes endosalpingeal inflammation, mucosal deciliation, and tubal scarring that impairs blastocyst transport through the fallopian tube.

probes.q: What is the risk of ectopic pregnancy if a patient conceives with an intrauterine contraceptive device in place?
probes.a: Although an intrauterine contraceptive device markedly reduces overall pregnancy rates, if failure occurs and a pregnancy implants, the proportion of ectopic gestations is significantly higher.

rubric.text: Inquires specifically about previous ectopic pregnancies and recurrence risks
Asks about previous tubal surgery, sterilisation, or adhesiolysis
Explores past pelvic inflammatory disease, sexually transmitted infections, and salpingitis
Identifies contraceptive failure with intrauterine contraceptive devices
Screens for assisted conception and the possibility of heterotopic gestation

skill.present.ectopic.case.title: Presenting the ectopic pregnancy case
skill.present.ectopic.case.oneLine: Structured bedside presentation of early pregnancy pain, ultrasound, and management decision
skill.present.ectopic.case.why: In acute gynaecology, a crisp structured case presentation clearly articulates haemodynamic stability, diagnostic imaging findings, and the justification for medical versus surgical therapy.

teach.heading: The sixty-second early pregnancy presentation
teach.body:
Open with age, parity, and gestational age calculated from the last menstrual period.

State clearly whether she is haemodynamically stable or unstable, her presenting complaints, and the key pelvic examination findings including cervical motion tenderness and adnexal fullness.

Conclude with the transvaginal ultrasound findings, baseline serum beta-hCG, and whether she meets criteria for medical management or requires immediate surgical intervention.

teach.heading: Key elements to highlight to the senior clinician
teach.body: Emphasise four critical decision points: first, vital signs and signs of intra-abdominal bleeding or peritonism; second, the serum beta-hCG in relation to the transvaginal discriminatory zone; third, adnexal mass dimensions and presence of embryonic cardiac activity; fourth, patient compliance and suitability for outpatient methotrexate versus inpatient surgery.

skill.present.ectopic.case.practice: Rehearse presenting an unruptured ectopic pregnancy case to a consultant in sixty seconds, summarising history, examination, transvaginal scan, hCG level, and medical management eligibility.
pitfalls: Presenting extensive non-contributory background before stating the haemodynamic stability and vital signs.
Omitting the transvaginal ultrasound adnexal mass diameter or the baseline serum beta-hCG.
Proposing methotrexate without stating whether baseline hepatic, renal, and haematological labs have been confirmed normal.

probes.q: What is the first clinical detail to communicate when presenting a suspected ectopic pregnancy?
probes.a: The patient haemodynamic stability and vital signs, to determine immediately whether resuscitation and emergency theatre transfer are required.

probes.q: Which three ultrasound measurements must be reported when presenting a stable ectopic pregnancy for medical management?
probes.a: The presence or absence of an intrauterine gestation, the maximum diameter of the adnexal mass, and the presence or absence of embryonic cardiac activity.

rubric.text: States age, parity, gestation, and immediate haemodynamic stability in the opening sentence
Summarises the classic triad, cervical excitation, and localized peritoneal findings
Quotes transvaginal scan features, mass size, cardiac activity, and quantitative beta-hCG
Justifies the selected management pathway according to established safety criteria

skill.hx.post.risk.title: Risk factors and background in prolonged pregnancy
skill.hx.post.risk.oneLine: Accurate menstrual dates, prior post-term births, maternal weight and risks that mandate timely delivery
skill.hx.post.risk.why: Gestational age determines every obstetric threshold. The commonest cause of an apparently post-term pregnancy is inaccurate dates, while true prolonged pregnancy carries risk of placental senescence, oligohydramnios and stillbirth. Taking a meticulous history of menstrual regularity, early dating ultrasound, prior post-term births and maternal risk factors separates spurious dating errors from genuine prolonged gestation requiring induction.

asks.text: What was the exact first day of your last normal menstrual period, and were your cycles regular at 28 to 30 days before conceiving? Regular cycles are essential for applying the rule of adding 9 months and 7 days to calculate the true expected date of delivery.

Did you have an early ultrasound scan during the first three months of pregnancy? An ultrasound measurement of crown-rump length between 11 and 14 weeks provides the most accurate estimation of gestational age.

Have you had any previous deliveries that went past your due date, or did you require induction of labour in earlier pregnancies? A history of a prior prolonged pregnancy carries a recurrence risk of up to 30 percent.

Have you had any high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid disease, or other medical illnesses during this pregnancy? Medical co-morbidities worsen placental insufficiency and lower the threshold for intervention.
Have you noticed regular fetal movements every day, or has there been any recent slowing down of the baby kicks? Decreased fetal movements in a late-term pregnancy can herald placental failure.
Have you noticed any watery fluid leaking from the vagina, bloody discharge, or painful uterine contractions? Leaking fluid may signify prelabour rupture of membranes compounding oligohydramnios.

skill.hx.post.risk.practice: Take a focused dating and risk history from a multiparous woman presenting at 41 weeks, verifying menstrual regularity, early scan confirmation, prior prolonged deliveries, and danger symptoms.
pitfalls: Relying on the date a period was missed rather than the first day of the last normal bleeding episode.
Assuming dates are accurate when the woman had irregular cycles or conceived immediately after stopping oral contraceptive pills.
Overlooking decreased fetal movements as an urgent sign of placental compromise in late gestation.

probes.q: What is the commonest cause of an apparent post-term pregnancy?
probes.a: Inaccurate menstrual dating due to irregular cycles or miscalculated last menstrual period is the commonest cause.

probes.q: What ultrasound parameter in the first trimester gives the most reliable estimation of gestational age?
probes.a: Crown-rump length measurement between 11 and 14 weeks gives the most accurate gestational age estimation within 5 days.

probes.q: Why does a history of previous post-term pregnancy matter in the current pregnancy?
probes.a: Prolonged pregnancy has a significant recurrence risk of 20 to 30 percent in subsequent pregnancies, warranting early dating and vigilant antenatal surveillance.

rubric.text: Verifies first day of last normal menstrual period and cycle regularity
Cross-checks dates against first-trimester dating ultrasound crown-rump length
Screens for prior post-term births, medical disorders, and decreased fetal movements

skill.present.post.case.title: Presenting the post-term pregnancy case
skill.present.post.case.oneLine: Maternal parity, confirmed gestational age, liquor and fetal status, Bishop score and induction plan
skill.present.post.case.why: Presenting a post-term pregnancy requires clear communication of dating reliability, maternal-fetal risk status, cervical readiness, and the proposed delivery plan. The listener needs the exact gestation in weeks and days, how it was verified, liquor status, and Bishop score to assess whether pre-induction cervical ripening or immediate delivery is required.
skill.present.post.case.body: Present a post-term obstetric case in a structured order: demographic particulars and parity, gestational age with dating basis, fetal surveillance findings, cervical Bishop score, and the step-by-step induction strategy.
keyPoints: State maternal age, parity, gravidity, and exact gestational age in completed weeks and days, confirming how dates were verified (regular LMP versus early dating scan).
Summarise the clinical history including absence or presence of labour pains, membrane rupture, vaginal bleeding, and fetal movement activity.
Report physical examination: maternal vitals, fundal height (noting any lag indicating oligohydramnios), Leopold manoeuvres with presentation and station, and baseline fetal heart rate.
Present investigation findings clearly: ultrasound biometry, single deepest pocket or amniotic fluid index, and non-stress test or CTG categorisation.
Detail the pre-induction cervical assessment: calculate and break down the modified Bishop score out of 13, classifying the cervix as favourable (8 or above) or unfavourable (5 or less).

Conclude with an actionable management plan: method of cervical ripening (dinoprostone gel, oral misoprostol, or Foley balloon) or oxytocin induction, monitoring protocol, and thresholds for caesarean delivery.
pitfalls: Failing to explain the evidence on which gestational age was established.
Recommending oxytocin induction without stating the Bishop score or cervical ripening status.
Omitting amniotic fluid volume and CTG findings when presenting fetal well-being.

probes.q: What essential information must be included in the opening sentence of a post-term pregnancy presentation?
probes.a: Maternal age, gravidity, parity, accurate gestational age in weeks and days, and how the dates were confirmed.

probes.q: Why must the pre-induction Bishop score be presented before detailing the induction regimen?
probes.a: Because cervical favourability dictates the induction method: a score of 5 or less requires cervical ripening with prostaglandins or balloon, whereas a score of 8 or more allows direct amniotomy and oxytocin.

rubric.text: Opens with maternal particulars, exact gestational age, and dating confirmation
Presents liquor volume and CTG findings systematically
Reports Bishop score and provides an appropriate cervical ripening or induction plan

skill.hx.twin.risk.title: Risk factors, conception background, and complications in multiple pregnancy
skill.hx.twin.risk.oneLine: Conception history, family twinning, severe hyperemesis, pre-eclampsia warnings, and early labour signs
skill.hx.twin.risk.why: A detailed multiple pregnancy history identifies risk factors for twinning (such as assisted reproductive technology, ovulation induction, advanced maternal age, and maternal family history of dizygotic twins), verifies menstrual dating before discordance develops, and screens proactively for major obstetric complications including severe hyperemesis, early-onset pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, severe anaemia, and preterm labour.

asks.text: Did this pregnancy occur naturally, or did you receive ovulation-inducing medications, intrauterine insemination, or in-vitro fertilisation? Ovulation induction and assisted reproductive technology dramatically increase dizygotic and higher-order multifetal conceptions.

What was the exact first day of your last normal menstrual period, and were your cycles regular before conceiving? Establishing accurate gestational dating in the first trimester is critical before discordant growth can confound assessment.

Did you have an ultrasound scan between 11 and 14 weeks of pregnancy? Early ultrasound provides definitive documentation of chorionicity and amnionicity, which stratifies all subsequent risk and surveillance.
Do you or your mother or sisters have a history of twin pregnancies? A maternal family history of twins indicates a genetic predisposition to polyovulation and dizygotic twinning.

Have you experienced persistent severe nausea, vomiting, or inability to keep fluids down during the first three months? Markedly elevated beta-hCG and human placental lactogen in multifetal pregnancy frequently cause severe hyperemesis gravidarum.

Have you noticed severe frontal headaches, visual blurring, flashes of light, swelling of your hands or face, or upper abdominal pain? Women with twins have a three-to-four-fold increased risk of developing pre-eclampsia at earlier gestational ages.

Have you felt regular painful abdominal tightenings, lower backache, pelvic pressure, watery vaginal leaking, or bloody discharge? Uterine overdistension predisposes to spontaneous preterm labour and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes.

skill.hx.twin.risk.practice: Take a comprehensive multiple pregnancy history from a primigravida at 18 weeks, verifying conception mode, menstrual dates, first-trimester scan documentation, hyperemesis, and warning symptoms of pre-eclampsia and preterm labour.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about fertility medications or embryo transfer numbers which influence zygosity and risk profiles.
Dismissing pronounced first-trimester vomiting as normal pregnancy nausea without assessing hydration, electrolytes, or weight loss.
Overlooking mild early hypertensive symptoms which can rapidly escalate to severe pre-eclampsia in multifetal gestation.

probes.q: Why is maternal family history relevant to dizygotic but not monozygotic twinning?
probes.a: Dizygotic twinning is influenced by a hereditary maternal tendency to multiple ovulation, whereas monozygotic twinning occurs at a constant rate of approximately 3.5 to 4 per 1,000 births without familial predisposition.

probes.q: Why is early first-trimester dating especially critical in multiple pregnancy?
probes.a: Because fetal growth restriction and inter-twin growth discordance can develop later in pregnancy, making late biometry unreliable for establishing true gestational age.

probes.q: Name three maternal medical complications that occur with significantly higher frequency in twin gestation.
probes.a: Pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes mellitus, severe hyperemesis gravidarum, and iron-deficiency anaemia.

rubric.text: Inquires about natural versus assisted conception and confirms first-trimester dating
Verifies whether early ultrasound established chorionicity and amnionicity
Systematically screens for hyperemesis, pre-eclampsia warnings, and preterm contractions
