skill.present.twin.case.title: Presenting the twin pregnancy case
skill.present.twin.case.oneLine: Maternal parity, confirmed gestational age, chorionicity, fetal presentations, growth concordance, and delivery plan
skill.present.twin.case.why: Presenting a multifetal pregnancy to senior obstetricians requires an efficient, structured delivery that highlights gestational age, chorionicity, fetal presentations, growth concordance, amniotic fluid adequacy, maternal blood pressure, and a comprehensive delivery or surveillance plan. Clear articulation of chorionicity immediately frames whether the consultation focuses on monochorionic vascular complications or standard multifetal surveillance.
skill.present.twin.case.body: Present a multifetal obstetric case in a structured order: demographic particulars and parity, gestational age with dating basis, first-trimester chorionicity determination, fetal lie and presentations (particularly Twin A), ultrasound biometry and growth concordance, amniotic fluid volumes, maternal blood pressure and laboratory screening, and the structured surveillance or delivery schedule.
keyPoints: Open with maternal age, parity, gravidity, exact gestational age, and confirmed chorionicity and amnionicity from early scan.
Summarise relevant history including conception mode (spontaneous versus assisted), family history, and absence of pre-eclampsia warning symptoms or preterm labour pains.
Report physical examination: blood pressure, abdominal symphysis-fundal height discrepancy, Leopold palpation identifying multiple fetal poles, and two distinct fetal heart rates.

Present ultrasound findings systematically: presentation of Twin A and Twin B, individual estimated fetal weights, calculated growth discordance percentage, deepest vertical pool in each sac, and Doppler indices.
State maternal screening results: urinalysis for proteinuria, complete blood count for anaemia, and oral glucose tolerance testing.

Conclude with a definitive, chorionicity-tailored management plan: fortnightly scans for MCDA or monthly scans for DCDA, nutritional supplements, preterm labour advice, and planned delivery timing and route based on the presentation of Twin A.
pitfalls: Failing to state chorionicity in the opening sentence of the presentation.
Omitting the presentation of Twin A, which is the single most critical determinant of planned vaginal birth versus caesarean section.
Neglecting to report amniotic fluid discordance and Doppler parameters when presenting monochorionic twins.

probes.q: What essential information must be communicated in the very first sentence of a twin pregnancy case presentation?
probes.a: Maternal age, gravidity, parity, exact gestational age in weeks, and whether the pregnancy is monochorionic or dichorionic.

probes.q: Why is the presentation of Twin A presented before Twin B when discussing the delivery plan?
probes.a: Because the presentation of Twin A dictates the route of delivery: if Twin A is cephalic, vaginal birth is feasible; if Twin A is non-cephalic, planned caesarean delivery is indicated regardless of Twin B.

rubric.text: States maternal particulars, exact gestational age, and chorionicity upfront
Presents Twin A presentation, growth discordance, and liquor status clearly
Outlines an appropriate surveillance interval and evidence-based delivery timing

skill.hx.fetal.symptoms.title: Symptoms and maternal signs in suspected fetal growth restriction
skill.hx.fetal.symptoms.oneLine: Perception of fetal movements, small abdominal girth, fluid leakage, and maternal warning signs
skill.hx.fetal.symptoms.why: Fetal growth restriction is clinically silent in its early stages until maternal awareness of small abdominal size or declining fetal movements prompts medical attention. Inquiring systematically about the onset and tempo of fetal activity, changes in abdominal girth, loss of fluid per vaginam, and features of coexisting gestational hypertensive disorders enables early detection of chronic placental compromise before irreversible fetal acidemia develops.

asks.text: Have you noticed any change or reduction in your baby movements over recent days? A sudden reduction in fetal kicks is a cardinal symptom of worsening placental perfusion and chronic hypoxaemia.

Have you felt that your baby bump is not growing as expected or seems smaller than other women at the same stage of pregnancy? Maternal perception of static abdominal size often corresponds to lagging fundal height.
Have you noticed any continuous or sudden trickling of clear watery fluid from your vagina? Rupture of membranes must be differentiated from intact membranes with reduced liquor production.
Have you experienced any vaginal spotting, fresh bleeding, or sudden abdominal pain? Bleeding and pain may indicate concealed placental abruption complicating uteroplacental insufficiency.

Do you have any severe persistent headache, flashing lights or blurred vision, or sharp pain just below your ribs? These pre-eclampsia danger signs warn of multi-organ maternal disease accompanying placental dysfunction.

How has your appetite and nutritional intake been, and have you been gaining weight on your antenatal check-up card? Maternal undernutrition and poor gestational weight gain contribute to suboptimal fetal growth.

skill.hx.fetal.symptoms.practice: Take a focused symptom history from a pregnant woman presenting at 34 weeks with lagging abdominal growth, specifically screening for reduced fetal movements, fluid leakage, and pre-eclampsia symptoms.
pitfalls: Dismissing maternal reporting of decreased fetal movement as normal late-pregnancy slowing without cardiotocography and ultrasound.
Failing to ask about watery discharge to exclude prelabour rupture of membranes as the primary cause of oligohydramnios.
Overlooking hypertensive warning signs like epigastric pain or persistent headache in a woman with an undersized uterus.

probes.q: What symptom reported by the mother is the most urgent indicator of acute-on-chronic fetal compromise in growth restriction?
probes.a: A sudden reduction or cessation of fetal movements indicates worsening fetal hypoxaemia and mandates immediate cardiotocography and ultrasound Doppler evaluation.

probes.q: Why must you ask about watery vaginal fluid leakage in a woman found to have oligohydramnios on palpation?
probes.a: Watery leakage indicates premature rupture of membranes, which must be distinguished from intact membranes where oligohydramnios is caused by reduced fetal urine output secondary to placental insufficiency.

rubric.text: Inquires specifically into the timing and pattern of fetal movements
Screens for fluid leakage to differentiate membrane rupture from oligohydramnios
Identifies coexisting maternal hypertensive warning signs

skill.hx.fetal.risk.title: Risk factors and background in fetal growth restriction and oligohydramnios
skill.hx.fetal.risk.oneLine: Previous small-for-gestational-age birth, maternal vascular disorders, nutritional status, and substance exposure
skill.hx.fetal.risk.why: Defective spiral artery invasion and secondary placental insufficiency cluster in women with identifiable pre-pregnancy and early-gestational risk factors. Eliciting a history of a prior growth-restricted newborn, recurrent stillbirths, chronic hypertension, renal disease, antiphospholipid antibodies, pre-gestational diabetes, severe anaemia, undernutrition, or tobacco exposure establishes pre-test probability, dictates surveillance frequency, and determines eligibility for prophylactic aspirin in subsequent pregnancies.

asks.text: What were the birth weights and gestational ages of your previous babies, and were any admitted to the special newborn care unit? A history of a previous small-for-gestational-age infant is the single strongest clinical predictor of recurrence.

Have you had any history of stillbirth, unexplained fetal loss, or recurrent miscarriages in past pregnancies? Recurrent pregnancy loss points towards parental chromosomal anomalies, thrombophilia, or severe uteroplacental vasculopathy.

Did you have high blood pressure, protein in the urine, or kidney problems before this pregnancy or early in gestation? Chronic vascular and renal diseases impede physiological trophoblastic remodelling of maternal spiral arteries.

Do you consume tobacco in any form, including bidi smoking or chewing gutkha and khaini? Nicotine and carbon monoxide cause maternal vasoconstriction, impair placental oxygen transport, and restrict fetal growth.

Were you started on low-dose aspirin tablets during the first four months of this pregnancy? Early initiation of aspirin by 16 weeks reduces the incidence of placenta-mediated growth restriction and pre-eclampsia in high-risk women.

Did you experience any high fever with skin rash, joint pains, or glandular swelling during the first trimester? Early maternal viral infections such as cytomegalovirus or rubella can cause symmetrical fetal growth failure.

skill.hx.fetal.risk.practice: Take a comprehensive obstetric and medical background history from a woman with suspected fetal growth restriction, evaluating prior birth weights, medical comorbidities, and substance use.
pitfalls: Recording a previous birth without inquiring whether the baby was born small for gestational age or required neonatal nursery admission.
Missing smokeless tobacco consumption, which is widely used in rural and semi-urban Indian communities and significantly impairs placental perfusion.
Failing to verify whether prophylactic low-dose aspirin was prescribed and taken regularly from early pregnancy.

probes.q: Which historical risk factor confers the highest recurrence risk for fetal growth restriction in the current pregnancy?
probes.a: A previous pregnancy affected by fetal growth restriction or delivery of a small-for-gestational-age infant is the strongest predictor of recurrence.

probes.q: Why should low-dose aspirin prophylaxis be initiated prior to 16 weeks of gestation in women with major risk factors for placental insufficiency?
probes.a: Aspirin inhibits thromboxane synthesis and improves deep trophoblastic invasion of the spiral arteries, which is completed by 16 to 20 weeks of gestation.

rubric.text: Extracts detailed birth weights and outcomes of previous pregnancies
Identifies maternal chronic vascular, renal, or autoimmune disorders
Inquires about tobacco consumption and adherence to low-dose aspirin prophylaxis

skill.present.fetal.case.title: Presenting the fetal growth restriction and oligohydramnios case
skill.present.fetal.case.oneLine: Maternal particulars, dating certainty, biometry discrepancy, Doppler stage, and delivery plan
skill.present.fetal.case.why: A senior obstetrician evaluates a fetal growth restriction case to decide whether the fetus is safer continuing in utero under surveillance or being delivered into neonatal intensive care. Presenting clearly requires stating the exact gestational age and its dating basis, the degree of abdominal circumference and estimated fetal weight deficit, the Doppler staging sequence, liquor volume, and a concrete delivery recommendation balanced against prematurity.
skill.present.fetal.case.body: Present a case of fetal growth restriction and oligohydramnios in a standardised clinical sequence: demographic particulars with dating accuracy, clinical and fundal lag, ultrasound biometry centiles, multi-vessel Doppler progression, liquor status, and an evidence-based delivery recommendation.
keyPoints: Open with maternal age, gravidity, parity, exact gestational age in completed weeks and days, and how dating was established using first-trimester crown-rump length or regular menstrual dates.
Summarise the clinical history including fetal movement perception, maternal perception of abdominal growth, and absence of membrane rupture or vaginal bleeding.
Report maternal physical examination: blood pressure, presence or absence of oedema, symphysis-fundal height with exact centimetres of lag, and abdominal palpation of fetal parts.
Present ultrasound biometry: specify abdominal circumference and estimated fetal weight centiles, head-sparing ratio, and confirmation of anatomical normality.

Detail the multi-vessel Doppler status: umbilical artery pulsatility index and presence, absence, or reversal of end-diastolic flow; middle cerebral artery pulsatility index and cerebroplacental ratio; and ductus venosus a-wave.
State the amniotic fluid volume using single deepest vertical pocket and amniotic fluid index.

Conclude with an actionable management plan: antenatal corticosteroids, magnesium sulphate if preterm delivery is planned, continuous fetal heart monitoring, and mode of delivery with neonatal team mobilization.
pitfalls: Presenting an estimated fetal weight without stating the exact gestational centile and whether previous scans show static growth.
Failing to report Doppler findings in logical vascular sequence from umbilical artery to middle cerebral artery and ductus venosus.
Recommending urgent delivery without stating antenatal corticosteroid coverage or neonatal intensive care readiness.

probes.q: What fundamental dating information must be stated at the beginning of a fetal growth restriction presentation?
probes.a: Maternal age, gravidity, parity, exact gestational age in weeks and days, and the method used to verify dating certainty.

probes.q: Why must the ductus venosus Doppler waveform be presented before deciding on delivery in early-onset severe growth restriction?
probes.a: Because ductus venosus a-wave reversal reflects advanced myocardial decompensation and acidemia, serving as a critical trigger for emergency delivery prior to 32 weeks.

rubric.text: Presents maternal demographics, verified gestational age, and dating criteria
Reports biometry centiles, liquor volume, and Doppler progression systematically
Concludes with a concrete delivery plan, steroid coverage, and neonatal coordination

skill.hx.rh.symptoms.title: Maternal symptoms and fetal movement monitoring in Rh negative pregnancy
skill.hx.rh.symptoms.oneLine: Systematic questioning to detect silent sensitisation, fetal movements, hydrops warnings, and mirror syndrome
skill.hx.rh.symptoms.why: Unsensitised Rh-negative pregnancy is completely symptomless, and even severe fetal haemolytic disease develops silently in utero. Inquiring deliberately into fetal movement patterns, maternal perception of abdominal enlargement, generalised oedema, and hypertensive symptoms allows the clinician to identify impending hydrops fetalis and maternal mirror syndrome before fetal demise occurs.

asks.text: How are the movements of your baby over recent days, and have you noticed any reduction in kicks? A sudden reduction in fetal kicks is a cardinal symptom of worsening fetal compromise and severe haemolytic anaemia.
Have you felt that your baby bump is growing unusually fast or seems much larger than expected? Rapid abdominal enlargement suggests polyhydramnios and placentomegaly secondary to fetal hydrops.
Have you noticed sudden swelling of your legs, hands, or face, or rapid weight gain? Severe fetal hydrops can provoke maternal mirror syndrome with generalized anasarca.
Do you have any severe persistent headache, flashing lights before your eyes, or upper stomach pain? Maternal mirror syndrome often mimics severe pre-eclampsia with hypertensive danger signs.
Have you experienced any shortness of breath or difficulty breathing when lying flat? Maternal pulmonary oedema can develop as part of the generalized fluid overload in mirror syndrome.
Have you had any bleeding from the vagina or clear watery fluid leaking? Antepartum haemorrhage triggers further fetomaternal haemorrhage, while membrane rupture requires urgent evaluation.

skill.hx.rh.symptoms.practice: In an antenatal clinic, demonstrate taking a targeted history from an Rh-negative pregnant woman, focusing on fetal movement trends, abdominal distension, and signs of maternal mirror syndrome.
pitfalls: Assuming that absence of maternal symptoms guarantees fetal health when fetal anaemia develops silently
Dismissing rapid abdominal growth and maternal edema as normal third-trimester physiological changes
Failing to ask specifically about the daily tempo of fetal kicks in an alloimmunised pregnancy

probes.q: Why does an Rh-negative pregnant woman carrying a severely anaemic fetus often have no physical symptoms herself?
probes.a: Maternal Rh isoimmunisation affects fetal red blood cells through transplacental IgG antibodies, so the mother remains asymptomatic while the fetus develops progressive extravascular haemolysis and anaemia.

probes.q: What is maternal mirror syndrome in severe Rh alloimmunisation, and what clinical features characterise it?
probes.a: Maternal mirror syndrome, or Ballantyne syndrome, is maternal generalised oedema and pre-eclampsia-like features that mirror severe fetal hydrops and placentomegaly.

rubric.text: Inquires specifically into the timing and pattern of fetal movements
Screens for signs of polyhydramnios and maternal mirror syndrome
Checks for coexisting antepartum bleeding, leaking, and hypertensive symptoms

skill.hx.rh.risk.title: Sensitising events, transfusion history and past obstetric outcomes in Rh negative pregnancy
skill.hx.rh.risk.oneLine: Systematic inquiry into prior pregnancies, blood transfusions, invasive procedures and anti-D prophylaxis
skill.hx.rh.risk.why: Maternal alloimmunisation requires prior exposure to foreign RhD-positive erythrocytes. Identifying whether sensitisation has occurred and quantifying recurrence risk requires a meticulous history of previous childbirths, abortions, ectopic pregnancies, invasive procedures, antepartum haemorrhages, blood transfusions, and whether adequate anti-D immunoglobulin was administered within the therapeutic window.

asks.text: What is your exact blood group and Rh status, and what is your husband blood group? Incompatibility requires an Rh-negative mother and an Rh-positive biological father.

In your previous deliveries, did the baby develop jaundice, and did you receive an anti-D injection within 72 hours? Omission of postnatal anti-D after an Rh-positive infant is the primary cause of isoimmunisation.
Have you had any miscarriages, abortions, or ectopic pregnancies, and did you receive anti-D each time? Early pregnancy bleeding and uterine curettage can cause significant fetomaternal haemorrhage.

Have you had any procedures during pregnancy, such as amniocentesis, CVS, or turning of the baby? Invasive intrauterine interventions disrupt the choriodecidual junction and require anti-D prophylaxis.
Have you had any vaginal bleeding or abdominal trauma during this pregnancy? Any antepartum haemorrhage or trauma warrants evaluation for fetomaternal haemorrhage and anti-D administration.
Have you ever received a blood transfusion or blood product transfusion in your life? Inadvertent transfusion of Rh-positive red cells or platelets can stimulate intense anti-D antibody production.

skill.hx.rh.risk.practice: Demonstrate taking a complete obstetric history in an Rh-negative woman, identifying every potential sensitising event and verifying whether anti-D prophylaxis was received.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about early pregnancy losses or terminations where anti-D was frequently omitted
Assuming anti-D was administered after a prior hospital delivery without checking written records
Neglecting the paternal blood group and zygosity in estimating fetal risk

probes.q: Within what time window should prophylactic anti-D immunoglobulin ideally be administered following a potentially sensitising event?
probes.a: Anti-D immunoglobulin should be administered as soon as possible and within 72 hours of a potentially sensitising event, but some protection is still conferred if given up to 28 days.

probes.q: Why does an Rh-negative woman carrying her first Rh-positive pregnancy rarely have an infant affected by severe haemolytic disease?
probes.a: Primary maternal sensitization usually occurs during delivery, so maternal IgM antibodies form too late to affect the first baby, while high-affinity IgG anti-D antibodies threaten subsequent Rh-positive pregnancies.

rubric.text: Confirms maternal Rh-negative status and paternal blood group and Rh typing
Exhaustively checks prior deliveries, abortions, procedures, trauma and transfusions
Verifies the timing and administration of anti-D immunoglobulin for each event

skill.present.rh.case.title: Presenting the Rh isoimmunisation case
skill.present.rh.case.oneLine: Structured clinical presentation of an Rh-negative pregnant woman with alloimmunisation and fetal risk stratification
skill.present.rh.case.why: Presenting an Rh-alloimmunised pregnancy to a senior obstetrician or multi-disciplinary fetal medicine team demands concise communication of critical risk parameters. The presentation must immediately convey parity, gestational age, maternal antibody titre, paternal status, middle cerebral artery Doppler velocity, ultrasound features of hydrops, and a clear plan regarding intrauterine transfusion or timed delivery.
skill.present.rh.case.body: A structured presentation begins with the patient identity, obstetric score, and reliable gestational age. State clearly: Mrs X is a G3P1L1A1 at 28 weeks of gestation with known blood group O Rh-negative and husband B Rh-positive, presenting with a rising indirect Coombs test titre of 1:32. Proceed immediately to the obstetric history: past delivery with neonatal jaundice and no anti-D prophylaxis, followed by an unprophylaxed miscarriage. Summarise the current fetal assessment: middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity of 48 cm/s (exceeding 1.5 multiples of the median, indicating moderate-to-severe fetal anaemia) without hydrops on ultrasound. Conclude with the management plan: tertiary fetal medicine admission, cordocentesis and intrauterine blood transfusion, antenatal corticosteroids, and serial Doppler surveillance.
keyPoints: State maternal and paternal blood groups, gestational age, and reliable dating basis upfront
Highlight prior sensitising events and whether anti-D prophylaxis was omitted
Report antibody titration, critical threshold status, and serial trends
Present fetal MCA Doppler peak systolic velocity in cm/s and multiples of the median (MoM)
State the presence or absence of ultrasound features of hydrops fetalis
Formulate an actionable management plan covering tertiary referral, fetal transfusion, steroids and delivery timing
pitfalls: Reporting maternal antibody titre without stating the centre critical titre threshold or previous values
Failing to convert raw MCA Doppler peak systolic velocity into multiples of the median for gestational age
Recommending immediate preterm delivery before evaluating feasibility of intrauterine transfusion

probes.q: What essential parameters must be highlighted in the opening summary of an Rh-sensitised pregnancy case presentation?
probes.a: The opening summary must state maternal and paternal blood groups, parity, reliable gestational age, maternal antibody titre and trend, and whether the critical titre threshold has been exceeded.

probes.q: How should the fetal surveillance status be communicated when presenting an Rh-isoimmunised patient?
probes.a: Communicate the fetal status by stating the middle cerebral artery peak systolic velocity in multiples of the median, presence or absence of hydrops on ultrasound, and need for intrauterine transfusion.

rubric.text: Presents maternal and paternal blood groups, gestational age, and antibody titre clearly
Accurately conveys MCA Doppler PSV, multiples of the median, and hydrops status
Proposes an evidence-based management plan balancing intrauterine transfusion against delivery

skill.hx.puerperal.symptoms.title: Maternal symptoms and clinical presentation of puerperal pelvic infection
skill.hx.puerperal.symptoms.oneLine: Systematic inquiry into postpartum fever, shivering, lower abdominal pain, lochia alterations, and systemic danger signs
skill.hx.puerperal.symptoms.why: Puerperal sepsis is a leading preventable cause of maternal mortality. Early infection often presents with non-specific malaise and mild lower abdominal ache before progressing rapidly to fulminant septic shock. A systematic symptom enquiry identifies the source of infection, detects uterine subinvolution and infected lochia, and flags systemic hypoperfusion early.

asks.text: When did the fever begin, how high was it, and was it accompanied by shaking chills or rigors? High-grade fever with rigors within the first 10 days postpartum strongly suggests invasive bacterial genital tract infection or bacteremia.

Where is your abdominal pain, and does it feel like worsening cramps or constant tenderness? Persistent lower abdominal pain and tenderness over the uterine fundus indicates puerperal endometritis or parametritis.

What is the colour, amount, and smell of your vaginal discharge (lochia)? Foul-smelling, purulent, or dark brownish lochia with clots indicates anaerobic or polymicrobial endometritis, though Group A Streptococcus may produce scant, serosanguinous, non-odorous discharge.

Do you have severe pain, burning, or swelling in your perineum, episiotomy site, or caesarean wound? Severe localised perineal pain suggests episiotomy wound infection, breakdown, haematoma, or necrotising fasciitis.

Have you noticed painful or burning urination, increased frequency, or pain in the flanks? Dysuria and flank tenderness help distinguish acute urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis from uterine infection.
Are your breasts painful, engorged, or red, and are you able to breastfeed comfortably? Unilateral breast erythema and wedge-shaped tenderness suggest acute mastitis rather than pelvic sepsis.

skill.hx.puerperal.symptoms.practice: Practise taking a focused postpartum history from a mother with fever on day 3 following delivery, distinguishing genital tract infection from urinary, breast, and wound causes.
pitfalls: Overlooking Group A Streptococcal endometritis which may present with scant, odorless lochia and rapid septic collapse
Dismissing lower abdominal cramping as normal postpartum afterpains in a febrile woman
Failing to inquire directly about the offensive odor of lochia on perineal pads

probes.q: What clinical symptom triad classically points to acute puerperal endometritis?
probes.a: Maternal fever, lower abdominal or pelvic pain, and abnormal or foul-smelling lochia.

probes.q: Why might a woman with life-threatening Group A Streptococcus puerperal sepsis not have foul-smelling lochia?
probes.a: Streptococcus pyogenes is an invasive non-putrefactive pathogen that causes fulminant bacteremia and shock with scant, serosanguinous, odorless lochia, unlike putrefactive anaerobic infections.

rubric.text: Inquires systematically into fever onset, temperature spikes, rigors, and systemic symptoms
Evaluates lochia colour, volume, consistency, clots, and offensive odour
Screens for alternative postpartum fever foci including breasts, surgical wounds, and urinary tract

skill.hx.puerperal.risk.title: Obstetric risk factors and predisposing events for puerperal sepsis
skill.hx.puerperal.risk.oneLine: Detailed history of antenatal, intrapartum, and postpartum risk factors predisposing to genital tract sepsis
skill.hx.puerperal.risk.why: The risk of puerperal sepsis increases dramatically with specific intrapartum events such as prolonged rupture of membranes, multiple unsterile vaginal examinations, prolonged labour, and operative intervention. Identifying these predisposing factors in the history establishes high pre-test probability, guides empirical antibiotic selection, and directs urgent investigation.

asks.text: When did your water break, and how many hours elapsed between membrane rupture and delivery of your baby? Rupture of membranes exceeding 18 hours allows ascending vaginal organisms to colonise the uterine cavity and fetal membranes.

How many internal vaginal examinations were performed during labour, and where did the delivery take place? Frequent vaginal examinations, particularly in unhygienic or home settings without sterile gloves, introduce exogenous pathogens into the genital tract.
How long did your labour last, and were you pushing for an extended duration? Prolonged labour leads to maternal exhaustion, dehydration, devitalised tissue, and increased microbial ascendancy.

How was your baby delivered, and were instruments or a caesarean section required? Emergency caesarean section carries a 5- to 20-fold increased risk of postpartum endometritis compared with uncomplicated vaginal delivery.

Did the afterbirth come out spontaneously and completely, or did the attendant have to remove it manually? Manual removal of the placenta and retained placental cotyledons create a large nidus for bacterial proliferation.

Did you have severe anaemia, diabetes, or malnutrition during your pregnancy? Pre-existing maternal anaemia (haemoglobin < 10 g/dL) and poorly controlled hyperglycemia impair host cellular immunity and wound healing.

skill.hx.puerperal.risk.practice: Role-play taking an intrapartum and delivery history to uncover predisposing sepsis factors in a woman transferred from a primary rural birth centre.
pitfalls: Neglecting to ask about the duration of ruptured membranes when evaluating a febrile postpartum woman
Failing to ask whether manual removal of the placenta was attempted during delivery
Underestimating the risk of severe sepsis following an emergency caesarean section

probes.q: What is the single most important risk factor for postpartum endometritis?
probes.a: Caesarean section, particularly emergency caesarean delivery following prolonged labour or ruptured membranes.

probes.q: How does prolonged rupture of membranes predispose to puerperal sepsis?
probes.a: Prolonged rupture breaks the physical barrier and allows ascending cervicovaginal bacteria to invade the amniotic cavity, decidua, and exposed placental bed.

rubric.text: Quantifies hours of ruptured membranes and identifies prolonged rupture (> 18 hours)
Explores duration of labour, frequency of vaginal examinations, delivery mode, and placenta delivery
Evaluates underlying anaemia, gestational diabetes, nutrition, and immunosuppression

skill.present.puerperal.case.title: Presenting the puerperal sepsis case
skill.present.puerperal.case.oneLine: Structured presentation of a postpartum mother with pelvic infection, systemic sepsis stratification, and resuscitation plan
skill.present.puerperal.case.why: Presenting a septic postpartum mother to a consultant obstetrician or intensive care team requires rapid, structured delivery of essential clinical information. The presenter must immediately state maternal age, parity, delivery details, postpartum day of presentation, hemodynamic stability, localising pelvic examination findings, and an urgent Sepsis Six management plan.
skill.present.puerperal.case.body: A structured presentation begins with the patient identity, obstetric history, and mode of birth: Mrs X is a 23-year-old P2L2, presenting on postpartum day 4 following a home delivery complicated by 22 hours of membrane rupture and unsterile vaginal examinations, presenting with high fever, rigors, lower abdominal cramps, and foul lochia. Proceed immediately to vital signs and sepsis screening: she is febrile at 39.1 degrees C, tachycardic at 116 beats per minute, tachypneic at 24 breaths per minute, with a blood pressure of 94/60 mmHg and serum lactate of 2.6 mmol/L, meeting obstetric sepsis criteria. Summarise key physical findings: uterine subinvolution at the umbilicus, marked uterine tenderness, purulent foul lochia, and cervical motion tenderness without peritonism. Conclude with the resuscitation and treatment plan: immediate Sepsis Six bundle including high-flow oxygen, blood and lochia cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum IV triple antibiotics (ampicillin, gentamicin, and metronidazole), IV crystalloid fluid boluses, strict catheterised urine monitoring, and pelvic ultrasound to exclude retained products of conception.
keyPoints: State maternal identity, parity, mode, location, and postpartum day of delivery upfront
Highlight major intrapartum predisposing factors including duration of ruptured membranes and unsterile examinations
Present vital signs, modified obstetric early warning score, and serum lactate immediately
Describe abdominal and pelvic examination findings: fundal height, uterine tenderness, lochia characteristics, and cervical motion tenderness
State diagnostic differentials and exclude secondary sources including breasts, wound, chest, and urinary tract
Formulate an actionable management plan based on the Sepsis Six bundle, antimicrobial choice, and ultrasound imaging
pitfalls: Presenting maternal history chronologically without immediately highlighting hemodynamic instability and sepsis vitals
Omitting whether blood and high vaginal cultures were collected prior to initiating intravenous antibiotics
Failing to mention the plan for pelvic ultrasound to rule out retained placental tissue

probes.q: What critical vitals and hemodynamic parameters must be delivered in the opening statement of a maternal sepsis presentation?
probes.a: Temperature, pulse rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, and serum lactate.

probes.q: What is the recommended timing for pelvic imaging in a woman presenting with puerperal endometritis?
probes.a: Pelvic ultrasound should be performed promptly after starting antimicrobial therapy and fluid resuscitation to identify retained infected products of conception or pelvic abscess.

rubric.text: Presents maternal identity, delivery complications, vital signs, and shock parameters clearly
Accurately conveys uterine fundal height, tenderness, lochia characteristics, and pelvic exam findings
Proposes an urgent Sepsis Six protocol, triple parenteral antibiotic regimen, and diagnostic ultrasound

skill.hx.heart.symptoms.title: Cardiovascular symptoms, functional capacity and decompensation warnings in pregnancy
skill.hx.heart.symptoms.oneLine: Systematic inquiry into gestational breathlessness, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, palpitations, and NYHA functional staging
skill.hx.heart.symptoms.why: Normal pregnancy physiological changes like expanded blood volume and cardiac output mimic mild cardiovascular symptoms. Distinguishing benign gestational dyspnoea from true pathological decompensation requires meticulous inquiry into symptom onset, exercise tolerance, nocturnal orthopnoea, and rapid heart rate changes to identify women at risk of acute pulmonary oedema.

asks.text: Are you experiencing any shortness of breath when walking on level ground or climbing stairs, and how far can you walk before needing to stop? Quantifying exercise tolerance establishes the baseline NYHA functional class and flags early cardiovascular compromise.

Do you need extra pillows to sleep comfortably at night, or do you have to sit upright in bed because of breathing difficulty? True orthopnoea indicates elevated left atrial and pulmonary venous pressures rather than mechanical gravid fundal pressure.

Do you wake suddenly from sleep gasping for breath and needing to open an outside window? Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea is a cardinal sign of interstitial pulmonary congestion and impending pulmonary oedema.

Have you noticed any racing, pounding, or irregular heartbeats, and do they make you feel dizzy or lightheaded? Tachycardia and atrial arrhythmias critically shorten diastolic filling time across a stenotic mitral valve, provoking pulmonary oedema.

Have you experienced any chest tightness, heaviness, or pain during exertion or at rest? Chest discomfort warrants urgent evaluation for myocardial ischaemia, severe pulmonary hypertension, or aortic dissection.
Have you had any episodes of blackouts, sudden fainting, or feeling faint on minimal exertion? Syncope in a pregnant woman indicates fixed cardiac output obstruction or significant bradyarrhythmia.
Have you coughed up any blood, pink frothy sputum, or blood-streaked phlegm? Haemoptysis in mitral stenosis reflects ruptured thin-walled bronchial veins under high pulmonary venous pressure.
Have you noticed swelling of your ankles, feet, or legs that persists in the morning after waking? Rapidly progressive or generalised oedema suggests right heart strain or biventricular failure.

skill.hx.heart.symptoms.practice: In an antenatal clinic or high-risk obstetric ward, demonstrate taking a structured cardiac history from a pregnant patient, systematically distinguishing physiological breathlessness from NYHA class II to IV symptoms and eliciting orthopnoea.
pitfalls: Attributing orthopnoea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea to normal late pregnancy mechanical diaphragm elevation
Overlooking palpitations and sudden tachycardia as triggers for acute decompensation in mitral stenosis
Failing to quantify daily functional capacity against specific domestic or occupational tasks using NYHA criteria

probes.q: How can a clinician distinguish physiological dyspnoea of pregnancy from pathological cardiac breathlessness?
probes.a: Physiological dyspnoea occurs early in gestation, improves when rested or seated, and is not associated with orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, nocturnal cough, or functional deterioration.

probes.q: Why is a sudden rise in maternal heart rate or the onset of atrial fibrillation dangerous in a pregnant woman with mitral stenosis?
probes.a: Tachycardia markedly reduces diastolic filling time across the narrowed mitral valve, raising left atrial pressure acutely and triggering pulmonary venous congestion and pulmonary oedema.

rubric.text: Quantifies exercise tolerance and assigns NYHA functional class
Screens specifically for orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, and cough
Inquires about palpitations, tachycardia episodes, syncope, and haemoptysis

skill.hx.heart.risk.title: Prior cardiac disease, rheumatic fever, structural interventions and medication reconciliation in pregnancy
skill.hx.heart.risk.oneLine: Systematic inquiry into childhood sore throat and polyarthritis, prosthetic valves, percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty, and teratogenic cardiac drugs
skill.hx.heart.risk.why: Rheumatic heart disease remains the dominant maternal cardiac pathology in lower- and middle-income countries. A detailed history of childhood rheumatic fever, secondary penicillin prophylaxis adherence, previous balloon mitral valvuloplasty, prosthetic valve types, and current medications such as ACE inhibitors or anticoagulants is vital to assess structural vulnerability and prevent fetal teratogenicity or maternal valve thrombosis.

asks.text: Did you suffer from repeated sore throats, joint swelling with pain moving from one joint to another, or abnormal involuntary twitches during childhood? A positive childhood history confirms acute rheumatic fever as the underlying aetiology of valvular disease.

Have you ever taken monthly injections of penicillin into the hip or daily penicillin tablets, and when was your last dose? Assessing adherence to secondary rheumatic fever prophylaxis determines ongoing vulnerability to recurrent streptococcal carditis.

Have you ever had an operation on your heart, a balloon inserted to stretch a valve, or a valve replacement? Establishing prior balloon mitral valvuloplasty or valve surgery identifies prosthetic valve status and residual stenotic or regurgitant lesions.

If you have an artificial valve, was it a mechanical metal valve or a biological tissue valve, and what blood thinner do you take? Mechanical valves carry high risks of catastrophic valve thrombosis and require strict therapeutic anticoagulation.

What daily cardiac or blood pressure tablets were you taking before and during this pregnancy? Immediate medication reconciliation identifies teratogenic medications such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and atenolol for prompt substitution.

How did your heart behave during any previous pregnancies, labours, or miscarriages? A history of cardiac decompensation or pulmonary oedema in a past pregnancy strongly predicts recurrence in the current gestation.

Were you born with any heart murmur, hole in the heart, or blue skin discolouration as an infant? Screening for congenital heart disease identifies maternal shunts, coarctation, or cyanotic lesions that require specialised surveillance.

skill.hx.heart.risk.practice: Demonstrate taking a focused cardiac background history from an antenatal patient, covering childhood joint pain and chorea, previous cardiac surgery, mechanical versus bioprosthetic valves, and current medications.
pitfalls: Failing to ask about childhood sore throats and migrating polyarthritis when evaluating a pregnant woman with heart disease
Continuing teratogenic medications such as ACE inhibitors or ARBs into the second and third trimesters
Missing a history of mechanical prosthetic valve replacement that requires immediate anticoagulation management

probes.q: Why is it essential to determine whether a prosthetic cardiac valve is mechanical or tissue in a pregnant patient?
probes.a: Mechanical valves have a high risk of valve thrombosis requiring continuous therapeutic anticoagulation, whereas bioprosthetic tissue valves have lower thrombotic risk and typically do not require full anticoagulation in sinus rhythm.

probes.q: Which major classes of cardiovascular medications are strictly contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal toxicity, and what adverse effects do they cause?
probes.a: ACE inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers are contraindicated because they cause fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, and neonatal renal failure.

rubric.text: Explores childhood rheumatic fever, chorea, and adherence to secondary prophylaxis
Clarifies prior cardiac surgeries, balloon interventions, and prosthetic valve types
Reconciles pre-existing medications and screens for teratogenic agents

skill.present.heart.case.title: Presenting the pregnant patient with heart disease
skill.present.heart.case.oneLine: Synthesising obstetric parameters, cardiovascular lesion, functional NYHA class, modified WHO risk category, and multidisciplinary delivery plan
skill.present.heart.case.why: Presenting a pregnant cardiac patient demands integrating two complex clinical fields: maternal gestational status and hemodynamic vulnerability. A structured presentation clearly communicates lesion severity, functional NYHA classification, modified WHO risk category, fetal wellbeing, and the coordinated intrapartum plan between obstetrics, cardiology, and obstetric anaesthesia.
steps: State the patient age, parity, gravidity, period of gestation, and booking status in the opening sentence.
Summarise the specific cardiovascular diagnosis, underlying aetiology (rheumatic, congenital, or cardiomyopathy), and current NYHA functional class.
Present the presence or absence of cardiac decompensation features: orthopnoea, nocturnal dyspnoea, haemoptysis, and peripheral oedema.
Detail relevant past history, including childhood rheumatic episodes, secondary penicillin prophylaxis, and previous cardiac surgical or balloon interventions.
Report pertinent physical examination findings: pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, elevated JVP, cardiac murmurs, lung crackles, and obstetric abdominal findings.
Review essential diagnostic investigations: ECG rhythm, echocardiographic valve area and gradients, pulmonary artery systolic pressure, and fetal growth parameters.
State the calculated modified WHO maternal risk category and CARPREG II score to articulate maternal event risk.

Conclude with the comprehensive management strategy: antenatal medical optimisation, fetal surveillance, and the multidisciplinary labour plan specifying timing, route, anaesthesia, and postpartum monitoring.
skill.present.heart.case.practice: Present an antenatal inpatient with rheumatic mitral stenosis or congenital heart disease to an interdisciplinary team, stating obstetric age, specific lesion, NYHA class, mWHO risk category, and intrapartum labour strategy.

probes.q: What four core clinical components must always be included in the opening diagnostic summary of a pregnant cardiac case presentation?
probes.a: The obstetric profile (gravidity, parity, gestational age), the specific structural cardiac lesion with aetiology, the functional NYHA class, and the modified WHO maternal risk category.

probes.q: Why is the modified WHO classification preferred over isolated clinical impression when presenting maternal cardiac risk to a multidisciplinary team?
probes.a: The modified WHO classification integrates maternal cardiac lesions into evidence-based risk categories predicting maternal mortality and morbidity, standardising care level and delivery location.

rubric.text: Delivers a structured opening combining obstetric profile, cardiac lesion, NYHA class, and mWHO category
Presents vital signs, auscultatory signs, echocardiographic parameters, and fetal wellbeing accurately
Outlines a multidisciplinary delivery plan detailing timing, route, epidural analgesia, and postpartum safety
